alignments.differs: Irving's ghost only chants a psalm tune, and a farmer reports Ichabod alive; Gogol's dead clerk comes back with his fists and strips the cloak off the man who scolded him.

question: Irving lets a rival dressed as a goblin drive Ichabod out of the valley into a career; Gogol lets the dead clerk come back as a robber of cloaks. Which ending gives the poor scribe more?

substitution.note: Only Sleepy Hollow has the poor man of the pen going home alone at midnight from a richer man's feast, an inventory of his bundle when he is gone, and a ghost of him in the town's talk. Canterville Ghost and The Haunted and the Haunters have ghosts but no victim made into one; Rip Van Winkle comes home alive and is not inventoried; Young Goodman Brown walks at night but from no feast and is not robbed. No other story in the graph has a clerk robbed on his way home. The Million Pound Bank-Note has a poor clerk dining at a rich house, but he is never set upon, does not die and leaves no ghost; The House of the Seven Gables and The Scarlet Letter have town legends of the dead but no poor man robbed on his way home.

claim: A man of the pen serves superiors who rule his wording, and rank shows him the door. Werther, who loves to transpose, is eased out of a noble assembly by a kind count and smarts at the gossip; Akaki, who can only copy, is shouted out of a great man's room and dies.

from.exact: altering the headings of various documents, and here and there changing the first personal pronoun into the third

to.exact: he has a deadly antipathy to all those transpositions of which I am so fond

alignments.same: An office paper is judged word by word, and a change in its wording sets the clerk apart from his superior.
alignments.differs: Werther wants to transpose and a pedant forbids it; Akaki is asked by a kind director to change a pronoun, sweats over it and begs to be given something to copy.

from.exact: with whom you are speaking? Do you consider before whom you are standing?

to.exact: I perceive the company is rather displeased at your being here.

alignments.same: Before onlookers, a man of rank tells a subordinate he has come where his rank does not admit him.
alignments.differs: The count speaks kindly at a window and Werther bows out smiling; the Superintendent shouts to impress a friend, and Akaki has to be dragged out half conscious.

from.exact: In his whole life he had never been so scolded by a superior official

to.exact: the minister gave me a reprimand,—a gentle one it is true, but still a reprimand

alignments.same: A reprimand from above falls on the subordinate and stays with him.
alignments.differs: Werther's minister softens his with a generous letter and Werther is at peace for a week; Akaki's scolding sends him out into the storm, and he dies of the fever.

question: Werther leaves the assembly and drives off to read Homer at sunset; Akaki goes out into the storm. What does Gogol's clerk lack that lets Goethe's hero turn an insult into a sorrow?

substitution.note: Only Werther has a subordinate whose papers a superior rules word by word, a reprimand from a minister and a scene where a man of rank shows him out of company. Northanger Abbey turns Catherine out of a great house, but she is no clerk and no one judges her wording; Gulliver's Travels has courts and ministers but no copying subordinate. No other story in the graph has a clerk judged on his wording. The Million Pound Bank-Note has a poor clerk, but no superior rules his wording and rank opens doors to him instead of showing him out; Candide is kicked out of a baron's house, but he is no man of the pen.

claim: A copyist who wants only to copy or be let alone baffles his office, and one man there feels him a brother. Akaki begs to go on copying and is mocked to his grave; Bartleby prefers not to, stops copying, and his employer's brotherly pity turns to fear.

from.exact: he said, and gently disappeared behind the screen

to.exact: No! Please give me again something to copy.

alignments.same: Given a task beyond plain copying (a report to recast, copies to check against the original), the clerk declines it.
alignments.differs: Akaki tries, sweats and begs to go back to copying for life; Bartleby says he would prefer not to, gives no reason, and later gives up copying too.

from.exact: I would prefer to be left alone here

to.exact: Do leave me alone! Why do you always want to disturb me at work?

alignments.same: Crowded by his fellow clerks at his desk, the copyist asks only to be left alone.
alignments.differs: Akaki's colleagues pelt him with paper and only one is shamed; Bartleby's 'prefer' gets into the other clerks' mouths, though they would kick him out or black his eyes.

from.exact: For both I and Bartleby were sons of Adam.

to.exact: Am I not your brother?

alignments.same: A man of the office is struck by the copyist into a sense of kinship as a fellow human.
alignments.differs: Gogol's young clerk hears the words for years and hides his face at men's cruelty; Melville's lawyer feels a fraternal melancholy that, he admits, soon turns to fear and repulsion.

question: Akaki's 'Am I not your brother?' changes a young clerk for life; the lawyer's 'sons of Adam' ends with him moving his offices. What does Melville's narrator do with his pity that Gogol's young clerk does not?

substitution.note: Only The Overcoat has a copying clerk who refuses a task beyond copying, begs to be left alone at his desk, and moves a fellow of the office to brotherhood. Werther has an office and a pedantic superior, but Werther is no copyist and no one pities him as a brother; Rip Van Winkle shirks work but in no office; The Minister's Black Veil withdraws behind a veil, but he is no clerk and has no employer. The Million-Pound Bank-Note has a poor clerk, but a broker's clerk who copies nothing and is pitied by no one at his desk; The Custom-House has an office of old officials, but none copies papers, begs to be let alone or is felt a brother; Hadleyburg, A Connecticut Yankee, The House of the Seven Gables, The Scarlet Letter, Tobermory and the Seven Gables and Yankee prefaces have no copying clerk.

claim: Melville twice sets a man before a wall. Ahab calls the whale the wall a prisoner must strike through, and calls his hunt decreed; Bartleby, a sentry at a desk by a window, only stares at a dead wall, and it is his employer who calls the matter predestined, to excuse doing nothing.

from.exact: he would stand looking out, at his pale window behind the screen, upon the dead brick wall

to.exact: How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved near to me.

alignments.same: A man stands facing a blank wall that shuts him in.
alignments.differs: Ahab would thrust through, and makes the whale his wall; Bartleby only stands and looks at it, and dies at the foot of the prison wall.

from.exact: He was a perpetual sentry in the corner.

to.exact: Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries.

alignments.same: Manhattan's men of the desk stand like sentries, fixed in reverie.
alignments.differs: Ishmael's landsmen leave their desks on the Sabbath to gaze at the sea, and he ships out; Bartleby keeps his corner even on Sunday, his reveries facing a wall.

from.exact: had been all predestinated from eternity

to.exact: This whole act’s immutably decreed.

alignments.same: Faced with a will that will not bend, a man calls what is happening decreed before time.
alignments.differs: Ahab says it to drive his crew on against Starbuck's plea; the lawyer says it to let Bartleby stay and do nothing, and drops it when his friends talk.

question: Ahab strikes at his wall and Bartleby stares at his. Which of them refuses more?

substitution.note: Only Moby-Dick has a wall that shuts a man in, Manhattan's desk-bound men posted like sentinels, and a man who calls the matter decreed. The Yellow Wallpaper has a woman staring at a wall, but no desk, no sentinels and no decree; Frankenstein and The Hound of the Baskervilles have pursuit but no wall; Twenty Thousand Leagues has a captain but no clerk; The Minister's Black Veil has a man behind a veil but no wall or decree. The House of the Seven Gables has a man shut up for years and a curse on a family, but no wall he must strike through, no hunt and no sentinels of the desk; The Scarlet Letter, The Custom-House, Hadleyburg, A Connecticut Yankee, The Million-Pound Bank-Note, Tobermory and the Seven Gables and Yankee prefaces have no wall, no hunt and no decree.

claim: Gogol's poor official saves for a coat with a cheap fur collar, is passed over like a fly, and seizes a man of rank only as a ghost. Dostoevsky's official borrows for a cheap beaver collar and, alive, runs into an officer shoulder to shoulder; the officer never looks round.

from.exact: I pitched upon a piece of cheap German beaver

to.exact: They did not buy marten fur, for it was too dear, but chose the best catskin in the shop

alignments.same: A poor official wants a fine fur collar on his coat, finds the real fur too dear and buys a cheap imitation.
alignments.differs: Akaki needs a new coat against the frost and only dreams of the collar; the underground man has a warm coat and changes the collar to pass for an officer.

from.exact: I had been treated like a fly

to.exact: they took no more notice than if a fly had flown through the room

alignments.same: The official is passed over as if he were a fly.
alignments.differs: Gogol's narrator says it of Akaki, who goes on copying; the underground man says it of himself, after an officer moves him aside without a word, and nurses the insult for years.

from.exact: we ran full tilt, shoulder to shoulder, against one another!

to.exact: Suddenly he felt a powerful hand seize him by the collar.

alignments.same: The slighted man at last lays hands on a man of rank in the street.
alignments.differs: Akaki does it as a ghost and the great man gives up his cloak in terror; the underground man does it alive, and the officer pretends not to notice.

question: Gogol needs a ghost before his clerk can touch the great man; Dostoevsky's clerk does it alive, in a borrowed collar, and the officer does not look round. Which revenge leaves the little man smaller?

substitution.note: Only The Overcoat has a poor official who buys a cheap imitation fur collar with money from the office, is passed over like a fly, and lays hands on a man of rank in the street. Sorrows of Young Werther has a slighted subordinate but no coat or street encounter; Dorian Gray and Jekyll and Hyde have men of rank but no clerk; no other work in the graph has a fur collar bought to be equal. Bartleby has a copyist and an office but no coat, collar or encounter in the street. The works merged before this step (The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg, The House of the Seven Gables and its preface, The Million Pound Bank-Note, Tobermory) have no poor official with a cheap fur collar: Hadleyburg tests a town with a sack of gold, The Million Pound Bank-Note's clerk is first scorned and then fawned on for a note, not a collar, and lays hands on no one; Seven Gables has a Judge of rank but no slighted clerk; Tobermory is a talking cat at a house party.

claim: A man in a respectable post hides petty vices of the night, is ashamed of them, and writes out a confession of his double life. Jekyll cannot bear the two halves together and buys them separate bodies with a drug; the underground man keeps hero and mud in one head and wants the contrast.

from.exact: Hence it came about that I concealed my pleasures

to.exact: And so, furtively, timidly, in solitude, at night, I indulged in filthy vice, with a feeling of shame which never deserted me

alignments.same: A man with a respectable post keeps a petty vice secret and is ashamed of it.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's shame comes from his high aims and drives him to hide the vice in another body; the underground man took to vice from a craving for contrast, shame and all.

from.exact: to assume, like a thick cloak, that of Edward Hyde

to.exact: the hero was a cloak for the mud

alignments.same: One self is worn over the other like a cloak.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's cloak is the low self, a second body put on by a drug to keep the respected one safe; the underground man's cloak is the dreamed hero, worn over his own mud.

from.exact: as I lay down the pen and proceed to seal up my confession

to.exact: Such confessions as I intend to make are never printed nor given to other people to read.

alignments.same: The man sets down his double life in a written confession.
alignments.differs: Jekyll writes to a friend, to be read after his end, and seals the paper; the underground man says he writes for no one, yet keeps addressing 'gentlemen'.

question: Jekyll wants the two natures 'housed in separate identities'; the underground man wants neither hero nor mud without the other. Which of the two is more divided?

substitution.note: Only Notes from Underground has a man with a post who hides a petty vice of the night in shame, calls one self a cloak for the other and writes a confession of it. Dorian Gray hides vices in obscure haunts but writes no confession and is told in the third person; Werther and The Yellow Wallpaper write in the first person but hide no vice. On the other side, only Jekyll has the cloak, the confession and the night pleasures together. Of the works merged before this step: in The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg Richards confesses aloud a wrong he kept hidden, not a hidden vice of the night or a double self in writing; Seven Gables' Judge hides his settled temper but writes no confession; Tobermory's cat reveals the guests' secrets, they do not confess them; Bartleby, The Million Pound Bank-Note and the Seven Gables preface have no hidden vice or confession.

claim: A clerk's household stakes years of want on one fine thing, shows it off one night at a superior's party and loses it going home. Akaki's own cloak is paid for by hunger beforehand, and its loss kills him; Mathilde's necklace is borrowed, and the hunger comes after: ten years for a copy of a fake.

from.exact: She no longer had the necklace around her neck!

to.exact: Robbed of his cloak, and feeling frozen to the marrow

alignments.same: Home after midnight from a superior's party where the treasure was admired, the poor owner finds it gone.
alignments.differs: Akaki's cloak is torn off by men in a dark square; Mathilde's necklace slips away unseen, no thief is ever found, and she hides the loss from its owner.

from.exact: late at night he often copied manuscript for five sous a page

to.exact: copy his documents in his landlady's room, in order to economise the fuel in his own

alignments.same: A clerk copies papers by night and cuts the household's food and comfort to pay for one costly thing.
alignments.differs: Akaki goes without tea and supper for a year before, to own a cloak; Loisel copies for ten years after, to pay usurers for a necklace that was never theirs.

from.exact: Why, my necklace was paste!

to.exact: chose the best catskin in the shop, which was a very good imitation of the former

alignments.same: The precious thing is cheaper stuff passing for dearer: catskin for marten, paste for diamonds.
alignments.differs: Akaki and his tailor pick the imitation knowingly to save money; Mathilde learns hers was false only after paying the price of real diamonds.

question: Akaki dies for a cloak that was truly his; Mathilde gives ten years for a necklace worth five hundred francs. Does the paste empty her sacrifice, or is her proud smile at the end something Akaki never had?

substitution.note: Only The Overcoat has a clerk's treasure, bought or replaced at the cost of years of want, admired at a superior's party and lost on the way home after midnight, with an imitation fur matching the paste. The Bank-Note has a lent valuable but no loss; Notes from Underground buys a beaver collar on borrowed money but loses nothing; Vanka is not in this step's graph. No other work joins night copying for a debt, a lost treasure and a fake. Hadleyburg has a poor couple tempted by a sack of gold, but no clerk, no party, nothing bought by want and lost; Tobermory has a house party but no treasure lost.

claim: A poor person is lent, for a set time, a thing of great worth whose look admits them among the rich, and runs into debt on its account. Twain's note is real, unspent and handed back whole, and makes a fortune; Maupassant's necklace is paste and lost, and costs ten years of real francs.

from.exact: It is lent to you for thirty days, without interest.

to.exact: Will you lend me this, only this?

alignments.same: A poor stranger to wealth is lent a costly thing for a time, to be given back.
alignments.differs: Rich men making a bet hand Adams the note unasked, and he does not know why; Mathilde begs the necklace from a friend and picks it herself for one night's show.

from.exact: Harris was so grateful that he forced loans upon me, and would not be denied

to.exact: He did borrow, asking a thousand francs of one, five hundred of another, five louis here, three louis there.

alignments.same: Because of the borrowed valuable, the poor man runs into debt with many lenders.
alignments.differs: Lenders press money on Adams for the note they have seen; Loisel begs from usurers to buy a copy of a necklace no one must know was lost.

from.exact: Have you the million-pound note?

to.exact: You should have returned it sooner; I might have needed it.

alignments.same: At the end the lender asks for the valuable, and it is handed back.
alignments.differs: Adams returns the very note, unspent, with £200,000 earned by its look; Mathilde returns a substitute bought with ruin, and her friend never opens the case.

question: Twain's note is worth a million and buys nothing; Maupassant's necklace is worth five hundred francs and costs thirty-six thousand. Which story says that how a thing looks is worth more than what it is, and which says it costs more?

substitution.note: Only The Necklace has a costly thing lent for a set time to someone poor, debts run up on its account, and the lender asking for it back. The Overcoat's cloak is bought, not lent; Candide and A Connecticut Yankee have money and innocence but no loan; Notes from Underground borrows money but is lent no valuable. Hadleyburg's sack is left with the Richardses only to be handed on, and buys them no entry among the rich and no debt; Tobermory has no loan.

claim: A poor dependent sends one plea up a chain of hands to the one person who might save him. Akaki skips the chain, reaches the great man and is shouted into a fatal fever; Vanka trusts post-box and mailcart with an address that reaches no one, and sleeps sure it is read.

from.exact: letters were put in post-boxes, and from the boxes were carried about all over the earth in mailcarts with drunken drivers and ringing bells

to.exact: This in due course would have passed through the hands of the chief clerk and director of the bureau.

alignments.same: A poor petitioner is told by others how a plea travels, hand to hand or cart to cart, before it reaches the one who can help.
alignments.differs: Akaki hears the channel from the great man after going around it; Vanka hears it from shopmen and trusts it, and no one tells him a letter needs an address.

from.exact: without putting on his little greatcoat, ran out into the street as he was in his shirt

to.exact: felt the cloak snatched away from him, and simultaneously received a kick which stretched him senseless in the snow

alignments.same: On the night of his hope, a poor man is out in the winter street with no coat on his back.
alignments.differs: Akaki's new cloak, bought with a year of hunger, is torn off by robbers and the cold kills him; Vanka leaves his own off for gladness, and the frost spares him.

from.exact: On the stove was sitting his grandfather, swinging his bare legs, and reading the letter to the cooks.

to.exact: At another time he seemed to be listening to the Superintendent's severe reprimand, and asking his forgiveness.

alignments.same: The petitioner's last scene is in bed, where his mind shows him the one he petitioned answering his plea.
alignments.differs: Akaki in fever hears the great man's reprimand again and begs pardon, and dies; Vanka in sweet sleep sees his grandfather read the letter aloud, and the story stops before morning.

question: Gogol follows Akaki's plea to its answer and its death; Chekhov stops while Vanka's letter is still in the box. Is the reader who knows it will not arrive kinder or crueller than the Superintendent?

substitution.note: Only The Overcoat has a poor petitioner told how his plea must pass hand to hand, out in the winter night without his coat, and ending in bed with the one he begged. Bartleby has the office and the undelivered letter but no plea of the clerk's own and no frost; Sleepy Hollow has a poor man going home at night but no petition; Werther's letters reach their reader. No other story in the graph sends a poor man's plea up a chain of officials or posts. Of the later works: Hadleyburg and The Million-Pound Bank-Note test men with money but no poor petitioner sends a plea up a chain; The Necklace's clerk's wife borrows a jewel and pleads with no one; the Underground clerk's unsent letter is a challenge, not a plea for help; Tobermory has no petitioner.

claim: Melville's narrator ends by imagining the Dead Letter Office: charity and hope sent too late to the dead, carted to the flames. Chekhov writes one such letter from the other end: the hungry child is alive and asks for the help, and his address makes the letter dead before it leaves his hand.

from.exact: To grandfather in the village.

to.exact: Dead letters! does it not sound like dead men?

alignments.same: A letter is written to someone it can never reach.
alignments.differs: Melville's letters fail because their readers are dead, and the narrator says so; Vanka's grandfather is alive, the address names no place, and nobody in the story says it will fail.

from.exact: I am fearfully hungry

to.exact: a bank-note sent in swiftest charity:—he whom it would relieve, nor eats nor hungers any more

alignments.same: Help for a hungry person goes by letter and does not meet him in time.
alignments.differs: In Bartleby the help is sent and the hungry man has died; in Vanka the hungry child himself writes asking for help, and no help is coming back.

from.exact: carried about all over the earth in mailcarts with drunken drivers and ringing bells

to.exact: For by the cart-load they are annually burned.

alignments.same: Letters are hauled by the cart-load.
alignments.differs: Vanka has heard only of the carts that carry letters everywhere, with bells; Melville's narrator knows the other carts, which take the undeliverable letters to be burned.

question: Melville's narrator weeps over dead letters he never saw; Chekhov shows a dead letter being written and never says it is dead. Which leaves the reader more responsible for the letter?

substitution.note: Only Bartleby has a letter that cannot reach its reader, charity to the hungry that comes too late and carts of letters. The Overcoat has a petition through channels but no letter; Werther and Frankenstein are told in letters that do arrive; Dracula's letters and journals reach their readers. No other story in the graph has a dead letter. Of the later works: the Underground clerk writes a letter he never sends, but it is a challenge to an officer, not help asked of or sent to the hungry; the Bank-Note envelope reaches the hungry man and is read at once; Hadleyburg's letters arrive; The Necklace and Tobermory have no undeliverable letter.

claim: Two men cut off from people for years write out what books have made of them. Dostoevsky's clerk says we all prefer life in books and would be lost without them, and stays dreaming in his hole; Chekhov's lawyer, after fifteen years of nothing but books, despises books and life alike and walks out.

from.exact: And I despise your books, despise all wordly blessings and wisdom.

to.exact: we are all privately agreed that it is better in books

alignments.same: A man who has lived apart from people gives his verdict on books against real life.
alignments.differs: The underground man says we cling to books because we loathe real life; the lawyer has had only books for fifteen years and despises the books and the life together.

from.exact: In your books I cast myself into bottomless abysses, worked miracles, burned cities to the ground, preached new religions, conquered whole countries

to.exact: preaching new ideas and fighting a victorious Austerlitz against the obscurantists

alignments.same: Shut in his room, the man lives through conquests and the preaching of new ideas he never performs.
alignments.differs: The underground man's triumphs are his own daydreams, which he mocks and keeps; the lawyer's come from the poets' books and he calls them all a mirage.

from.exact: like the mice underground

to.exact: creep ignominiously into its mouse-hole. There in its nasty, stinking, underground home

alignments.same: The mouse underground stands for a man's place in the world.
alignments.differs: Dostoevsky's man is himself the conscious mouse, spiteful in its hole; Chekhov's lawyer puts the proud and wise of the world in the mice's place, wiped out by death.

question: Both men are forty and have learned the world from books. Why does one stay underground writing notes while the other gives up two millions to leave five minutes early?

substitution.note: Only Notes from Underground has a man shut away who says life is better in books, dreams of conquest and preaching in his corner, and calls himself the mouse underground. Bartleby is shut away but reads nothing and dreams nothing aloud; Rip Van Winkle sleeps his years; The Overcoat's clerk copies but does not read; Jekyll confesses but lives in the world; The Yellow Wallpaper's narrator is shut in and writes, but is kept from work and books, not fed them. No other story in the graph weighs books against life. Hadleyburg, The Necklace and Tobermory have no one shut away weighing books against life.

claim: A man of business keeps a silent man shut in his premises, is tempted alone to kill him, and turns aside. Melville's lawyer is saved by a commandment and never learns why Bartleby refuses money and work; Chekhov's banker is stopped by the prisoner's written reasons for refusing two millions, and weeps.

from.exact: I have only to take and throw this half-dead thing on the bed, smother him a moment with the pillow

to.exact: I remembered the tragedy of the unfortunate Adams and the still more unfortunate Colt in the solitary office of the latter

alignments.same: Alone with the motionless man he cannot be rid of, the man of business thinks of killing him.
alignments.differs: Melville's lawyer recalls another man's murder as a warning to himself; Chekhov's banker plans his own, a pillow and the watchman to blame.

from.exact: kissed the head of the strange man, and began to weep

to.exact: A new commandment give I unto you, that ye love one another.

alignments.same: What turns the would-be killer aside is love for the strange man.
alignments.differs: Melville's lawyer remembers a commandment before he knows anything of Bartleby's mind; the banker is turned by reading the prisoner's own letter, and weeps in contempt for himself.

from.exact: That I may show you in deed my contempt for that by which you live, I waive the two millions

to.exact: you have not even touched that money yet

alignments.same: The shut-away man leaves untouched the money his keeper must pay him.
alignments.differs: Bartleby gives no reason and only prefers not to; the lawyer writes out his contempt and breaks the agreement on purpose to lose the money.

question: Melville's narrator never reads a word of Bartleby's; Chekhov's banker reads the prisoner's letter and locks it in his safe. Which keeper understands his prisoner better?

substitution.note: Only Bartleby has an employer alone with a motionless man in his premises who thinks of murder, is turned by love, and sees his money left untouched. Notes from Underground has a man shut away but no keeper; The Overcoat's superiors scold but never think of killing; The House of the Seven Gables has Clifford released and the Judge's threats but no murder resisted and no money refused. Hadleyburg, The Necklace and Tobermory have no keeper tempted to kill a shut-away man.

claim: Rich men settle an argument by betting a great sum on whether a man can last a fixed term. Chekhov's lawyer stakes his own freedom, lasts fifteen years and waives the millions in contempt; Twain's stranger is staked without being asked, lasts thirty days, and comes out rich and married, the end Chekhov's banker dreaded.

from.exact: Brother B said he would bet twenty thousand pounds that the man would live thirty days

to.exact: You stake two millions, I my freedom

alignments.same: An argument among rich men is settled by a bet on how long a man can last under set terms.
alignments.differs: Twain's brothers bet on a stranger who is never asked and does not know the terms; Chekhov's lawyer makes the bet himself and stakes his freedom.

from.exact: I earned it by thirty days’ judicious use of that little loan you let me have.

to.exact: I waive the two millions of which I once dreamed as of paradise

alignments.same: At the end of the term the man meets the money the bet has put before him.
alignments.differs: Twain's man claims his winnings and shows a profit; Chekhov's lawyer leaves five minutes early so that he cannot claim them.

from.exact: For it gave me my Portia.

to.exact: He will take away my last farthing, marry, enjoy life, gamble on the Exchange

alignments.same: The man who lasts the term may come out with money and a wife.
alignments.differs: In Twain this happens, with the bettor's own stepdaughter; in Chekhov it is only the ruined banker's dread, and the lawyer refuses it.

question: Twain's bet makes everyone happy and Chekhov's nearly ends in murder. Is the difference in the bettors, in the term, or in what the man does with it?

substitution.note: Only The Bet has a bet among rich men on how long one man can last under set terms. Connecticut Yankee and Candide have no wager on a man; Rip Van Winkle loses twenty years without any stake; Bartleby's money is wages, not a stake. With any other work the bet, the term and the money waived at its end fall away. Hadleyburg's stranger bets only with himself on the town's honesty, with no term to last; The Necklace has a loan repaid over ten years but no bet; Tobermory has no stake.

claim: A young wife married to a minor official she cannot look up to wants another life, finds it briefly among admirers away from home, then keeps a secret for years. Mathilde's one night costs ten years of drudgery repaying a borrowed jewel; Anna's holiday brings a lover who follows her home, and her secret has no end.

from.exact: She was not sure whether her husband had a post in a Crown Department or under the Provincial Council

to.exact: so she let herself be married to a little clerk of the Ministry of Public Instruction

alignments.same: The young wife is married to a minor official and thinks little of his post.
alignments.differs: Mathilde knows his ministry and resents his small pay; Anna does not even know which office her husband serves, only that he is 'a flunkey'.

from.exact: in his buttonhole there was some badge of distinction like the number on a waiter

to.exact: Her husband had been sleeping since midnight in a little deserted anteroom

alignments.same: At the public evening the official husband is a small figure at the edge while other men watch his wife.
alignments.differs: Loisel sleeps apart while his wife dances with the Cabinet; Von Diderits bows at her side in the stalls, and her lover is waiting for him to leave.

from.exact: they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning

to.exact: This life lasted ten years.

alignments.same: The bright escape is followed by years of a life hidden from others.
alignments.differs: Mathilde's hidden years are counted, paid off and ended by the truth about the paste; Chekhov's lovers stand at the start of theirs, with no sum and no end.

question: Mathilde wants a necklace and a ball; Anna says only 'I wanted to live!' Is Anna's wish larger than Mathilde's, or the same wish without an object?

substitution.note: Only The Necklace has a young official's wife who scorns his post, a night among admirers away from her husband, and years of secret life after. The Scarlet Letter's Hester is married to a scholar and her shame is public; Werther's Charlotte honours Albert; The Yellow Wallpaper's wife is kept at home by a respected physician; The Million-Pound Bank-Note and The Overcoat have no wife.

claim: A respected man loves a married woman in secret and keeps one face for the world. Hawthorne's minister cannot bear the split, Hester plans their flight, and he dies confessing; Chekhov's Gurov finds the hidden life the true one, and he and Anna plan and plan, the way out always about to appear.

from.exact: He had two lives: one, open, seen and known by all who cared to know, full of relative truth and of relative falsehood

to.exact: No man, for any considerable period, can wear one face to himself and another to the multitude

alignments.same: A man in good standing keeps a public face and a hidden life of love.
alignments.differs: Hawthorne says the double face leaves a man unsure which is true; Gurov is sure: the hidden life is true and the open one is the false sheath.

from.exact: And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin

to.exact: Begin all anew!

alignments.same: Alone together, the lovers look for a way out of hiding into a new life.
alignments.differs: Hester has the way at once, forest, ship and a new name, and it is undone by the minister's confession; Chekhov's lovers clutch their heads and the way stays a little ahead.

from.exact: like "the woman who was a sinner" in an old-fashioned picture

to.exact: an object to remind him of the image of Divine Maternity

alignments.same: The fallen woman is seen as a figure in a religious painting.
alignments.differs: Hester stands upright on the public scaffold and recalls sinless motherhood by contrast; Anna droops in a hotel room like the penitent, while Gurov eats water-melon.

question: Dimmesdale's secret kills him and Gurov's secret makes him, for the first time, sincere. What does each story need the public world to be for its verdict to hold?

substitution.note: Only The Scarlet Letter has secret lovers, one a respected man with a double face, who plan together a way out into a new life. Jekyll and Hyde has the double life but no beloved and no shared plan; The Minister's Black Veil and Young Goodman Brown have hidden sin but no lovers; Werther has love for a married woman but no double life and no plan of flight.

claim: A lover cannot see why a marriage should stand between him and the woman fate meant for him. Werther loves alone, says farewell for ever and dies to claim Charlotte in the next world; Chekhov's lovers are both married, part for ever at a station, and meet again in this one, in secret, with no end.

from.exact: they could not understand why he had a wife and she a husband

to.exact: And what do they mean by saying Albert is your husband? He may be so for this world

alignments.same: The lover finds the marriage that divides him from his beloved beyond understanding.
alignments.differs: Werther questions one marriage, Charlotte's, and looks past it to the next world; Gurov and Anna question two, their own, and stay in this one.

from.exact: it seemed to them that fate itself had meant them for one another

to.exact: if thou hadst destined this happiness for me

alignments.same: The love is read as something destiny meant.
alignments.differs: Werther knows destiny gave Charlotte to Albert and only wishes; Chekhov's lovers feel fate chose them and blame the cages they were caught in.

from.exact: We are parting forever—it must be so, for we ought never to have met.

to.exact: we shall recognise each other under every possible change!

alignments.same: A farewell is spoken as if it were the last.
alignments.differs: Werther, meaning to die, promises a meeting beyond death; Anna means the parting for ever, and Gurov finds her months later in her provincial theatre.

question: Werther dies so that the marriage will not matter in the next world. Gurov and Anna live on inside both their marriages. Which story takes marriage more seriously?

substitution.note: Only Werther has a lover who calls a marriage meaningless against a destined love and a farewell for ever that is not the end. The Scarlet Letter's lovers do not question Hester's marriage, only flee its keeper; The Necklace has no lover; Notes from Underground's Liza is not married; Dracula's Mina is loved only by her husband.

claim: Both stories shut a wife in an upstairs room with a window, under a husband's loving will. Gilman's teller, kept by John's care behind barred windows, locks herself in and creeps; Chopin's Louise, at an open window, names a kind intention a crime and opens her own door, and her husband's return kills her.

from.exact: There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair.

to.exact: the windows are barred for little children

alignments.same: A wife alone in an upstairs room sits by a window that looks out on trees, sky and the road.
alignments.differs: Gilman's windows are barred and what the teller sees outside are creeping women; Chopin's window is open, and spring air, rain, song and blue sky come in to her.

from.exact: A kind intention or a cruel intention made the act seem no less a crime

to.exact: He is very careful and loving, and hardly lets me stir without special direction.

alignments.same: A husband's will directs his wife's days, and the wife grants that the will is meant kindly.
alignments.differs: Gilman's teller calls John's direction care and herself 'basely ungrateful'; Louise, in one hour alone, calls even a kind imposed will a crime.

from.exact: Louise, open the door! I beg, open the door — you will make yourself ill.

to.exact: It is no use, young man, you can’t open it!

alignments.same: Someone begs at the locked door of a wife's room, and from inside she refuses to let them in.
alignments.differs: Gilman's teller has thrown the key away and John faints when he gets in; Louise opens the door herself, goes down to her returning husband, and she is the one who falls dead.

question: John faints at the sight of his wife; Louise dies at the sight of her husband. Which story lets the wife's freedom outlast the moment the husband comes through the door?

substitution.note: Only The Yellow Wallpaper shuts a wife alone in an upstairs room with a window under a husband's loving direction and ends with someone at her locked door. The Birth-Mark has a husband's kind will that kills, but Georgiana has no window or locked room and never calls it a crime; Usher's Madeline is shut in by a brother; The Turn of the Screw and Herland have no husband ruling a wife; in Rip Van Winkle the wife rules. No other story in the graph fits all three pairs. The Necklace has a husband who gives way to his wife, and no locked room or window. The Lady with the Dog has a wife in love beyond her marriage but no husband's loving rule, window room or locked door; The Bet's lawyer shuts himself in by a wager, with no wife; Hadleyburg and Tobermory have no wife kept by a husband.

claim: Irving makes a wife's death a joke for henpecked husbands: Rip hears the news, takes a drop of comfort, and goes in and out as he pleases. Chopin gives that news and that secret gladness to a wife, then brings the husband home alive: his return, not his death, is what kills her.

from.exact: She did not stop to ask if it were or were not a monstrous joy that held her.

to.exact: There was a drop of comfort, at least, in this intelligence.

alignments.same: Told that a spouse is dead, the survivor feels, under the expected grief, something like gladness.
alignments.differs: Irving lets Rip take his 'drop of comfort' with a narrator's wink; Chopin has Louise ask whether her joy is monstrous and wave the question off herself.

from.exact: There would be no one to live for her during those coming years; she would live for herself.

to.exact: he had got his neck out of the yoke of matrimony, and could go in and out whenever he pleased

alignments.same: The surviving spouse looks ahead to years of coming and going at will, free of the other's rule.
alignments.differs: Rip is freed from a scold's 'petticoat government' and the village laughs with him; Louise is freed from a loving husband's will and can only whisper it alone.

from.exact: It was Brently Mallard who entered, a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his grip-sack and umbrella.

to.exact: it’s twenty years since he went away from home with his gun, and never has been heard of since

alignments.same: A husband given up for dead comes home with his gear in hand, not knowing what his absence has meant.
alignments.differs: Rip comes back after twenty years to find his wife already dead and his freedom made; Brently comes back within the hour, and his living face ends Louise's freedom and her life.

question: Rip's village laughs with him at his release; no one in the Mallard house could be told of Louise's. What makes the same gladness comic in one story and unspeakable in the other?

substitution.note: Only Rip Van Winkle has a spouse's death heard as news and taken with comfort, years of going in and out at will, and a husband given up for dead walking home. The Scarlet Letter's Chillingworth is thought lost and returns, but no one is glad of his death; Werther dies but no spouse rejoices; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod vanishes with no wife; The Yellow Wallpaper has no death. No other story in the graph fits all three pairs. The Necklace has no death of a spouse and no husband coming home. The Lady with the Dog, Hadleyburg, The Bet and Tobermory have no spouse's death taken as release and no husband given up for dead coming home.

claim: Both tales follow a youth who finds the common world ugly, finds romance at a shabby theatre and lives for beautiful things until he dies by his own hand. Wilde's narrator says a book poisoned Dorian; Cather's says Paul scarcely read, and no portrait bears his sins: he wears his spoils for eight days and jumps.

from.exact: Several of Paul's teachers had a theory that his imagination had been perverted by garish fiction; but the truth was, he scarcely ever read at all.

to.exact: Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book.

alignments.same: A youth's turn to a life of sensation is laid to a corrupting book.
alignments.differs: Wilde's narrator says the yellow book poisoned Dorian, though Lord Henry denies it; Cather gives the theory to Paul's teachers and denies it: music, not novels, is his spark.

from.exact: the stage entrance of that theatre was for Paul the actual portal of Romance

to.exact: I passed by an absurd little theatre, with great flaring gas-jets and gaudy play-bills

alignments.same: A youth weary of the grey, grimy city finds his romance at a cheap theatre with a cracked orchestra.
alignments.differs: Dorian loves an actress there and casts her off when she acts badly; Paul loves no one, wants no part on the stage, only to breathe the painted air behind the scenes.

from.exact: As he fell, the folly of his haste occurred to him with merciless clearness

to.exact: It would kill the past, and when that was dead, he would be free.

alignments.same: Cornered by his past, the youth strikes a blow meant to free him, and it kills him.
alignments.differs: Dorian stabs the portrait to kill his past and is found withered, knifed in the heart; Paul jumps knowing it is death, and sees as he falls all he left undone.

question: Dorian's ruin is laid to a book and stored in a portrait; Paul's is laid to nothing but Cordelia Street. Which story makes the love of beauty itself the cause of the fall?

substitution.note: Only Dorian Gray gives a youth who scorns the common world a shabby theatre for his romance, a book blamed for his fall, and a death by his own blow. Werther reads and kills himself, but has no theatre and no book blamed for him; Notes from Underground and The Bet have books and confinement but no theatre and no suicide; The Necklace has the hunger for luxury but no theatre, book or death; Jekyll and Hyde has a self-made death but no theatre or love of beauty; The Lady with the Dog and Tobermory have no theatre, blamed book or death.

claim: Both tales give someone from a thrifty home, who feels born for luxury, one bright spell among the rich on money not their own. Mathilde pays for a borrowed paste necklace with ten years of scrubbing and lives on; Paul's father repays the theft at once, and Paul jumps rather than go home.

from.exact: these were his own people, he told himself

to.exact: Mathilde suffered ceaselessly, feeling herself born to enjoy all delicacies and all luxuries.

alignments.same: Someone from a narrow, thrifty home holds that the life of the rich is the one they were made for.
alignments.differs: Mathilde suffers the want of it at home and gets no more than one ball; Paul says it standing in the Waldorf's corridors, his way paid with stolen bank notes.

from.exact: He reflected upon the mysterious dishes that were brought into the dining-room, the green bottles in buckets of ice

to.exact: she thought of delicious dishes served on marvellous plates

alignments.same: Shut out, the dreamer pictures the dishes served at rich tables.
alignments.differs: Mathilde dreams them over her husband's soup and never tastes them; Paul dreams them in the rain outside the Schenley, then eats them at the Waldorf with champagne.

from.exact: The firm of Denny & Carson announced that the boy's father had refunded the full amount of his theft

to.exact: At the end of ten years they had paid everything, everything

alignments.same: The money that bought the bright spell is paid back in full.
alignments.differs: Mathilde repays it herself through ten years of hard work and lives on; Paul's father repays it at once, and the news of it sends Paul to his death.

question: Mathilde survives her debt and keeps the memory of the ball; Paul cannot survive being forgiven his. Which is the harsher sentence, the bill or the return home?

substitution.note: Only The Necklace has someone of a thrifty home who feels born to luxury, dreams of rich dishes from outside, gets one bright spell on money not their own, and has it paid back in full. In The £1,000,000 Bank-Note the loan is never spent or repaid and Henry does not feel born to luxury; The Overcoat's Akaki wants a cloak, not luxury; Dorian Gray is rich from the start; The Story of an Hour has no money; Hadleyburg's money is a trap, not a spell of pleasure; The Lady with the Dog and Tobermory have no stolen or borrowed spell of luxury.

claim: Two boys of drab streets dress a longed-for place in Eastern enchantment and end in the dark, looking up. Paul steals his way into the Waldorf, finds it all he dreamed, and dies when the money runs out; the boy of Araby reaches his bazaar, finds it closing over counted coins, and turns his scorn on himself.

from.exact: cast an Eastern enchantment over me

to.exact: Paul had his secret temple, his wishing-carpet, his bit of blue-and-white Mediterranean shore

alignments.same: In a grimy city, a boy's longing for a place takes the dress of an Eastern tale.
alignments.differs: Paul's wishing-carpet is a theatre he enters night after night; the boy has only the name of a bazaar he has never seen, spoken by the girl he loves.

from.exact: two men were counting money on a salver. I listened to the fall of the coins.

to.exact: money was everything, the wall that stood between all he loathed and all he wanted

alignments.same: At the end the place of the dream is seen to rest on money.
alignments.differs: Paul learns it as a wall he cannot pass and jumps; the boy hears it as coins counted by the bazaar's curtain, and his florin buys nothing.

from.exact: The upper part of the hall was now completely dark.

to.exact: Paul wondered whether he were destined always to shiver in the black night outside, looking up at it.

alignments.same: The lights go out and the boy stands in the dark, looking up toward the place he longed for.
alignments.differs: Paul stands outside the hotel still wanting in; the boy is inside his bazaar, and looking up into its dark he sees himself 'driven and derided by vanity'.

question: Paul is never let down by the Waldorf, only shut out of it; the boy of Araby gets in and is let down at once. Which story blames the dream, and which the world that will not pay for it?

substitution.note: Only Paul's Case has a boy of a drab city who dresses a longed-for place as an Eastern tale, learns that money is what the place rests on, and is left in the dark looking up at it. Northanger Abbey's Catherine reaches her dreamed place but it is no Eastern tale, money does not stand in her way, and she is not left in the dark; The Necklace has the longing for luxury but no boy, no Eastern dress and no darkness; Dorian Gray and The Lady with the Dog have no place longed for from outside; Candide's Eldorado is reached and left without disenchantment; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod covets a farm, not a place of romance.

claim: A girl and a boy are carried away by the name of a place they have never seen, reach it, find modern wares where they looked for romance, and judge their own fancy as folly. Henry's rebuke wakes Catherine, who forgives herself within a day; no one speaks to the boy of Araby, who wakes alone in anguish and anger.

from.exact: The syllables of the word Araby were called to me through the silence in which my soul luxuriated

to.exact: Northanger Abbey! these were thrilling words

alignments.same: The bare name of a place the young dreamer has never seen is enough to carry them away.
alignments.differs: Catherine's name comes with an invitation to stay there near Henry; the boy's comes from a girl who cannot go, and he must go alone at night to bring her something.

from.exact: examined porcelain vases and flowered tea-sets

to.exact: The furniture was in all the profusion and elegance of modern taste.

alignments.same: Inside the dreamed place the visitor finds fashionable household goods instead of the romance its name promised.
alignments.differs: Catherine still hunts the abbey for secrets in chests and cabinets; the boy at the Eastern bazaar finds English china, sold by a lady with an English accent who serves him from duty.

from.exact: I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

to.exact: The visions of romance were over. Catherine was completely awakened.

alignments.same: The dreamer wakes from a romance and judges it as their own folly.
alignments.differs: Henry's words wake Catherine, who cries and is happy again by the next day; no one says a word to the boy, and the story ends on his anguish.

question: Catherine's romance came from novels and is cured by the man she loves; the boy's came from love itself and has no one to correct it. Is the last sentence of Araby a cure, or the first wound?

substitution.note: Only Northanger Abbey has a young dreamer excited by a place's very name, who finds modern furnishings inside it and then calls the romance folly. Paul's Case has a dreamed place, but the Waldorf matches Paul's dream and he never calls it folly; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod is driven off, not disenchanted; The Necklace's ball does not disappoint Mathilde; Turn of the Screw's Bly is never seen as ordinary; Rip Van Winkle wakes to change, not to his own folly; Phoebe reaches the House of the Seven Gables without having dreamed of it; the haunted houses of Usher, Canterville, Dracula, Bulwer's tale and The Yellow Wallpaper are feared or mocked, never found ordinary and called folly.

claim: A boy and a married man watch a woman lit at a rail from the shadow, hold their desire in by pressing their palms, and at the end see themselves as fools. The boy's sight of himself ends in anguish and anger; Gabriel's shame turns to generous tears for a dead rival, and his self fades into falling snow.

from.exact: He stood still in the gloom of the hall, trying to catch the air that the voice was singing and gazing up at his wife.

to.exact: The light from the lamp opposite our door caught the white curve of her neck, lit up her hair that rested there and, falling, lit up the hand upon the railing.

alignments.same: From the shadow a man gazes at a woman at a rail, the light on her hair, and builds a romance on what he sees.
alignments.differs: The girl at the railing speaks to the boy of the bazaar; Gretta on the banisters listens to a song that calls up another man, and Gabriel would paint her as Distant Music.

from.exact: only the stress of his nails against the palms of his hands held the wild impulse of his body in check

to.exact: I pressed the palms of my hands together until they trembled

alignments.same: Alone with his longing, the lover presses his palms until they tremble to hold it in.
alignments.differs: The boy prays to love in the dark room where the priest died; Gabriel checks his lust on the hotel stairs behind a wife whose thoughts are with a dead boy.

from.exact: He saw himself as a ludicrous figure, acting as a pennyboy for his aunts

to.exact: Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

alignments.same: At the end the lover sees himself from outside as a fool made by his own fancy.
alignments.differs: The boy's story stops in that burning anger; Gabriel's shame gives way to generous tears, pity for his wife and the snow falling on the living and the dead.

question: Both men find that the woman they dreamed about was elsewhere in her thoughts. Why does the boy end in anger at himself while Gabriel ends in tears that are not about himself at all?

substitution.note: Only Araby has a male lover who gazes from the shadow at a woman lit at a rail, presses his palms together to hold in his longing, and ends seeing himself as a fool. The Lady with the Dog's Gurov sees himself in a glass but not as a fool and watches no woman at a rail; Paul's Case and Northanger Abbey have a dreamer let down but no beloved watched at a rail; The Sorrows of Young Werther has the lover watching but ends in death, not self-scorn; The Birth-Mark and Rappaccini's Daughter have a man watching a woman but no pressed palms or self-sight; Notes from Underground has self-scorn but no beloved at a rail.

claim: Two men past youth, in a hotel room with a weeping woman, see themselves in a glass, think of her beauty fading and withering, and learn that they have never loved. Gurov finds that love in himself, late, for the woman crying for him; Gabriel knows it only as what a dead boy felt for his wife.

from.exact: As he passed in the way of the cheval-glass he caught sight of himself in full length

to.exact: at that moment he saw himself in the looking-glass.

alignments.same: In a hotel room with a woman in tears, the man catches sight of himself in a glass and finds himself older and plainer than he thought.
alignments.differs: Gurov sees his greying hair while his hands are on the shoulders of a woman who weeps for him; Gabriel sees his well-filled shirt-front while his wife weeps for another man.

from.exact: Better pass boldly into that other world, in the full glory of some passion, than fade and wither dismally with age.

to.exact: He felt compassion for this life, still so warm and lovely, but probably already not far from beginning to fade and wither like his own.

alignments.same: Beside the woman, the man thinks of her life and his own as bound to fade and wither with age.
alignments.differs: Gurov's compassion binds him to her fading life; Gabriel envies the boy who died at seventeen in passion rather than fade.

from.exact: He had never felt like that himself towards any woman but he knew that such a feeling must be love.

to.exact: And only now when his head was grey he had fallen properly, really in love—for the first time in his life.

alignments.same: A man who has courted or married learns late that he has never loved before.
alignments.differs: Gurov finds love at last in himself and it is returned; Gabriel recognises love only in the feeling of a dead rival, which he has never had.

question: Gurov's late love begins a new and harder life; Gabriel's late knowledge of love ends with his identity fading into snow. Is Gabriel's discovery a beginning, like Gurov's, or only a farewell?

substitution.note: Only The Lady with the Dog has a man past youth who sees himself in a glass in a hotel room beside a weeping woman, thinks of her life fading and withering like his own, and learns he has never loved. The Sorrows of Young Werther and The Scarlet Letter have love across a marriage but no late discovery of never having loved; Dorian Gray has the self seen in a picture but no beloved weeping beside him; The Necklace and The Story of an Hour have no man learning love; Araby's boy sees himself as a fool but is young and has never courted.

claim: Gilman's teller reads a broken neck into the wallpaper John laughs at and hides a rope for the woman she frees; John only faints. Glaspell moves the reading outside the absent wife: neighbors find a wrung neck among kitchen things the men laugh at, and the rope was round the husband's neck.

from.exact: "Nothing here but kitchen things," he said, with a little laugh for the insignificance of kitchen things.

to.exact: He laughs at me so about this wallpaper!

alignments.same: A man laughs at the household thing a woman attends to, and the story's truth is hidden in that thing.
alignments.differs: John laughs at his wife's study of her own wallpaper; the sheriff laughs at the kitchen of a wife who is gone, and two other women do the studying.

from.exact: Its neck—look at its neck! It's all—other side to.

to.exact: There is a recurrent spot where the pattern lolls like a broken neck and two bulbous eyes stare at you upside-down.

alignments.same: A woman looking hard at a wife's surroundings finds a broken neck turned the wrong way.
alignments.differs: Gilman's broken neck is a figure the teller sees in the paper and comes to share; Glaspell's is a real canary wrung by the husband, and it tells the neighbors why he died.

from.exact: 'He died of a rope round his neck,' says she; and just went on pleatin' at her apron.

to.exact: I’ve got a rope up here that even Jennie did not find.

alignments.same: A wife kept to a lonely house ends the story with a rope, and her husband is laid low.
alignments.differs: Gilman's teller means the rope for the creeping woman, herself, and John only faints in her path; Minnie's rope was round John Wright's neck, and she sits pleating her apron.

question: Gilman gives the wife her own voice; Glaspell never lets Minnie speak except in Mr. Hale's report. What does each story gain from where it puts the one who reads the pattern?

substitution.note: Only The Yellow Wallpaper has a husband who laughs at the household thing his wife studies, a broken neck turned upside-down found in her surroundings, and a wife ending with a rope. The Story of an Hour has a loving husband's will but no laughter, neck or rope; The Birth-Mark's Aylmer studies his wife himself; Usher's Madeline is shut in by a brother; The Purloined Letter's searchers laugh but there is no wife or rope. No other story in the view fits all three pairs. Araby and The Dead, added later, have no laughter at a wife's household thing, no broken neck and no rope.

claim: Chopin gives one wife an hour alone: she calls a kind husband's will a crime, hears singing and sparrows, and dies while doctors name the wrong joy. Glaspell's wife has already acted and is gone; her song and bird are dead, and her neighbors name the crime and keep the reason from the men.

from.exact: That was a crime! That was a crime! Who's going to punish that?

to.exact: A kind intention or a cruel intention made the act seem no less a crime

alignments.same: A woman names as a crime the slow stifling of a wife's life, a wrong no court would try.
alignments.differs: Louise calls her husband's imposed will a crime; Martha Hale calls her own staying away a crime, while the law makes ready to punish Minnie for the one act it can see.

from.exact: a thing that sang. She used to sing. He killed that too.

to.exact: The notes of a distant song which some one was singing reached her faintly, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves.

alignments.same: Singing and birds stand for the life a wife's marriage has shut out.
alignments.differs: Louise hears a stranger's song and sparrows coming in at the news of her husband's death; Minnie's own singing stopped in her marriage, and her husband strangled her one canary.

from.exact: it's all perfectly clear, except the reason for doing it.

to.exact: When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of the joy that kills.

alignments.same: Men arrive after the event and give, or look for, the reason for what happened in a wife's house.
alignments.differs: Chopin's doctors name a reason, wrongly and with confidence, and no one corrects them; Glaspell's attorney knows he lacks the reason, and the two women who hold it keep it from him.

question: Louise's secret dies with her; Minnie's is kept by two women who choose to keep it. Is their silence a freedom for her or another kind of confinement?

substitution.note: Only The Story of an Hour has a woman calling a husband's will a crime, song and birds standing for the wife's shut-out life, and men arriving afterwards to give the reason for a wife's act or death. The Yellow Wallpaper has no crime named, no song or bird and no verdict after; Rip Van Winkle's wife dies offstage and no one seeks a reason; The Birth-Mark's Georgiana dies under her husband's hand but no one names it a crime. No other story in the view fits all three pairs. Araby and The Dead, added later, name no crime and bring no men to give the reason for a wife's act; Gretta's song in The Dead calls back a dead boy, not a life her marriage shut out.

claim: Poe's Prefect laughs at the hint that the case is too plain; Dupin reads a soiled letter against its owner's neat habits and pockets it for the police. Glaspell's men laugh at quilting talk; two wives read one crooked block against Minnie's even sewing and pocket the dead bird to keep it from the law.

from.exact: There was a laugh for the ways of women, a warming of hands over the stove

to.exact: “What nonsense you do talk!” replied the Prefect, laughing heartily.

alignments.same: The official in charge laughs off the idea that what he seeks lies in something ordinary.
alignments.differs: The Prefect laughs at Dupin's hint that the case is too simple; the sheriff laughs at the women's talk of quilting, not knowing that their talk is the search.

from.exact: All the rest of them have been so nice and even—but—this one.

to.exact: the soiled and torn condition of the paper, so inconsistent with the true methodical habits of D——

alignments.same: The searcher notices one thing whose disorder breaks its owner's known neat habits.
alignments.differs: Dupin reads the soiled letter as the minister's deliberate disguise; the women read the crooked block as Minnie's shaking hand, and Martha Hale unpicks it so no one else can read it.

from.exact: Martha Hale snatched the box from the sheriff's wife, and got it in the pocket of her big coat

to.exact: I stepped to the card-rack, took the letter, put it in my pocket, and replaced it by a fac-simile

alignments.same: The finder pockets the evidence while the others look away and leaves a false surface behind.
alignments.differs: Dupin's letter goes to the Prefect for fifty thousand francs; Martha Hale's bird goes nowhere, and the false surface she leaves is a word to the attorney: 'knot it.'

question: Dupin outwits the police in order to serve them; the two wives outwit the sheriff in order to judge for themselves. Which is the better reader of evidence, and which the better judge?

substitution.note: Only The Purloined Letter has an official who laughs at the ordinary, a searcher who reads one item's disorder against its owner's neat habits, and the evidence pocketed and replaced behind others' backs. In Murders in the Rue Morgue Dupin scorns the police but pockets nothing; in Mysterious Affair at Styles Poirot reads ornaments straightened twice, but no one laughs at his search and what he hides goes to the law in the end; in Scandal in Bohemia Holmes never gets the photograph; in The Blue Cross Father Brown swaps parcels but reads no broken habit and hands the cross back. No other story in the view fits all three pairs. Araby and The Dead, added later, have no official, no search and no evidence pocketed.

claim: Each narrator says a solitary man's life deserves a book he cannot write, tells late of the post the man lost, and finds him alone with a few crumbs. Melville's lawyer has only a rumour and is horrified; Anderson tells Wing's ruin as fact and shows him eating crumbs like a priest at prayer.

from.exact: The story of Wing Biddlebaum’s hands is worth a book in itself. Sympathetically set forth it would tap many strange, beautiful qualities in obscure men. It is a job for a poet.

to.exact: I believe that no materials exist for a full and satisfactory biography of this man. It is an irreparable loss to literature.

alignments.same: The narrator declares the hidden life of an obscure, odd man worth a book, and says he cannot give it.
alignments.differs: Melville's lawyer lacks the materials and has only what he saw; Anderson's narrator has the facts but says the telling needs a poet's sympathy.

from.exact: In his youth Wing Biddlebaum had been a school teacher in a town in Pennsylvania.

to.exact: The report was this: that Bartleby had been a subordinate clerk in the Dead Letter Office at Washington, from which he had been suddenly removed by a change in the administration.

alignments.same: Late in the story the narrator gives the man's former post and how he was suddenly put out of it.
alignments.differs: Bartleby's past is an unchecked rumour about a government office; Wing's is told as fact: a loved teacher beaten and driven out of town over his hands.

from.exact: A few stray white bread crumbs lay on the cleanly washed floor by the table; putting the lamp upon a low stool he began to pick up the crumbs, carrying them to his mouth one by one with unbelievable rapidity.

to.exact: in a newspaper a few crumbs of ginger-nuts and a morsel of cheese

alignments.same: The solitary man's meal is a few crumbs, eaten alone in the place where he lives.
alignments.differs: The lawyer finds only the crumbs Bartleby left and is struck by the horror of his solitude; Anderson watches Wing eat each crumb, kneeling like a priest at his rosary.

question: Melville's lawyer cannot learn Bartleby's past; Anderson's narrator knows Wing's past and still says the story needs a poet. What is each narrator admitting he cannot do?

substitution.note: Only Bartleby has a narrator who says the strange man's life deserves a book that cannot be written, gives the man's lost former post only late, and finds him alone with a few crumbs. The Overcoat tells Akaky's birth and naming at the start, not a lost post at the end, and its narrator never says the life is beyond him; Vanka, Notes from Underground and The Lady with the Dog have no narrator holding back a stranger's past; Moby-Dick's Ishmael tells of Ahab's lost leg early and there is no meal of crumbs; Araby, Paul's Case and The Dead have no solitary man watched by a narrator.

claim: A boy at a fair emptied of its crowd hears its silence and sees himself as a small thing driven along, his feeling for a girl unspoken. Araby's boy stands there without her and ends in anguish and anger; George sits silent beside Helen in the dark grand-stand, and the silence gives both what they need.

from.exact: It has itched and squirmed with life and now it is night and the life has all gone away. The silence is almost terrifying.

to.exact: I recognised a silence like that which pervades a church after a service.

alignments.same: The boy is in a fair emptied of its crowd and feels its silence as something solemn or fearful.
alignments.differs: Araby's boy comes late and alone to a bazaar that is closing; George brings Helen to the fair ground after the fair, and the silence deepens his thought and his love of life.

from.exact: With a little gasp he sees himself as merely a leaf blown by the wind through the streets of his village.

to.exact: Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

alignments.same: With a shock the boy sees himself from outside as a small thing driven along.
alignments.differs: Araby's boy sees vanity driving him, and the sight ends his story in anger; George sees a leaf in the wind, and the sight sends him to look for Helen's understanding.

from.exact: In the darkness in the grand-stand Helen White and George Willard remained silent.

to.exact: I did not know whether I would ever speak to her or not or, if I spoke to her, how I could tell her of my confused adoration.

alignments.same: The boy cannot put into words what he feels for the girl.
alignments.differs: Araby's boy never tells his adoration and goes home with nothing; George and Helen sit silent together, and the silence itself is what they came for.

question: Both boys are left in the dark at an emptied fair. Why does the girl's absence turn Araby's silence into self-contempt, while Helen's silent presence turns George's into reverence?

substitution.note: Only Araby has a boy who reaches a fair once its crowd is gone, hears its church-like silence, sees himself as a thing driven by vanity, and never tells the girl what he feels. Northanger Abbey's Catherine is a girl whose letdown is a house, not a fair, and she is scolded into waking; Paul's Case has a boy dreaming of fine places but no girl and no emptied fair; The Dead has a fool's self-sight but at a party with his wife; Rip Van Winkle and Sleepy Hollow have rural frolics but no boy alone in the silence after them.

claim: After a night of music and dancing, a man in the dark beside a woman thinks of all who lived before him, feels his self dwindle, and weeps. Gabriel, beside a wife who loved a dead boy, fades into the snow; George weeps for love of his living town, and Helen makes his smallness bearable.

from.exact: the countless figures of men who before his time have come out of nothingness into the world, lived their lives and again disappeared into nothingness

to.exact: His soul had approached that region where dwell the vast hosts of the dead.

alignments.same: The man's mind turns to the multitude of those who lived and died before him.
alignments.differs: Gabriel's host is the dead, among them the boy his wife loved; George sees all men passing out of nothingness, and the fair ground's ghosts are of the living.

from.exact: In the darkness under the roof of the grand-stand, George Willard sat beside Helen White and felt very keenly his own insignificance in the scheme of existence.

to.exact: His own identity was fading out into a grey impalpable world: the solid world itself which these dead had one time reared and lived in was dissolving and dwindling.

alignments.same: Beside a woman in the dark, his own self shrinks to nothing against all who have lived.
alignments.differs: Gabriel's identity fades into a dissolving world while his wife sleeps; George's smallness is eased by Helen, who is awake and close and renews him.

from.exact: One shudders at the thought of the meaninglessness of life while at the same instant, and if the people of the town are his people, one loves life so intensely that tears come into the eyes.

to.exact: Generous tears filled Gabriel’s eyes.

alignments.same: The thought of lives that end brings tears to his eyes.
alignments.differs: Gabriel's tears are for his wife and the dead boy who loved her; George's are love for the life of his own town's people.

question: Both men feel their selves dwindle before the host of those who lived before. Why does Gabriel's dwindling leave him alone with the snow, while George's sends him to hold Helen's hand?

substitution.note: Only The Dead has, after a night of music and dancing, a man in the dark beside a woman who thinks of the host of those who lived before him, feels his self dwindle, and weeps. Araby's boy weeps in anger at a closing bazaar, with no thought of the dead; The Lady with the Dog's Gurov, beside Anna at Oreanda, thinks of the sea sounding when we are no more, but after no dance and without tears; The Sorrows of Young Werther has a dance, a storm and tears, but the tears come when Lotte names Klopstock, not from a self dwindling among the dead; The Story of an Hour's widow feels release, not dwindling.

claim: Both stories keep a death out of a party till the guests are gone, then bring a host before a poor dead young man, and end past words. Gabriel bars the dead from his speech, meets the boy only in fancy and loses himself among the dead; Laura begs to stop the party, sees the body, and stammers about life.

from.exact: I’ll remember it again after the party’s over, she decided.

to.exact: I will not let any gloomy moralising intrude upon us here tonight.

alignments.same: A host of the party resolves to keep thoughts of death out of it until the celebration is over.
alignments.differs: Gabriel himself shuts the dead of the past out of the feast; Laura wanted the party stopped for a man killed that morning, and gives in once her mother hands her a hat.

from.exact: There lay a young man, fast asleep—sleeping so soundly, so deeply, that he was far, far away from them both.

to.exact: in the partial darkness he imagined he saw the form of a young man standing under a dripping tree.

alignments.same: After the party the host faces a young man of the poorer sort who has died, a carter or a boy from the gasworks.
alignments.differs: Gabriel only imagines Michael Furey, dead for love years ago, and feels the dead drawing him into their dissolving world; Laura stands over the carter's body and finds him peaceful, content and far from parties.

from.exact: But what life was she couldn’t explain.

to.exact: He was conscious of, but could not apprehend, their wayward and flickering existence.

alignments.same: At the close the host is moved by what the dead show and cannot grasp or say it.
alignments.differs: Gabriel's failure to grasp is about the dead and ends in his own identity fading under the snow; Laura's unfinished word is about life, said aloud to a brother who 'quite understood'.

question: Gabriel is left alone beside his sleeping wife while the snow falls on the living and the dead; Laura is met by her brother, who says he understands. Does Laura's 'Isn't life—' end in the same place as Gabriel's swoon, or somewhere else?

substitution.note: Only The Dead has a party whose host keeps death out of it, a dead young man of the poorer sort met by that host after the guests leave, and a closing sense the host cannot grasp. The Picture of Dorian Gray stops its shooting party for the dead beater and ends in no wordless insight; Bartleby's narrator finds the dead man seemingly asleep and ends 'Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!', but there is no party; The Story of an Hour has a death reported to a house, no party and no body seen; The Overcoat's party comes before the clerk's own death; The Sorrows of Young Werther ends with the lover's death, not a host facing a dead man; The Necklace has a ball but no death. Winesburg, Ohio's 'Death' brings George Willard to his mother's body, but there is no party, the dead is a woman, not a poor young man, and he speaks his feeling aloud.

claim: Each girl sees herself made beautiful in a mirror, is the beauty of the party, and afterwards wants to hide her clothes from women of another class. Mathilde's borrowed necklace lifts her above her station and she shrinks from women in furs; Laura's gift hat sets her above the poor and she longs to hide in their shawls.

from.exact: There, quite by chance, the first thing she saw was this charming girl in the mirror

to.exact: was lost in ecstasy at her reflection in the mirror.

alignments.same: Before the party a young woman sees in the mirror a beauty she had not known she could have, made by a single ornament.
alignments.differs: Mathilde's diamonds are borrowed from a rich friend to raise her above her station; Laura's hat is her mother's gift, and the sight of it quiets her pity for the dead carter.

from.exact: Laura, you look quite Spanish. I’ve never seen you look so striking.

to.exact: Madame Loisel was a great success. She was prettier than any other woman present

alignments.same: At the party she is admired above everyone, and she glows with the praise.
alignments.differs: Mathilde's success is among strangers of a higher rank, the minister himself; Laura's praise comes from her own kind at her own family's party.

from.exact: To be away from those staring eyes, or to be covered up in anything, one of those women’s shawls even.

to.exact: She felt this and wished to escape so as not to be remarked by the other women, who were enveloping themselves in costly furs.

alignments.same: After the party, among women of another class, she is ashamed of what she wears and wants to escape their eyes.
alignments.differs: Mathilde hides her poor wraps from rich women in furs; Laura, going down to the poor, is ashamed of her shining frock and hat and wishes for a poor woman's shawl.

question: Mathilde spends ten years paying for one night's finery; Laura asks the dead man to 'Forgive my hat'. Which of them learns more from being looked at by women of another class?

substitution.note: Only The Necklace has a woman made beautiful in a mirror for a party, admired above the rest there, and afterwards ashamed of her clothes before women of another class. Paul's Case has the toilet watched in a mirror and a luxurious dining-room, but nobody praises Paul and his shame is of his home, not his clothes; The Overcoat's new coat is admired at a party with no mirror and no shame; The £1,000,000 Bank-Note dresses Adams on credit but he hides from no other class; Northanger Abbey has balls but no mirror-made beauty or class shame; The Dead's Gabriel sees himself in a glass but is no beauty at the party. Winesburg, Ohio's Elizabeth Willard makes herself up to be beautiful, but for no party, with no praise, and with no shame before another class.

claim: Both travellers vow to stay home, blame fate for sending them out again, and set their own word against travellers' tales.
