Sindbad's voyages end in riches, alms and a feast that rewards the listener; Gulliver's last ends with him loathing the family that thought him dead and disowning tales told to amuse.

from.exact: although my evil destiny so ordered, that she had not power to hinder me

to.exact: but evidently it was my fate to rove, and after a year of repose I prepared to make a sixth voyage, regardless of the entreaties of my friends and relations

alignments.same: The people at home plead with the traveller to stay, and he says a fate stronger than their pleas sent him to sea again.
alignments.differs: Sindbad, rich and rested, sails once more against his friends' entreaties and comes back richer; Gulliver closes Part II on his wife's protest and promises the reader that his 'evil destiny' will overrule it.

from.exact: My wife and family received me with great surprise and joy, because they concluded me certainly dead; but I must freely confess the sight of them filled me only with hatred, disgust, and contempt

to.exact: since that time I have rested from my labours, and given myself up wholly to my family and my friends

alignments.same: The last voyage ends with the traveller home among his family for good.
alignments.differs: Sindbad gives himself wholly to family and friends; Gulliver's family, who had given him up for dead, fill him only with hatred and disgust.

from.exact: I could, perhaps, like others, have astonished thee with strange improbable tales; but I rather chose to relate plain matter of fact

to.exact: were mere travellers' tales invented to give pleasure to the hearers, but now I perceived that they were surely true

alignments.same: The traveller sets his own account against the tales travellers tell to give pleasure.
alignments.differs: Sindbad finds the sailors' tale of the diamond valley true and tells his wonders at a feast; Gulliver, after talking horses and a flying island, disowns tales that astonish and says he writes to inform.

question: Sindbad's voyages make him rich and pay a poor porter to listen; Gulliver's leave him unable to bear his own house. What does each book say a traveller brings home?

substitution.note: Only Sindbad, among the works this step sees, has a traveller who vows after a voyage to stay home and sails again, pleads fate, ends among his family, and tests his wonders against travellers' tales. Twenty Thousand Leagues, Journey to the Centre, The Lost World and Frankenstein's Walton tell one voyage; Moby-Dick's Ishmael blames the Fates for one whaling voyage but makes no vow and has no homecoming; Prendick in Moreau comes home loathing men but from one wreck, with no vow and no feast; The Time Machine's traveller tells one journey to doubting guests and leaves for good; Candide travels on and settles in a garden, not at home; Rip Van Winkle comes home once; A Jury of Her Peers has no voyage at all. Swapping Gulliver for Micromégas, Herland or A Connecticut Yankee leaves no series of voyages and no family homecoming. The Garden Party, The Dead and Winesburg, Ohio keep their people ashore at a party or in one town, with no voyage, vow or travellers' tale.

claim: Both castaways are carried free by a Portuguese captain, offered a captain's own suit and given money at Lisbon. Crusoe signals for rescue, wears the suit and praises his benefactor; Gulliver hides from his rescuers, is tied and heaved aboard, refuses a Yahoo's clothes and bears Don Pedro's kindness as an animal's.

from.exact: the captain would carry me gratis to Lisbon

to.exact: I will carry you thither in charity

alignments.same: Portuguese seamen find a lone Englishman in a small boat far from home, and their captain will carry him for nothing.
alignments.differs: Crusoe signalled with a flag and a gun and offered the captain all he had; Gulliver hid behind a stone, begged leave to go, and was tied with cords.

from.exact: abhorring to cover myself with any thing that had been on the back of a Yahoo

to.exact: with a very good suit of clothes of his own, which had been worn but very little

alignments.same: The captain who saves him offers the castaway, still dressed in skins, a suit of clothes from his own back.
alignments.differs: Crusoe puts it on, finding it only awkward at first, and appears as governor; Gulliver refuses anything worn by a Yahoo and takes only two washed shirts.

from.exact: Don Pedro accompanied me to the ship, and lent me twenty pounds

to.exact: he pulls out an old pouch, and gives me one hundred and sixty Portugal moidores in gold

alignments.same: At Lisbon the Portuguese captain puts money into the returned traveller's hand.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's old friend pays him out of a plantation kept in trust; Don Pedro lends twenty pounds to send Gulliver home to a family he loathes, and his parting embrace is only borne.

question: When Gulliver treats Don Pedro's charity as a Yahoo's, is the satire aimed at Gulliver himself, or at the grateful castaway that Crusoe was?

substitution.note: Only Robinson Crusoe has a castaway carried free by a Portuguese captain, clothed in a captain's own suit and handed money at Lisbon. Sindbad is taken up by ships whose captains return his bales, but no Portuguese, no suit, no Lisbon; Candide reaches Lisbon by wreck and is helped by Jacques the Anabaptist, not a captain who carries him free; Moreau's Prendick is picked up twice but by no Portuguese ship and given no suit or money. Replacing Gulliver's Travels: no other work has a castaway who refuses his rescuer's clothes as unclean.

claim: Both castaways stand alone on a wreck's shore among riches that cannot feed them, build a raft from the wreckage and blame their love of roving. Sindbad loads his raft with rubies and trusts his lucky star; Crusoe loads bread and cheese, keeps the coin only on second thoughts, and calls his roving an original sin.

from.exact: what art thou good for? Thou art not worth to me

to.exact: but all these things only added to the desolation of the scene

alignments.same: On the wreck's shore the castaway finds heaped riches and sees they are worth nothing to a man who cannot leave.
alignments.differs: Crusoe says one knife outweighs the whole heap of coin and keeps it as an afterthought; Sindbad's jewels deepen the desolation until he packs them as his first cargo.

from.exact: the first of these I filled with provisions—viz. bread, rice, three Dutch cheeses

to.exact: I then made up many packages of rubies, emeralds, rock crystal, ambergris, and precious stuffs, and bound them upon my raft

alignments.same: Alone, he builds a raft from what the wreck has left and loads it before he sets out.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's raft carries bread, rice and cheese to keep him alive on the island; Sindbad's carries rubies and emeralds away from it, down a river into the dark.

from.exact: the opposition to which was, as I may call it, my original sin

to.exact: I regretted bitterly the roving disposition which was always bringing me into such straits

alignments.same: Facing death alone, he blames his own restless wish to wander for bringing him there.
alignments.differs: Sindbad regrets a disposition and still trusts he was 'born under a lucky star'; Crusoe calls his defiance of his father's advice an original sin that Providence has punished.

question: Sindbad brings riches home from every wreck; why does Crusoe's island make coin useless and bread precious, and what is left of the merchant's tale?

substitution.note: Only Sindbad has a lone survivor on a shore heaped with wreck treasure who builds a raft and loads it with jewels. Gulliver builds a canoe of Yahoo skins but finds no riches; Journey to the Centre builds a raft for an underground sea with no treasure; Twenty Thousand Leagues has the Vigo galleons' gold but no castaway or raft; Moby-Dick's Ishmael floats on a coffin; Moreau's Prendick has no riches. Replacing Robinson Crusoe: no other work has a castaway who loads his raft with provisions, scorns coin as worth less than a knife, and calls his roving an original sin.

claim: Both end with one man alive from a boat drawn round into a whirl and lifted out on a floating cask or coffin. Poe's fisherman reasons from what the whirl spares, lashes himself to the cask and leaves his brother; Ishmael, dropped astern by chance, does nothing, and the coffin bursts up to him.

from.exact: Round and round, then, and ever contracting towards the button-like black bubble at the axis of that slowly wheeling circle, like another Ixion I did revolve.

to.exact: Round and round we swept—not with any uniform movement—but in dizzying swings and jerks

alignments.same: The survivor is carried round and round the inside of the whirl, slowly, toward its centre.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman rides the funnel at its height and studies its moonlit walls; Ishmael reaches it only after it 'had subsided to a creamy pool' and turns like Ixion bound to his wheel.

from.exact: the coffin life-buoy shot lengthwise from the sea, fell over, and floated by my side

to.exact: I resolved to lash myself securely to the water cask upon which I now held, to cut it loose from the counter, and to throw myself with it into the water.

alignments.same: A buoyant barrel-shaped float is what carries the one survivor up out of the vortex.
alignments.differs: The fisherman picks the cask because he has seen that cylinders sink slowest; Queequeg's coffin is thrown up to Ishmael by the vortex itself, 'by reason of its cunning spring'.

from.exact: It so chanced, that after the Parsee’s disappearance, I was he whom the Fates ordained to take the place of Ahab’s bowsman

to.exact: with a bitter struggle, I resigned him to his fate

alignments.same: Of the boat's men only the teller lives; the others go down with the vessel.
alignments.differs: The fisherman chooses to live, leaving his brother clinging to the ring-bolt; Ishmael says chance and 'the Fates' chose him, and he leaves no one behind by any act of his.

question: Poe's fisherman earns his escape by watching the whirl; the whirl hands Ishmael his. Which of the two has the better right to say he alone escaped to tell it?

substitution.note: Only Poe's tale has a boat carried round inside a whirl toward its centre and one man lifted out on a floating cask while his brother goes down. Twenty Thousand Leagues spins a boat in the maelstrom but Aronnax is senseless and rides no float; Journey to the Centre's raft turns in whirlpools but no one is lost and nothing floats them out; Usher's narrator flees on foot as the tarn closes; Candide, Gulliver and Frankenstein have shipwreck or ice but no vortex and no cask. Replacing Moby-Dick: no other work has a coffin thrown up from a vortex. Works added later in order: Robinson Crusoe's boat is carried off by a current and brought back by an eddy, with no whirl drawing it round to a centre, no cask or coffin lifting him out and no one lost; Sindbad's ships are wrecked and he floats on planks, but no whirlpool turns them; Araby, The Garden Party, A Jury of Her Peers, The Dead and Winesburg have no sea; the Crusoe and Arabian Nights prefaces and O'Brien's notes are paratexts with no voyage. Claim false with each.

claim: Verne ends his voyage in Poe's whirl off Lofoden: whales and a bear swallowed, a small boat spinning till the teller is giddy, rescue by Lofoden fishermen, a story that may not be believed. But Poe's fisherman stays awake and tells exactly how he got out; Aronnax is knocked senseless and cannot tell.

from.exact: There, not only vessels, but whales are sacrificed, as well as white bears from the northern regions.

to.exact: A bear once, attempting to swim from Lofoden to Moskoe, was caught by the stream and borne down

alignments.same: The whirl's victims are listed as ships, whales and a bear from the north.
alignments.differs: Poe quotes Jonas Ramus by name and has his narrator smile at the whale and bear 'anecdotes'; Verne gives them as what 'we knew', with no source and no doubt.

from.exact: My head struck on a piece of iron, and with the violent shock I lost all consciousness.

to.exact: I took courage, and looked once again upon the scene.

alignments.same: Inside the whirl the teller's small boat spins and he waits for death.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman opens his eyes and studies the funnel until its floating wreckage shows him a way out; Aronnax is struck senseless, so how the boat escaped he 'cannot tell'.

from.exact: Shall I be believed? I do not know. And it matters little, after all.

to.exact: I told them my story—they did not believe it.

alignments.same: Taken in by fishermen of Lofoden, the survivor doubts that his story will be believed.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman was disbelieved and tells it again to a stranger on the cliff; Aronnax says belief 'matters little' and rests on his record: 'Not a fact has been omitted'.

question: Poe's survivor lives because he keeps looking; Verne's lives without seeing anything. What does Verne's ending lose, or gain, by leaving the escape untold?

substitution.note: Only Poe's tale has the whirl off Lofoden with its whales and bear, a giddy spinning boat, rescue by Lofoden fishermen and a disbelieved survivor. Moby-Dick's vortex is a sinking ship's, with no Lofoden, bear or fishermen; Journey to the Centre's raft whirls underground and comes out at Stromboli; Rip Van Winkle's story is doubted but there is no sea; Frankenstein and Gulliver have no whirlpool. Replacing Twenty Thousand Leagues: Moby-Dick's Ishmael keeps his senses and is picked up by the Rachel, not by Lofoden fishermen. Works added later in order: Robinson Crusoe's boat is carried off by a current and brought back by an eddy, with no whirl drawing it round to a centre, no cask or coffin lifting him out and no one lost; Sindbad's ships are wrecked and he floats on planks, but no whirlpool turns them; Araby, The Garden Party, A Jury of Her Peers, The Dead and Winesburg have no sea; the Crusoe and Arabian Nights prefaces and O'Brien's notes are paratexts with no voyage. Claim false with each.

claim: Stevenson takes three things from Crusoe's island: the castaway who finds God there, the parrot's voice that wakes a sleeper, and the mutineers left ashore instead of hanged. His maroon's piety comes with rum and buried gold, the parrot cries for money, and the men left behind beg not to be left to die.

from.exact: But it were Providence that put me here. I’ve thought it all out in this here lonely island, and I’m back on piety.

to.exact: I had been well instructed by father and mother

alignments.same: Alone on the island, the castaway blames his fall on leaving a pious parent's teaching and finds Providence in being put there.
alignments.differs: Crusoe repents in earnest and reads his Bible; Ben Gunn keeps 'a thimbleful for luck' of rum and whispers in the same breath, 'I’m rich.'

from.exact: start upright in bed with the sharp voice of Captain Flint still ringing in my ears

to.exact: I was awaked out of my sleep by a voice calling me by my name several times

alignments.same: A parrot's voice breaks into the sleeper's rest and makes him start up in fright.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's Poll cries the lament he taught it, 'Poor Robin Crusoe', and goes home with him; Silver's bird screams 'Pieces of eight', and Jim still hears it in nightmares.

from.exact: to take them home for the gibbet would have been a cruel sort of kindness

to.exact: I told them I thought they had made a right choice; that if the captain had carried them away they would certainly be hanged.

alignments.same: Rather than carry the mutineers home to be hanged, the ship leaves them on the island with arms and stores.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's rebels choose to stay, thank him and learn his way of living; Stevenson's three kneel on the sand begging not to be left, then fire at the ship.

question: Ben Gunn has Crusoe's goats, piety and island years; what does Stevenson change by making him a pirate who found the treasure and loses his share in nineteen days?

substitution.note: Only Robinson Crusoe has a lone islander who blames his fall on a pious parent's teaching, a parrot that wakes him calling his name, and mutineers left on the island instead of hanged. Sindbad's castaway has no parrot or mutiny; Gulliver is set ashore by his own mutinous crew but leaves no one behind; Moby-Dick and Descent into the Maelström have no island; Moreau's Prendick finds no piety and leaves the Beast People. Replacing Treasure Island: no other work in the graph has a marooned man back 'on piety', a parrot's cry in a sleeper's ears and mutineers deserted on the island.

claim: Both voyages hang on a one-legged seaman an owner vouches for, who braces his leg in the deck and holds out gold to the crew. Ahab lost his leg to the whale he hunts, stands rigid, and pays for revenge; Silver lies about his leg, sways with every roll, and wants the money.

from.exact: Long John Silver, he is called, and has lost a leg; but that I regarded as a recommendation, since he lost it in his country’s service, under the immortal Hawke.

to.exact: ever since he lost his leg last voyage by that accursed whale, he’s been a kind of moody

alignments.same: Before sailing, the man who fitted out the ship tells how the one-legged seaman lost his leg and vouches for him.
alignments.differs: Peleg tells the truth and warns of moods; the squire repeats Silver's own lie about Hawke, which hides a leg lost in the pirate Flint's broadside.

from.exact: wedge the foot of the crutch against a bulkhead, and propped against it, yielding to every movement of the ship

to.exact: His bone leg steadied in that hole; one arm elevated, and holding by a shroud; Captain Ahab stood erect

alignments.same: On the rolling deck the one-legged man fixes his bone leg or crutch into the ship's timber to keep his footing.
alignments.differs: Ahab stands erect and still, staring beyond the prow; Silver yields to every movement and goes on cooking, as he will go over to whichever side is winning.

from.exact: it’s hundreds of pounds instead of hundreds of farthings in their pockets

to.exact: he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!

alignments.same: The one-legged man binds the crew to his voyage by holding gold before them.
alignments.differs: Ahab nails his doubloon to the mast as the prize for sighting the whale he means to kill; Silver promises shares of Flint's treasure and banks his own, 'some here, some there'.

question: Melville's one-legged captain is ruled by the wound and Stevenson's one-legged cook by money; which of them does the crew have more reason to fear?

substitution.note: No other work in the graph has a one-legged seaman: Twenty Thousand Leagues' Nemo and Descent into the Maelström's fisherman are whole, Gulliver's and Crusoe's captains are two-legged and hold out no gold, Sindbad's captains have no false leg. Replacing Moby-Dick: no other work has an owner vouching for a man who lost his leg, a leg braced in the deck and gold held out to the crew; replacing Treasure Island the same fails.

claim: Both crews row a ship's boat into surf they know will swamp it, and the waves throw the teller ashore while others drown. Crusoe commits his soul to God, fights each wave and thanks God he alone was saved; Crane's correspondent is flung over the boat by chance, and the best swimmer lies drowned before an indifferent shore.

from.exact: All we can do is to work her in as far as possible, and then when she swamps, pile out and scramble for the beach.

to.exact: we committed our souls to God in the most earnest manner; and the wind driving us towards the shore, we hastened our destruction with our own hands

alignments.same: The men row toward a shore whose surf they know will overturn the boat.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's crew commit their souls to God and row 'like men going to execution'; Crane's captain gives it as a drill, and the men appeal only, in rage, to 'this old ninny-woman, Fate'.

from.exact: A large wave caught him and flung him with ease and supreme speed completely over the boat and far beyond it.

to.exact: I could feel myself carried with a mighty force and swiftness towards the shore

alignments.same: A breaking wave carries the swimmer bodily a long way toward the beach.
alignments.differs: Crusoe holds his breath, grips a rock and times each run, sharing the work with the sea; Crane's correspondent does nothing and calls it 'an event in gymnastics, and a true miracle of the sea'.

from.exact: In the shallows, face downward, lay the oiler.

to.exact: reflecting upon all my comrades that were drowned, and that there should not be one soul saved but myself

alignments.same: Ashore, the survivor learns that the sea has kept a companion.
alignments.differs: Crusoe, saved alone, gives thanks for his 'deliverance' and finds only hats and odd shoes of the drowned; Crane's dead man is the oiler, who led the swim, lying where a man could wade.

question: Crusoe reads his landing as a deliverance meant for him; the oiler, the best swimmer, drowns a few yards from Crane's correspondent. What is left of Crusoe's thanks if the sea chooses like this?

substitution.note: Only Crusoe has a ship's boat rowed on purpose into surf known to swamp it, a teller thrown ashore wave by wave, drowned comrades and thanks to God for being the one saved. Gulliver's boat is overset by a flurry far out and he swims 'as fortune directed' and walks ashore, seeing no one drowned; Sindbad is washed ashore on wreckage or floats on a raft, with no boat rowed into breakers; Candide reaches Lisbon on a plank after a wreck; Moby-Dick, Twenty Thousand Leagues and the Maelström have no beach. Replacing The Open Boat: no other work has a man flung over his boat by a wave while the strongest swimmer drowns in the shallows. Treasure Island (added later to this stage's view) also fails: the overloaded jolly-boat is rowed for the beach with 'We mustn't mind if we swamp her now', but it 'sank by the stern, quite gently, in three feet of water', with no surf, no one thrown ashore and no one drowned.

claim: Both put men in a small boat before a sea that should drown them. Poe's fisherman counts his life paltry before God's power, gazes at the whirl in admiration and reasons his way out; Crane's men have no time to look, the correspondent pleads 'I love myself', and a wave, not a plan, frees him.

from.exact: When it occurs to a man that nature does not regard him as important, and that she feels she would not maim the universe by disposing of him

to.exact: how foolish it was in me to think of so paltry a consideration as my own individual life, in view of so wonderful a manifestation of God’s power

alignments.same: Facing drowning, the man sees his own life as a small thing to the power that holds him.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman blushes for valuing his life and grows composed; Crane's man wants to throw bricks at the temple, then pleads 'Yes, but I love myself' and is answered by 'a high cold star'.

from.exact: Viewed from a balcony, the whole thing would doubtlessly have been weirdly picturesque. But the men in the boat had no time to see it

to.exact: Never shall I forget the sensations of awe, horror, and admiration with which I gazed about me.

alignments.same: The sea around the boat is a spectacle to be looked at.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman gazes in admiration at the funnel's walls and its rainbow; Crane's men, bailing and rowing, see only the next wave, and the picturesque is left to an onlooker on a balcony.

from.exact: But later a wave perhaps whirled him out of this small deadly current

to.exact: The result was precisely what I had hoped it might be.

alignments.same: The teller is carried free of the current that held him.
alignments.differs: Poe's fisherman gets out by what he has seen of floating cylinders and by a plan; Crane's correspondent does not know what freed him ('a wave perhaps'), and the oiler, who swam best, drowns.

question: Poe's fisherman finds the whirl magnificent and escapes by watching it; Crane's men are too busy to look and are saved or drowned by chance. Which teller has more right to say what the sea means?

substitution.note: Only the Maelström has a man in a small boat who calls his own life paltry before God's power, gazes at the sea in admiration and escapes by a plan drawn from what he sees. Moby-Dick's Ishmael is saved by chance and reasons nothing; Twenty Thousand Leagues' Aronnax is knocked senseless in the maelstrom; Robinson Crusoe commits his soul to God and fights the surf but admires nothing; Journey to the Centre's raft spins in a storm with no plan to get out; Sindbad trusts his luck. Replacing The Open Boat: no other work has men too busy to look at the sea and a teller saved by a wave he cannot explain while the best swimmer drowns. Treasure Island (added later to this stage's view) also fails: Jim in the coracle 'devoutly recommended my spirit to its Maker' and studies the rollers to steer ashore, but he 'could not bear to look upon my fate', counts no life paltry before God's power and admires nothing.

claim: Both put the men of a lost ship in a small boat at night and ask what they owe each other and the dead. Crane's crew grow into a silent brotherhood under a captain who mourns his men; the Patna's officers, who fled first, turn on Jim and talk as if the ship were empty.

from.exact: Over the lives borne from under the shadow of death there seems to fall the shadow of madness.

to.exact: It would be difficult to describe the subtle brotherhood of men that was here established on the seas.

alignments.same: The teller stops to say what a small boat on the open sea, after the ship is lost, does to the men in it.
alignments.differs: Crane finds a brotherhood that warms each man and is the correspondent's best experience; Marlow finds madness, the officers barking 'You ain't fit to live!' and Jim ready to kill them.

from.exact: He noticed that they talked as though they had left behind them nothing but an empty ship.

to.exact: this captain had on him the stern impression of a scene in the greys of dawn of seven turned faces

alignments.same: The men in the boat have just seen their ship go down, as they believe, with people still aboard.
alignments.differs: Crane's captain carries the seven faces in a voice 'deep with mourning'; the Patna's officers, who left eight hundred pilgrims, cheer each other that she 'shot down like a flat-iron'.

from.exact: Suddenly the skipper howled ‘Mein Gott! The squall! The squall! Shove off!’

to.exact: The mind of the master of a vessel is rooted deep in the timbers of her, though he commanded for a day or a decade

alignments.same: The captain's tie to his sinking ship is tested in the moment she goes.
alignments.differs: Crane's hurt captain stayed with his ship and still commands the dinghy calmly; the Patna's skipper is in the boat first, howling to shove off from the ship and the sleeping pilgrims.

question: Crane's men are bound by what they lost together; the Patna's men are bound by what they left. Is Jim, who hates them, any less one of them than the oiler is one of Crane's crew?

substitution.note: Only The Open Boat has the men of a ship that went down with people aboard sharing a small boat at night, a captain who mourns them, and a teller who stops to say what the boat made of the men. Robinson Crusoe's boat is overset within a mile and its crew drown at once; Gulliver's six are overset by a flurry; Sindbad and Moby-Dick's Ishmael are saved alone; the Maelström's brothers are in their own smack, no ship lost; Twenty Thousand Leagues' three escape the Nautilus, which is not sunk; Treasure Island's jolly-boat leaves a ship still afloat. Replacing Lord Jim: no other work in view has officers who fled their ship cursing the man who joined them.

claim: Both young seamen leap from their post in a fright they cannot explain, are cursed as cowards in the boat, and are left facing the sea's immensity. Pip leaps out of the boat and is abandoned for a whale; Jim leaps from the pilgrims' ship into the officers' boat, and the abandonment is his.

from.exact: of the cause that tore him out of his immobility, he knew no more than the uprooted tree knows of the wind that laid it low

to.exact: The involuntary consternation of the moment caused him to leap, paddle in hand, out of the boat

alignments.same: The leap happens in an instant, without a decision the jumper can afterwards name.
alignments.differs: Pip leaps from the safe boat into the sea at a whale's rap; Jim, who stood still by the davit, finds himself in the boat, the pilgrims left behind.

from.exact: Where did you get the pluck to jump—you coward?

to.exact: the poor little negro was assailed by yells and execrations from the crew

alignments.same: Once in the boat, the jumper is cursed as a coward by its crew.
alignments.differs: Pip's crew curse him for losing them a whale; Jim's are the officers who deserted first, and they curse him for joining them, 'You ain't wanted here'.

from.exact: A silence of the sea, of the sky, merged into one indefinite immensity still as death around these saved, palpitating lives.

to.exact: The intense concentration of self in the middle of such a heartless immensity, my God! who can tell it?

alignments.same: After the leap the jumper is alone with an immensity of sea that gives back nothing.
alignments.differs: Pip floats alone in the water, a mile from any boat, and comes back mad; Jim sits safe among three men and feels that every man on earth but they has drowned.

question: Stubb leaves Pip for a whale and says a man is worth less than one; Jim leaves eight hundred pilgrims for his own life. Who in each book has abandoned whom, and which leap can be lived down?

substitution.note: Only Moby-Dick has a young seaman leap from his post in a fright he did not choose, cursed as a coward by the boat's crew and left alone in the sea's immensity. The Open Boat's correspondent jumps when the captain orders it; the Maelström's teller leaps lashed to a cask by plan; Treasure Island's Jim Hawkins slips into the mutineers' boat on a whim and no one curses him; Crusoe, Gulliver and Sindbad are thrown from or left by their ships, not leaping in fear. Replacing Lord Jim: no other work in view has a man leap from a ship he thinks sinking into the boat of those who fled.

claim: Both books give a captain who owns no master a mate who levels a loaded gun at him, wrestles with himself and cannot fire; both captains die unrepentant. Ahab hates a malice he thinks hides behind the world and dies striking at it; Larsen thinks life mere ferment and dies blind, spelling 'bosh' to immortality.

from.exact: He did not care to serve God. He cared to serve nothing.

to.exact: Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I’d strike the sun if it insulted me.

alignments.same: To the one man aboard who can follow him, the captain declares he will bow to no power over him, God included.
alignments.differs: Ahab would strike through the mask at a reasoning malice he believes is there; Larsen, who can only 'almost believe in God', praises Milton's Lucifer for refusing to serve.

from.exact: And yet I wrestled with myself and could not pull the triggers.

to.exact: The yet levelled musket shook like a drunkard’s arm against the panel; Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel

alignments.same: A mate resolved to kill the captain levels a loaded gun at him from close by, shakes, wrestles with himself and does not fire.
alignments.differs: Starbuck aims through a door at Ahab asleep and turns away when Ahab cries out; Van Weyden faces Larsen awake, who tells him his morality will not let him shoot.

from.exact: It was Wolf Larsen’s last word, “bosh,” sceptical and invincible to the end.

to.exact: to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee.

alignments.same: The captain's last words are a refusal; he dies without yielding.
alignments.differs: Ahab dies in the act, caught round the neck by his harpoon line; Larsen dies by inches, blind and paralysed, writing his scorn with a pencil Maud holds in his hand.

question: Starbuck lowers the musket thinking of his wife and child; Larsen says Van Weyden cannot fire because a code was drummed into him. Is either refusal the mate's own choice?

substitution.note: Only Moby-Dick has a mate who raises a loaded gun at his sleeping captain, shakes and puts it back, and a captain who dies spitting defiance. Twenty Thousand Leagues has no gun raised at Nemo, and Nemo is last heard begging God for an end; Frankenstein's Walton faces a mutiny but no one aims at him; Moreau is killed by his puma, not held at gunpoint by Prendick; Candide, Gulliver and Usher have no such captain. Lord Jim's Patna skipper flees his ship and no mate aims at him, and Jim dies yielding to Doramin; Crusoe, Sindbad, Treasure Island and The Open Boat have no such captain. Replacing The Sea-Wolf: no other work's mate fails to fire at a captain who then dies unrepentant.

claim: Both books take a scholar from the sea after a collision and keep him aboard under a captain with a cabin library, till he steals off by boat past that captain. Nemo makes Aronnax his guest and is left sobbing out remorse; Larsen makes Van Weyden cabin-boy and is left mute with pain.

from.exact: And mind you, it’s for your own soul’s sake. It will be the making of you.

to.exact: You will remain on board my vessel, since fate has cast you there.

alignments.same: The captain refuses to set ashore the man he took from the sea and tells him that staying aboard will be good for him.
alignments.differs: Nemo offers Aronnax the run of the ship and 'the land of marvels'; Larsen makes Van Weyden cabin-boy at twenty dollars a month, to learn to stand on his own legs.

from.exact: Against the wall, near the head of the bunk, was a rack filled with books.

to.exact: These are the only ties which bind me to the earth.

alignments.same: The captive is astonished to find that the captain who holds him keeps a library aboard.
alignments.differs: Nemo shows his twelve thousand volumes, bought before he quit the world, and lends them; Van Weyden finds Larsen's rack, and a pencil-marked Browning, while making his bed.

from.exact: I spoke to him, but he made no answer, though his head was still rocking from side to side and he was not asleep.

to.exact: His breast was swelling with sobs; and I heard him murmur these words (the last which ever struck my ear):

alignments.same: On the night he flees in a small boat, the captive comes within reach of the captain, who does nothing to keep him.
alignments.differs: Nemo, having sunk a warship, glides past sobbing a plea to God; Larsen lies in his bunk, head rocking with pain, while Van Weyden takes his guns.

question: Aronnax half wants to stay for Nemo's books and marvels. Does Van Weyden take anything from the Ghost besides its guns and stores that he did not choose to learn?

substitution.note: Only Twenty Thousand Leagues has a scholar thrown into the sea by a collision, kept aboard by a captain with a library, who escapes by boat past him at night. Moby-Dick's Ishmael signs on freely and Ahab keeps no books; Frankenstein's Walton takes Victor from the ice but holds no one; Moreau's Prendick is picked up by a drunken captain without books and flees an island, not a ship; Gulliver's captains free him. Crusoe and Sindbad are wrecked and land alone, not held aboard; Treasure Island's Jim slips off by coracle but was never taken from the sea or kept by a captain with books; Lord Jim's Patna is struck, but Jim leaps and is held by no one. Replacing The Sea-Wolf: no other work keeps a rescued scholar captive aboard.

claim: Both hunts are written down, at the companions' asking, by a man the treasure made rich who would not go again, and both pass a dead man marking the route. Jim withholds the bearings and Flint's skeleton is a killer's joke; Quatermain prints the map, and its maker sits frozen where he wrote it.

from.exact: First reason: Because Sir Henry Curtis and Captain John Good asked me.

to.exact: Squire Trelawney, Dr. Livesey, and the rest of these gentlemen having asked me to write down the whole particulars about Treasure Island

alignments.same: The narrator says he writes the history because the gentlemen who shared the hunt asked him to.
alignments.differs: Jim keeps back 'the bearings of the island' because treasure still lies there; Quatermain sends his reader to 'the rough copy and translation of old da Silvestra’s map'.

from.exact: There he sat, the dead man, whose directions, written some ten generations ago, had led us to this spot.

to.exact: The body pointed straight in the direction of the island, and the compass read duly E.S.E. and by E.

alignments.same: On the way to the treasure the seekers come on a dead man's body that belongs to the directions they follow.
alignments.differs: Flint laid out a man he had killed as a pointer, and Silver shivers at the joke; Silvestra wrote the directions himself, starving in that cave, and Quatermain pities him.

from.exact: but I do not think I would go through the last fifteen or sixteen months again for it

to.exact: Oxen and wain-ropes would not bring me back again to that accursed island

alignments.same: The narrator, made rich by the hunt, swears that no wealth would take him back.
alignments.differs: Jim says it last, leaving the bar silver buried and dreaming of the parrot's cry; Quatermain says it first, an old hunter 'almost sick of adventure' who has made his pile.

question: Jim hides the island's bearings and Quatermain prints the dead man's map: what does each narrator expect his reader to do with the treasure?

substitution.note: Replacing Treasure Island: The Lost World's dead forerunner leaves chalk arrows and a sketch-book, its skeleton (Colver) marks no route, and Lord John means to go back; Journey to the Centre's Saknussemm leaves a cipher and carved initials but no body; Robinson Crusoe returns to his island; Sindbad sails again; Moby-Dick, Twenty Thousand Leagues, Gulliver's Travels and Lord Jim (Marlow's tale, no treasure hunt) have no history written at companions' asking with a dead man on the route. Replacing King Solomon's Mines with any of these fails the same way.

claim: Both parties follow a dead forerunner's marks into a walled-off country, win a native people's war with rifles, and bring home diamonds known by Kimberley's blue clay. Haggard's forerunner sits frozen as a warning, and the king they crown shuts out white men; Doyle's is a pioneer to honour, and the stones fund a museum.

from.exact: He had some presentiment that worthy footsteps would follow close behind him.

to.exact: a sad memento of the fate that so often overtakes those who would penetrate into the unknown

alignments.same: The dead man who went first has left the marks the party follows toward the unknown country.
alignments.differs: Challenger greets Maple White's chalk arrow as a pioneer's welcome to 'worthy footsteps'; Quatermain, before Silvestra's frozen body, reads the fate of those who press into the unknown.

from.exact: since by our strange powers we had aided them to destroy their hereditary foe

to.exact: No other white man shall cross the mountains, even if any man live to come so far.

alignments.same: The white strangers' guns win a native people's war, and that people then holds the only way out of its country.
alignments.differs: The grateful Accala Indians may not let their strangers go, and the ape-men are wiped out; Ignosi, crowned, sends his friends home and bars every white man after them.

from.exact: That was the great De Beers Diamond Mine of Kimberley—what? So you see I got diamonds into my head.

to.exact: Then it is clear that you have never seen the diamond diggings at Kimberley. You may depend on it that this is Solomon’s Diamond Mine.

alignments.same: A man who knows Kimberley recognises a diamond pit by its blue clay.
alignments.differs: Quatermain's pit leads to Solomon's chests, where the treasure nearly entombs them; Lord John digs alone with a spud, tells no one, and shares the stones out so Challenger can found a museum.

question: Ignosi shuts his land to white men 'with their guns and gin', while the Accala Indians may simply keep their strangers: which book gives the native people the last word?

substitution.note: Replacing King Solomon's Mines: Treasure Island has no native war and no diamonds; Journey to the Centre has Saknussemm's marks but no people to fight for; A Connecticut Yankee wins battles with modern arms but has no dead forerunner or diamond pit; Gulliver fights Lilliput's war without guns; The Time Machine and Moreau have no forerunner or diamonds; Lord Jim wins Doramin's war with guns in a walled-off Patusan but follows no dead man's marks and digs no diamonds. Replacing The Lost World: none of these has a forerunner's body, a war won for a native king and a Kimberley-like pit together.

claim: Both tales put a few white men with rifles among a hidden mountain people who take them for more than men, and both rule out a marriage across that line. Haggard's men admit they are men, crown a native heir and go home; Kipling's loafer keeps the godhood, crowns himself, takes a bride and bleeds.

from.exact: Neither god nor devil but a man!

to.exact: We come from another world, though we are men such as ye

alignments.same: The hidden people's question about the white strangers is whether they are gods or men.
alignments.differs: Quatermain answers it himself with a lie that still grants they are men; Dravot never answers it, and the priests shout it when his bitten neck bleeds.

from.exact: How can daughters of men marry gods or devils? It’s not proper.

to.exact: for the sun may not mate with the darkness, nor the white with the black.

alignments.same: Someone of the land declares that a woman of the land cannot marry the white stranger.
alignments.differs: Foulata says it of herself, dying for Good, and Quatermain calls her death fortunate; Billy Fish says it because Dravot is a god, and Dravot forces the wedding.

from.exact: I’d hand over the crown—this crown I’m wearing now—to Queen Victoria on my knees

to.exact: No other white man shall cross the mountains, even if any man live to come so far. I will see no traders with their guns and gin.

alignments.same: The new ruler of the mountain kingdom decides whether more white men and their guns shall come in.
alignments.differs: Ignosi, the native heir they crowned, shuts the passes to white men; Dravot, a white loafer crowned by the people, would send for Englishmen and Sniders and kneel to the Queen.

question: Haggard's white men leave a native king on the throne and go home, Kipling's stay to rule: what does each tale make the price of being taken for a god?

substitution.note: Replacing King Solomon's Mines: Lord Jim's Patusan credits Jim with supernatural powers but nobody forbids his marriage to Jewel and no native heir shuts the country; Connecticut Yankee's Hank wins by an eclipse too, but marries Sandy and means to bring the nineteenth century in; The Lost World's party is never taken for gods; Robinson Crusoe, Sindbad (married abroad on his fourth voyage, no bar) and Gulliver's Travels have no hidden people ruled through a god-belief. Replacing The Man Who Would Be King with any of these fails the same way.

claim: Both white men win a remote people with guns, are credited with more than human power, and die before that people for a failure that cost a native friend his life. Dravot claimed godhood and is driven to a rope-bridge; Jim never claimed his legend and walks unarmed to his friend's father to be shot.

from.exact: Already the legend had gifted him with supernatural powers.

to.exact: They think we’re gods.

alignments.same: After the white men's guns win the first fights, the people credit them with powers beyond men's.
alignments.differs: Jim's legend grows out of guns hauled up a hill and he never claims it; Dravot names himself a god and son of Alexander and rules by it.

from.exact: Jim came up slowly, looked at his dead friend, lifting the sheet, than dropped it without a word.

to.exact: There was a man called Billy Fish, a good friend of us all, and they cut his throat, Sir, then and there, like a pig

alignments.same: The native chief who stood by the white ruler is killed for the white man's mistake.
alignments.differs: Billy Fish chooses to die beside Dravot, whose wish for a wife brought the ruin; Dain Waris is shot by Brown, whom Jim let go, and Jim must look on his body.

from.exact: They say that the white man sent right and left at all those faces a proud and unflinching glance.

to.exact: Out he goes, looking neither right nor left

alignments.same: The fallen white lord goes to his death before the people with a fixed, proud bearing.
alignments.differs: Dravot is prodded to the bridge like an ox and calls for the cut himself; Jim comes ready and unarmed to Doramin and is shot by his friend's father.

question: Dravot asks Peachey's forgiveness and Jim leaves Jewel crying that he is false: to whom does each white lord think he owes his death?

substitution.note: Replacing The Man Who Would Be King: King Solomon's Mines' white men are taken for men from the stars but none rules or dies, and Ignosi lives; Connecticut Yankee's Hank is called the Boss and wins with guns but has no native friend killed for his fault and dies in his bed in another century; Robinson Crusoe, Treasure Island and The Lost World have no white lord of a native people. Replacing Lord Jim: The Sea-Wolf's Wolf Larsen rules only a ship, King Solomon's Mines' men go home alive, and none of the other novels and tales in view has a white ruler of a native people who walks to his death before them.

claim: Both books give Marlow's tale to an unnamed listener who sets him in the dark among silent men, where he becomes a voice. Heart of Darkness keeps one Thames evening that ends when he stops; Lord Jim makes it one evening of many, and finishes the tale in a letter to one listener.

from.exact: with the very first word uttered Marlow’s body, extended at rest in the seat, would become very still, as though his spirit had winged its way back into the lapse of time and were speaking through his lips from the past.

to.exact: For a long time already he, sitting apart, had been no more to us than a voice.

alignments.same: Once Marlow is talking in the dark, his body drops away for the listeners and only his voice is left.
alignments.differs: Heart of Darkness has one pitch-black night on a yawl; Lord Jim's 'would' makes it a habit, on many verandahs in distant parts of the world.

from.exact: Marlow paused to put new life into his expiring cheroot, seemed to forget all about the story, and abruptly began again.

to.exact: then a match flared, and Marlow’s lean face appeared, worn, hollow, with downward folds and dropped eyelids

alignments.same: The frame narrator breaks into the tale to show Marlow pausing to light his tobacco.
alignments.differs: In Heart of Darkness the pause follows a listener's sigh that Marlow snaps at, and the flare shows a worn face; in Lord Jim the pause is idle.

from.exact: there was only one man of all these listeners who was ever to hear the last word of the story.

to.exact: Marlow ceased, and sat apart, indistinct and silent, in the pose of a meditating Buddha.

alignments.same: When Marlow stops talking, the listeners sit on in silence.
alignments.differs: Heart of Darkness ends its tale and its book with that silence; Lord Jim's evening leaves the story unfinished, and its end reaches one listener by letter two years later.

question: Why does Lord Jim need a letter to finish what one night on the Thames could hold in Heart of Darkness?

substitution.note: Replacing Heart of Darkness: The Turn of the Screw's frame is a manuscript read aloud by the fire, not a teller recalling his own past in the dark; The Man Who Would Be King's journalist hears Peachey alone in a lit office; Sindbad tells his voyages over feasts by day; Frankenstein and Moby-Dick have no silent circle of listeners. Replacing Lord Jim: none of the other novels and tales in view has a frame narrator among silent men in the dark round a teller who becomes a voice.

claim: Both white men take worship from a remote people and boast of what their will can make of them; each tale ends on severed heads. Dravot orders the worship, is seen to bleed, and his own head comes home in a bag; Kurtz is never unmasked and sets other men's heads on stakes.

from.exact: By the simple exercise of our will we can exert a power for good practically unbounded

to.exact: I’ll make a damned fine Nation of you, or I’ll die in the making!

alignments.same: The white man set over a remote people declares what his will alone can make of them.
alignments.differs: Dravot says it to the people themselves and drills them into an army; Kurtz writes it in a report for a Society at home, and his own postscript reads 'Exterminate all the brutes!'

from.exact: were offered up to him—do you understand?—to Mr. Kurtz himself

to.exact: every morning Dravot sat by the side of old Imbra, and the people came and worshipped. That was Dravot’s order.

alignments.same: The people bring their worship to the white man himself.
alignments.differs: Dravot orders it, sitting by a village idol as part of his plan; Kurtz's rites end 'unspeakable' midnight dances, and Marlow can hardly bring himself to name them.

from.exact: those heads on the stakes, if their faces had not been turned to the house

to.exact: the dried, withered head of Daniel Dravot!

alignments.same: Severed heads are the token that shows what the white king's rule came to.
alignments.differs: Dravot's own head is carried back to the newspaper office by his partner and crowned on the table; Kurtz's stakes hold the heads of men he called rebels, turned toward his house.

question: Dravot is killed when his people see him bleed, Kurtz is mourned to the last: which tale is harder on the man who would be worshipped?

substitution.note: Replacing The Man Who Would Be King: King Solomon's Mines' white men are taken for men from the stars but ask no worship and plan no nation, and the head Sir Henry cuts off is Twala's, a native king's; Lord Jim's legend gives Jim supernatural powers but no rites and no heads; The Island of Doctor Moreau's Beast Folk chant Moreau's praises but he is a surgeon remaking beasts, not a man made a god, and no head is cut off; Connecticut Yankee's Boss means to build a republic by will but takes no worship. Replacing Heart of Darkness: none of these has a white ruler worshipped by the people who ends among severed heads.

claim: Both narrators meet a white master whom his creatures approach on their knees, and come home unable to bear city crowds. Moreau's beasts creep back to the animal when his hand lifts; Conrad's master himself crawls on all-fours toward the fires, and Marlow hates in the crowds not the beast but their safety.

from.exact: the chiefs came every day to see him. They would crawl

to.exact: they began to cringe towards Moreau and chant

alignments.same: The creatures the white master rules come before him low on the ground.
alignments.differs: Moreau's Beast People cringe chanting his Law, which forbids going on all-fours; Kurtz's chiefs crawl in ceremonies Marlow refuses to hear described, under no law but Kurtz's word.

from.exact: He can’t walk—he is crawling on all-fours—I’ve got him.

to.exact: As soon as my hand is taken from them the beast begins to creep back, begins to assert itself again.

alignments.same: Going back to the beast is pictured as a creeping that the master's hand must hold down.
alignments.differs: Moreau means the beasts he made, who creep back when he lets go; in Conrad the master himself crawls off on all-fours toward the drums, and Marlow drags him back.

from.exact: I found myself back in the sepulchral city resenting the sight of people hurrying through the streets

to.exact: I would go out into the streets to fight with my delusion, and prowling women would mew after me

alignments.same: Home in a European city, the survivor cannot bear the people passing him in the streets.
alignments.differs: Prendick sees the animal surging up through every face; Marlow resents faces that are too safe, intruders who cannot know the things he knows.

question: Prendick fears the beast in other men, Marlow despises men who have never met it: which of them has learned more from the master he served?

substitution.note: Replacing The Island of Doctor Moreau: Gulliver's Travels sends Gulliver home unable to bear his family as Yahoos, but his master is a Houyhnhnm whom nobody worships on their knees; The Man Who Would Be King has worship but its narrator never goes to Kafiristan and Peachey comes back to die, not to walk the streets; Frankenstein, The Time Machine and Lord Jim have no worshipped master and no return to crowds. Replacing Heart of Darkness: none of the other novels and tales in view has both a master worshipped on the knees and a narrator home among crowds he cannot bear.

claim: Kim takes three scenes from the loafers' tale: a stranger in a train signalling a brotherhood for help, a man turned holy beggar to pass hostile eyes, Masonry as a white wanderer's passport. In the tale they serve a grab for a throne; in Kim they save an agent's life and return a bazar boy to the Sahibs.

from.exact: Oh, there is no caste where men go to—look for tarkeean,

to.exact: I am hoping that you will give him the message on the Square—for the sake of my Mother as well as your own.

alignments.same: In a railway carriage a stranger in trouble makes himself known by the set words of a secret brotherhood and asks a fellow member for help.
alignments.differs: Carnehan's brotherhood is the Craft and he wants a message carried to Dravot; E23's is the Game, he is hunted for his life, and the boy he signals has been in it two days.

from.exact: We must make thee a yellow Saddhu all over.

to.exact: Who’d touch a poor mad priest?

alignments.same: A man who must pass unknown before hostile eyes is made over, with rags and patter, into a wandering holy man.
alignments.differs: Dravot plays a mad priest of his own making to smuggle twenty rifles to a throne; Kim makes the hunted E23 a Saddhu in a crowded carriage and curses the Jat into silence.

from.exact: Assuming that he is the son of a Mason, the sooner he goes to the Masonic Orphanage the better.

to.exact: The Craft’s the trick so help me!

alignments.same: Freemasonry carries a white wanderer across the line between native life and power over it.
alignments.differs: Dravot finds the Craft among the hill priests and uses it to make himself god and king; Kim's dead father's Lodge papers deliver the bazar boy to a regiment and a school for Sahibs.

question: Kipling hands the tale's loafer tricks, the brotherhood sign and the holy man's rags, to a boy in the Great Game. Does Kim redeem those tricks by putting them in the Government's service, or only give them a better master?

substitution.note: Replacing The Man Who Would Be King: King Solomon's Mines has no brotherhood sign and no disguise as a holy man; A Scandal in Bohemia's Holmes goes as a clergyman, but to enter one house, with no train meeting and no Masonry; Lord Jim, Connecticut Yankee, Sea-Wolf, Treasure Island, Robinson Crusoe and Sindbad have none of the three scenes. Replacing Kim with any of these fails the same way. Heart of Darkness (added in the ordered view) has no train meeting, no holy-man disguise and no Masonry.

claim: Both boys empty an enemy's box of instruments and papers, take what lies at the bottom wrapped in oilskin, and hand the packet to grown men who can read it. Jim's becomes the gentlemen's hunt for gold; Kim, a Sahib who 'cannot very well steal', throws the instruments down the hill and wants only to be rid of the papers.

from.exact: At the very bottom was an embroidered bag covering a sealed, gilded, and illuminated document such as one King sends to another.

to.exact: there lay before us, the last things in the chest, a bundle tied up in oilcloth, and looking like papers

alignments.same: Under the instruments, papers and gear in an enemy's box, the prize lies at the very bottom.
alignments.differs: The dead captain's bundle lies beside a bag of gold and goes unread; the Russians' kilta holds a king's sealed letter that Kim knows at once for the prize.

from.exact: But after all, a Sahib cannot very well steal, and the things might be inconvenient evidence later.

to.exact: I’ll have my dues, and not a farthing over.

alignments.same: Those who rifle the box set a limit on what they will take, so that taking is not stealing.
alignments.differs: Mrs Hawkins counts out only the captain's score while Jim pockets the packet besides; Kim keeps every paper and throws compass and theodolite down the cliff.

from.exact: for the present need on his soul was to get rid of the loot.

to.exact: said I, and gave him the oilskin packet.

alignments.same: The boy hands the oilskin packet to the grown man who will know what it means.
alignments.differs: Livesey pockets Jim's packet unopened and it starts the voyage for gold; Kim, sick, only longs to be rid of his, and Hurree tears the oilskin open for the office.

question: Jim's packet leads to treasure and Kim's to an official report with his name in it. What does each boy get for what he took, and does he want it?

substitution.note: Replacing Treasure Island: King Solomon's Mines' map comes from a dead man's hand, not from a box a boy empties; Robinson Crusoe strips the wreck for his own use and hands nothing on; The Man Who Would Be King, Lord Jim, Sea-Wolf, Lost World and Sindbad have no boy who takes an enemy's papers. Replacing Kim with any of these fails the same way. Heart of Darkness (added in the ordered view): Marlow is handed Kurtz's packet by its owner, not taken by a boy from an enemy's box.

claim: Both books open with a Briton and an Asian of another faith meeting among holy things as friends, and close on a Sahib and an Asian together. Kipling's pair trade spectacles for a pencase and the lama wins salvation for his chela; Forster's friends are refused by earth and sky: 'No, not yet.'

from.exact: That makes no difference. God is here.

to.exact: as a sign of friendship between priest and priest

alignments.same: In the first chapters a Briton and an Asian believer of another faith meet among holy things, and respect for the other's faith begins a friendship.
alignments.differs: Kipling's Curator trades spectacles for the lama's pencase as scholar to scholar; Mrs Moore is the intruder in Aziz's mosque, shouted at until he learns her shoes are off.

from.exact: Then you are an Oriental.

to.exact: To those who follow the Way there is neither black nor white, Hind nor Bhotiyal.

alignments.same: The Asian friend tells the European-born friend that the line between East and West does not hold for them.
alignments.differs: The lama denies the line for every soul on the Way, though Kim says he is a Sahib; Aziz grants her the East as praise, then says Indians may not enter her club.

from.exact: they said in their hundred voices, “No, not yet,” and the sky said, “No, not there.”

to.exact: as a man may who has won salvation for himself and his beloved.

alignments.same: The last sentence of each book settles the friendship of a Sahib and an Asian after a long road together.
alignments.differs: Kim ends with the lama sitting by his chela, sure of deliverance for both; Forster's riders swerve apart, and rocks, temples and sky refuse the friendship its time and place.

question: Kipling's friends trade gifts in the first chapter and sit together in the last; Forster's are parted by the land itself. Is it the men, the empire or the ground that makes the friendship possible in one book and 'not yet' in the other?

substitution.note: Replacing Kim: The Man Who Would Be King (no meeting among holy things; Billy Fish dies and the tale ends on a severed head), King Solomon's Mines (Umbopa is crowned and shuts out white men; no shared faith or holy house), Heart of Darkness (Marlow befriends no Asian; it ends on a lie to a white woman), Lord Jim (Jim and Dain Waris, but no first meeting among holy things, and both die), Robinson Crusoe (Friday is converted, his faith not respected), Sindbad and Gulliver's Travels make the claim false. Replacing A Passage to India with any of these fails the same way.

claim: Both books carry Europeans into a land older than speech, where their best words fail, and end on one sentence about what happened there. Kurtz's own postscript undoes his eloquence and Marlow lies to spare a woman; Forster's caves turn every word to 'boum', and the woman who went in tells the truth.

from.exact: They are older than anything in the world.

to.exact: Going up that river was like traveling back to the earliest beginnings of the world

alignments.same: The country the travellers go into is set back before the world's beginning, older than men and their history.
alignments.differs: Conrad's forest is a stillness 'brooding over an inscrutable intention' that looks at Marlow with vengeance; Forster's hills hold no intention at all, and 'nothing, nothing attaches to them'.

from.exact: all its divine words from “Let there be Light” to “It is finished” only amounted to “boum.”

to.exact: This was the unbounded power of eloquence—of words—of burning noble words.

alignments.same: The noblest words a European brings into the interior, a mission's or a gospel's, come to nothing there.
alignments.differs: Kurtz undoes his own report with a scrawled 'Exterminate all the brutes!'; Mrs Moore's Christianity is undone by no one, only by an echo that makes every sound 'boum'.

from.exact: Dr. Aziz never followed me into the cave.

to.exact: The last word he pronounced was—your name.

alignments.same: Pressed by a questioner near the end, one sentence decides what the dark place will be said to have done.
alignments.differs: Marlow lies to Kurtz's Intended so that the women stay 'out of it'; Adela, the woman who went in, tells the truth in open court, and the English rise to stop her.

question: Marlow keeps the truth from a woman who never went in; Adela, who went in, takes back her own charge. Which book thinks what happened in the dark can be told, and what does the telling cost?

substitution.note: Replacing Heart of Darkness: Journey to the Centre and The Lost World go back into the earth's past, but no European words come to nothing there and no closing sentence is lied or recanted; Lord Jim (Patusan is not set before the world; Jim's end is told, not lied about), King Solomon's Mines, The Man Who Would Be King, The Island of Doctor Moreau, The Time Machine and Kim fail on the words or the closing sentence. Replacing A Passage to India with any of these fails the same way.

claim: Both narrators follow a man who left Europe into the tropics, where a visitor finds a knowledge men should not have, then sit with the woman he left. Kurtz's knowledge is a cry Marlow edits and lies to hide; Strickland's is a painted house he has burnt, and the narrator omits only his native wife and son.

from.exact: It was the work of a man who knew things which it is unholy for men to know.

to.exact: Being alone in the wilderness, it had looked within itself, and, by heavens! I tell you, it had gone mad.

alignments.same: A white visitor up from the coast reaches the man who left Europe, at his end far in the wild, and finds in him a knowledge men should not have.
alignments.differs: Dr. Coutras reads it in the walls Strickland painted and, though afraid, cries 'this is genius'; Marlow reads it in Kurtz's own soul and calls it madness.

from.exact: he made her promise that she would set fire to the house and not leave it till it was burned to the ground and not a stick remained.

to.exact: I offered him the report on the ‘Suppression of Savage Customs,’ with the postscriptum torn off.

alignments.same: After the man's death, what he made out there passes into other hands that decide what the world will see of it.
alignments.differs: Strickland orders his own masterpiece burnt and Ata does it against the doctor's plea; Kurtz wanted his pamphlet kept, and Marlow keeps it but tears off the one line that tells the truth.

from.exact: I thought it unnecessary to say anything of Ata and her boy

to.exact: The last word he pronounced was—your name.

alignments.same: Home again, the narrator sits with the woman the man left in Europe and keeps from her what his last life was.
alignments.differs: Marlow lies to a girl who begs for one word to live with; Maugham's narrator only leaves out a native wife and son, before a widow who hangs Strickland's pictures as 'essentially decorative'.

question: Marlow cannot tell the Intended 'the horror'; Maugham's narrator tells everything but Ata. Is his silence kinder than Marlow's lie, or only easier?

substitution.note: Replacing Heart of Darkness: Lord Jim's Marlow visits Jim in Patusan, but finds no forbidden knowledge, keeps no work of Jim's and sits with no woman left in Europe (Jewel is of Patusan); The Man Who Would Be King and King Solomon's Mines bring no one home to a wife or betrothed; The Island of Doctor Moreau, Robinson Crusoe and The Sea-Wolf have no man who left Europe for good and no visitor at his end. Replacing The Moon and Sixpence: none of these has a narrator who reaches the man's end, decides the fate of what he made, then keeps the truth from the woman at home. A Passage to India (added later): Fielding and Mrs Moore are visitors, but no man has left Europe for good, no work of his is burnt or edited after his death, and no narrator keeps his last life from a woman at home.

claim: In both books a blade raised against a painting is stopped as if it were a crime, and a girl's poisoning leaves the man who dropped her unshaken. Dorian's portrait bears his sins and he knows Sibyl's death for murder; Strickland's nude bears only his genius, and he calls Blanche's death her own folly.

from.exact: I had nearly committed a dreadful crime.

to.exact: It would be murder!

alignments.same: A man in a studio takes a blade to a painted canvas, and cutting it is spoken of as a crime against a person.
alignments.differs: Basil would cut his own portrait and is stopped by Dorian, whose self is in it; Stroeve would cut his rival's nude of his wife and is stopped only by its greatness.

from.exact: Blanche Stroeve didn’t commit suicide because I left her, but because she was a foolish and unbalanced woman.

to.exact: Yet the roses are not less lovely for all that.

alignments.same: A young woman poisons herself after the man she loved turns from her, and he goes on untouched by her death.
alignments.differs: Dorian calls it murder and then lets Lord Henry make it a play he has watched; Strickland denies any part in it, calls her 'an entirely unimportant person' and offers to show his pictures.

from.exact: He had found, not himself, as the phrase goes, but a new soul with unsuspected powers.

to.exact: every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist, not of the sitter.

alignments.same: A painting of someone close to the painter shows, to those who look, the painter's soul more than the sitter.
alignments.differs: Basil hides his portrait because it would show his worship of Dorian; Strickland's nude of Blanche shows a new soul and no love for her, and he leaves it with its face to the wall.

question: Stroeve spares the nude because it is great art, though it records his wife's ruin. Would Basil, who would cut his best picture to save a friend, have spared it?

substitution.note: Replacing The Picture of Dorian Gray: The House of the Seven Gables has a portrait but no blade raised to it and no girl poisoned; Rappaccini's Daughter has a girl dying of poison but no painting; The Birth-Mark kills a wife by a perfecting draught but with no canvas; Jekyll and Hyde, Frankenstein and Northanger Abbey have neither. Replacing The Moon and Sixpence: no other work in this view has a blade stopped before a painting as before a crime, beside a young woman's poisoning shrugged off by the man who left her. A Passage to India (added later): no blade is raised to a painting and no young woman poisons herself after a man turns from her.

claim: Both heroines tour the great house of the family they misjudge, read a portrait there as evidence of its master, and are humbled. Catherine reads the General's cruelty into his wife's portrait and blames her novels; Elizabeth reads Darcy's regard into his portrait and his servant's praise, and blames her own vanity.

from.exact: It was a large, well-proportioned room, handsomely fitted up.

to.exact: She saw a large, well-proportioned apartment

alignments.same: The heroine enters a large, well-proportioned room in the house of the man she has misjudged.
alignments.differs: Catherine, who came looking for a scene of crime, finds a bright modern bedroom and feels shame; Elizabeth surveys the dining-parlour and thinks 'of this place I might have been mistress!'

from.exact: she beheld a striking resemblance of Mr. Darcy, with such a smile over the face, as she remembered to have sometimes seen, when he looked at her

to.exact: A portrait—very like—of a departed wife, not valued by the husband! he must have been dreadfully cruel to her!

alignments.same: A family portrait, said to be very like, becomes evidence for the heroine's judgement of the master of the house.
alignments.differs: Catherine reads a dead wife's portrait, hung away from the General's rooms, as proof of his cruelty; Elizabeth finds in Darcy's portrait the smile he turned on her, and softens toward him.

from.exact: But vanity, not love, has been my folly.

to.exact: it seemed as if the whole might be traced to the influence of that sort of reading which she had there indulged

alignments.same: The humbled heroine traces her false judgement to a cause.
alignments.differs: Catherine, rebuked by Henry, lays her delusion on the novels she read in Bath; Elizabeth, alone with Darcy's letter, lays hers on her own vanity, flattered by Wickham and offended by Darcy.

question: Catherine's error comes from what she read and Elizabeth's from what she was told and felt: which of them is more to blame, and does either novel let its heroine off too lightly?

substitution.note: Only Northanger Abbey has a heroine who tours the house of a family she misjudges, reads a 'very like' portrait there as proof against its master, and, humbled, traces her error to a cause. The House of the Seven Gables has the Colonel's portrait ruling the house but no visitor who misjudges and is humbled; The Turn of the Screw's governess guesses at hidden horrors but is never shown wrong; Dorian Gray's portrait is the hero's own and no woman reads it; Araby's boy names his folly but tours no house. Replacing Pride and Prejudice: no other work has a heroine whose reading of a portrait and a servant's praise corrects a misjudgement. Later additions fail too: A Passage to India's Adela misjudges Aziz and is humbled, but tours no house and reads no portrait; The Moon and Sixpence's pictures are judged by a man, not by a woman in the house of a family she misjudged; The Garden Party's Laura enters a poor cottage, not a great house; the sea, jungle and Indian tales have no heroine misjudging a family.

claim: Both women lack the fortune to marry well and take the modest man to hand. Charlotte, plain and twenty-seven, chooses Collins as her provision, asks only a comfortable home and makes one by not hearing him; Mathilde, pretty, lets herself be married, wants to be envied, and sits across from her husband's soup dreaming of silver.

from.exact: She had no dowry, no expectations, no way of being known, understood, loved, married by any rich and distinguished man; so she let herself be married to a little clerk of the Ministry of Public Instruction.

to.exact: it was the only honourable provision for well-educated young women of small fortune

alignments.same: A young woman without fortune takes the modest husband who offers.
alignments.differs: Charlotte makes marriage her object and feels the good luck of gaining Collins; Mathilde, who might have pleased a rich man, merely 'let herself be married' and takes the clerk as a fall.

from.exact: She would have liked so much to please, to be envied, to be charming, to be sought after.

to.exact: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home

alignments.same: The wife names what she wants from life once married.
alignments.differs: Charlotte asks only a comfortable home and says so to her friend; Mathilde wants to be envied and sought after, and keeps away from her rich friend because the visits make her sad.

from.exact: opposite her husband, who uncovered the soup tureen and declared with a delighted air

to.exact: When Mr. Collins could be forgotten, there was really a great air of comfort throughout

alignments.same: The wife sits at home with a husband who is delighted with small things.
alignments.differs: Charlotte forgets Collins and enjoys her neat, small house; Mathilde, facing her husband over his soup, thinks of shining silverware and whispered gallantries.

question: Charlotte gets what she asked for and Mathilde loses ten years to a borrowed necklace: is Austen rewarding Charlotte's prudence, or is her 'comfortable home' as sad as Mathilde's dream?

substitution.note: Only Pride and Prejudice has a woman of small fortune who takes the modest suitor as her provision, asks only a comfortable home, and makes her small house comfortable by forgetting a husband pleased with little. The Lady with the Dog's Anna married young a husband she calls a flunkey, but no want of fortune or home is named; A Jury of Her Peers has a cheerless farm marriage but no choice for want of a dowry; The Story of an Hour and The Yellow Wallpaper have wives but no marriage taken as provision; The Overcoat's clerk has no wife. Replacing The Necklace: no other work has a dowerless girl who lets herself be married to a clerk and dreams of luxury over his soup. Later additions fail too: Winesburg, Ohio's Elizabeth Willard married unhappily, but not as a provision for want of fortune, and no wife dreams of luxury over her husband's soup; A Passage to India's Adela breaks off her match rather than taking it as provision; The Moon and Sixpence's Mrs. Strickland is no dowerless girl; the sea, jungle and Indian tales have no such marriage.

claim: Both governesses keep a master's ward in a lonely house, love the master, and walk out at dusk half expecting someone. Jane, fearing a spirit, meets the master, and the madwoman upstairs proves his wife; James's governess, longing for the master, sees a stranger on the tower whom no one else sees.

from.exact: Someone would appear there at the turn of a path and would stand before me and smile and approve.

to.exact: No Gytrash was this,—only a traveller taking the short cut to Millcote.

alignments.same: Walking alone near the house at dusk, the governess pictures who may come upon her, and a figure appears.
alignments.differs: Jane expects a spirit from Bessie's tales and finds her master fallen on the ice; James's governess wishes for the master's approving face and sees a stranger on the tower.

from.exact: an insane, an unmentionable relative kept in unsuspected confinement

to.exact: Bertha Mason is mad; and she came of a mad family; idiots and maniacs through three generations!

alignments.same: A mad relative kept shut up in the house is the secret the governess must reckon with.
alignments.differs: At Thornfield the madwoman is real, and Rochester names her and shows her; at Bly it is a passing guess, and the secret stays a dead servant only the governess sees.

from.exact: she couldn’t tell her story without its coming out

to.exact: Portrait of a Governess, disconnected, poor, and plain.

alignments.same: A governess loves the gentleman who employs her and knows the match is past hope.
alignments.differs: Jane sentences herself to draw her plain portrait, yet speaks her love and is asked to marry; James's governess saw her employer twice, and her love shows only in her written story.

question: Jane is told the truth about Thornfield's third storey, and James's governess never learns the truth about Bly: does knowing make Jane's story less frightening, or James's more?

substitution.note: Only Jane Eyre has a governess for a master's ward who loves the master, meets him on a lonely walk in place of the spirit she feared, and finds a mad relative really kept upstairs. Northanger Abbey's Catherine guesses at a shut-up wife but is a guest, not a governess, and loves no master; The Yellow Wallpaper's confined woman is the narrator, a wife; The House of the Seven Gables and The Fall of the House of Usher keep their secrets in a family, with no hired woman. Replacing The Turn of the Screw: no other work has a governess whose wish to meet her master is answered by a figure no one else sees.

claim: Both heroines sense a secret behind an old house's shut doors and laugh off gothic fears with a household trifle. Catherine's prisoner wife is her invention, and a washing-bill and Henry's 'we are English' cure her; Jane mocks her alarm with Grace Poole's pot of porter and is wrong: the wife is there.

from.exact: like a corridor in some Bluebeard’s castle

to.exact: receiving from the pitiless hands of her husband a nightly supply of coarse food

alignments.same: The heroine pictures a closed part of the house as a husband's prison for a wife.
alignments.differs: Catherine builds her picture on the General's late hours and believes it; Jane only borrows a nursery tale for a passage of shut doors, and the laugh there is the wife's.

from.exact: oh, romantic reader, forgive me for telling the plain truth!

to.exact: An inventory of linen, in coarse and modern characters, seemed all that was before her!

alignments.same: A household commonplace, a washing-bill or a pot of porter, answers a gothic expectation.
alignments.differs: Austen's washing-bill is the truth and shames Catherine; Jane's pot of porter is carried up for a madwoman, so the 'plain truth' she offers the romantic reader is the false one.

from.exact: “That is my wife,” said he.

to.exact: Remember that we are English, that we are Christians.

alignments.same: A man answers the fear of what an English gentleman's house can hide.
alignments.differs: Henry calls on laws, neighbours and religion to show such a crime is impossible; Rochester, stopped at the altar, unlocks the third-storey room and shows the wife he has kept hidden for years.

question: Austen makes Catherine ashamed of reading horrors into a house: does Jane Eyre take that lesson back, or show that the sensible heroine can be fooled too?

substitution.note: Only Northanger Abbey has a heroine who imagines a husband keeping his wife shut up in the house, is cured by a washing-bill, and is told by the man she loves that in England such a thing could not happen. The Turn of the Screw's governess names 'an unmentionable relative' but drops the guess and is never rebuked by a household trifle; The Canterville Ghost and The Haunted and the Haunters mock the ghost, not a suspected crime. Replacing Jane Eyre: no other work has a heroine who laughs off a 'romantic' alarm with a homely detail and then finds the hidden wife is real.
