claim: Both put a wife, shut in by her husband, in a room at the top of the house, going on all fours. Brontë shows Bertha from outside, through the governess who sees her face under her own bridal veil; Gilman tells it from inside the barred room, where the wife becomes the creeping woman.

from.exact: the windows are barred for little children, and there are rings and things in the walls.

to.exact: In a room without a window, there burnt a fire guarded by a high and strong fender, and a lamp suspended from the ceiling by a chain.

alignments.same: The wife's room at the top of the house is fitted to keep its occupant in and from harm.
alignments.differs: Rochester's room is a cell for the wife he hides; Gilman's is a nursery her physician husband chose for her rest, and she takes its bars and rings for a child's.

from.exact: It is the same woman, I know, for she is always creeping

to.exact: it grovelled, seemingly, on all fours; it snatched and growled like some strange wild animal

alignments.same: The confined woman goes on all fours.
alignments.differs: Bertha is seen by the wedding party as 'it', a beast that springs at her husband; Gilman's narrator watches the creeping woman without blame and ends by creeping herself.

from.exact: I’ve got out at last,” said I, “in spite of you and Jane!

to.exact: At that moment I saw the reflection of the visage and features quite distinctly in the dark oblong glass.

alignments.same: The sane woman meets the confined woman as a figure of herself.
alignments.differs: Jane sees Bertha's face under her own wedding veil in the glass, faints, and stays Jane; Gilman's narrator speaks at the end as the woman got out of the paper.

question: Jane Eyre lets us see the confined wife only through the woman who would replace her, and Gilman gives the confined wife the whole story: what does each book gain by where it stands?

substitution.note: Only Jane Eyre has a husband who keeps his wife in a room at the top of his house, a woman seen going on all fours, and a second woman who sees her face in a glass under her own veil. The Turn of the Screw and Northanger Abbey only guess at a confined relative; The Story of an Hour's wife is shut in her room by grief, not by her husband; The Fall of the House of Usher's Madeline is entombed by her brother. Replacing The Yellow Wallpaper: no other work tells the confined wife's side from inside her room.

claim: Both heroines say their soul is the same as, or equal to, the man's they love, and a marriage stands between them. Jane keeps the law, leaves Rochester, and answers when he cries her name at an open window; Catherine marries Edgar thinking nothing need change, and Heathcliff's cry at the window brings no one.

from.exact: Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same; and Linton’s is as different as a moonbeam from lightning, or frost from fire.

to.exact: it is my spirit that addresses your spirit; just as if both had passed through the grave, and we stood at God’s feet, equal,—as we are!

alignments.same: The heroine claims her soul is one with, or equal to, the soul of a man her rank or fortune puts beneath or above her.
alignments.differs: Jane says it to Rochester's face as one soul to another; Catherine says it to Nelly after Heathcliff has slipped out, and in the same breath takes Linton.

from.exact: He’ll be as much to me as he has been all his lifetime. Edgar must shake off his antipathy, and tolerate him, at least.

to.exact: I will keep the law given by God; sanctioned by man.

alignments.same: The heroine decides what the man she loves may be to her once a marriage to someone else stands between them.
alignments.differs: Jane will not live with Rochester while his wife lives, and leaves Thornfield; Catherine means to marry Edgar and keep Heathcliff as before, as if the marriage changed nothing.

from.exact: Cathy, do come. Oh, do—once more!

to.exact: replied, ‘I am coming: wait for me;’

alignments.same: Alone at an open window at night, the man cries out the absent woman's name and begs her to come.
alignments.differs: Rochester's cry is answered by Jane's voice and she comes back to him alive; Heathcliff calls to Catherine's ghost, and only snow and wind come in and blow out the light.

question: Jane says her soul is equal to Rochester's and leaves him; Catherine says her soul is Heathcliff's and marries Linton: which claim costs more, and who in each book pays for it?

substitution.note: Only Jane Eyre has a heroine who tells the man she loves that their spirits are equal, refuses him because his marriage stands, and hears him cry her name at an open window and answers. Pride and Prejudice's Elizabeth refuses Darcy, but no marriage stands between them and no one calls across distance; The Lady with the Dog and Rip Van Winkle have marriages in the way but no claim of one soul and no call; Werther loves Charlotte, who is married to Albert, and she sends him away, but he never cries her name at a window and is never answered; The Scarlet Letter's Hester, whose marriage stands between her and Dimmesdale, plans flight with him in the forest but claims no sameness of soul, and no one cries her name across distance; Northanger Abbey, The Yellow Wallpaper and The Turn of the Screw have no lovers' souls declared. The claim is false for every other work tried. The Open Boat and Treasure Island have no heroine, no lovers and no marriage in the way. Heart of Darkness, Kim, King Solomon's Mines, Lord Jim, The Man Who Would Be King and A Passage to India have no heroine who claims one soul with a man while a marriage stands between them, and no cry at a window; The Moon and Sixpence's Blanche Stroeve leaves her husband for Strickland, but no one cries her name across distance.

claim: Both novels reach their story through a stranger's dated pages: a gentleman alone in a wild place writes down, in the teller's own words, a tale heard over many sittings, then sees its end himself. Walton hears the hero and meets his creature; Lockwood hears a servant, condenses her, and finds only quiet graves.

from.exact: 1801—I have just returned from a visit to my landlord—the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with.

to.exact: I shall commit my thoughts to paper, it is true; but that is a poor medium for the communication of feeling.

alignments.same: The book opens in the dated pages of a gentleman alone in a remote place, before he has heard the story he will set down.
alignments.differs: Walton writes letters to his sister and longs for a friend; Lockwood keeps a diary for no one and boasts of a 'misanthropist's Heaven' shared with his landlord.

from.exact: I’ll continue it in her own words, only a little condensed.

to.exact: to record, as nearly as possible in his own words, what he has related during the day.

alignments.same: The listener, held by ice or by illness, writes down a long story heard over many sittings in the teller's own words.
alignments.differs: Walton's teller is the hero, who later corrects the notes himself; Lockwood's is the housekeeper, a witness and servant, whose story he trims and whose style he judges.

from.exact: wondered how any one could ever imagine unquiet slumbers for the sleepers in that quiet earth.

to.exact: He was soon borne away by the waves, and lost in darkness and distance.

alignments.same: The frame closes with the writer seeing for himself what is left of the story he was told.
alignments.differs: Walton meets the creature over Victor's body and watches him go off to die; Lockwood finds three headstones and, against the shepherd boy's ghosts, pictures the sleepers at rest.

question: Victor corrects Walton's notes, and Lockwood condenses Nelly: whose story are we reading in each book, and does the listener's frame make the tale easier or harder to believe?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has a frame in which a gentleman alone in a wild place writes dated pages, records a long tale over many sittings 'as nearly as possible in his own words', and at the end sees the story's last survivor himself. The Turn of the Screw's frame reads out a written manuscript at a house party; Sleepy Hollow and Rip Van Winkle are one sitting's tale from a found paper; Werther's editor collects letters and tells no told story; Dracula's journals are written by those who live the story, not a listener; Moby-Dick's Ishmael tells his own voyage; Twenty Thousand Leagues' Aronnax narrates what he lived; Notes from Underground, The Scarlet Letter and The Island of Doctor Moreau have a found manuscript but no listener at sittings; Jekyll and Hyde's Utterson reads written statements; Jane Eyre is told in the first person with no frame. The claim is false for every other work tried. Treasure Island's Jim writes down his own adventure at the Squire's request, with no teller heard at sittings; The Open Boat is told in the third person with no frame. Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim have Marlow tell aloud in one evening to listeners who write no dated pages and do not see the end themselves; The Man Who Would Be King's journalist hears Carnehan in one night in a newspaper office; The Moon and Sixpence's narrator knew Strickland himself and pieces the end together from several tellers; King Solomon's Mines is told by Quatermain, who lived it; Kim and A Passage to India have no frame.

claim: Both heroines take their notion of life from what they read at fifteen, and both books put novel-reading on trial. Austen's narrator defends novels, and Catherine, shamed out of her fancies, owns them her own; Flaubert leaves the charge to Emma's mother-in-law, and Emma, let down, decides that life itself is the lie.

from.exact: Emma, at fifteen years of age, made her hands dirty with books from old lending libraries

to.exact: from fifteen to seventeen she was in training for a heroine

alignments.same: At fifteen the girl is schooled by the books a heroine reads.
alignments.differs: Catherine's reading stocks her with quotations from Pope and Gray; Emma's novels, slipped to her at the convent, teach her lovers who are always well dressed and weep like fountains.

from.exact: So it was decided to stop Emma reading novels.

to.exact: Yes, novels; for I will not adopt that ungenerous and impolitic custom so common with novel-writers

alignments.same: The novel stops to judge the reading of novels.
alignments.differs: Austen's narrator steps in to defend novels against their foes; in Flaubert the mother-in-law blames them for Emma's vapours and stops her library subscription, and the narrator says nothing.

from.exact: nothing was worth the trouble of seeking it; everything was a lie

to.exact: The visions of romance were over.

alignments.same: The romance the heroine looked for fails her.
alignments.differs: Catherine wakes, traces her fancies to her reading and resolves on good sense; Emma blames not her books but life, and still dreams of a being strong and beautiful.

question: Austen defends the novel and cures her reader; Flaubert lets the novel's enemies speak and leaves his reader uncured. Which book takes reading more seriously?

substitution.note: Turn of the Screw's governess knows Udolpho, but she is no girl of fifteen schooled by novels and nobody judges her reading. Pride and Prejudice has Collins read Fordyce aloud and Mary moralise, but no heroine taught by romances. Notes from Underground learns life from books, but he is a man and no one tries the novel. Lady with the Dog, Necklace, Story of an Hour, Yellow Wallpaper and the rest have no reading heroine. Jane Eyre reads Bewick and Gulliver as a child of ten, not novels at fifteen, and nobody tries her reading; Robinson Crusoe and Winesburg, Ohio have no reading heroine. Wuthering Heights has no heroine schooled by novels at fifteen and puts no reading on trial.

claim: Both follow a young wife bored by her husband into a lover's room. Emma's first fall is a triumph, out of her books, with a practised lover who finds her like all the rest, and the adultery sinks into marriage's platitudes; Anna's is a shame, and her practised lover, grey-haired, first loves her as a wife.

from.exact: I am a bad, low woman; I despise myself and don't attempt to justify myself.

to.exact: She tasted it without remorse, without anxiety, without trouble.

alignments.same: Just after her first fall, the young wife who scorns her husband looks at what she has done.
alignments.differs: Emma, before her glass, sings with the adulterous heroines of her books and feels a revenge; Anna sits like the sinner in an old picture and despises herself.

from.exact: but he had never once loved; it was anything you like, but not love.

to.exact: Emma was like all his mistresses

alignments.same: A man practised with many women sets the new mistress among the others.
alignments.differs: Rodolphe finds Emma's passion the old monotony and leaves her; Gurov, who had sorted his women into kinds, finds he never loved any of them, and loves Anna.

from.exact: Anna Sergeyevna and he loved each other like people very close and akin, like husband and wife

to.exact: Emma found again in adultery all the platitudes of marriage.

alignments.same: Lovers meeting in secret in hotel rooms come to be as husband and wife.
alignments.differs: For Emma and Léon the likeness to marriage means boredom and weariness of each other; for Gurov and Anna it means the love has changed them both.

question: Emma's lovers tire of her; Gurov does not tire of Anna. Is the difference in the women, in the men, or in what each writer thinks a love affair can become?

substitution.note: The Scarlet Letter has an adulterous wife but no hotel room, no practised seducer and no affair that turns into a marriage; Werther loves a wife but never wins her. The Necklace's wife wants another life but takes no lover; The Dead and Story of an Hour have no adultery. Northanger and Pride and Prejudice have no married heroine. Jane Eyre's Rochester is married, but Jane refuses to be his mistress and leaves; Winesburg, Ohio has wives bored by their husbands but no lovers' rooms that turn into a marriage. Wuthering Heights' Catherine, married to Edgar, loves Heathcliff but takes no practised lover to a room, and no affair settles into marriage.

claim: Both wives, married below their dreams, sit across from a husband pleased with his dinner, are lifted by one grand ball, and live on its memory. Mathilde is the ball's beauty and pays in ten years of toil; Emma dances once, brings home a stranger's cigar-case, and makes the ball a dream of Paris.

from.exact: opposite her husband, who uncovered the soup tureen and declared with a delighted air

to.exact: Even at table she had her book by her, and turned over the pages while Charles ate and talked to her.

alignments.same: At dinner, across from a husband content with plain fare, the wife lives elsewhere.
alignments.differs: Mathilde dreams of silver, tapestries and trout out of her own longing; Emma keeps a novel open by her plate and reads Sue and Balzac for furniture and lovers.

from.exact: She danced with rapture, with passion, intoxicated by pleasure

to.exact: Her journey to Vaubyessard had made a hole in her life

alignments.same: One night at a grand ball lifts the wife above her station.
alignments.differs: Mathilde, in borrowed diamonds, is the beauty whom ministers notice; Emma cannot waltz until the Viscount leads her, and comes home with a hole in her life.

from.exact: she thought of that gay evening of long ago, of that ball where she had been so beautiful and so admired.

to.exact: The memory of this ball, then, became an occupation for Emma.

alignments.same: Long after, the wife's thoughts go back to the one ball.
alignments.differs: Mathilde recalls it at her window after ten years' toil for the lost necklace; Emma, weeks after, turns it into a dream of Paris she goes on seeking.

question: Mathilde pays for one night in ten years of honest work; Emma never stops paying for hers. Which story is harder on the dream of the ball?

substitution.note: Northanger and Pride and Prejudice have balls, but their heroines are unmarried and dream of no luxury. The Garden Party's girl dreams in a mirror at a party but has no husband and no ball. Paul's Case dreams of luxury but has no marriage; Lady with the Dog has a bored wife but no ball and no dinner table. Story of an Hour, The Dead and the rest fail on the ball. Jane Eyre has a great party at Thornfield, but Jane is a governess watching, not a wife; Winesburg, Ohio's wives dream away from dull husbands but go to no ball. Wuthering Heights' Catherine marries above her, not below her dreams, and there is no grand ball.

claim: Both wives are left by a lover whose farewell note pleads love, turn from their children, and choose their deaths. Rodolphe's letter is a calculated performance, and Emma, ruined by debts, eats arsenic before her husband; Robert's one line is honest, and Edna, owing nothing, strips on an empty beach and swims out.

from.exact: “I love you. Good-by—because I love you.”

to.exact: “Courage, Emma! courage! I would not bring misery into your life.”

alignments.same: The lover who will not take the married woman away leaves her a written farewell that gives his love for her as the reason.
alignments.differs: Rodolphe drafts at length, weighs each phrase for effect and signs 'Your friend'; Robert scrawls one line on a piece of paper and is gone before Edna comes home to him.

from.exact: The children appeared before her like antagonists who had overcome her

to.exact: “It is very strange,” thought Emma, “how ugly this child is!”

alignments.same: A mother feels her own child as something set against her.
alignments.differs: Emma pushes Berthe away so that she cuts her cheek, then finds her ugly; Edna, who would die for her sons, sees them dragging her soul into slavery and slips away.

from.exact: The water was deep, but she lifted her white body and reached out with a long, sweeping stroke.

to.exact: withdrawing it full of a white powder, she began eating it.

alignments.same: Left by her lover, the wife goes alone to a death she takes with her own hands.
alignments.differs: Emma, hunted by debts and refused by her lovers, eats arsenic from the druggist's locked room and dies in agony; Edna walks into the Gulf and swims until her strength is gone.

question: Cather in 1899 called Edna a 'Creole Bovary'. Do Robert's honest note and Edna's quiet swim answer Flaubert's novel, or retell it more gently?

substitution.note: Only Madame Bovary has a married woman whose lover breaks off in a farewell letter pleading her good, a mother who finds her child set against her, and a death the wife takes herself. Werther has the farewell letter and the suicide, but the lover dies and Lotte turns from no child; The Scarlet Letter has Hester and Pearl but no farewell letter and no suicide; The Lady with the Dog, The Necklace, The Story of an Hour and The Dead have no lover's note and no chosen death; Jane Eyre's Rochester begs Jane to stay, and Jane leaves him alive; The Yellow Wallpaper and A Jury of Her Peers have no lover; Northanger Abbey and Pride and Prejudice end in marriage; in Wuthering Heights Catherine dies in childbed loving Heathcliff, with no farewell note and no death taken by her own hand; The Open Boat has the sea and a drowning but no wife or lover. The Moon and Sixpence's Blanche Stroeve leaves her husband for Strickland and drinks oxalic acid while she lives with him, but she has no child and gets no farewell note; Lord Jim, Heart of Darkness and A Passage to India have no wife who takes her own life.

claim: Chopin's two wives claim body and soul against anyone's right to dispose of them. Louise finds that freedom alone in an hour, only because her husband is reported dead, and dies when he walks in travel-stained; Edna says it aloud with her husband alive, arrives travel-stained herself, and carries it into the sea.

from.exact: But they need not have thought that they could possess her, body and soul.

to.exact: "Free! Body and soul free!" she kept whispering.

alignments.same: A wife claims her body and soul as her own against those who would possess her.
alignments.differs: Louise whispers it alone in her room at the news of her husband's death; Edna thinks it of her living husband and her children while swimming out beyond her strength.

from.exact: I am no longer one of Mr. Pontellier’s possessions to dispose of or not. I give myself where I choose.

to.exact: There would be no powerful will bending hers in that blind persistence with which men and women believe they have a right to impose a private will upon a fellow-creature.

alignments.same: A wife denies that anyone has a right to bend her will or dispose of her self.
alignments.differs: Louise can think it only with her husband dead and only to herself; Edna says it aloud to her lover while her husband lives, and laughs at the thought of being handed over.

from.exact: looking tired and a little travel-stained

to.exact: a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his grip-sack and umbrella

alignments.same: An arrival 'a little travel-stained' comes just before the wife's death.
alignments.differs: In the story the husband, alive after all, walks in and ends Louise's hour of freedom; in the novel Edna herself arrives at the island, and walks on alone to the sea.

question: Louise's freedom needs her husband's death and ends at his return; Edna's needs no death but her own. Is the novel a harder answer to the story, or the same hour drawn out?

substitution.note: Only The Story of an Hour has a wife who claims body and soul as her own, denies a husband's right to bend her will, and dies just after a travel-stained arrival. The Yellow Wallpaper has a husband's loving will but no claim of body and soul and no arrival; A Jury of Her Peers has a stifled wife and a dead husband but no freedom claimed in her words; Madame Bovary's Charles imposes no will; Jane Eyre claims an independent will but is no wife; Rip Van Winkle's travel-worn return finds the wife already dead; The Necklace and The Lady with the Dog have no claim to self against a husband; Wuthering Heights' Catherine says she is Heathcliff, the opposite of a claim to a self of her own, and The Open Boat has no wife. Of the later novels, The Moon and Sixpence gives the claim to freedom to a husband, Strickland, and A Passage to India's Adela is no wife; none has a wife whose freedom comes with a husband's reported death.

claim: Elizabeth and Lily, both without fortune, turn aside a rich suitor's first proposal and face him again after scandal has touched them. Darcy renews his offer unchanged despite Lydia's disgrace; Rosedale loves Lily more yet withdraws because the stories about her have changed the bargain, and the provision Charlotte Lucas took is closed to her.

from.exact: I’m confoundedly gone on you—that’s about the size of it—and I’m just giving you a plain business statement of the consequences.

to.exact: His sense of her inferiority—of its being a degradation—of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination

alignments.same: A rich man declares his love to a woman without fortune and, in the same speech, sets out what the match means in rank or money.
alignments.differs: Darcy dwells on what marrying her costs him and is refused outright; Rosedale counts what it will buy her, and Lily, fearing what he knows, asks only for time.

from.exact: I’m more in love with you than I was this time last year; but I’ve got to face the fact that the situation is changed.

to.exact: My affections and wishes are unchanged, but one word from you will silence me on this subject for ever.

alignments.same: Months after his first offer, and after scandal has fallen on her family or her name, the suitor tells her his love has not lessened.
alignments.differs: Darcy renews the offer despite Lydia's elopement and leaves the word to Elizabeth; Rosedale, though Lily now offers herself, will marry her only if she first buys back her standing.

from.exact: In our imperfectly organized society there is no provision as yet for the young woman who claims the privileges of marriage without assuming its obligations.

to.exact: it was the only honourable provision for well-educated young women of small fortune

alignments.same: Marriage is called the 'provision' for a young woman who has no money of her own.
alignments.differs: Charlotte, plain and twenty-seven, takes Collins as that provision and is secured; Van Alstyne uses the word to excuse gossip about Lily, who has taken men's money and attentions without marrying.

question: Rosedale says a change of heart counts 'in novels' but not 'in real life'. What must be true of a society for Darcy's second proposal to happen, and is Wharton's book answering Austen's?

substitution.note: Only Pride and Prejudice has a heroine without fortune who turns aside a rich suitor's first proposal, hears his love declared unchanged after a scandal touches her family, and a friend who takes marriage as a poor woman's 'provision'. Jane Eyre is proposed to once by Rochester and returns to him an heiress; Wuthering Heights' Catherine accepts Edgar; Northanger Abbey's Catherine refuses no one and is cast off for her lack of fortune; Madame Bovary, The Awakening and The Lady with the Dog begin with marriages already made; The Necklace and The Story of an Hour have no suitor. King Solomon's Mines has no heroine choosing or refusing a marriage. Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Man Who Would Be King and The Moon and Sixpence have no heroine weighing a rich suitor's offer; A Passage to India's Adela is not poor, breaks her own engagement after the trial, and no one calls marriage her provision.

claim: After parting from the man she loves, each heroine lies awake and sees her future plainly. Edna holds waking better than illusion, sees her children as antagonists and swims out; Lily, appalled by that lucidity, wants darkness, takes extra chloral at one chance in a hundred, and dies with an imagined child on her arm.

from.exact: darkness, darkness was what she must have at any cost

to.exact: perhaps it is better to wake up after all, even to suffer, rather than to remain a dupe to illusions all one’s life.

alignments.same: Sleepless and seeing her life without illusion, the woman chooses between staying awake to it and the dark.
alignments.differs: Edna tells the Doctor it is better to wake and suffer than be a dupe of illusions; Lily shrinks from 'the glare of thought' and must have darkness at any cost.

from.exact: Nettie Struther’s child was lying on her arm

to.exact: The children appeared before her like antagonists who had overcome her

alignments.same: On her last night a child presses on the heroine's mind as she lets go of her life.
alignments.differs: Edna's sons rise as antagonists dragging her into the soul's slavery; Lily, childless, feels Nettie's baby warm on her arm and holds her breath not to wake it.

from.exact: If sleep came at all, it might be a sleep without waking.

to.exact: She did not look back now, but went on and on

alignments.same: Alone at night or on an empty beach, the woman takes an act that may end her life.
alignments.differs: Edna swims out past her strength and does not look back; Lily calls the extra drops 'but one chance in a hundred', and the doctor finds an overdose 'by mistake'.

question: Edna wakes and walks into the sea; Lily wants sleep and dies in it. Is Lily's death any less chosen than Edna's, and what does the imagined child give her that Edna's real children could not?

substitution.note: Only The Awakening has a heroine who, after parting from the man she loves, spends a wakeful night, says waking is better than illusion, feels her children as antagonists, and takes her own death at the end. Madame Bovary's Emma eats arsenic awake and finds her child ugly, but she has lived by illusions to the last and has no choice between waking and the dark; The Story of an Hour has no child and no lover; The Dead has a wakeful night beside a sleeping wife but no death taken; Werther's suicide is a man's, with no child; Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights and Pride and Prejudice end otherwise; Frankenstein, Moby-Dick and The Open Boat have no such heroine. King Solomon's Mines has no heroine. Heart of Darkness, Kim and The Man Who Would Be King have no such heroine; The Moon and Sixpence's Blanche takes poison after Strickland leaves her, but has no child and no wakeful night choosing between lucidity and the dark; A Passage to India's Adela lives.

claim: Selden tells Lily the free country can be found; she is cast out at a dinner, and his word comes after her death. In the later novel Ellen, who has been beyond, calls that country a delusion; the family sends her off with a dinner, and Archer, free at last, will not go up.

from.exact: Oh, my dear—where is that country? Have you ever been there?

to.exact: There never is—it’s a country one has to find the way to one’s self.

alignments.same: A place of freedom from money and convention is spoken of as a country that the lovers might reach together.
alignments.differs: Selden, who has not been there, tells Lily it can be found; Ellen has been beyond and tells Archer it ends at Boulogne or Monte Carlo.

from.exact: the way of people who dreaded scandal more than disease, who placed decency above courage

to.exact: Miss Bart is not going back to the yacht

alignments.same: At the end of a dinner, society parts itself from a woman whose name has been joined with a man's.
alignments.differs: Bertha casts Lily off in one public sentence; May's family sends Ellen away at a dinner in her honour, and no word is said.

from.exact: It's more real to me here than if I went up

to.exact: he had found the word he meant to say to her, and it could not wait another moment to be said.

alignments.same: Years or a night after parting, the man goes to the woman he loved, meaning to speak.
alignments.differs: Selden hurries up the stairs and finds Lily dead; Archer, a widower free to go up, sits below her window and turns back.

question: Lily never reaches the country Selden describes, and Ellen says no one does. Is The Age of Innocence correcting The House of Mirth, or telling the same story from the side of the one who stayed?

substitution.note: Only The House of Mirth has a man who calls a life free of money and convention a 'country' to find the way to, a woman cast out by her set at a dinner table, and a man who comes to her with his word too late. The Lady with the Dog's lovers keep meeting and seek a plan; The Awakening's Edna seeks her freedom alone and Robert leaves; Madame Bovary's Emma begs Rodolphe to take her away and he writes to refuse; Jane Eyre leaves Rochester and returns to him; Pride and Prejudice, Wuthering Heights and The Story of an Hour have no such country and no such exclusion. Added in the order correction: Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no free country named to a lover, no woman cast off by her set at a dinner and no late visit with a word to say, so the claim fails for each.

claim: Archer and Gurov, both married, come to hold their love as their real life, hidden beneath an open one. Gurov and Anna go on meeting in secret and seek a plan; Ellen says there is no 'us' and will not deceive those who trust them, and Archer counts the flower of life missed.

from.exact: he had built up within himself a kind of sanctuary in which she throned among his secret thoughts and longings

to.exact: He had two lives: one, open, seen and known by all who cared to know

alignments.same: A married man keeps beside his public life a secret one, and holds the secret one as his real life.
alignments.differs: Gurov's hidden life is spent with Anna in a Moscow hotel; Archer's sanctuary holds only his thoughts of Ellen, who has stopped writing.

from.exact: For us? But there's no us in that sense! We're near each other only if we stay far from each other.

to.exact: Let us talk now, let us think of some plan.

alignments.same: The lovers, both bound elsewhere, come to the question of what plan they can make together.
alignments.differs: Gurov and Anna take counsel on how to escape the secrecy; Ellen answers Archer's 'plan for us' by refusing that there is an 'us'.

from.exact: Something he knew he had missed: the flower of life.

to.exact: And only now when his head was grey he had fallen properly, really in love—for the first time in his life.

alignments.same: A man past his youth measures his whole life against one love.
alignments.differs: Gurov finds that love late and keeps it; Archer, at the end of a dutiful marriage, counts it as the prize he never drew.

question: Gurov believes 'every man had his real, most interesting life under the cover of secrecy'. Ellen thinks such a life would make them only cousins deceiving those who trust them. Which of them is right about Archer?

substitution.note: Only The Lady with the Dog has a married man past his youth who keeps his love as his real life in secret beneath an open, false one, and lovers who ask what plan could free them. In Madame Bovary and The Awakening the hidden life is the wife's, and it ends in her death; The House of Mirth's Selden is unmarried and Lily has no secret lover; Rochester in Jane Eyre hides a wife, not a love; Wuthering Heights' Catherine, married to Edgar, sees Heathcliff under her husband's roof and dies of it; The Necklace, The Story of an Hour and The Dead have no lovers who meet in secret. Added in the order correction: in Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India no married man keeps a secret love as his real life beneath an open one; Strickland leaves his wife openly and Blanche Stroeve leaves her husband openly, so the claim fails for each.

claim: Poe reuses the Rue Morgue's frame: a friend tells of a ruined recluse of old family whose reasoning is explained only after it succeeds. He moves it from a Paris murder to buried gold, has the narrator take the reasoner for a lunatic, and makes the opening question a cipher's language instead of a voice's.

from.exact: He was of an ancient Huguenot family, and had once been wealthy; but a series of misfortunes had reduced him to want.

to.exact: This young gentleman was of an excellent, indeed of an illustrious family, but, by a variety of untoward events, had been reduced to such poverty

alignments.same: The narrator introduces his friend as the last of an old family whom misfortune has reduced to poverty and a recluse's life.
alignments.differs: Dupin shares his shuttered Paris rooms with the narrator; Legrand lives in a hut on a sand island with a freed slave, and the narrator only visits from Charleston.

from.exact: By this time what little doubt I might have entertained of my poor friend’s insanity, was put finally at rest.

to.exact: we should have been regarded as madmen—although, perhaps, as madmen of a harmless nature.

alignments.same: The reasoner's way of living or acting looks like madness to anyone who does not know its purpose.
alignments.differs: In Paris only outsiders would think them mad, and the narrator shares the life; on the island the narrator himself thinks his friend a lunatic, and Legrand feeds the belief.

from.exact: the first question regards the language of the cipher

to.exact: each one spoke of it as that of a foreigner

alignments.same: The solver begins with signs nobody can read and asks first what language they belong to.
alignments.differs: Dupin finds that the voice fits no witness's language and so is no human tongue; Legrand settles on English through a pun, the kid drawn as Kidd's signature.

question: Legrand plays up his madness to punish the narrator, while Dupin's narrator shares his seclusion: what does the doubting friend add to the reasoner's story?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue has a reasoner of illustrious family reduced to poverty, a seclusion that would pass for madness, and testimony about a voice whose language each witness misplaces. The Purloined Letter shares Dupin but not the ruined family or the language puzzle; Holmes, Father Brown and Poirot are not ruined recluses and read no unknown tongue. Replacing The Gold-Bug: no other work in the graph has a cipher whose language is fixed by a pun, kept by a friend the narrator thinks insane. Also tried The Age of Innocence, Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Man Who Would Be King, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India: none has a ruined recluse of old family whose reasoning is explained after it succeeds, and none reads a cipher or an unknown tongue; Maugham's narrator thinks Strickland mad, but Strickland is a painter, not a reasoner.

claim: Both reasoners find what another hid by measuring the hider's mind. Legrand judges Kidd crude, so the cipher is simple and the secret lay in a dirty parchment's hidden ink, seen from one ledge only; Dupin judges the Minister subtle, so the soiled letter is not hidden at all but left where everyone looks.

from.exact: my measures were adapted to his capacity, with reference to the circumstances by which he was surrounded

to.exact: from what is known of Kidd, I could not suppose him capable of constructing any of the more abstruse cryptographs

alignments.same: The reasoner first weighs the intellect of the man who hid the thing and fits his method to it.
alignments.differs: Legrand measures Kidd as a crude sailor and expects a simple cipher; Dupin measures the Minister as poet and mathematician and expects no hiding place at all.

from.exact: These, like the over-largely lettered signs and placards of the street, escape observation by dint of being excessively obvious

to.exact: the circular opening in question is visible from no other attainable point of view than that afforded by the narrow ledge upon the face of the rock

alignments.same: Each tale turns on where a sign can be seen from: the hider counts on how and where the seeker will look.
alignments.differs: Kidd's mark shows from a single ledge and nowhere else; Dupin's map game hides a word by stretching it across the whole chart, in sight of everyone.

from.exact: This last was much soiled and crumpled.

to.exact: a scrap of what I took to be very dirty foolscap

alignments.same: The document worth a fortune looks like a dirty scrap fit to be crumpled and thrown away.
alignments.differs: The parchment is dirty by accident and its writing appears only under heat; the Minister soils and tears the letter on purpose, as a disguise in plain sight.

question: Kidd's treasure is found because he hid it too well for an ordinary eye, and the letter because the Minister did not hide it: which hider does the reasoner understand better?

substitution.note: Only The Gold-Bug pairs a solver who measures a dead hider's intellect with a dirty scrap that holds the secret and a mark visible from one point alone. The Rue Morgue has no hider to measure; A Scandal in Bohemia and The Blue Cross have no scrap whose worth is hidden; Treasure Island's map is plain and needs no measuring of Flint's mind. Replacing The Purloined Letter: no other work in the graph hides a soiled letter in plain sight after weighing a poet-mathematician's mind. Also tried The Age of Innocence, Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Man Who Would Be King, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India: none has a seeker who finds a hidden thing by weighing the hider's mind; Kim's spying hides papers but no one measures the hider's intellect to find them.

claim: Stevenson takes the Gold-Bug's pirate directions: a bearing to a tall tree, a dead man's body as the sight, and helpers killed after the burying. He changes who reads them: Legrand's lone deciphering wins the gold, while Flint's plain note leads a crew of mutineers along a skeleton's line to an empty pit.

from.exact: Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder, bearing a point to the N. of N.N.E.

to.exact: forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes northeast and by north main branch seventh limb east side

alignments.same: The pirate's paper names a tall tree and a compass bearing that lead from a landmark to the buried gold.
alignments.differs: Kidd's directions are in cipher and fix one ledge for a telescope; Flint's note is plain, read aloud in the boat, and fits three tall trees.

from.exact: this one he hauled here and laid down by compass

to.exact: shoot from the left eye of the death’s-head a bee line

alignments.same: The pirate sets a dead man's remains to mark the line toward the treasure.
alignments.differs: Kidd nails a skull high in the tree and drops the line through its eye; Flint lays a skeleton on the ground, hands pointing, and his men call it his joke.

from.exact: Him and these six was alone here; he killed ’em, every man

to.exact: he may have thought it expedient to remove all participants in his secret

alignments.same: The pirate who buried the treasure killed the men who helped him dig.
alignments.differs: Legrand only guesses it from skeletons in the pit, and finds it 'dreadful to believe'; Silver tells it as known fact, and the murdered men frighten the treasure-seekers.

question: Legrand's error of one eye costs only a second digging, but Silver's crew reaches the right spot and finds it rifled: why does Stevenson empty the pit that Poe filled?

substitution.note: Only The Gold-Bug has pirate directions giving a tree and a bearing, a dead man's remains used as the sight, and helpers murdered at the burying. Robinson Crusoe and Sindbad have no buried treasure; Moby-Dick's doubloon is nailed to the mast, not buried; Descent into the Maelström has no map. King Solomon's Mines has a dead man's map and his frozen body on the way, but no tree and bearing, no body set as a sight and no murdered helpers. Replacing Treasure Island: no other work in the graph follows a pirate's bearings past a skeleton laid by compass. Also tried The Age of Innocence, Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Man Who Would Be King, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India: none follows a pirate's directions to buried treasure; The Man Who Would Be King has treasure and a crowned head but no bearing, no tree and no body set as a sight.

claim: Both detectives beat the police by heeding a small mark the culprit left, and both trails end at someone who meant no crime. Dupin's flawless chain from the nail finds an ape; Cuff's sound reasoning from the paint smear accuses innocent Rachel, and the smear finally names Franklin, who took the diamond under opium.

from.exact: In all my experience along the dirtiest ways of this dirty little world, I have never met with such a thing as a trifle yet.

to.exact: it was the retention of this spring which had been mistaken by the police for that of the nail

alignments.same: A small mark where the culprit passed, which the police passed over, becomes the detective's starting point.
alignments.differs: The police read the nail as proof the window stayed shut, and it shows the way out; Seegrave blames the maids' petticoats, and the smear only proves a garment brushed the door.

from.exact: That result satisfied me that my view was the right one.

to.exact: There was no flaw in any link of the chain.

alignments.same: The detective builds a chain of inference from the trace and declares it closed on one person.
alignments.differs: Dupin's chain ends at the true agent; Cuff's, built as carefully from the smear and Rachel's refusal to open her wardrobe, ends at Rachel, who is innocent and shielding someone else.

from.exact: on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered Myself as the Thief.

to.exact: I perfectly well know that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue.

alignments.same: The hand that did the deed carried no guilty will, and the man the evidence leads to is innocent of the crime.
alignments.differs: Poe splits the deed between a beast and its blameless owner, who confesses to Dupin; Collins puts both in one man, who finds his own name on the stained nightgown.

question: Dupin's reasoning never fails, while Cuff reads the right evidence and accuses the wrong person: why does Collins need a detective who is wrong?

substitution.note: Only the Rue Morgue joins a small mark the police misread at the culprit's way through (the nail), a reasoner's chain he calls flawless, and an agent without guilty will whose owner is innocent. The Purloined Letter and The Gold-Bug have no misread physical mark and no innocent agent; A Study in Scarlet, A Scandal in Bohemia, The Blue Cross, The Hound of the Baskervilles and The Mysterious Affair at Styles end at culprits who meant their crimes; Jekyll and Hyde has a divided agent but no detective's trace. Replacing The Moonstone: no other work in the graph has a detective who reasons rightly from a paint smear to the wrong person while the thief is the man who acted unknowingly under opium. Added after the earlier stages merged: The Age of Innocence, Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no detective reading a trace the police passed over; Aziz in A Passage to India is innocent but no one reasons to him from a mark.

claim: Stoker builds his novel in Collins's form: a case told in turn through its witnesses' own papers, with spoken words taken down in shorthand or by machine. Collins's narrators write afterwards to clear innocent names; Stoker's write as events happen, Mina types and orders them during the hunt, and the finished typescript proves nothing.

from.exact: Mrs. Harker says that they are knitting together in chronological order every scrap of evidence they have.

to.exact: the idea is that we should all write the story of the Moonstone in turn—as far as our own personal experience extends, and no farther.

alignments.same: The story is made of several witnesses' accounts set one after another, each covering what its writer knew.
alignments.differs: Franklin commissions the narratives after the case is over and fixes where each must stop; Stoker's diaries and letters were written as things happened and are collated while the Count is still loose.

from.exact: I have copied out the words on my typewriter, and none other need now hear your heart beat, as I did.

to.exact: I understand the art of writing in shorthand; and I was able to take down the patient’s ‘wanderings’, exactly as they fell from his lips.

alignments.same: Words spoken without design, by a sick man or into a phonograph, are taken down whole and turned into written evidence by another hand.
alignments.differs: Jennings fills the gaps in Candy's delirious phrases to recover what the doctor did; Mina types Seward's cylinders so no one need hear his grief, and the hunters mine them for dates.

from.exact: there is hardly one authentic document; nothing but a mass of typewriting

to.exact: The memories of innocent people may suffer, hereafter, for want of a record of the facts to which those who come after us can appeal.

alignments.same: The compilers think of their papers as a record for later readers who may want proof.
alignments.differs: Franklin gathers the narratives so that the innocent can be cleared by appeal to them; Harker, seven years on, finds the typescript proves nothing and asks no one to believe it.

question: Collins's witnesses write so that later readers can judge the innocent; Stoker's admit their papers prove nothing. What does each book want its reader to do with the evidence?

substitution.note: Only The Moonstone sets witnesses' narratives in turn by agreement, takes down a sick man's words in shorthand as evidence, and compiles the papers to clear the innocent. Jekyll and Hyde ends in two documents but not a commissioned series and has no transcript; Frankenstein, Wuthering Heights and The Turn of the Screw are framed tellings by one or two voices; Werther is letters with an editor; The Hound of the Baskervilles has Watson's reports alone. Replacing Dracula: no other work in the graph has a typist collating diaries, letters and phonograph cylinders during the pursuit and then doubting the typescript as proof. Added after the earlier stages merged: Heart of Darkness and The Moon and Sixpence gather what others tell into one narrator's voice, with no witness writing his own paper and nothing taken down in shorthand or by machine; The Age of Innocence, Kim and A Passage to India are told by one narrator throughout.

claim: Doyle takes over Collins's plot: a British soldier gets Indian jewels by a killing in a fortress at war, vengeance follows them to an English house, and they end beyond English reach. Collins's avengers, priests of a god, restore the stone; Doyle's, a robbed English thief, scatters the gems in the Thames.

from.exact: Ere he could stagger to his feet the Sikh was upon him, and buried his knife twice in his side.

to.exact: I saw John Herncastle, with a torch in one hand, and a dagger dripping with blood in the other.

alignments.same: At night inside an Indian stronghold at war, a British soldier gets a hoard of jewels by killing the Indians who carry or guard it.
alignments.differs: Herncastle stabs the guards himself in the sack and keeps the stone alone; Small trips a fleeing merchant for a Sikh's knife in a planned ambush and shares the box with three Sikhs.

from.exact: upon his chest was fixed a torn piece of paper, with the words ‘The sign of the four’ scrawled across it

to.exact: The Moonstone will have its vengeance yet on you and yours!

alignments.same: The robbed party marks the man who took the jewels, and the threat runs on to his family in England.
alignments.differs: A dying guardian curses Herncastle for robbing a god; Small pins the four thieves' sign on Sholto's corpse because his partner cheated them of loot they had killed for.

from.exact: It is my treasure; and if I can’t have the loot I’ll take darned good care that no one else does.

to.exact: And there, in the forehead of the deity, gleamed the yellow Diamond

alignments.same: At the end the jewels pass for good out of reach of the English family that held them.
alignments.differs: Collins sends the diamond home to the moon-god's forehead in its sacred city; Doyle's convict scatters the gems along five miles of the Thames, and the empty box frees Watson to propose.

question: Collins gives the stolen diamond a rightful owner who takes it home; Doyle gives the Agra treasure none. Who in Doyle's novel has the best claim to it, and why does no one get it?

substitution.note: Only The Moonstone joins jewels got by a British soldier's killing inside an Indian fortress at war, the robbed party's mark on the holder that threatens his English family, and an end that puts the jewels beyond English reach. King Solomon's Mines finds its diamonds in a treasure-chamber and brings them home; Treasure Island and The Gold-Bug dig up pirate hoards with no Indian keepers and no vengeance on a family; The Man Who Would Be King takes no jewels to England; A Study in Scarlet's vengeance comes from Utah over a girl, not loot. Replacing The Sign of the Four: no other work in the graph carries loot from an Indian war into an English house pursued by those it was taken from. Heart of Darkness's ivory is traded, not taken in an Indian fortress; Kim, A Passage to India and The Moon and Sixpence have no stolen jewels.

claim: Both novels end with a captured avenger telling Holmes the wrong abroad behind a London death and the word he left there. Hope wrote RACHE to mislead and killed for a dead girl; Small left the four's sign for his comrades and claims the loot as wages, and the love story passes to Watson.

from.exact: so I scrawled down the sign of the four of us, as it had been on the chart, and I pinned it on his bosom

to.exact: so I dipped my finger in my own blood and printed it on a convenient place on the wall

alignments.same: The avenger leaves a written word by the dead man that those who find it cannot read.
alignments.differs: Hope prints RACHE in his own blood to send the police after secret societies; Small pins the sign from the treasure plans on Sholto as a token for his comrades.

from.exact: Whose loot is this, if it is not ours?

to.exact: You may consider me to be a murderer; but I hold that I am just as much an officer of justice as you are.

alignments.same: In handcuffs before the police, the avenger answers their law with a right of his own.
alignments.differs: Hope's right is a murdered father and a girl forced to marry, and he killed only the two men to blame; Small's is a dead merchant's jewels, paid for in the Andamans.

from.exact: I should never marry myself, lest I bias my judgment.

to.exact: held Lucy’s marriage ring in front of his eyes

alignments.same: A marriage stands at the close of the case.
alignments.differs: In the first book the ring is a dead bride's, shown to her persecutor as he dies; in the second the marriage is Watson's own, and Holmes sets it against cold reason.

question: Holmes faults Watson for working a love-story into A Study in Scarlet. Where does the romance go in The Sign of the Four, and does the new book keep Holmes's rule?

substitution.note: Only A Study in Scarlet ends with a captured avenger telling Holmes and the police the wrong done abroad behind a London death, after leaving a written word by the dead. The Moonstone's Indians leave no word and tell no tale; The Hound of the Baskervilles' Stapleton dies unconfessed; The Murders in the Rue Morgue's sailor tells his story but avenged nothing; A Scandal in Bohemia has no death; Jekyll and Hyde ends in a full statement but no avenger. Replacing The Sign of the Four: no other work in the graph answers RACHE with a thieves' sign and a claim to loot. Heart of Darkness, Kim, A Passage to India and The Moon and Sixpence have no captured avenger telling Holmes his tale.

claim: Father Brown unmasks a man in clerical black by his theology and says how he knows evil. Flambeau, a false priest, attacks reason, and Brown, taught by penitents, brings the police; Wilfred, a true curate, prayed on heights until he thought himself God, and Brown, finding the devils in his own heart, leaves him to confess.

from.exact: But he saw all men walking about like insects.

to.exact: Though they seemed as small as insects, Valentin could see that one of them was much smaller than the other.

alignments.same: From a height the watcher sees the people below as small as insects and picks out the one he is after.
alignments.differs: Valentin, looking across the Heath, goes down to arrest the tall priest; Wilfred, looking down from the belfry, takes the green hat for a poisonous insect and drops the hammer.

from.exact: and he fancied he was God. So that, though he was a good man, he committed a great crime.

to.exact: “You attacked reason,” said Father Brown. “It’s bad theology.”

alignments.same: Brown names the criminal's error as a fault of theology.
alignments.differs: Flambeau's attack on reason shows he is no priest at all; Wilfred is a real curate whose lonely prayer on high places led him to take God's judgement into his own hand.

from.exact: “I am a man,” answered Father Brown gravely; “and therefore have all devils in my heart.

to.exact: a man who does next to nothing but hear men’s real sins is not likely to be wholly unaware of human evil

alignments.same: Asked how he could know the criminal's mind, Brown answers that he knows human evil.
alignments.differs: To Flambeau he cites the sins he hears in confession, with police behind the tree; to Wilfred he points to his own heart's devils and seals what he knows as a confession.

question: Brown hands the thief to the police but leaves the fratricide free to give himself up: what has changed between the priest on the Heath and the priest on the tower?

substitution.note: Only The Blue Cross has Father Brown unmask a man in priest's clothes by his theology, after the pursuers watch two black figures 'as small as insects' from across the Heath, and credit his knowledge of evil to the confessional. The Scarlet Letter and The Minister's Black Veil have a guilty or veiled clergyman but no reasoner who unmasks him by his theology; the Rue Morgue, the Purloined Letter, Scandal, Study in Scarlet, Styles and The Moonstone have reasoners, and Godfrey Ablewhite a pious face, but no theology unmasks anyone; in The Man Who Would Be King Dravot is taken for a god, with no priest to judge him. Replacing The Hammer of God: no other work in the graph has a true curate who kills from a belfry after seeing men as insects, and a priest who keeps the secret. The Sign of the Four, Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no priest unmasked by his theology: Holmes reasons without it, Kurtz is worshipped but judged by no priest, and Kim's lama unmasks no one.

claim: Both reasoners find the answer where everyone could see it and explain it by a law of physics. Dupin's inertia is a figure for the Minister's mind, and he contrives the Minister's fall without pity; Brown's gravitation is the weapon itself, a small hammer dropped from the tower, and he pulls the murderer back from the parapet.

from.exact: There is at least the mystery of why so big a man should attempt so big a blow with so little a hammer.

to.exact: Perhaps the mystery is a little too plain

alignments.same: The reasoner corrects the others' sense of how much mystery the case holds.
alignments.differs: The Prefect calls the affair simple yet baffling and laughs at 'too plain'; the cobbler sees no mystery in the strong smith, and Brown finds one in the lightest hammer.

from.exact: The force that smashed that skull was a force well known to scientists

to.exact: The principle of the vis inertiæ, for example, seems to be identical in physics and metaphysics.

alignments.same: The reasoner points to a law of physics to explain the case.
alignments.differs: Dupin's inertia is an analogy for how a great intellect moves; Brown's gravitation is literal, the force that turned a small hammer dropped from the tower into a giant's blow.

from.exact: “Not by that door,” he said quite gently; “that door leads to hell.”

to.exact: In the present instance I have no sympathy—at least no pity—for him who descends.

alignments.same: The case closes on the guilty man's way down from a height, spoken of as the way to hell.
alignments.differs: Dupin sets the Minister's fall in motion and leaves him a taunting verse; Brown catches the curate by the collar at the parapet and leaves the next step, giving himself up, to him.

question: Dupin takes fifty thousand francs and his revenge, while Brown keeps what he knows under the seal of confession: what does each reasoner think his discovery is for?

substitution.note: Only The Purloined Letter has a reasoner call the case 'a little too plain', give the inertia of large bodies as a figure for the opponent's intellect, and close by arranging the guilty man's descent without pity. The Rue Morgue and The Gold-Bug have Dupin's or Legrand's reasoning but no physical law offered as the key and no culprit's fall; The Mysterious Affair at Styles hides a letter in plain sight on a mantelpiece, but its key is a chemical precipitate and Poirot neither pities nor ruins the murderer from a height; The Blue Cross has no law of physics, and The Moonstone's theft is explained by an opium experiment, with no hiding place in plain sight. Replacing The Hammer of God: no other work in the graph kills with a small hammer dropped from a tower and pulls the murderer back from the parapet. The Sign of the Four has Holmes trace a climber across a roof but gives no law of physics as the key and no culprit pulled back from a fall; Heart of Darkness, Kim, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no reasoner solving a crime.

claim: Chesterton returns to Gregory's false bishop. In Thursday a man in gaiters cries down reason, is nabbed, and learns that the safe disguise is his own creed; in The Blue Cross a thief in a priest's clothes doubts reason before a real priest, who names it bad theology, and the harmless-looking cleric proves the detective.

from.exact: “You attacked reason,” said Father Brown. “It’s bad theology.”

to.exact: When on my first appearing in episcopal gaiters in a drawing-room I cried out in a voice of thunder, ‘Down! down! presumptuous human reason!’ they found out in some way that I was not a bishop at all.

alignments.same: A criminal dressed as a churchman gives himself away by speaking against reason.
alignments.differs: Gregory thunders in a drawing-room and never learns how he was found out; Flambeau murmurs his doubt on the Heath, and a real priest tells him why it betrayed him.

from.exact: When it came to the last case, Valentin gave it up and almost laughed.

to.exact: I preached blood and murder to those women day and night, and—by God!—they would let me wheel their perambulators.

alignments.same: A man is passed over as harmless because he looks exactly what he is.
alignments.differs: Gregory's open anarchism hides a real bomb-maker from the women of Saffron Park; Father Brown's open simplicity hides, from the great detective, the priest who leads both thief and police.

from.exact: a man who does next to nothing but hear men’s real sins is not likely to be wholly unaware of human evil

to.exact: The ordinary detective goes to pot-houses to arrest thieves; we go to artistic tea-parties to detect pessimists.

alignments.same: Each explains how a man who is no ordinary policeman comes to know the criminal.
alignments.differs: The philosophical policeman leaves thieves to others and hunts pessimists through sonnets; Brown learns from the common sins of the confessional, and with that knowledge catches a thief.

question: Gregory is safest dressed as an anarchist; Flambeau is caught dressed as a priest. What does each story say a disguise can never cover?

substitution.note: Replacing Thursday: only Thursday has a criminal who dresses as a churchman and is found out for crying down reason, and a man passed over because he looks just what he is. The Hammer of God has a true curate, not a disguise; in Scandal in Bohemia Holmes, the detective, wears the clergyman's dress and Irene Adler sees through it without any talk of reason; The Moonstone's Godfrey Ablewhite has a pious face but is unmasked by evidence. Replacing The Blue Cross: no other work in the graph has a real priest unmask a false one by his theology, or a harmless-looking cleric who turns out to be leading the police. Rechecked with works merged later in order: in The Sign of the Four Holmes goes disguised as an old seaman, not a churchman, and no one is found out for attacking reason; Heart of Darkness, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no false or true priest and no detective.

claim: Both books give one man a good face and a brutal one, on both sides of the law. Jekyll's drug splits them into two bodies worn by turns, and the evil one wins; Sunday's beast and god are the back and front of one body, and his victims question him at the feast.

from.exact: But when I saw him from behind I was certain he was an animal, and when I saw him in front I knew he was a god.

to.exact: Even as good shone upon the countenance of the one, evil was written broadly and plainly on the face of the other.

alignments.same: One man shows a good face and a bestial one.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's two faces belong to two bodies he takes by turns through a drug; Sunday's are the front and back of one body, seen by walking round him in the sunlight.

from.exact: When I see the horrible back, I am sure the noble face is but a mask. When I see the face but for an instant, I know the back is only a jest.

to.exact: In my eyes it bore a livelier image of the spirit, it seemed more express and single, than the imperfect and divided countenance I had been hitherto accustomed to call mine.

alignments.same: The man who looks at the two faces must judge which is the true one.
alignments.differs: Jekyll finds the evil face the more single and welcomes it as himself; Syme suspects each face of being a mask, and comes to trust the good one.

from.exact: If you were the man in the dark room, why were you also Sunday, an offense to the sunlight?

to.exact: I had but to drink the cup, to doff at once the body of the noted professor, and to assume, like a thick cloak, that of Edward Hyde.

alignments.same: One man holds a respected place and also its criminal opposite.
alignments.differs: Jekyll wears Hyde to escape the law for his pleasures and hides him from all; Sunday heads police and anarchists alike to try his recruits by terror, and must answer them.

question: Jekyll's double ends in a locked cabinet and a written confession; Sunday's ends at a feast where his victims question him. Does either book think the two faces can be reconciled?

substitution.note: Replacing Jekyll: Dorian Gray keeps a beautiful face while the portrait bears his evil, but the two never stand on both sides of the law, and no one walks round one body to see a beast and a god; Usher, Young Goodman Brown, the Rue Morgue's 'double Dupin' and the Underground Man split or mirror a self without a drug and without a respected office worn with its criminal opposite; The Moonstone's laudanum makes Franklin Blake a thief unawares, with no second face. Replacing Thursday: no other work in the graph has one figure who is beast from behind and god from in front and commands both police and plotters. Rechecked with works merged later in order: Heart of Darkness's Kurtz speaks nobly and acts brutally, but with no drug, no second body or back-and-front, and no post on both sides of the law; The Sign of the Four, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India give no one man two such faces.

claim: Both novels make the London bomb plot something the law has a hand in. Conrad's outrage is ordered by an embassy from its own spy and kills the simple boy who carries it; Chesterton's council of anarchists turns out to be all policemen under one chief, and its dead dynamiter is a joke.

from.exact: They have but two objects, to destroy first humanity and then themselves. That is why they throw bombs instead of firing pistols.

to.exact: The attack must have all the shocking senselessness of gratuitous blasphemy.

alignments.same: A bomb is meant to strike at something larger than any victim, an idea rather than a king.
alignments.differs: Chesterton's policeman finds that creed in the anarchists' inner ring; Conrad puts it in the mouth of an embassy secretary who dictates it to his paid spy to frighten England.

from.exact: I am the man in the dark room, who made you all policemen.

to.exact: The terrorist and the policeman both come from the same basket.

alignments.same: The plotters and the police are found to belong to one body.
alignments.differs: Sunday says it as the chief of both, and the discovery ends the nightmare; Conrad's Professor sneers at both as idlers, and stays the one real bomb-maker outside the game.

from.exact: his death was as self-denying as his life, for he died through his faith in a hygienic mixture of chalk and water

to.exact: All round fragments of a man’s body blown to pieces.

alignments.same: Each plot opens on a dead man of the bomb trade.
alignments.differs: The old Thursday's death is a joke in the chairman's speech about chalk and water; the Greenwich bomb kills Stevie, who only carried the can, and is gathered up in fragments.

question: Chesterton's plotters are all policemen and nobody is killed; Conrad's are idle talkers and a boy is blown up. Which book takes the bomb more seriously?

substitution.note: Replacing The Secret Agent: no other work in this view has a bomb outrage at all, let alone one ordered by a state or one that kills its carrier. Replacing The Man Who Was Thursday: the begin view's other anarchist-free detective tales (Blue Cross, Hammer of God, Scandal in Bohemia, Sign of the Four) have no anarchist council, no bomb and no chief who turns out to command both sides; Jekyll and Hyde has one man on both sides of the law but no plot or police. Recheck with works merged later in order: The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no bomb, no anarchist ring and no chief over both sides; the Mansfield and Nevinson reviews are not stories.

claim: Both books call in Lombroso's criminal type. Mina uses it on the Count and the hunters follow his habit home; Conrad gives it to Ossipon, who reads it in a harmless boy's ears and a frightened widow's teeth, while Yundt answers that the law, not the skull, marks the criminal.

from.exact: That’s what he may be called scientifically. Very good type too, altogether, of that sort of degenerate. It’s enough to glance at the lobes of his ears. If you read Lombroso—

to.exact: The Count is a criminal and of criminal type. Nordau and Lombroso would so classify him, and quâ criminal he is of imperfectly formed mind.

alignments.same: Lombroso's type is named to class someone as a criminal by nature.
alignments.differs: Mina classes the real criminal and so foresees his flight; Ossipon classes Stevie, a gentle boy drawing circles, who will be the bomb's victim, not its maker.

from.exact: Teeth and ears mark the criminal? Do they? And what about the law that marks him still better—the pretty branding instrument invented by the overfed to protect themselves against the hungry?

to.exact: The criminal always work at one crime—that is the true criminal who seems predestinate to crime, and who will of none other.

alignments.same: Each asks what makes a man a criminal.
alignments.differs: Van Helsing answers that he is born so, with a child-brain; Yundt answers that the law brands him so, and calls Lombroso an ass.

from.exact: He gazed at her, and invoked Lombroso, as an Italian peasant recommends himself to his favourite saint.

to.exact: ‘Dos pou sto,’ said Archimedes. ‘Give me a fulcrum, and I shall move the world!’

alignments.same: Criminal science is called on at the turn of the hunt for a killer.
alignments.differs: Van Helsing's science gives the hunters a lever and wins; Ossipon's is a prayer to a saint, the type he reads in Winnie's teeth only frightens him into robbing her and leaving.

question: Lombroso helps Stoker's hunters and only frightens Conrad's anarchist. What does each book think a face can tell about a crime?

substitution.note: Replacing Dracula: Lombroso is named nowhere else in our sources (grep of content/sources and content/contexts finds only dracula-5 and secret-agent-1/-3); Jekyll and Hyde gives Hyde an ape-like look but no theory of a criminal type, and the Holmes and Dupin tales read traces, not skulls. Replacing The Secret Agent: no other work in the view has a character who reads a criminal type in a face and is mocked for it. Recheck with works merged later in order: Lombroso is not named in moon-and-sixpence-1/-2, passage-to-india-1/-3 or the two reviews, and no one there reads a criminal type in a face.

claim: Both give a wife one evening of being free. Louise Mallard's freedom comes from her husband's reported death and fills the years ahead until he walks in alive; Winnie Verloc's comes from her brother's death, she makes it complete with the carving knife, and it leaves her nothing to do.

from.exact: She had her freedom. Her contract with existence, as represented by that man standing over there, was at an end. She was a free woman.

to.exact: She said it over and over under her breath: "free, free, free!"

alignments.same: A wife alone with news of a death finds herself free.
alignments.differs: Louise is freed by her husband's death; Winnie by her brother's, which ends the bargain of marrying for his sake while the husband stands alive before her.

from.exact: She had become a free woman with a perfection of freedom which left her nothing to desire and absolutely nothing to do

to.exact: But she saw beyond that bitter moment a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely.

alignments.same: The freedom is pictured as something absolute that the wife now owns.
alignments.differs: Louise's fills the coming years with days of her own; Winnie's, after the knife, empties them, with nothing left to want or do.

from.exact: “Where are we going to, Tom?” she asked timidly. Mrs Verloc was no longer a free woman.

to.exact: When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of the joy that kills.

alignments.same: The freedom ends the same evening it begins.
alignments.differs: Louise's ends when her husband walks in alive and her heart stops; Winnie's ends when, having killed hers, she clings in terror to a new man.

question: Chopin's wife is freed by a death she did not cause, Conrad's by one she did. Why does neither keep her freedom past the evening?

substitution.note: Replacing The Story of an Hour: The Jury of Her Peers has a wife who kills her husband but no moment when she or anyone calls her free; The Awakening's Edna seeks freedom with her husband alive and away; Madame Bovary dies before her husband; Rip Van Winkle's release is a husband's. Replacing The Secret Agent: no other work in the view has a wife declared 'a free woman' by a death that is not her husband's, who then kills him. Recheck with works merged later in order: no wife in The Moon and Sixpence or A Passage to India is called free by a death (Blanche Stroeve leaves a living husband, Mrs Strickland is left by hers); the two reviews are not stories.

claim: Both novels hold that plotters hide best by not hiding. Chesterton's anarchists breakfast on a balcony as anarchists, and his actor cannot shed his part; Buchan's German spies vanish into English tennis, golf and bridge, and Hannay finds them out only by one remembered gesture.

from.exact: The Black Stone didn’t need to bolt. They were quietly absorbed into the landscape.

to.exact: He said that if you didn’t seem to be hiding nobody hunted you out.

alignments.same: The plotters' cover is to show themselves openly where anyone could look.
alignments.differs: Sunday's council flaunts itself on a Leicester Square balcony as anarchists; the Black Stone shows itself only as three suburban Englishmen, and no plotter is in view.

from.exact: A fool tries to look different: a clever man looks the same and is different.

to.exact: ‘Why, then, dress up as an anarchist, you fool!’

alignments.same: Each sets a rule of disguise against the fool who dresses up.
alignments.differs: Sunday's rule is a paradox, wearing one's real creed so that no one believes it; Peter Pienaar's is a craft, keeping one's face and changing one's life, and it nearly beats Hannay.

from.exact: Those chaps didn’t need to act, they just turned a handle and passed into another life, which came as naturally to them as the first.

to.exact: I acted the paralytic Professor so well, that now I can’t leave off.

alignments.same: A man takes on a played part so wholly that it becomes his nature.
alignments.differs: Chesterton's policeman is stuck in his old man's act, comically; Buchan's spies pass in and out of English life at will, and a tapping of fingers betrays one.

question: Chesterton's open plotters turn out to be policemen; Buchan's turn out to be exactly the enemy. Does hiding in plain sight mean the same thing in a nightmare as in a spy story?

substitution.note: Replacing The Man Who Was Thursday: no other work in this view has a ring of plotters who hide by showing themselves, or a stated rule of disguise; The Purloined Letter hides a letter, not men, and Kim's and Scandal in Bohemia's disguises are costumes the wearer puts on, not lives. Replacing The Thirty-Nine Steps: The Secret Agent's anarchists meet in a back parlour and its spy hides behind a shop, not in open English leisure; Blue Cross and Hammer of God have one disguised thief, no ring.

claim: Both find the enemy in a mild man of learning on the moor and turn on seeing through a respectable face. Holmes covers a portrait's hat and curls and sees Stapleton; Hannay, who is no Sherlock Holmes, sits at cards with his man and knows him only by a tapping of fingers.

from.exact: His face was round and shiny, like Mr Pickwick’s, big glasses were stuck on the end of his nose, and the top of his head was as bright and bare as a glass bottle.

to.exact: In that impassive colourless man, with his straw hat and his butterfly-net, I seemed to see something terrible—a creature of infinite patience and craft, with a smiling face and a murderous heart.

alignments.same: The quiet collector in a lonely moorland house is the murderers' chief behind a mild face.
alignments.differs: Watson comes to suspect the naturalist only after many meetings; Hannay runs into the archaeologist's house for refuge and knows him within minutes by eyelids hooded like a hawk's.

from.exact: It was the movement I remembered when I had stood before him in the moorland farm, with the pistols of his servants behind me.

to.exact: My eyes have been trained to examine faces and not their trimmings. It is the first quality of a criminal investigator that he should see through a disguise.

alignments.same: The villain is known at last by something beneath his outward look.
alignments.differs: Holmes strips the trimmings from a portrait with a trained eye; Hannay reads nothing in the three faces and is saved by a gesture he chanced to see.

from.exact: An observer with a telescope on one of the higher hills might have discovered the truth, but only herds went there, and herds do not carry spy-glasses.

to.exact: I see him every day through my telescope upon the roof.

alignments.same: A telescope over the moor could find out what hides on it.
alignments.differs: Frankland's telescope watches the moor and catches Holmes's boy, not the convict; on Buchan's moor nobody carries one, so the spies' aerodrome stays hidden.

question: Holmes trusts a trained eye to see through any disguise; Hannay says he was no Sherlock Holmes and wins by a chance glance. What does Buchan's chase keep from the detective story, and what does it give up?

substitution.note: Replacing The Hound: no other work in this view sets the criminal in a scholar's house on a moor, and the other Holmes tales (Study in Scarlet, Sign of the Four, Scandal in Bohemia) have no moor, no telescope and no villain known by a face under its trimmings; Dracula's Count is known by his own looks, not through a respectable disguise. Replacing The Thirty-Nine Steps: Thursday's disguised Professor is a policeman, not the enemy, and there is no moor.

claim: Both put a great power's paid spies behind a London plot and make anarchism the story told over it. Conrad's embassy orders an outrage the anarchists will be blamed for; Scudder first tells Hannay of anarchists framing Berlin, and his notebook shows German agents taking the naval plans.

from.exact: It will all be an infernal lie, of course, but the case will look black enough to the world.

to.exact: A dynamite outrage must be provoked. I give you a month.

alignments.same: A blow in London is set for a date, with the blame arranged beforehand.
alignments.differs: Vladimir's embassy means the anarchists to be blamed so that England will crush them; in Scudder's tale the anarchists plan Karolides' death to lay the blame on Vienna and Berlin.

from.exact: All his yarns about the Balkans and the Jew-Anarchists and the Foreign Office Conference were eyewash, and so was Karolides.

to.exact: “Anarchist,” stated Mr Verloc in a deadened tone.

alignments.same: Behind the anarchist story stands a foreign government's agent.
