alignments.differs: Verloc wears the anarchist's name as the cover his paymasters need; Buchan's anarchists exist only in Scudder's yarn, and the real spies wear the look of English gentlemen.

from.exact: This man was more than a spy; in his foul way he had been a patriot.

to.exact: There is no occupation that fails a man more completely than that of a secret agent of police.

alignments.same: Each book weighs what kind of man the spy is.
alignments.differs: Conrad's agent is a lazy man whom his trade has emptied; Buchan's old spy, caught, burns with a hawk's pride, and Hannay grants him a foul patriotism.

question: Conrad's spy serves an embassy that despises him; Buchan's serves his country to the end. Which book makes spying the more frightening trade?

substitution.note: Replacing The Secret Agent: no other work in this view has a foreign power's spies at work in London; Thursday's anarchist council is all policemen, with no embassy and no frame-up, and Dracula's foreign Count is no state's agent. Replacing The Thirty-Nine Steps: Thursday has no spy of a foreign government and no blame laid beforehand on another party.

claim: Poe gives the close of Usher to the murderer himself: a man of acute senses hears the heart of one he put under the floor and shrieks his secret. Usher's sister was buried alive and returns; the old man was killed and stays dead, so the beat can come only from the narrator.

from.exact: And have I not told you that what you mistake for madness is but over-acuteness of the sense?

to.exact: Said I not that my senses were acute?

alignments.same: The speaker reminds his hearer that he has already called his senses acute, to vouch for a sound no one else is sure of.
alignments.differs: Usher says it after the sound, to prove he heard his sister in the coffin; the narrator says it before the murder, to prove he is not mad.

from.exact: It is the beating of his hideous heart!

to.exact: Do I not distinguish that heavy and horrible beating of her heart?

alignments.same: The man who laid a body under the floor or in the vault hears its heart beating through what lies between.
alignments.differs: Madeline is alive and comes through the door; the old man lies cut up and dead under the planks, so the beat can only be the hearer's own.

from.exact: “Villains!” I shrieked, “dissemble no more! I admit the deed!

to.exact: Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!

alignments.same: The tale ends as he shrieks an insult at his listener and blurts out what he has kept back.
alignments.differs: Usher calls his friend a madman and owns a hasty burial; the narrator calls the smiling officers villains, owns a murder and bids them tear up the planks.

question: Usher really hears Madeline, who is alive; the old man is stone dead. Whose heart does the narrator hear, and does the earlier tale help decide?

substitution.note: Only Usher has a man who cites his own acute senses while hearing the heart of someone he shut in below, and ends shrieking an insult at his listener. The Country of the Blind hears heartbeats but buries no one; Dracula entombs Lucy but no hearer hears her; The Diamond Lens feels Simon's pulse but hears nothing after. Replacing The Tell-Tale Heart: Notes from Underground has over-acuteness without a body or a heartbeat. The Secret Agent's Winnie stabs Verloc but hears no heart and shrieks no confession; in The Thirty-Nine Steps Scudder's body lies in Hannay's flat, but nobody hears a heart.

claim: Both narrators answer a 'you' who thinks them mad by blaming an excess of perception. Poe's over-acute hearing drives him to kill and then to shriek his deed to the police; Dostoevsky's over-acute consciousness leaves him unable to act at all, and he writes his confession for himself alone.

from.exact: You think, gentlemen, perhaps that I am mad? Allow me to defend myself.

to.exact: but why will you say that I am mad?

alignments.same: The narrator turns on a listener who, he supposes, thinks him mad and sets out to answer the charge.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator offers the cunning of his murder as proof of a sound mind; the underground man defends man's right to want against reason, and his 'gentlemen' are the believers in reason.

from.exact: it was all in accord with the normal fundamental laws of over-acute consciousness, and with the inertia that was the direct result of those laws

to.exact: what you mistake for madness is but over-acuteness of the sense

alignments.same: The narrator names an over-acuteness, not madness, as the cause of what he is.
alignments.differs: Poe's sharpened hearing catches the old man's heart and goads him to leap into the room; the underground man's consciousness brings only inertia, so that he 'could do absolutely nothing'.

from.exact: Such confessions as I intend to make are never printed nor given to other people to read.

to.exact: I admit the deed!—tear up the planks!—here, here!

alignments.same: The narrative moves toward a confession of what the narrator is ashamed of.
alignments.differs: Poe's confession is shrieked at the police, forced out by a sound he thinks they hear; the underground man writes his in secret, to test whether one can be open even with oneself.

question: Poe's narrator is undone by a sense that will not stop working, Dostoevsky's by a consciousness that stops him from acting: which of them is the madman his 'you' suspects?

substitution.note: Replacing The Tell-Tale Heart: The Diamond Lens's murderer denies he is mad but claims no sharpened sense; Usher claims acute senses but is not the narrator and answers no one who calls him mad; Ahab's 'They think me mad' (Moby-Dick) is a soliloquy with no over-acuteness. Replacing Notes from Underground: no other graph work sets an over-acute consciousness, a 'you' who thinks the narrator mad and a confession side by side. The Secret Agent, The Thirty-Nine Steps, The Moon and Sixpence and A Passage to India have no narrator who answers a 'you' calling him mad.

claim: Both murderers plan with care, feel the victim's heart, satisfy the law and deny they are mad. Poe's narrator is undone by the heart he stilled, whose beat drives him to confess to the officers; O'Brien's Linley gets a verdict of suicide, feels no guilt, and is broken instead by losing what he killed for.

from.exact: with the other I discovered as accurately as I could by pulsation the exact locality of the heart

to.exact: I placed my hand upon the heart and held it there many minutes. There was no pulsation.

alignments.same: The murderer lays his hand on the victim's breast and feels for the pulse of the heart.
alignments.differs: Linley feels it before the blow, to aim the creese; Poe's narrator feels it afterwards to be sure it has stopped, and yet hears it beating again within hours.

from.exact: All the other evidence corresponded—the door locked inside, the position of the corpse, the burned papers.

to.exact: The officers were satisfied. My manner had convinced them.

alignments.same: The killer's precautions satisfy the officers of the law who come to look into the death.
alignments.differs: The inquest returns suicide and Linley is never found out; Poe's narrator seats the officers over the corpse, and while they chat he breaks and gives himself up.

from.exact: They say now that I am mad; but they are mistaken.

to.exact: but why will you say that I am mad?

alignments.same: Telling his story, the murderer rejects the madness others charge him with.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator offers the cunning of the murder as proof of sanity; Linley is called mad for mourning a creature in a drop of water, and the murder never enters the charge.

question: Linley's murder is never found out and never troubles him, while Poe's narrator cannot keep his secret a night: what has O'Brien taken from the murderer's tale, and what does he put in place of the beating heart?

substitution.note: Replacing The Tell-Tale Heart: Dorian Gray hides Basil's body and is never charged, but feels no pulse, faces no officers in the room and denies no madness; Usher's heartbeat comes from no murder. Replacing The Diamond Lens: no other graph work has a murderer who feels the victim's heart, passes an inquest and says he is not mad. The Secret Agent's Winnie kills Verloc on impulse, feels for no pulse and denies no madness; Hannay in The Thirty-Nine Steps is suspected of a murder he did not commit.

claim: Poe retells the close of his earlier tale: the police are satisfied, the murderer boasts over the hidden body, and a sound from the hiding place undoes him. But now his own heart beats calmly, and the sound is the walled-up cat's scream, which every officer hears; they open the wall without his confession.

from.exact: My heart beat calmly as that of one who slumbers in innocence.

to.exact: It is the beating of his hideous heart!

alignments.same: At the height of the police search the narrator reports on a beating heart.
alignments.differs: The new murderer feels his own heart beat calmly, like an innocent man's; the old one hears the dead man's heart pound louder until he cannot bear it.

from.exact: I rapped heavily, with a cane which I held in my hand, upon that very portion of the brick-work behind which stood the corpse of the wife of my bosom.

to.exact: placed my own seat upon the very spot beneath which reposed the corpse of the victim.

alignments.same: In his triumph the murderer puts himself on the very spot that hides the corpse.
alignments.differs: The old man's killer only sits above the planks and chats; the wife's killer strikes the wall with his cane, and his own blows call out the answering cry.

from.exact: No sooner had the reverberation of my blows sunk into silence, than I was answered by a voice from within the tomb!

to.exact: “Villains!” I shrieked, “dissemble no more! I admit the deed!

alignments.same: A sound from the hiding place ends the concealment, and the body is uncovered before the police.
alignments.differs: Before, only the narrator heard it and he shrieked his own confession; here the whole party hears the cat, and they tear down the wall while he staggers away.

question: The Aristidean first called The Black Cat a reproduction of the Tell-tale Heart, then 'an amplification of one of its phases'. Which phase is amplified, and what changes when the betraying sound is one everyone can hear?

substitution.note: Closest substitutes: Usher (a sound from the tomb, but no murderer and no police), The Diamond Lens (an inquest satisfied, but nothing hidden that cries out), A Jury of Her Peers (the hidden evidence is found by the women, not given away by the killer). None has the satisfied police, the boast at the hiding place and the betraying sound together.

claim: Both confessions, written at the edge of death, trace a murder to an evil called primitive in man and set loose by drink. Poe's narrator stays one man, changed by gin, who kills with his own hand and will hang; Jekyll's draught gives the evil a body of its own, so the murder is Hyde's.

from.exact: I learned to recognise the thorough and primitive duality of man

to.exact: perverseness is one of the primitive impulses of the human heart

alignments.same: Each confessor turns his fall into a law of human nature and calls the evil he found in himself primitive.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator names one impulse in every heart, to do wrong because it is wrong; Jekyll finds two whole natures and dreams of housing them in separate bodies.

from.exact: My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring.

to.exact: My original soul seemed, at once, to take its flight from my body and a more than fiendish malevolence, gin-nurtured, thrilled every fibre of my frame.

alignments.same: After a drink a fiend takes over the man, and he strikes a creature that cannot resist.
alignments.differs: Gin leaves Poe's narrator in his own body with his soul fled; Jekyll's draught builds the devil a body of its own, so the hand that kills is Hyde's.

from.exact: Will Hyde die upon the scaffold? or will he find courage to release himself at the last moment?

to.exact: But to-morrow I die, and to-day I would unburthen my soul.

alignments.same: The confession is written by a man who knows the gallows waits for the one who did the deed.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator writes in his cell the day before he hangs; Jekyll cannot tell whether Hyde will hang or kill himself, and ends his own life when he stops writing.

question: Jekyll needs a second body to disown his crime; Poe's narrator has only a cat, which ends by bearing the gallows on its breast. Which confessor takes more of the blame on himself?

substitution.note: Closest substitutes: Dorian Gray (evil given an outward image, opium, a murder, but no written confession before death and no 'primitive' law), Notes from Underground (a confession and a theory of the will, but no drink and no murder), The Tell-Tale Heart (a murderer's confession, but no drink and no general law of man).

claim: Both narrators name a wish that philosophy leaves out: to choose, knowingly, what harms oneself. Poe's narrator calls it perverseness, a sin that made him hang his cat and will hang him; the Underground man calls it caprice, man's most advantageous advantage, and turns it against the laws of nature.

from.exact: But I repeat for the hundredth time, there is one case, one only, when man may consciously, purposely, desire what is injurious to himself, what is stupid, very stupid

to.exact: Who has not, a hundred times, found himself committing a vile or a silly action, for no other reason than because he knows he should not?

alignments.same: Each says a man will knowingly choose the harmful or silly thing, and appeals to what has happened a hundred times.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator offers the vile act as common experience, to make his cruelty familiar; the Underground man claims the stupid wish as a right, to keep a will of his own.

from.exact: which comes under no classification and against which all systems and theories are continually being shattered to atoms.

to.exact: Of this spirit philosophy takes no account.

alignments.same: Both say the philosophers' account of man has no place for this impulse.
alignments.differs: For Poe's narrator it is a spirit that came to his final overthrow; for Dostoevsky's it is the advantage that shatters every system, prized for that very reason.

from.exact: but what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic, when, for some reason I dislike those laws and the fact that twice two makes four?

to.exact: Have we not a perpetual inclination, in the teeth of our best judgment, to violate that which is Law, merely because we understand it to be such?

alignments.same: Each finds in himself a wish to go against a law only because it is a law.
alignments.differs: Poe's Law is God's, and breaking it means hanging a cat that loved him; the Underground man's laws are nature's and arithmetic's, and he owns he cannot break the wall.

question: Poe's narrator calls perverseness a sin; the Underground man calls caprice a right. Does each man's story bear out his own name for the impulse?

substitution.note: Closest substitutes: Bartleby (a refusal without reason, but no one theorizes it), Jekyll and Hyde (a law of man's double nature, not of willing one's own harm), The Tell-Tale Heart (no account of perverseness at all). Only Notes from Underground argues the same wish against philosophy.

claim: Poe walls up a victim again and turns the ending round. The Black Cat's killer hides a corpse in the cellar wall, feels satisfied, and is undone when a cry answers his rapping cane. Montresor brings his trowel, walls in a living man, answers the screams himself, and no one opens the wall for fifty years.

from.exact: producing a trowel from beneath the folds of my roquelaire.

to.exact: I determined to wall it up in the cellar—as the monks of the middle ages are recorded to have walled up their victims.

alignments.same: Each murderer settles on walling his victim up below the house.
alignments.differs: The cat's killer hits on the wall only after weighing fire, a grave and the well; Montresor has carried his trowel from the start, for a man still alive.

from.exact: I placed my hand upon the solid fabric of the catacombs, and felt satisfied.

to.exact: When I had finished, I felt satisfied that all was right.

alignments.same: The builder looks to his masonry and feels satisfied.
alignments.differs: Montresor is satisfied halfway, his hand on granite while his victim screams; the cat's killer is satisfied with fresh plaster that gives way after one tap of his cane.

from.exact: I re-echoed—I aided—I surpassed them in volume and in strength.

to.exact: No sooner had the reverberation of my blows sunk into silence, than I was answered by a voice from within the tomb!

alignments.same: A scream from inside the new wall meets the man who built it.
alignments.differs: The cat's scream answers the killer's blows before the police, who tear the wall down; Montresor answers Fortunato's screams himself, louder, with no one else to hear.

question: Montresor says a wrong is unredressed unless the avenger makes himself felt as such. Fifty years on, unpunished and still telling it, has he won what the Black Cat's killer lost when the wall spoke, or is his telling a confession too?

substitution.note: Closest substitutes: The Tell-Tale Heart (the body hidden under planks, not walled up, and the sound a heart, not a cry), Usher (a vault and an iron door, no masonry and no murder), The Murders in the Rue Morgue (a body thrust up a chimney, nothing built over it). None has the killer's own masonry, his satisfaction with it and a scream from behind it.

claim: Both tales leave a living body in a damp vault below the family house, by torches dimmed in foul air, and the one who left it hears it struggle. Usher dared not speak, and his sister breaks out and bears him down dead; Montresor stops work to listen with satisfaction, and the niche stays shut.

from.exact: in which the foulness of the air caused our flambeaux rather to glow than flame.

to.exact: our torches, half smothered in its oppressive atmosphere, gave us little opportunity for investigation

alignments.same: Torches burn low in the foul air of the deep vault where the body will be left.
alignments.differs: Usher and his friend carry down a coffined body they take for dead; Montresor walks his victim down alive, drunk and joking, on his own feet.

from.exact: that I might hearken to it with the more satisfaction, I ceased my labors and sat down upon the bones.

to.exact: I now tell you that I heard her first feeble movements in the hollow coffin.

alignments.same: The man who shut a living body in hears its first struggles from inside.
alignments.differs: Usher heard them for days and dared not speak, sick with terror; Montresor lays down his trowel and sits on the bones to enjoy the rattling chain.

from.exact: For the half of a century no mortal has disturbed them.

to.exact: Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!

alignments.same: Each tale ends on what becomes of the one buried alive.
alignments.differs: Madeline breaks out of her vault, bloody, and falls dead upon her brother; Fortunato never comes out, and the bones stacked against his wall lie undisturbed.

question: Usher is destroyed by what he heard and kept silent; Montresor hears more and shouts back. Why does Poe give the living burial first to a frightened brother and later to a satisfied avenger, and which ending is the more terrible?

substitution.note: Closest substitutes: The Black Cat (the cat walled up alive by chance, its killer hears nothing until the police search), Jane Eyre (Bertha shut up alive and breaking out, but in an attic, not a tomb, and no one hears her as one buried), The Tell-Tale Heart (the body dead and under the floor), Dracula (Lucy leaves her tomb undead, not buried alive, and no one hears her), Northanger Abbey (Mrs Tilney's living imprisonment is only Catherine's fancy). None has a living body laid in the family vault by torchlight and its struggles heard by the one who put it there.

claim: Both narrators meet a ghost with science: nerves, and signals sent along wires. Bulwer's theorist calls spectres purposeless and pulls down the room that sends them; the signal-man's spectre warns precisely, and Dickens's narrator, whose unspoken words come back in the driver's cry, can end only by pointing out a coincidence.

from.exact: I showed him how that this figure must be a deception of his sense of sight, and how that figures, originating in disease of the delicate nerves that minister to the functions of the eye, were known to have often troubled patients

to.exact: Now, my theory is that the supernatural is the impossible, and that what is called supernatural is only a something in the laws of Nature of which we have been hitherto ignorant.

alignments.same: The narrator meets an apparition with a natural theory before he will grant a ghost.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator holds his theory as armour for his own night in the house; Dickens's offers another man a doctor's account of the eye's nerves while a frozen finger traces his own spine.

from.exact: and to the wild harp it makes of the telegraph wires!

to.exact: still am I persuaded that these are but agencies conveyed, as by electric wires, to my own brain from the brain of another.

alignments.same: Wires that carry signals over a distance enter the explanation of the haunting.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's wire figures a far brain's will, cut off by razing one room; Dickens's real telegraph wires only make the wind cry like a voice, and the warning still comes.

from.exact: If it came, on those two occasions, only to show me that its warnings were true, and so to prepare me for the third, why not warn me plainly now?

to.exact: These apparitions come for little or no object,—they seldom speak when they do come

alignments.same: The tale asks what an apparition comes for and what it says.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's theorist finds spectres objectless and mute; the signal-man's spectre cries a precise warning, and his torment is a meaning he cannot read in time.

question: Bulwer's narrator ends by stopping the haunting, Dickens's by pointing out a coincidence: which narrator's reason survives his story?

substitution.note: Only The Haunted and the Haunters has a narrator who sets out a nerve-and-mesmerism theory of ghosts, figures the haunting as signals 'as by electric wires' and declares apparitions objectless. Usher's narrator blames nerves and the place but offers no theory of spectres; Canterville's Otises meet the ghost with patent cleaners, not science; Turn of the Screw, Yellow Wallpaper and Jekyll have no reasoner who argues the ghost into nature; Dracula's Van Helsing argues the other way. Northanger's Henry Tilney reasons away a suspected crime, not an apparition, and Seven Gables' Holgrave mesmerizes without a theory of ghosts. Replacing The Signal-Man: no other work in the graph has telegraph wires in a ghost story or a spectre whose warning comes true. Among works added later: The Black Cat's narrator explains the gallows-cat on the plaster by natural causes and The Tell-Tale Heart's pleads over-acute senses, but neither meets an apparition with a theory of spectres or of wires; Heart of Darkness, A Passage to India and the rest have no ghost.

claim: Each tale gives a ghost to a guardian of others' lives and ends in a death by day. Dickens's signal-man, tested, sees nothing, dares not telegraph a nameless danger, and dies under the engine himself; James's governess sees Miss Jessel when her witness cannot, will not write to the master, and holds Miles as his heart stops.

from.exact: Where on earth do you see anything?

to.exact: “No,” he answered. “It is not there.”

alignments.same: The seer and a companion look together at the spot where the spectre stood.
alignments.differs: At the cutting the haunted man himself sees nothing and the test settles nothing; at the lake the governess sees Miss Jessel plainly, and her witness's blindness leaves her alone.

from.exact: By writing to him that his house is poisoned and his little nephew and niece mad?

to.exact: I should get into trouble, and do no good. They would think I was mad.

alignments.same: The one who sees the danger will not report it to the superior who could act, for fear of being thought mad.
alignments.differs: The signal-man wants a warning plain enough to telegraph; the governess, sure of the danger, keeps it from the master and takes the whole charge on herself.

from.exact: We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.

to.exact: It was just at broad day. He had struck the light, and had the lamp in his hand.

alignments.same: The haunting ends in a death in broad daylight.
alignments.differs: The signal-man, the watcher, is killed with his back to the warned-of engine; the governess survives, holding the boy who dies as she points at a Quint he cannot see.

question: The signal-man is believed by no one and dies; the governess is believed by no one and lives: whose watch failed, and who was it for?

substitution.note: Only The Signal-Man has a watcher with lives in his charge who is tested at the spot and sees nothing, fears being called mad if he reports, and dies by day. Haunted and the Haunters and Canterville have no witness test or withheld report; Yellow Wallpaper's narrator sees what her husband does not but guards no one and nobody dies; Wuthering Heights' Heathcliff sees Catherine alone but answers to no master; Usher and Jekyll end in deaths but not in daylight after a refused report. Northanger, Seven Gables and Dracula have no lone seer whose witness sees nothing at the spot. Replacing The Turn of the Screw: no other work in the graph has a governess who sees a ghost her witness cannot and keeps it from her employer. Among works added later: The Black Cat, The Tell-Tale Heart and The Cask of Amontillado end in murder, not a ghost given to a guardian of lives; Heart of Darkness, The Secret Agent, The Thirty-Nine Steps and A Passage to India have no spectre and no tested witness.

claim: Stevenson turns Victor's night work among graves into a trade. Victor gathers the dead alone for his own discovery, and the body he quickens comes back alive to kill; Fettes and Macfarlane rob graves for pay and buy murdered bodies, and the dead come back only as a murdered man's face in their sack.

from.exact: Hell, God, Devil, right, wrong, sin, crime, and all the old gallery of curiosities—they may frighten boys, but men of the world, like you and me, despise them.

to.exact: a church-yard was to me merely the receptacle of bodies deprived of life, which, from being the seat of beauty and strength, had become food for the worm.

alignments.same: A young student of the dead declares that the terrors of the churchyard have no hold on him.
alignments.differs: Victor was bred free of superstition and turns his calm into research; Fettes boasts it over dinner with a murderer's gold in his pocket, and the drive home with the corpse undoes him.

from.exact: The coffin was forced, the cerements torn, and the melancholy relics, clad in sackcloth, after being rattled for hours on moonless byways, were at length exposed to uttermost indignities before a class of gaping boys.

to.exact: I collected bones from charnel houses; and disturbed, with profane fingers, the tremendous secrets of the human frame.

alignments.same: The dead are taken from their rest by night to be cut open for science.
alignments.differs: Victor gathers alone and in secret for one discovery of his own; Stevenson's graves are robbed for a trade, paid for at the door and laid before a whole anatomy class.

from.exact: bearing along with it, sole occupant of the gig, the body of the dead and long-dissected Gray.

to.exact: nearly in the light of my own vampire, my own spirit let loose from the grave, and forced to destroy all that was dear to me.

alignments.same: A body the man of science took from the dead comes back on him.
alignments.differs: Victor's creature lives, walks and kills his family; Gray comes back only as a dead face in a sack, never explained, and calls up the murder the two doctors hid.

question: Victor says a churchyard held no terror for him, and Fettes says he despises 'the old gallery of curiosities'. What at last frightens each man, and is it the same thing?

substitution.note: Replacing The Body Snatcher: The Island of Doctor Moreau cuts living animals bought for the purpose, not the dead from graves; in Dracula the doctors open Lucy's tomb to destroy her, not to study her, and no anatomy class is fed; Usher's vault is guarded against the doctors, not robbed by them; Jekyll and Hyde has no bodies taken. Replacing Frankenstein: no other work in the graph has a student gather the dead for a discovery of his own and quicken a body that lives and kills; Moreau makes his beasts from the living, and Rappaccini and The Birth-Mark work on living daughters and wives. Works added in order before this step: Poe's Tell-Tale Heart, Black Cat and Cask of Amontillado hide one murdered body and rob no grave for science; the Signal-Man's spectre and the Mugby Junction frame have no anatomist; Heart of Darkness, The Secret Agent, The Moon and Sixpence, A Passage to India and The Thirty-Nine Steps have no bodies bought for dissection.

claim: Stevenson asks twice how a doctor of good name lives with secret crime. In The Body Snatcher one self squares its nights against its days and an ugly look only crosses the respected face; in Jekyll the doctor splits himself, gives the guilt to Hyde's separate body and welcomes the ugly face in his glass.

from.exact: It was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, that was guilty.

to.exact: For his day of work he indemnified himself by nights of roaring, blackguardly enjoyment; and when that balance had been struck, the organ that he called his conscience declared itself content.

alignments.same: A man of medicine pays for respectable days with nights of vice, and his conscience is at ease.
alignments.differs: Fettes squares day and night inside one self, like an account; Jekyll gives the nights to another body, so that the doctor wakes blameless.

from.exact: I stood already committed to a profound duplicity of life.

to.exact: The more things are wrong the more we must act as if all were right.

alignments.same: A doctor keeps up a respectable front over what he has done in secret.
alignments.differs: Macfarlane's front is a rule two accomplices agree on to hide a murder; Jekyll's duplicity grows from his own shame at small pleasures and leads him to think man is two.

from.exact: And yet when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome.

to.exact: A horrible, ugly look came and went across his almost venerable countenance.

alignments.same: An ugly second face shows itself in a doctor of good name.
alignments.differs: On Macfarlane it flickers for a moment before witnesses and is masked again; Jekyll's ugly face is a whole body that he meets in his mirror and welcomes.

question: Fettes quiets his conscience by habit and Macfarlane's rule, Jekyll by a drug. Which way of living with a crime does Stevenson judge more harshly, and how can you tell?

substitution.note: Replacing The Body Snatcher: Dorian Gray is no doctor, and his portrait, not one self, carries the guilt; in The Scarlet Letter Dimmesdale's conscience is never at ease and the physician Chillingworth hides revenge, not a crime he shares; The Moonstone's Godfrey Ablewhite leads a double life but is no doctor and has no ugly look; Frankenstein hides his making but his conscience gives him no rest. Replacing Jekyll and Hyde: Dorian gives his sins to a picture, not a second body, and is no doctor; The Invisible Man's drug makes Griffin unseen, not two; Rappaccini's science works on his daughter, not on himself. Works added in order before this step: Poe's murderers in The Tell-Tale Heart, The Black Cat and The Cask of Amontillado are no doctors of good name and do not split; Verloc in The Secret Agent and Kurtz in Heart of Darkness are no doctors; the Signal-Man, the Mugby Junction frame, The Moon and Sixpence, A Passage to India and The Thirty-Nine Steps keep no secret crime under a respected face.

claim: Jacobs gives Victor's wish to a grieving mother and takes away the science. Victor reasons toward renewing life in the dead, sees his made being wake and flees, listening all night for it; Mrs White wants only her buried son back, and the father, hearing the knocks, wishes it away before anyone sees what came.

from.exact: Go down and get it quickly, and wish our boy alive again.

to.exact: renew life where death had apparently devoted the body to corruption.

alignments.same: Someone hopes to bring a dead body back to life.
alignments.differs: Victor reasons toward it as a discovery to serve all; Mrs White wants one son back at once, by a fakir's charm, ten days after his burial.

from.exact: Do you think I fear the child I have nursed?

to.exact: No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve their’s.

alignments.same: The one who would give life to the dead speaks as a parent of a child.
alignments.differs: Victor dreams of a grateful new species and flees his creature when it wakes; the mother trusts the son she nursed, and the father will not open the door.

from.exact: He stood motionless, his breath suspended until the knock was repeated.

to.exact: listening attentively, catching and fearing each sound as if it were to announce the approach of the demoniacal corpse to which I had so miserably given life.

alignments.same: At night a man listens in terror for a corpse brought back to life to come to him.
alignments.differs: Victor has seen the creature's eyes and grin; Mr White never sees what knocks, and spends his last wish so the door opens on an empty road.

question: Victor flees the being he made, and Mr White wishes away what knocks before he sees it. Is the father's last wish a failure of love, as his wife's wail says, or the only mercy left?

substitution.note: Replacing The Monkey's Paw: in The Body Snatcher the dead come back only as a body in a sack, and no one wishes them alive; in Dracula Lucy returns undead but no one called her back, and the men who loved her destroy her; Wuthering Heights has Heathcliff beg Catherine's ghost to haunt him, but there is no body to quicken and no maker; Moreau, Rappaccini and The Birth-Mark work on the living. Replacing Frankenstein: no other work in the graph has a man set out to renew life in dead bodies and then flee and listen for the corpse he quickened; The Body Snatcher's doctors only cut the dead, and Moreau makes his beasts from the living. Works merged since (G17 order): The Cask of Amontillado walls a living man up and no one wishes the dead back; The Thirty-Nine Steps has Scudder murdered but no one tries to quicken him or listens for his return; Buchan's dedication to Nelson and Stevenson's review of Poe tell no such story.

claim: Both tales price a dead body and bring the dead back by night to those paid. K— buys bodies and asks no questions, and the lamp shows Gray's face in the sack; the Whites get two hundred pounds for their son, wish him back, and unwish him before his face is seen.

from.exact: They admit no liability at all, but in consideration of your son’s services, they wish to present you with a certain sum as compensation.

to.exact: ‘They bring the body, and we pay the price,’ he used to say, dwelling on the alliteration—‘quid pro quo.’

alignments.same: A firm pays money for a dead body and takes no blame for how it died.
alignments.differs: K— buys strangers' bodies for dissection, no questions asked; Maw and Meggins pay parents for their own son, and the sum is the one the father wished for.

from.exact: I could only recognize him by his clothing. If he was too terrible for you to see then, how now?

to.exact: ‘Hold that lamp,’ said the other. ‘I must see her face.’

alignments.same: At night men weigh whether to look on the face of a dead body brought back to them.
alignments.differs: Macfarlane uncovers the face and finds Gray, whom they killed; Mr White, who saw his son's ruined body once, will not have it seen again.

from.exact: The street lamp flickering opposite shone on a quiet and deserted road.

to.exact: bearing along with it, sole occupant of the gig, the body of the dead and long-dissected Gray.

alignments.same: Each tale ends on a night road with the returned dead.
alignments.differs: Stevenson leaves Gray's body seen and driven off alone in the gig; Jacobs leaves nothing on the road, so whether the dead son came back is never proved.

question: The firm pays the Whites two hundred pounds, and K— pays the resurrection men their price. In which tale does taking the money make people guilty, and of what?

substitution.note: Replacing The Monkey's Paw: Frankenstein has bodies taken from charnel houses but no price paid and no one wishing the dead back; Dracula opens Lucy's tomb and looks on her face, but no money is paid for her; in Wuthering Heights Heathcliff gets the sexton to uncover Catherine's coffin and sees her face again, and bribes him only to loosen the coffins for his own burial, so no one is paid for her body; The Signal-Man's death by an engine brings no compensation and no return. Replacing The Body Snatcher: Frankenstein's creature is seen and lives; Dracula and The Haunted and the Haunters have no sum paid for a body; The Moonstone and The Sign of the Four pay for treasure, not for the dead. Works merged since (G17 order): in The Cask of Amontillado Fortunato is walled up alive, no price is paid for his body and he never comes back; in The Thirty-Nine Steps Scudder's corpse is left in the flat, not sold or returned by night; Buchan's dedication and Stevenson's Poe review tell no story.

claim: Both theorists meet a haunting worked through an old Latin-inscribed object. Bulwer's investigator calls ghosts natural law, refuses fear, and later burns the tablet; James's professor denies the supernatural, blows a whistle he cannot read, cries out, and is saved by the Colonel, who throws it into the sea.

from.exact: The laws which govern winds are really not at all perfectly known

to.exact: what is called supernatural is only a something in the laws of Nature of which we have been hitherto ignorant

alignments.same: Each man explains the marvel by laws of nature that are not yet known.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's theorist lets the unknown law admit the ghost; Parkins uses it only to explain a fishing superstition away, then offers his own whistling as the example.

from.exact: its one power was that of frightening

to.exact: unless I fear I cannot be harmed

alignments.same: The haunting's power over a man is said to lie in the fear it makes.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator tells himself this in the room and wills away fear; the Colonel says it afterwards, of a professor who cried out and was nearly forced through the window.

from.exact: At the end of it the Colonel left the hotel door carrying a small object between his finger and thumb, which he cast as far into the sea as a very brawny arm could send it.

to.exact: Mr. J——burned the tablet and its anathema.

alignments.same: The old object with a Latin inscription that worked the haunting is destroyed at the end.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's investigator digs the tablet out after the haunting and reads its curse; Parkins dug up the whistle himself and blew it without construing its Latin.

question: Bulwer's investigator keeps his theory and his nerve; Parkins loses both. Is James's tale a refutation of the theorist, or only of the theorist who does not expect to be tested?

substitution.note: Only The Haunted and the Haunters pairs a narrator's theory of ghosts as unknown natural law, the belief that the haunting harms only through fear, and an inscribed Latin object destroyed at the end. The Signal-Man's narrator explains by nerves but there is no object; Canterville's Otises disbelieve but fear nothing and destroy nothing; The Monkey's Paw has a talisman thrown on the fire but no theory or Latin; Dracula's Van Helsing reasons from science to belief, not the reverse; Usher, Jekyll and Turn of the Screw have no destroyed inscription. Replacing Whistle: no other tale in the graph has a disbelieving professor summon a ghost by blowing an object he cannot read. Added later: The Cask of Amontillado (a revenge walled up in a vault, with no ghost, sceptic or summons) and Stevenson's 1875 Academy review of Poe (a review, not a tale) fit none of the three points.

claim: Each tale has a faceless figure waving from afar and a call that seems to summon it. Dickens's narrator cries the spectre's words by chance and blames another man's nerves; Parkins blows 'Who is this who is coming?' on purpose, blames his own brain, and the thing comes for him.

from.exact: Well, the best way to find out is evidently to whistle for him.

to.exact: What made you cry ‘Halloa! Below there!’ to-night?

alignments.same: A visitor's own call is heard as the summons of the spectre.
alignments.differs: The narrator calls the spectre's words by chance and only frightens the signal-man; Parkins reads 'Who is this who is coming?', blows on purpose, and something comes.

from.exact: which he saw clearly enough could only be a morbid reflection of his walk and his thoughts on that very day

to.exact: I showed him how that this figure must be a deception of his sense of sight

alignments.same: A vision is explained away as a disorder of the nerves or the brain.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator explains another man's spectre and stays a visitor; Parkins explains his own dream of the pursued runner, and is himself the one pursued.

from.exact: couldn’t see its face; but it wived at him

to.exact: I never saw the face. The left arm is across the face, and the right arm is waved.

alignments.same: A figure whose face cannot be seen is seen waving from a distance.
alignments.differs: The spectre waves to the signal-man before each death on his line; the thing at Parkins's window waves at a boy, and Parkins blames a maid making the bed.

question: The signal-man's spectre comes uncalled and warns; Parkins's comes because he called it and does not warn. Which of the two sceptics, the narrator or the professor, is answered by his tale?

substitution.note: Only The Signal-Man has a sceptical visitor whose own call echoes the spectre, explains a vision as a disorder of the nerves, and hears of a faceless figure waving from a distance. The Haunted and the Haunters has the theory but no call or waving figure; Turn of the Screw's figures stand still on the tower and at the window; Canterville's ghost is seen face and all; Yellow Wallpaper's figure creeps, not waves. Replacing Whistle: no other tale in the graph has a sceptic summon a faceless waving thing by his own call. Added later: The Cask of Amontillado (a revenge walled up in a vault, with no ghost, sceptic or summons) and Stevenson's 1875 Academy review of Poe (a review, not a tale) fit none of the three points.

claim: Both hauntings use the second bed in a watcher's room, a child at a window, and a white face at a window. At Bly the ghosts stay outside and Miles dies in the governess's arms; at Burnstow the thing comes in, sits up in the empty bed, and drives Parkins half through the window.

from.exact: to see a figure suddenly sit up in what he had known was an empty bed

to.exact: Flora’s little bed was empty

alignments.same: At night the watcher finds the second bed in the room not as it should be, its sheets disordered.
alignments.differs: Flora's bed is empty because the child has gone to the window to look at someone outside; Parkins's spare bed, empty all along, has something in it.

from.exact: “Ow, I seen it wive at me out of the winder,” wailed the boy, “and I don’t like it.”

to.exact: squeezed in behind the blind and was peering out into the night

alignments.same: A child and a ghost meet through a window.
alignments.differs: Flora, inside, looks out at the figure and says nothing, and the governess reads complicity; the Burnstow boy, outside, sees the thing wave from within and runs crying.

from.exact: a horrible, an intensely horrible, face of crumpled linen

to.exact: the white face of damnation

alignments.same: At the climax a white face presses close at a window.
alignments.differs: Quint's face is at the glass, outside, while the governess holds Miles, who dies; the linen face is inside, thrust into Parkins's own, and nothing is left of it but bedclothes.

question: Henry James keeps his ghosts at the window and the stair, M. R. James puts one in the bed. Does bringing the ghost indoors make it more frightening, or less open to doubt?

substitution.note: Only Turn of the Screw combines a disordered second bed in the watcher's room, a child who sees a ghost through a window, and a white face at a window at the end. Wuthering Heights has Lockwood's window and the ghost child's face but no child witness or empty bed; Jane Eyre has a night visitor at the bedside but no child; Yellow Wallpaper has the bedroom and window but no child at it; Canterville's Virginia sees the ghost but not through a window. Replacing Whistle: no other tale in the graph has the ghost itself occupy the spare bed in the room of the man it haunts. Added later: The Cask of Amontillado (a revenge walled up in a vault, with no ghost, sceptic or summons) and Stevenson's 1875 Academy review of Poe (a review, not a tale) fit none of the three points.

claim: An ugly being serves others unseen and asks to be judged by the heart, not the eyes. Beauty learns to distrust her eyes, says yes, and the Beast becomes a prince; the Creature finds that hearing only in a blind old man, is beaten by the son who sees, and loses even a mate.

from.exact: these labours, performed by an invisible hand, greatly astonished them

to.exact: hoping that he might soon have an opportunity of thanking his considerate entertainer, whoever it might be. But no one appeared

alignments.same: An unseen host supplies the needs of people in want, who wonder at a hand they never see.
alignments.differs: The Beast's bounty is a palace's, and he appears the moment a rose is taken; the Creature gives firewood and cleared snow and stays hidden because of his face.

from.exact: a fatal prejudice clouds their eyes, and where they ought to see a feeling and kind friend, they behold only a detestable monster

to.exact: do not trust too much to your eyes

alignments.same: The ugly one's hope rests on someone who will not judge him by what the eyes show.
alignments.differs: The dream Prince teaches Beauty to distrust her eyes, and she learns it; the Creature can only lament the eyes' prejudice, and only the blind De Lacey hears him fairly.

from.exact: I demand a creature of another sex, but as hideous as myself

to.exact: Can you really love such an ugly creature as I am?

alignments.same: A being who knows his own ugliness asks for a companion's love.
alignments.differs: Beauty's yes breaks the spell and gives back a handsome prince; the Creature, sure no human will love him, asks for a mate as hideous as himself, and Victor destroys her.

question: The Beast is loved and changed back; the Creature stays hideous and alone. Does the difference lie in Beauty, in the De Laceys' eyes, or in the monster's body itself?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has an unseen servant of a poor family who asks not to be judged by the eyes and asks for a mate because of his ugliness. Jane Eyre has the ugly master but no secret service or blind judge; Moreau's Beast Folk ask for no love; The Invisible Man is unseen but serves no one; The Country of the Blind judges a sighted man, not an ugly one. Replacing Beauty and the Beast: no other tale in the view has the beast who asks 'will you marry me?'. The Cask of Amontillado has no ugly one asking for love, only a revenge walled up in a vault.

claim: Brontë keeps the tale's end: a woman returns to an ugly master grown half a beast without her, and takes him. But she refuses its magic. No charm can make Rochester handsome; Jane rehumanises him with a comb and teasing, and he stays blind and maimed when she marries him.

from.exact: A loving eye is all the charm needed

to.exact: to let her heart guide her, and not her eyes

alignments.same: Love, not what the eye sees, is what makes the ugly master acceptable to the woman.
alignments.differs: Beauty's love, once she distrusts her eyes, undoes the spell on his shape; Jane says a handsome Rochester is 'past the power of magic', and a loving eye needs none.

from.exact: Am I hideous, Jane?

to.exact: Can you really love such an ugly creature as I am?

alignments.same: Found again by the woman who left him, the broken master asks whether she finds him ugly.
alignments.differs: Beauty answers that she never knew how much she loved him, and he soon turns prince; Jane answers 'Very, sir: you always were, you know,' and he stays as he is.

from.exact: It is time some one undertook to rehumanise you

to.exact: restored my dear son to his natural form

alignments.same: The woman's return gives a man who has become half a beast back his human form.
alignments.differs: The Queen thanks Beauty for undoing an enchantment in a moment; Jane's rehumanising is combing a 'shaggy black mane' and bringing supper, and Rochester stays blind and one-handed.

question: Brontë keeps the beast and the woman's return but drops the transformation. What does Jane's marriage gain, or lose, because Rochester is never made handsome?

substitution.note: Only Jane Eyre has a woman who comes back to a maimed master likened to a wild beast, who asks 'Am I hideous?' and whom she sets out to 'rehumanise'. Frankenstein's Creature is refused, not returned to; Wuthering Heights' Catherine does not come back to Heathcliff; Moreau and Dorian Gray have no woman's return. Replacing Beauty and the Beast: no other tale in the view turns a beast back into a man by a woman's love. The Cask of Amontillado has no ugly one asking for love, only a revenge walled up in a vault.

claim: Both give a being of another kind who watches people unseen, longs to be loved by them, and pulls one from the water without thanks. Shelley's Creature, shot for it, swears vengeance and kills; Andersen's mermaid, handed the knife that would save her, throws it into the sea and is raised toward a soul.

from.exact: But to her he sent no smile; he knew not that she had saved him

to.exact: I rushed from my hiding-place, and, with extreme labour from the force of the current, saved her, and dragged her to shore

alignments.same: A creature hidden from people drags a drowning one to shore, and others take the rescued away without knowing who saved them.
alignments.differs: The girl's companion shoots the Creature; the mermaid hides in the sea foam and watches the prince smile at a girl from the temple instead.

from.exact: She grew more and more fond of human beings, and wished more and more to be able to wander about with those whose world seemed to be so much larger than her own

to.exact: my heart yearned to be known and loved by these amiable creatures

alignments.same: Watching people from hiding, a being of another kind longs to live among them and be loved.
alignments.differs: The Creature hopes the cottagers will love him as he is; the mermaid wants a human body and soul and pays the witch her tongue and tail for them.

from.exact: then she flung it far away from her into the waves

to.exact: Inflamed by pain, I vowed eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind

alignments.same: Wronged by the one they saved or loved, each is brought to the point of killing.
alignments.differs: The Creature turns his kindness into revenge and murder; the mermaid throws away the knife that would make her a mermaid again and chooses death.

question: Both are repaid for a rescue with nothing or with a wound. Why does the Creature turn to killing and the mermaid away from it, and what does Andersen gain by rewarding her with a soul?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has a being not human who watches people from hiding, longs for their love, saves one from drowning and is denied thanks, then is brought to kill. Beauty and the Beast's Beast is not hidden and saves no one from water; Moreau's Beast Folk and The Invisible Man rescue nobody; Jane Eyre's and Moby-Dick's rescues are by people. Replacing The Little Mermaid: no other tale in the view has the rescuer who refuses the knife.

claim: Andersen turns the tale round: the one who must be married to be changed is a mute girl, and the one who must answer is a prince. The Beast asks aloud each night and Beauty learns to look past her eyes; the mermaid cannot ask, and the prince trusts his eyes and weds another.

from.exact: the eyes of the little mermaid seemed to say

to.exact: Do you love me, Beauty? Will you marry me?

alignments.same: The one whose change hangs on a marriage asks the beloved for love.
alignments.differs: The Beast asks aloud each evening until Beauty says yes; the mermaid, her tongue cut out, asks only with her eyes, and the prince loves her as a child.

from.exact: unless a man were to love you so much that you were more to him than his father or mother

to.exact: restored my dear son to his natural form

alignments.same: Only the love and marriage of the other can change the being of another kind.
alignments.differs: Beauty's yes gives the Beast back the human shape he had lost; the prince's love could give the mermaid only a soul she never had, and he weds another.

from.exact: who saved my life when I lay dead on the beach

to.exact: to let her heart guide her, and not her eyes

alignments.same: Whether the right one is loved depends on seeing past what the eyes saw.
alignments.differs: Beauty learns to distrust her eyes and finds her prince in the Beast; the prince trusts what he saw on the beach and thanks the temple girl for the mermaid's rescue.

question: Beauty is taught not to trust her eyes; Andersen's prince never is. Is the mermaid lost by his blindness, or by the voice she gave up to reach him?

substitution.note: Only Beauty and the Beast has a being of another kind whose change waits on a marriage of love, asked for again and again, and a beloved told to look past her eyes. Frankenstein's Creature asks for a mate, not a marriage that would change him; Jane Eyre's Rochester is a man; Werther asks no change. Replacing The Little Mermaid: no other tale in the view has a mute suitor whose soul depends on a wedding.

claim: Wilde runs Andersen's bargain backwards. Andersen's mermaid pays a witch her voice for a human body, hoping a man's love will give her a soul; Wilde's Fisherman pays a witch a dance to be rid of his soul and live in the sea. She buys feet to dance for the prince; he leaves the footless Mermaid for a dancer's feet.

from.exact: ‘Thou hast a human soul,’ she answered. ‘If only thou wouldst send away thy soul, then could I love thee.’

to.exact: then his soul would glide into your body

alignments.same: A human soul stands between a sea-maiden and the man she would join, and love must settle what becomes of it.
alignments.differs: Andersen's mermaid has no soul and can gain one only through the prince's love; Wilde's Mermaid will love the Fisherman only if he throws his soul away.

from.exact: ‘Thou must dance with me, pretty boy,’ she murmured

to.exact: this voice you must give to me

alignments.same: The lover goes to a witch for the change and the witch names her price.
alignments.differs: Andersen's sea witch cuts out the mermaid's tongue so she may join the human world; Wilde's land witch asks a dance at the Sabbath and gives a knife so the man may leave it.

from.exact: he remembered that the little Mermaid had no feet and could not dance

to.exact: though each time her foot touched the floor it seemed as if she trod on sharp knives

alignments.same: Feet and dancing mark what the sea-maiden lacks in the human world, and a dance decides the love.
alignments.differs: Andersen's mermaid buys feet and dances in pain to please the prince; Wilde's Mermaid keeps her tail, and the Fisherman leaves her to find a girl who dances with naked white feet.

question: Andersen's mermaid would give anything for a soul; Wilde's Fisherman gives his away for love and cannot keep it gone. What does each tale think a soul is for, and which ending is kinder to its lover?

substitution.note: Only The Little Mermaid has a sea-maiden without a soul, a witch who takes a price for crossing between sea and land, and feet bought to dance for the beloved. Beauty and the Beast has no soul, witch or sea; Dorian Gray gives his soul by a wish, not to a witch; The Monkey's Paw prices a wish with no lover; Frankenstein's Creature asks no change of kind. Replacing the Fisherman: no other work in the view gives up a soul to marry into the sea.

claim: Wilde parts a man from his soul twice, and the parted soul drives him to crime. Dorian's soul is a locked-up picture that takes the marks of his sins; the Fisherman's goes out without a heart and learns evil. Each turns a knife on it: Dorian dies, but the Fisherman's knife fails, and only love lets the soul back in.

from.exact: For her body I would give my soul, and for her love I would surrender heaven.

to.exact: I would give my soul for that!

alignments.same: A young man says aloud that he would give his soul for what he desires.
alignments.differs: Dorian offers his soul to keep his own beauty unchanged; the Fisherman offers his for a mermaid's love and then cuts it away from him with a knife.

from.exact: ‘When thou didst send me forth into the world thou gavest me no heart, so I learned to do all these things and love them.’

to.exact: as though it had been suggested to him by the image on the canvas, whispered into his ear by those grinning lips

alignments.same: The man's parted soul whispers to him to strike, and he does wrong at its prompting.
alignments.differs: Dorian's picture only bears the marks of sins he chose; the Fisherman's heartless soul has learned evil on its own and orders the theft, the blow to the child and the murder.

from.exact: with the little knife that had the handle of green viper’s skin he strove to cut from his feet that shadow of the body which is the body of the Soul

to.exact: As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work

alignments.same: To be free of his parted soul, the man turns a knife on it.
alignments.differs: Dorian stabs the picture and is found dead and withered; the Fisherman's knife has no power the second time, and the soul gets back into him only when his heart breaks with love.

question: Dorian's soul records his sins; the Fisherman's soul commits them. Which tale puts the evil in the man, and which in the soul cut off from his heart?

substitution.note: Only Dorian Gray has a man who says he would give his soul, a parted soul that whispers him to kill, and a knife turned on that soul. Jekyll's Hyde is a second body that does the crimes, no soul is offered and no knife is turned on him; The Canterville Ghost, Usher and Monkey's Paw have no parted soul. Replacing the Fisherman: Jekyll, Usher or Goodman Brown give no soul away for love.

claim: Both send a girl on aching feet after a boy who does not know her. The mermaid pays the sea witch her voice, the best thing she has, for a draught, and cannot weep; Gerda's red shoes are refused by the river, the Finland woman gives her no potion, and her own tears thaw Kay's heart.

from.exact: then she took off her red shoes, the most precious things she possessed, and threw them both into the river

to.exact: the best thing you possess will I have for the price of my draught

alignments.same: A girl gives up the most precious thing she owns to a power of the water to win back the one she loves.
alignments.differs: The sea witch takes the mermaid's voice and keeps it; the river washes Gerda's shoes back to the bank, as if it would not take what was dearest to her.

from.exact: I can give her no more power than what she has already

to.exact: I will prepare a draught for you

alignments.same: A wise woman who knows magic is asked for the means to reach the boy.
alignments.differs: The sea witch brews a draught and cuts out the mermaid's tongue as payment; the Finland woman refuses the reindeer's plea for a potion and says Gerda's power lies in her heart.

from.exact: Then little Gerda shed burning tears; and they fell on his bosom

to.exact: the mermaid sighed deeply, but she could not shed tears

alignments.same: The girl grieves beside a boy who does not know her for the one who came for him.
alignments.differs: The mermaid has no tears and no voice, and the prince never learns who saved him; Gerda's tears reach Kay's frozen heart, and he knows her.

question: The sea witch takes a price and the Finland woman refuses to sell anything. What changes when Gerda's power is something no one can sell her, and why does the mermaid's love need a bargain?

substitution.note: Only The Little Mermaid has a girl who pays a witch the best thing she owns for a draught to reach a boy who does not know her, and who cannot weep. Beauty and the Beast's Beauty gives up nothing and is asked for no price; Frankenstein's Creature buys no change from anyone; Jane Eyre's and Wuthering Heights' lovers strike no bargain with magic. Replacing The Snow Queen: no other tale in the view has the gift refused by the water and the potion denied. The Fisherman and His Soul has a witch who takes a price for the change, but its lover is a young man who gets what he asks, and no girl walks on aching feet or cannot weep, so the claim does not hold for it.

claim: Andersen's sprite makes a mirror that turns the good ugly, and its splinter freezes Kay's heart until Gerda's tears wash it out. Wilde's portrait is a magic mirror that shows truly the sin behind Dorian's fair face; he smashes his own glass in loathing, no love cleanses him, and the picture keeps its record.

from.exact: This portrait would be to him the most magical of mirrors

to.exact: he had made a mirror with the power of causing all that was good and beautiful when it was reflected therein, to look poor and mean

alignments.same: A magic glass shows the one who looks in it what the eye alone cannot see.
alignments.differs: The sprite's mirror lies, shrinking the good and swelling the ugly; Dorian's portrait tells the truth, showing the sin his unchanging face hides.

from.exact: flinging the mirror on the floor, crushed it into silver splinters beneath his heel

to.exact: it flew out of their hands and fell to the earth, where it was dashed in a hundred million and more pieces

alignments.same: A mirror is dashed down and broken into splinters.
alignments.differs: The sprites drop theirs by accident and its splinters go on working evil in eyes and hearts; Dorian breaks his hand-glass on purpose, loathing his beauty, and the portrait stays as it was.

from.exact: Some love might come across his life, and purify him

to.exact: they thawed the lumps of ice, and consumed the splinters of the looking-glass

alignments.same: The love of another is the cure for a soul the glass has spoiled.
alignments.differs: Gerda's tears melt Kay's heart and wash out the splinter; for Dorian that love stays a 'might', and when he spares Hetty Merton the portrait shows only a look of cunning.

question: Andersen's mirror lies and Wilde's tells the truth, yet each cuts a young man off from those who love him. Why can Gerda's tears cure Kay when no one's love can cleanse Dorian?

substitution.note: Only The Snow Queen has a magic mirror dashed into splinters whose pieces change how people see, and a love that washes the splinter out. Jekyll's mirror shows only the body the drug has made and is not broken; The Birth-Mark's mirror shows Georgiana her own mark truly; The Little Mermaid and Beauty and the Beast have no mirror. Replacing Dorian Gray: no other novel in the view has a picture that serves as a magic mirror of the soul, or a glass smashed in loathing. The Fisherman and His Soul has a Mirror of Wisdom that shows all things but the face of the one who looks; it is hidden whole, never broken, and no love washes it out, so it does not replace The Snow Queen.

claim: Both split one person into two natures that take turns in one body. Helga is born so: a wicked will under a fair face by day, a gentle heart in a frog by night, and love lets the better win. Jekyll splits himself by a drug, evil shows on Hyde's face, and the worse wins.

from.exact: Even as good shone upon the countenance of the one, evil was written broadly and plainly on the face of the other.

to.exact: By day it was charming in appearance as an angel of light, but with a temper wicked and wild

alignments.same: Each of the two bodies shows one side of a single person.
alignments.differs: Stevenson writes the evil plainly on Hyde's ugly face; Andersen hides the wicked will under the fair day face and puts the gentle heart in the hideous frog.

from.exact: I had gone to bed Henry Jekyll, I had awakened Edward Hyde

to.exact: in that part of the bed where her feet had been, lay, not the child, but a great, ugly frog

alignments.same: Someone wakes to find the other body in the bed where the first lay down.
alignments.differs: Jekyll wakes as Hyde unbidden, a sign the drug no longer rules him; in Andersen the sun makes the change daily, and the foster-mother wakes to find it.

from.exact: I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self, and becoming slowly incorporated with my second and worse.

to.exact: It was, in this transformation, as if two natures were striving together within her

alignments.same: Two natures strive for one person, and one of them is gaining.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's worse self grows until he cannot come back; Helga's frog heart passes into her day form with her first tears, and the better nature wins.

question: Andersen puts the evil in the beautiful body and the good in the ugly one; Stevenson puts it on Hyde's face. What does each gain by where it hides the bad self, and why can love save Helga but not Jekyll?

substitution.note: Only The Marsh King's Daughter has one person whose body changes each day by a fixed law, the wicked will in the fair form and the good heart in the ugly one, found by another in the bed, and whose better self wins. Dorian Gray's soul is a picture, not a second body; The Fisherman's soul walks apart; Usher's double is a sister; Beauty and the Beast's Beast has one nature. Replacing Jekyll: no other work in the view wakes in the other body.

claim: Andersen tells the cold-hearted child again from the inside. Kay is frozen by a splinter and a queen's kiss, cannot say the Lord's Prayer, and Gerda's tears thaw him. Helga is born cold; a foster-mother's kiss on the frog's forehead and Christ's name, found at last on her own lips, set her free.

from.exact: But love never entered thy heart; it is cold and clammy, like the plants on the moor.

to.exact: she had kissed away all feeling of cold from his body, and his heart was a lump of ice

alignments.same: A child under a spell has a heart too cold to love those who love it.
alignments.differs: Kay's heart is frozen from outside by a splinter of the troll's mirror; Helga's coldness is her father's nature, born in her with the marsh.

from.exact: she pressed a kiss on the forehead of the hideous frog-child

to.exact: and then she kissed his forehead. Ah! it was colder than ice

alignments.same: A woman's kiss on the child's forehead decides the spell.
alignments.differs: The Snow Queen's kiss freezes Kay and makes him forget his home; the Viking's wife kisses the hideous frog she has nursed, and the frog skin falls away for good.

from.exact: rose to her lips, and she uttered the words

to.exact: he tried to repeat the Lord's Prayer; but all he could do, he was only able to remember the multiplication table

alignments.same: Under the spell, holy words are what the child must say and cannot.
alignments.differs: Kay recalls only the multiplication table and is freed by Gerda's tears and hymn; Helga, having buried the priest who died for her, finds Christ's name herself.

question: Kay is saved by Gerda's tears; Helga must free a prisoner, bury him and find the holy name herself. Why does Andersen make the second child do the work of her own rescue?

substitution.note: Only The Snow Queen has a child whose heart is frozen by a spell, a kiss on the forehead that binds him, and a prayer he cannot say. The Little Mermaid's heroine is not cold and no kiss binds her; Beauty and the Beast's Beast is not cold-hearted and no holy words free him; Rappaccini's Beatrice is poisoned, not unloving. Replacing The Marsh King's Daughter: no other tale in the view frees a cold child by Christ's name on her own lips.

claim: Andersen turns Irving's homecoming into a death. Both lose a lifetime in what felt like one night and come back to be told they vanished long ago. Rip, who slept among ghosts, takes his seat again at the inn door; Helga, who lingered to look at heaven, has no place left and falls to dust.

from.exact: Three minutes only in heaven, and a whole night on earth had passed away!

to.exact: the whole twenty years had been to him but as one night

alignments.same: Years pass at home while the one away thinks only a night has gone.
alignments.differs: Rip sleeps after drinking the liquor of the ghostly bowlers; Helga begs for one more look at heaven at her own wedding feast.

from.exact: she vanished on the evening of her wedding day, many hundred years ago, and never came back

to.exact: it’s twenty years since he went away from home with his gun, and never has been heard of since

alignments.same: The returner asks after the past and is told the one in question vanished long ago and never came back.
alignments.differs: Rip's own daughter says it, and he can answer that he is her father; the stork speaks of a princess of his grandfather's time and tells Helga she dreamed it.

from.exact: The body crumbled into dust, and a faded lotus-flower lay on the spot on which Helga had stood.

to.exact: he took his place once more on the bench, at the inn door

alignments.same: The tale ends by settling where the returner belongs now.
alignments.differs: Rip is taken back into the village as an old man with a story; Helga's centuries cannot be lived, and only her soul rises while her body falls to dust.

question: Rip's lost years are a joke he lives to tell; Helga's are a judgment on a moment's longing. What does Andersen's lesson of the ostrich add to Irving's homecoming, and is the ending a punishment or a release?

substitution.note: Only Rip Van Winkle has a lifetime lost in what felt like one night and a returner told by those at home that the one asked for vanished and never came back. A Connecticut Yankee goes back thirteen centuries and is not told he vanished; The Time Machine's traveller returns the same evening; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod never returns. Replacing The Marsh King's Daughter: no other tale in the view ends the return in death.

claim: Stevenson folds the Grimms' twins into one man. The broom-maker's twins are alike and both good, so the one standing in for his lost brother keeps a sword between himself and the queen. Jekyll splits off an unjust twin, wills him his place, and can kill him only by killing himself.

from.exact: the unjust might go his way, delivered from the aspirations and remorse of his more upright twin

to.exact: The poor one had two children, who were twin brothers and as like each other as two drops of water.

alignments.same: A self is pictured as a pair of twins.
alignments.differs: Jekyll wants twins split into just and unjust, each free of the other; the broom-maker's twins are alike in face and in goodness, and promise to love each other till death.

from.exact: the said Edward Hyde should step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes

to.exact: It will be better if I pass myself off for him, and then I can rescue him more easily.

alignments.same: When one man goes missing, his double is to take his place in his house.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's will gives Hyde everything if Jekyll vanishes; the twin takes his brother's place only to find and free him, and lays a sword between himself and the queen.

from.exact: when I know how he fears my power to cut him off by suicide

to.exact: he became so jealous and angry that he drew his sword, and struck off his brother’s head.

alignments.same: One of the pair holds the other's life in his hand.
alignments.differs: The young king kills his twin in jealousy, repents, and the hare's root brings him back; Jekyll can end Hyde only by his own death, and pities him for loving life.

question: The Grimms' twin lays a sword in the bed he is given; Hyde takes all that Jekyll's will hands him. Is the faithful double a better self, or a double who was never made to want anything?

substitution.note: Replacing The Two Brothers: The Fall of the House of Usher has twins bound by sympathy, but neither takes the other's place or holds his life; Dorian Gray's double is a picture that takes no place in any house; The Man Who Was Thursday's Sunday is on both sides but no one is mistaken for another; Young Goodman Brown's fellow-traveller resembles him but is the devil, not a stand-in. No other work in the graph has a double take a missing man's place among his household and refuse his bed. Replacing Jekyll and Hyde: Dorian Gray splits no self into twins and wills no one his place; Usher's twins are sundered by burial, not by a will; Notes from Underground, The Yellow Wallpaper and The Murders in the Rue Morgue have doubles of the mind with no house to step into. Beauty and the Beast (merged during this stage): the Beast and the dream prince are one being in two shapes, but no double takes a missing man's place or holds his life, so it fails in either slot. Failed both ways, so passed. Works merged before this stage: The Fisherman and his Soul cuts his soul away and it comes back wicked, but it is no twin alike in goodness, takes no one's place in a household, and its death is not his; in The Marsh King's Daughter Helga is one girl split by day and night, with no twin to stand in for her and no will; The Little Mermaid, The Snow Queen and The Cask of Amontillado have no double; Andersen's memoirs and the Stevenson and Wilde reviews tell no such tale.

claim: Wilde turns the Grimms' life-token into a self. The knife in the tree rusts on the absent brother's side, and the twin who reads it rides to save him; Dorian reads only his own decay in the picture, and the blade he turns on it kills him.

from.exact: he himself would creep upstairs to the locked room, open the door with the key that never left him now

to.exact: he would just go and look at the knife that they had thrust in the trunk of a tree at their parting, that he might learn how his brother was.

alignments.same: A man back from his wanderings goes to look at the thing that shows how his other self is faring.
alignments.differs: The twin goes openly to a tree to learn of a brother far away; Dorian creeps to a locked room to see what his own life has made of his face.

from.exact: looking now at the evil and aging face on the canvas, and now at the fair young face that laughed back at him from the polished glass

to.exact: When he got there his brother’s side of the knife was half rusted, and half bright.

alignments.same: The token shows the spoiled and the bright side by side.
alignments.differs: Half-bright steel tells the twin his brother can still be saved, so he sets out; Dorian sets the bright face in the mirror against the spoiled one and only looks.

from.exact: He seized the thing, and stabbed the picture with it.

to.exact: he drew his sword, and struck off his brother’s head.

alignments.same: A man strikes with a blade at the double who has borne his part.
alignments.differs: The king cries that he has killed the brother who delivered him, and the root restores the twin; Dorian's knife is found in his own heart and the picture is whole again.

question: The Grimms' knife calls one brother to rescue the other; Dorian's picture calls no one but Dorian. What does Wilde make of a life-token that has no second person to read it?

substitution.note: Replacing The Two Brothers: Jekyll and Hyde has no token that shows a distant self's life (Jekyll's mirror shows Hyde only when he has changed); in The Fall of the House of Usher the fissure in the house is not read by anyone to learn a twin's state; The Monkey's Paw's charm grants wishes and shows nothing. No other work in the graph has an object left behind whose two halves tell whether an absent double lives, and a blade turned on that double. Replacing Dorian Gray: Jekyll strikes no blade at Hyde; Usher's Roderick buries his twin but strikes no blow; Frankenstein's Victor reads no token of the creature's state. Beauty and the Beast (merged during this stage): Beauty learns that the Beast is dying from a dream, not from a token left behind, and no blade is turned on a double, so it fails in either slot. Failed both ways, so passed. Works merged before this stage: The Snow Queen's mirror shard distorts Kay's sight but tells Gerda nothing of his life, and no blade is turned on it; The Fisherman and his Soul has no token of the absent soul's state, and he dies of grief, not by a blow; The Marsh King's Daughter and The Little Mermaid (whose sisters bring a knife she will not use on the prince) have no life-token; The Cask of Amontillado, Andersen's memoirs and the Stevenson and Wilde reviews have neither token nor double.

claim: MacDonald turns Andersen's sea tale round. Andersen's tearless mermaid saves a drowning prince unthanked and dies for him. MacDonald's prince 'saves' a princess who was only swimming, then drowns stopping her lake though she does not love him; she cannot keep his head above water, and her first tears bring him back and make her human.

from.exact: he brought her to shore in a fashion ignominious to a swimmer

to.exact: so she swam with the handsome prince to the beach

alignments.same: At night in the water, one of royal blood is carried to the shore by the one who will love them.
alignments.differs: The mermaid saves a drowning prince who never learns it was she; MacDonald's prince half drowns a princess who was only swimming, and she scolds him for it.

from.exact: But she never cried.

to.exact: only that the mermaids have no tears, and therefore they suffer more

alignments.same: The heroine who lives for the water cannot weep, even in her worst grief.
alignments.differs: The mermaid has no tears by her kind and suffers the more for it; the princess loses them to a curse and laughs at her parents' grief until her lake dies.

from.exact: She got hold of him, and held his head above the water

to.exact: She held his head above the water, and let the waves drift them where they would.

alignments.same: The heroine holds a drowning prince's head above the water.
alignments.differs: The mermaid's hold keeps her prince alive till morning; the princess's comes too late, for he has drowned stopping her lake, and he wakes only after she drags him home.
