question: Andersen's mermaid gives her life for a prince who never loves her; MacDonald gives the dying to the prince and lets it be undone. Is The Light Princess a comic answer to Andersen's sacrifice, or does it ask the same of love?

substitution.note: Only The Little Mermaid has a heroine of the water who cannot weep, a prince carried to shore at night, and a drowning head held above the water. Frankenstein's Creature drags a girl from a river but weeps and is never the one loved; Beauty and the Beast has no water rescue and Beauty weeps freely. Replacing The Light Princess: no other tale in the view gives the dying to the prince. Of the tales added to the view later: The Snow Queen and The Marsh King's Daughter have no drowning prince held above the water, and Wilde's mermaid in The Fisherman and His Soul is netted, not a rescuer.

claim: MacDonald moves the spell from the lover to the beloved. The Beast lies dying while Beauty forgets her promise, and her water and her avowal give him back his shape. The prince drowns by his own will for a princess who forgot him; she drags him from the water, and her grief breaks her own enchantment.

from.exact: As for the prince, she had forgotten him.

to.exact: I was dying because I thought you had forgotten your promise.

alignments.same: The lover comes near death while the beloved, taken up with something else, forgets him.
alignments.differs: The Beast dies of grief because Beauty stays at home too long; the prince chooses to drown in the hole of the lake for a princess who wants only her water back.

from.exact: Love and water brought back all her strength.

to.exact: she sprinkled it over his face, and, to her great delight, he began to revive

alignments.same: Finding her lover dying, the heroine brings him back with water.
alignments.differs: Beauty sprinkles fountain water on a fainting Beast; the princess must pull the drowned prince out of the water that killed him and row him home before he wakes.

from.exact: My darling child! she's found her gravity!

to.exact: I never knew how much I loved you until just now, when I feared I was too late to save your life.

alignments.same: Only the fear of losing her lover shows the heroine that she loves him, and the spell breaks.
alignments.differs: Beauty's love gives the Beast back his human shape; the princess's grief changes herself, and she falls to the floor with the weight she lacked.

question: Beauty's love disenchants the Beast; the princess's love disenchants herself. What does MacDonald gain by making the one who must change the one who is loved?

substitution.note: Only Beauty and the Beast has a lover dying of the beloved's forgetting who is revived with water and whose spell breaks when she owns her love. Jane Eyre returns to a maimed Rochester she never forgot; The Little Mermaid's prince is never revived by the one who loves him; Werther dies unrevived. Replacing The Light Princess: no other tale in the view puts the spell on the beloved. Of the tales added to the view later: in The Snow Queen Gerda never forgets Kay and no spell is on her, and in The Marsh King's Daughter the priest who dies for Helga is not revived; the claim is false for both.

claim: Both tales move on a captain who sails without a merchant and carries his goods, and on a king who has a stranger's story written into his archives. Sindbad claims his own bales and tells his tale to kings; Camaralzaman's jars find him through his disguised wife, who puts off hearing her own story from him.

from.exact: They belong to a merchant who was left behind

to.exact: but by mischance he was left behind upon a desert island where we had landed to fill up our water-casks

alignments.same: A captain tells a stranger of a merchant his ship sailed without, whose goods he still carries.
alignments.differs: Sindbad is that merchant and says 'look well at me' to claim his bales; Camaralzaman is a year away, and his wife, buying his olive jars, finds her talisman and sends for him.

from.exact: It shall be inscribed in the archives of my kingdom and published everywhere abroad.

to.exact: he ordered my adventures to be written in letters of gold and laid up in the archives of his kingdom

alignments.same: A king who has heard a stranger's whole story orders it written into his kingdom's archives.
alignments.differs: Sindbad's king keeps a sailor's wonders in gold letters as a treasure; the King of China records how a prince came disguised as an astrologer to win his daughter, and will publish it abroad.

from.exact: "I will hear it some other time," replied the princess.

to.exact: I told my story, concealing nothing

alignments.same: A stranger brought before a king offers him the whole strange story of how he came there.
alignments.differs: Sindbad's king hears it at once and rewards him; the king before Camaralzaman is Badoura in disguise, who puts off a story that is her own and answers it by taking off the king's dress.

question: Sindbad tells his own story at every port and at his own table; why does Camaralzaman's story have to be told by others, and kept from him by the wife who knows it?

substitution.note: Replacing Sindbad: no other work has both a captain carrying the goods of a merchant his ship left behind and a king who has a stranger's story written into his archives. Robinson Crusoe's goods are kept in trust by the Portuguese captain while he is thought dead, but no king records his tale; Gulliver tells his story to kings who keep no archive of it. Replacing Camaralzaman: no other work has the left-behind merchant's goods bought by a disguised wife and used to fetch him back.

claim: In both a stranger made king of a foreign people must take a wife there, and the wedding threatens to show what the king is. Badoura, a woman in her husband's clothes, tells her bride the truth, is kept secret and gives up the crown herself; Dravot seizes a terrified girl whose bite draws blood and shows him a man.

from.exact: I want a wife.

to.exact: take my daughter and my crown and stay with us

alignments.same: The foreigner on a throne is to be bound to the kingdom by marrying one of its women.
alignments.differs: Dravot demands a wife against his partner's warning and the Council's silence; Badoura has the bride pressed on her by a grateful old king and dares not refuse.

from.exact: The slut’s bitten me!

to.exact: I am not Prince Camaralzaman, but a princess like yourself and his wife

alignments.same: At the first meeting with the bride, the new king's secret is put to the test.
alignments.differs: Badoura tells her bride she is a woman and is embraced and kept secret; Dravot's bride, told she will die, bites him, and his blood gives him away.

from.exact: Neither god nor devil but a man!

to.exact: yesterday I was the king, to-day I am only the Princess of China

alignments.same: The false king is shown before the court for what he is.
alignments.differs: The priests' cry turns Dravot's army against him and ends in his death; Badoura unmasks herself, asks pardon for an innocent deception and hands the crown to her husband.

question: Badoura's deception is forgiven and Dravot's is punished; is the difference in the people deceived, in the bride, or in what each impostor wanted from the crown?

substitution.note: Replacing The Man Who Would Be King: Lord Jim marries Jewel in Patusan and King Solomon's Mines has Good and Foulata, but neither marriage threatens to unmask a stranger-king; Connecticut Yankee's Hank marries Sandy without being exposed; Heart of Darkness has Kurtz worshipped but no wedding; The Two Brothers' twin is taken for his brother the young King and passes himself off as him, but he takes another's place and is not made king by a wedding of his own. Replacing Camaralzaman: no other work has a disguised stranger made king through a royal marriage who confides in the bride.

claim: A princess who wants only the man she met by night is called mad, the healers fail, and her lover comes in a healer's robe. Badoura's madness is her father's word for her refusal, cured by a wedding he blesses; the Princess of Bengal plays mad herself, and the cure is a sham to steal her.

from.exact: she determined to feign madness

to.exact: You have lost your senses and you must be treated accordingly.

alignments.same: A princess who will marry no one but the stranger she met by night is held mad by the king who would marry her off.
alignments.differs: Badoura says plainly whom she wants and her father calls that madness and shuts her up; the Princess of Bengal chooses to rave so that the Sultan cannot wed her.

from.exact: as the cure depended neither on them nor their skill, but only on the princess herself

to.exact: This was the first of many suitors for the princess whose inability to cure her cost them their lives.

alignments.same: The king calls healers from far off with a reward for a cure, and every one of them fails.
alignments.differs: Badoura's failed curers are suitors who pay with their heads; the Sultan's doctors only go home, because the madness is hers to keep or end.

from.exact: Look at me, princess, and you will see that I am no doctor, but the Prince of Persia, who has come to set you free.

to.exact: As regards my person, your Majesty has rightly guessed that I am not an astrologer.

alignments.same: The lover in a healer's robe cures the princess by making himself known, and owns that he is no healer.
alignments.differs: Camaralzaman owns it to her father, who gives him her hand; Firouz whispers it to her alone and hides it from the Sultan, whose cure he then fakes in public.

question: Badoura is called mad for wanting her own husband, and the Princess of Bengal makes herself mad to keep hers; which tale gives the princess more say in her own cure?

substitution.note: Replacing Camaralzaman: no other work has a princess held mad for refusing a marriage whom a lover cures in a healer's disguise. Jane Eyre's Rochester disguises himself as a fortune-teller, but Jane is not held mad and no healers have failed; in Two Brothers and Beauty and the Beast no one feigns or is called mad. Replacing The Enchanted Horse: no other work has the madness feigned by the princess herself and the cure staged as a public sham.

claim: Both tales lose a saddled machine with paired controls to people who store it without knowing its use, and its rider wins it back by mounting it among them. The Time Traveller built it and keeps its levers; Firouz flies before learning its screws and recovers it only by a sham.

from.exact: this lever, being pressed over, sends the machine gliding into the future, and this other reverses the motion

to.exact: he discovered a tiny little peg, much smaller than the other, close to the right ear

alignments.same: A saddled machine is worked by one small control that sends it off and a second that brings it back.
alignments.differs: The Time Traveller explains both levers before anyone touches the model; Firouz turns the first screw before the Indian shows him the second, and hunts for it in the air.

from.exact: I have suspected since that the Morlocks had even partially taken it to pieces while trying in their dim way to grasp its purpose.

to.exact: he had ordered the enchanted horse to be taken to his treasury as a curiosity, though he was quite ignorant how it could be used

alignments.same: The machine is shut away by people who keep it but cannot work it.
alignments.differs: The Morlocks hide it in the Sphinx as bait for its maker; the Sultan keeps it as a curiosity and brings it out at the false doctor's word.

from.exact: But at last the lever was fixed and pulled over.

to.exact: Springing lightly up behind the lady, he leaned forward and turned the peg

alignments.same: The rider regains the saddle among those who hold the machine and is gone the moment he works the control.
alignments.differs: The Time Traveller fights off Morlock hands in the dark and leaves alone; Firouz hides in perfumed smoke before a crowd and carries his bride off with him.

question: The Time Traveller made his machine, while the horse came from an inventor no one sees, bought with a daughter; what does each tale make of a rider who does not understand what he rides?

substitution.note: Replacing The Enchanted Horse: no other work has a ridden machine taken and stored by people who cannot work it and won back by its rider among them. Twenty Thousand Leagues' Nautilus is never taken from Nemo; The Machine Stops has no machine one rides away on; Sindbad's roc is a bird he cannot steer and keeps nothing. Replacing The Time Machine: no other work has a saddled machine with paired controls explained, lost to captors and regained by fixing its lever.

claim: In both a stranger promises to break a spell before a seated ruler and a crowd, with smoke and meaningless words. Hank's show is the point and wins him the crowd while a pump does the work; Firouz invents the spell, and its smoke covers his flight with the princess.

from.exact: Behold, in another minute the spell will be broken, or no mortal can break it.

to.exact: a portion of its enchantment has by some means been communicated to her person, and it can only be dissipated by certain perfumes of which I possess the secret

alignments.same: A stranger who claims a secret says a spell lies on what others could not mend, and that he will lift it.
alignments.differs: Hank knows the well only leaks and stages the spell to beat Merlin; Firouz knows the princess only feigns, and makes the spell up from the Sultan's own tale.

from.exact: When you are going to do a miracle for an ignorant race, you want to get in every detail that will count

to.exact: give the court and the people one of the most astonishing spectacles they have ever witnessed

alignments.same: The healer asks for a public spectacle, with the ruler seated on a platform and the crowd held back.
alignments.differs: Hank sets the abbot's throne on his platform for effect; Firouz has the princess decked in crown jewels and seated on the horse, his means of escape.

from.exact: then slowly pronounced this ghastly word with a kind of awfulness which caused hundreds to tremble

to.exact: walked three times round the horse, muttering the while certain words

alignments.same: Amid smoke, the healer speaks words that mean nothing while the crowd watches.
alignments.differs: Hank's words and coloured fires are the show, ending with the water gushing; Firouz's muttering and smoke hide his leap into the saddle.

question: Hank's sham magic earns him a nation's awe and Firouz's earns him only a getaway; what does each tale think a crowd at a miracle is for?

substitution.note: Replacing A Connecticut Yankee: no other work has a stranger stage the breaking of a spell with smoke and gibberish before a seated ruler and a crowd. King Solomon's Mines' eclipse is foretold, not a spell broken, and has no smoke or words; Camaralzaman's astrologer cures by a letter without seeing the princess; The Man Who Would Be King's masonic signs are no spell. Replacing The Enchanted Horse: no other work's sham disenchantment is cover for an escape on what the crowd is watching.

claim: Both dress trained beasts as men and watch them turn back. Aesop's monkeys tear off their masks for a handful of nuts and the court laughs, sure of what they were; Moreau's Beast Folk shed their wrappings slowly, untempted, and Prendick comes home seeing Londoners as beasts about to revert.

from.exact: how they gave up bandagings and wrappings, abandoned at last every stitch of clothing

to.exact: Pulling off their masks and tearing their robes, they fought with one another for the nuts.

alignments.same: Beasts that were dressed to pass as men throw off the clothes and fall back into beasts.
alignments.differs: The monkeys strip in one moment, for a handful of nuts a courtier throws; the Beast Folk shed their wrappings over months, with no tempter, after their maker is dead.

from.exact: the stubborn beast-flesh grows day by day back again

to.exact: became (as indeed they were) Monkeys instead of actors

alignments.same: The teller says that under the training the animal was the animal all along.
alignments.differs: Aesop puts it in a parenthesis, a joke the audience shares; Moreau, who cut and taught his creatures himself, says it as a failure he still means to conquer.

from.exact: I could not persuade myself that the men and women I met were not also another Beast People

to.exact: they danced as well as any of the courtiers

alignments.same: Trained beasts in human dress pass among people as if they were people.
alignments.differs: Aesop's courtiers laugh at the monkeys once the masks fall; Prendick, back in London, turns the lesson round and fears the men and women he meets are beasts in human shape.

question: Aesop's audience laughs when the monkeys turn back; Prendick cannot laugh. What has changed between a beast that apes men and a man who suspects he is a beast?

substitution.note: Replacing Moreau: no other work has beasts trained to pass as men who shed their clothes and turn back. Tobermory's cat speaks but wears nothing and does not revert; Hyde is a man's own beast side, not a trained animal; the Rue Morgue ape copies its master's shaving but is never dressed or taught; Gulliver's Yahoos are men-shaped beasts nobody trained, and Gulliver's horror at his family has no shedding of dress before it. Replacing the fables: no other work has monkeys dressed for court who drop the act for nuts. Later works: the Little Mermaid and the Fisherman cross between kinds by a witch's bargain, not training, and never revert; Helga in the Marsh King's Daughter changes by day and night under a spell, not dress; the Snow Queen's crows and the Enchanted Horse play no man's part.

claim: In Aesop beasts flatter, plot and bait one another, and the reader takes the lesson. Saki's cat drops the flattery: asked about a guest's wit, he repeats her host's verdict. The people he quotes then sit like the mice in council, vote the cat poison, and set out bait he never takes.

from.exact: Sir Wilfrid protested that you were the most brainless woman of his acquaintance

to.exact: My good Crow, your voice is right enough, but your wit is wanting.

alignments.same: A talking animal tells a vain listener, who wants her gifts praised, that her wit is lacking.
alignments.differs: The fox flatters first to get the meat and gives the verdict as his own; Tobermory flatters no one and quotes Sir Wilfrid, so the insult lands on the host as well.

from.exact: both he and the stable cat must be done away with without delay

to.exact: the proposal to tie a bell to the neck of the Cat

alignments.same: A frightened company meets to decide what to do about a cat that goes where it likes among them.
alignments.differs: The mice want only warning of the cat's claws and no one dares bell him; the guests fear his tongue, want him dead, and Sir Wilfrid offers poison and drowning at once.

from.exact: A plateful of carefully dosed fish scraps was in readiness on the sideboard

to.exact: Ah, my good madam, even though you should turn into a meal-bag, we will not come near you.

alignments.same: One side lays a bait for the other and waits for it to come out, and it never comes.
alignments.differs: Aesop's cat baits the mice with her own feigned death and a mouse sees through it aloud; the guests bait the cat, who stays away only because the Rectory Tom has killed him.

question: Aesop's beasts teach men at a safe distance; what becomes of that distance when the beast sits at the tea-table quoting the guests by name?

substitution.note: Replacing Tobermory: no other work has a speaking animal who repeats men's verdicts on one another and is then condemned by a company in council. Moreau's Beast Folk talk but quote no one and are hunted for breaking the Law; Poe's black cat is killed by its owner alone and never speaks; Hadleyburg's town is shamed by a stranger's trick, not a beast. Replacing the fables: no other work has a council against a cat and a feigned bait the hunted refuse. Later works: the Snow Queen's crows talk and carry court news, but repeat no verdict on a listener and no company plots against them; the Marsh King's Daughter's storks gossip among themselves; no council, poison or bait in the Little Mermaid, Fisherman, Light Princess, Enchanted Horse or Adela Cathcart.

claim: Aesop's monkeys copy men and are caught out once: nuts end the court dance, the Fox mocks the boast among the tombs, and the audience laughs. Kipling makes the lapse a whole people's nature. The Bandar-log play at men in a dead king's city, forget at every falling nut, and are punished by never being noticed.

from.exact: scratch for fleas and pretend to be men

to.exact: Being naturally great mimics of men’s actions, they showed themselves most apt pupils

alignments.same: Monkeys copy men in a king's hall or a prince's court.
alignments.differs: Aesop's monkeys are taught by a prince and dance well enough to pass; the Bandar-log teach themselves in a dead king's council chamber and fool no one, not even themselves for long.

from.exact: the falling of a nut turns their minds to laughter and all is forgotten

to.exact: The Monkeys at the sight of the nuts forgot their dancing

alignments.same: A nut makes the monkeys forget what they were doing.
alignments.differs: In Aesop a courtier's thrown nuts end one show and the audience laughs; in Baloo's account any falling nut does it, and the laughter is the monkeys' own.

from.exact: The monkeys called the place their city, and pretended to despise the Jungle-People because they lived in the forest.

to.exact: are erected in honour of my ancestors, who were in their day freedmen and citizens of great renown

alignments.same: Among the stones of the dead, monkeys claim the builders' greatness as their own.
alignments.differs: Aesop's Fox answers one liar with a jibe that the dead cannot contradict him; Kipling's jungle answers the whole tribe by refusing to notice them, the one thing they crave.

question: Aesop's monkeys are laughed at; the Bandar-log are not even looked at. Which is the harder sentence on a creature that copies men, and why does Kipling's jungle need a Law to keep it?

substitution.note: Replacing Kaa's Hunting: no other work has a tribe of monkeys playing at men in a ruined king's city, forgetting at a falling nut, and shunned by beasts who will not notice them. Moreau's Ape-man copies speech but is one creature inside the Law; the Rue Morgue ape copies one man's shaving; Tobermory speaks but boasts of nothing. Replacing the fables: no other work has trained monkeys who drop their dance for nuts or a monkey boasting of ancestors among tombs.

claim: Kipling's Law of the Jungle is words a man-cub learns by heart so that beasts will help him; the monkeys who only steal words are outcasts, and a beating settles all scores. Wells turns it round: beasts chant a man's Law against their natures, an ape-man among them, and the House of Pain settles nothing.

from.exact: This Law they were ever repeating, I found, and ever breaking.

to.exact: he grew very tired of saying the same thing over a hundred times

alignments.same: The Law is a set of sayings learned by heart and said over and over.
alignments.differs: Mowgli recites so that every beast will help him, and the words save him in the Cold Lairs; the Beast Folk recite rules against their own natures and break them after dark.

from.exact: If ever I made a remark he did not understand, he would praise it very much, ask me to say it again, learn it by heart

to.exact: They have no speech of their own, but use the stolen words which they overhear when they listen

alignments.same: An ape repeats words it has overheard from others without understanding them.
alignments.differs: Kipling's monkey tribe steals the jungle's words and is shut out of its Law; Wells's Ape-man lives under the Law, calls himself a five-man, and makes borrowed words 'Big Thinks'.

from.exact: Evil are the punishments of those who break the Law. None escape.

to.exact: One of the beauties of Jungle Law is that punishment settles all scores. There is no nagging afterward.

alignments.same: Breaking the Law brings a set punishment that the learner is taught to expect.
alignments.differs: Bagheera's love-taps close the account and Mowgli rides home asleep on his back; the Beast Folk chant the House of Pain as an endless dread, and the Ape-man is branded.

question: Mowgli's Law lets a boy live among beasts; Moreau's Law asks beasts to live as men. Why does the one hold and the other break?

substitution.note: Replacing Moreau: no other work has beasts who chant a Law of sayings, an ape who learns men's words by heart, and a punishment house. The fables have no law the beasts learn; Gulliver's Houyhnhnms reason without a recited code; the Machine Stops has a book men consult, not beasts; Frankenstein's Creature learns words by overhearing but understands them and keeps no law; Tobermory repeats men's words to shame them, under no law. Replacing Kaa's Hunting: no other work has a child taught a beasts' Law word by word, with outcast monkeys who steal words and a punishment that settles all scores.

claim: In Kaa's Hunting a man-cub who knows the Snake Word is safe: cobras lower their hoods and ask only that he stand still, and the snake whose eyes hold beasts is his rescuer. In Rikki-Tikki-Tavi no word passes between boy and snake; a cobra freezes the family to strike, and the rescuer is a snake-killer.

from.exact: “I am Nag. The great God Brahm put his mark upon all our people

to.exact: “Even ssso! Down hoods all!” said half a dozen low voices

alignments.same: Cobras meet a newcomer and answer with their hoods.
alignments.differs: Mowgli gives the Snake's Call and the cobras lower their hoods; Rikki is a stranger with no word, and Nag spreads his hood and tells him to be afraid.

from.exact: Keep very still, all you three! If you move I strike, and if you do not move I strike.

to.exact: Stand still, Little Brother, for thy feet may do us harm.

alignments.same: A cobra tells a human child to keep still.
alignments.differs: The cobras ask Mowgli for stillness to keep their young from his feet, and he is safe; Nagaina's order buys Teddy nothing, since she means to strike either way.

from.exact: for a bird who looks at a snake’s eyes gets so frightened that she cannot move

to.exact: “Without thy order we cannot stir foot or hand, O Kaa!”

alignments.same: Whoever watches the snake cannot move.
alignments.differs: Kaa's dance holds the monkeys and even draws Baloo and Bagheera a step nearer; Darzee's wife will not look, and leads Nagaina away by pretending a broken wing.

question: Mowgli is saved by words he shares with the snakes, Teddy by a beast born to kill them. What does each story suppose a child needs to be safe among wild things?

substitution.note: Replacing Kaa's Hunting: no other work has cobras who lower their hoods to a child's word and bid him stand still, and a snake whose dance holds beasts motionless. Kim's cobra is spared but speaks no word; the fables' serpents only bite; Sindbad's serpent swallows men. Replacing Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: no other work has a cobra who freezes a family at table to strike a child.

claim: Aesop's serpents strike back at whoever hunts near them: the Crow that seizes a sleeping Serpent is bitten as it turns, and the Fowler watching a bird treads on a viper. Kipling's mongoose has studied that return stroke, picks where to bite the sleeping cobra, and lives; the fable's moral goes to a timid muskrat.

from.exact: Nag was asleep, and Rikki-tikki looked at his big back, wondering which would be the best place for a good hold.

to.exact: saw a Serpent asleep in a sunny nook, and flying down, greedily seized him

alignments.same: A hungry hunter finds a serpent asleep and attacks it.
alignments.differs: The Crow seizes greedily wherever it can; Rikki weighs back, neck and tail for an hour and chooses the head, so the snake cannot turn.

from.exact: but he was afraid of the terrible lashing return stroke of the cobra

to.exact: The Serpent, turning about, bit the Crow with a mortal wound.

alignments.same: The serpent turns on the one who has bitten or seized it.
alignments.differs: For Aesop the turn is the sting of the moral and kills the Crow; for Kipling it is a fact of natural history that a young mongoose fears and learns to avoid.

from.exact: “Those who kill snakes get killed by snakes,” said Chuchundra

to.exact: that while I purposed to hunt another, I am myself fallen unawares into the snares of death

alignments.same: The hunter of others will be killed by what he hunts.
alignments.differs: The Fowler learns it dying, and the fable bears him out; Kipling gives the saying to a muskrat who never dares the middle of the room, and the snake-killer survives.

question: Aesop's serpents teach that the hunter becomes the hunted; Kipling lets the muskrat say so and proves him wrong. Is the mongoose's skill an answer to the fable's warning, or only better luck?

substitution.note: Replacing the fables: no other work has a sleeping serpent seized by a hungry hunter and turning to bite, or a hunter of birds struck by the viper underfoot. Kaa's Hunting has snakes but none attacked asleep; Kim's cobra is left alone. Replacing Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: no other work has a beast that hunts a sleeping cobra and holds the head against the return stroke.

claim: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi takes the bungalow's side: Nag's claim to Brahm's mark is brushed off, a stick beats even a dead snake, and the garden is kept by killing. In Kim the lama stops the white boy's stick, calls the cobra a soul on the Wheel, and walks past its hood unharmed.

from.exact: “I have no stick—I have no stick,” said Kim. “I will get me one and break his back.”

to.exact: while Teddy’s father beat the dead Karait

alignments.same: A white man or boy reaches for a stick against a snake.
alignments.differs: Teddy's father beats a snake the mongoose has already killed; the lama stops Kim before he finds a stick, and the live cobra is let be.

from.exact: He is upon the Wheel as we are—a life ascending or descending—very far from deliverance.

to.exact: “Well,” said Rikki-tikki, and his tail began to fluff up again, “marks or no marks

alignments.same: The cobra is given a place in an Indian sacred order.
alignments.differs: Nag claims Brahm's mark himself, to frighten, and the mongoose waves it aside; the lama grants the cobra a soul and blesses it as a brother.

from.exact: He passed within a foot of the cobra’s poised head. It flattened itself among the dusty coils.

to.exact: till never a cobra dared show its head inside the walls

alignments.same: The cobra lowers its head before one who does not fear it.
alignments.differs: Rikki keeps the garden by killing until no cobra dares appear; the lama walks past a living cobra, which flattens and makes no sign.

question: Teddy's father calls the mongoose a providence; the lama calls the cobra a brother. Does Kim take back the sympathies of the earlier story, or only show the same garden from the other side?

substitution.note: Replacing Kim: no other work has a cobra spared because it is a soul on the Wheel, a boy's wish for a stick to break its back checked, and a holy man walking past its hood. Kaa's Hunting's cobras are kin by a word, not souls; A Passage to India's cobra is a stump. Replacing Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: no other work has a cobra claiming Brahm's mark and a garden kept by killing them.

claim: Ruskin turns the Grimms' luck into tests of charity. The Grimms' twins get rich on scraps fallen from a miser's roast, a huntsman's welcome to a cold old woman turns him to stone, and his twin frees him. Gluck gives his own slice away, refusing a cold old man ruins his brothers, and they stay stone.

from.exact: Gluck fitted the slice into the mutton again, with desperate efforts at exactitude

to.exact: she quickly killed a young cock, took out his heart and liver, and put them beside the golden bird

alignments.same: A piece goes missing from a miser's roast while a boy turns the spit, and someone hurries to hide the gap.
alignments.differs: The hungry twins eat the fallen bits by chance and wake to gold, and the wife hides the loss; Gluck cuts his own slice for a starving stranger, and the cut is found.

from.exact: I'll just let him in for a quarter of an hour.

to.exact: Come down, and warm thyself if thou art cold.

alignments.same: A cold old stranger begs for warmth, and a young man offers the fire.
alignments.differs: The Grimms' old woman is a witch who uses the welcome to turn the huntsman to stone; Ruskin's old man is the wind, and the brothers' refusal ruins them.

from.exact: And at the top of the cataract of the Golden River are still to be seen two black stones

to.exact: She took a wand and touched the stones, and then his brother with his animals came to life again

alignments.same: Brothers on a perilous errand are turned to stone.
alignments.differs: The Grimms' twin forces the witch to wake his brother; Ruskin's brothers, who mocked each other through prison bars, stay stone, and the place is named for them.

question: In the Grimms kindness to a cold old woman is a trap and chance makes the poor rich; in Ruskin every stranger is a test. Does Ruskin lose the Grimms' sense of luck, or answer it?

substitution.note: Only The Two Brothers has a miser's roast robbed at the spit, a cold old stranger asking to be warmed, and brothers turned to stone. Beauty and the Beast has a merchant sheltered in a palace but no spit, no petrified brothers; Rip Van Winkle sleeps but is not stone; The Monkey's Paw has no hospitality test; the double tales offered as peers (Jekyll and Hyde, Dorian Gray, Usher, The Fisherman and His Soul) have no robbed spit and no brothers turned to stone. Replacing The King of the Golden River: no other tale in the view leaves the brothers as stone. Also tried: The Marsh King's Daughter (a double-natured girl, a Viking's castle, a priest; no roast at the spit, no cold stranger warmed, no one turned to stone), Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (a mongoose fights cobras; no brothers, no hospitality test), the preface to The Jungle Book and Andersen's memoir of his childhood home (no story of either kind).

claim: Twain's stranger answers Ruskin's Southwest Wind. Both are slighted in passing and come back to ruin the whole place, and both tie gold to charity once shown a stranger in need. Ruskin's dying beggars are real tests that only the giver passes; Twain's beggar is invented, and his gilded lead catches men who lie that they gave.

from.exact: I wanted to damage every man in the place, and every woman—and not in their bodies or in their estate, but in their vanity

to.exact: after such a refusal of hospitality as I have just experienced, you will not be surprised if that visit is the last I ever pay you

alignments.same: A stranger who was slighted comes back to ruin all those who slighted him.
alignments.differs: Ruskin's wind takes the brothers' estate by flood and then drought; Twain's stranger spares bodies and estate and strikes at the town's pride in its honesty.

from.exact: There wasn’t any pauper stranger, nor any twenty-dollar contribution

to.exact: the water which has been refused to the cry of the weary and dying is unholy

alignments.same: Gold is promised to whoever once gave to a stranger in need.
alignments.differs: Ruskin's dying are real, and only the boy who gives his last water wins the river; Twain's pauper never existed, and the sack draws men who lie that they gave.

from.exact: Friends, they are only gilded disks of lead!

to.exact: we can put a great deal of copper into the gold without anyone's finding it out

alignments.same: The gold is not what it looks, and base metal hides under it.
alignments.differs: Ruskin's brothers debase gold to cheat buyers and lose their trade; Twain's stranger gilds lead as bait, and the cheat shames those who claim it, not its maker.

question: Ruskin's wind punishes the brothers for a refusal they made to his face; Twain's stranger punishes a town for an offence it may not know it gave. Which revenge is juster, and which tale still believes in its test?

substitution.note: Only The King of the Golden River has a stranger turned from the door who returns to ruin the place, gold won by charity to the dying, and debased gold. The Million Pound Bank-Note tests men with money but no slighted stranger; Young Goodman Brown has no gold; The Monkey's Paw grants money as a curse, not for charity; The Bet stakes money on a wager, with no beggar and no revenge. Replacing Hadleyburg: no other tale in the view invents the beggar. Also tried: The Marsh King's Daughter (no slighted stranger's revenge on a place, no gold tied to charity), Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (the snakes' revenge is on one household, with no gold or charity), the preface to The Jungle Book and Andersen's memoir of his childhood home (no such stranger or gold).

claim: Both comic tales keep the fairy tale's rules on purpose and bargain over the death the rules demand. MacDonald's prince haggles only to be fed while he truly drowns, and love must undo it; Grahame's saint and dragon fix the spot and the banquet beforehand, and the deadly combat harms no one.

from.exact: There ought to be a Princess. Terror-stricken and chained to a rock, and all that sort of thing.

to.exact: Of course he could not marry a mere woman, however beautiful; and there was no princess to be found worthy of him.

alignments.same: The hero's story is said to need a princess, as a rule of the kind rather than a wish of the heart.
alignments.differs: MacDonald's prince searches far and finds none worthy until he falls into her lake; St. George forgets her till the fight is fixed, asks the Boy to arrange one, and goes without.

from.exact: and that's where I come in

to.exact: the princess, your daughter, shall go with me, feed me with her own hands, and look at me now and then to comfort me

alignments.same: Before the deadly act, the one who is to lose it bargains over what he will get.
alignments.differs: The prince asks only to be fed and looked at while he really drowns; the dragon, who will not be hurt, bargains for the triumph and a seat at the banquet.

from.exact: the Saint had hit him in the spare place agreed upon, and it didn't even seem to tickle

to.exact: for he was resolved to die like a prince.

alignments.same: The death the tale demands is carried out with full ceremony before the court or the crowd.
alignments.differs: The prince dresses to die and truly drowns, and only the princess's love brings him back; the saint spears the dragon where they agreed, and the beast winks.

question: MacDonald lets his prince mean his sacrifice; Grahame lets no one mean the combat. Which tale takes the fairy tale's rules more seriously, and what is each one laughing at?

substitution.note: Only The Light Princess has a hero who treats the princess as a rule of his kind and haggles over terms before the death his tale demands. The Little Mermaid's bargain buys legs, not a death; A Connecticut Yankee mocks the rules from outside and strikes no terms with a foe; Beauty and the Beast's Beast dies unbargained. Replacing The Reluctant Dragon: no other tale in the view fixes the deadly fight beforehand. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (tried after it joined the view): its fights to the death are real and no one bargains over the death a fairy-tale rule demands.

claim: Both send a knight-errant into a land of tall tales about captive princesses and fire-breathing foes. Twain's Yankee sees through the tales, buys the princesses as hogs and routs knights with pipe smoke; Grahame's saint half doubts them yet keeps the rules, and the real dragon must relearn his fire to lose a fixed fight.

from.exact: Why, our villagers are the biggest story-tellers in all the country round.

to.exact: There never was such a country for wandering liars

alignments.same: The knight is sent to rescue on the word of tellers of wrongs who are known liars.
alignments.differs: The Yankee scorns the court for swallowing such tales and must ride out anyway; the Boy tells the saint the village lies, and the saint already found the tales 'not always quite convincing'.

from.exact: may there not be, at this very moment, some hapless Princess immured within yonder gloomy cavern?

to.exact: Her mistress was a captive in a vast and gloomy castle

alignments.same: A captive princess is imagined in the monster's gloomy hold.
alignments.differs: Sandy's princesses turn out to be hogs, which the Yankee buys and drives home; St. George's princess does not exist, and he is sorry he spoke of her.

from.exact: as to breathing fire, it's surprising how easily one gets out of practice

to.exact: then spouted a column of white smoke through the bars of my helmet

alignments.same: Smoke from the nostrils is what makes a dragon before mounted knights.
alignments.differs: The Yankee's pipe makes knights take a man for a dragon and yield; Grahame's real dragon must practise his fire again to play a beaten foe.

question: Twain's Yankee wins by refusing the knights' story; Grahame's Boy wins by staging it. Is The Reluctant Dragon kinder to chivalry than Twain, or does its fixed fight mock it more?

substitution.note: Only A Connecticut Yankee sends a knight out on liars' tales of princesses held in a gloomy hold, and has smoke breathed before knights make a dragon. The Light Princess has no dragon and no tale-tellers; Gulliver's Travels and Candide have no knights to rout; Sindbad's monsters are real. Replacing The Reluctant Dragon: no other tale in the view has a real dragon fake his own defeat. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (tried after it joined the view): a mongoose in a bungalow garden, with no knight, no tall tales and no captive princess.

claim: Both books ask who answers for a child nobody wanted. Victor flees his creature on its first night, and the Creature says misery made him a fiend. Oliver's mother dies, the surgeon goes to dinner, the parish rears him, and Fagin works solitude on him on purpose, yet he stays good.

from.exact: You needn’t mind sending up to me, if the child cries, nurse

to.exact: Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room

alignments.same: On the new being's first night, the man who brought it into the world turns his back on it and leaves.
alignments.differs: Victor flees in horror from the face of what he made and leaves it alone; the surgeon strolls off to dinner and leaves the crying child to a tippling nurse and the parish.

from.exact: If he could have known that he was an orphan, left to the tender mercies of churchwardens and overseers, perhaps he would have cried the louder.

to.exact: No father had watched my infant days, no mother had blessed me with smiles and caresses

alignments.same: A newborn has no father or mother to watch over it.
alignments.differs: The Creature learns his lack later, from watching a family, and holds it against his maker; Dickens's narrator says it over the crying infant, whom churchwardens and overseers will rear instead.

from.exact: he was now slowly instilling into his soul the poison which he hoped would blacken it, and change its hue for ever

to.exact: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.

alignments.same: Solitude and misery are named as what turns a young creature to evil.
alignments.differs: The Creature's solitude comes of his maker's desertion, and it does make him a murderer; Fagin plans Oliver's solitude in order to blacken him, and the poison never takes.

question: The Creature says misery made him a fiend; Oliver suffers hunger, beatings and Fagin's solitude and stays good. Does Dickens answer the Creature, or refuse to believe him?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has a maker who flees his new being on its first night, a creature who learns from watching a family that no father or mother watched him, and the plea that misery made him a fiend. Moreau stays with his beast men; Heathcliff is a foundling taken in, not fled; Jane Eyre and Mowgli lose parents but no maker turns from them. On the other side, only Oliver has a mother dying at the birth, a surgeon leaving for dinner, a parish rearing, and a Fagin who uses solitude to corrupt.

claim: Brontë takes Dickens's starved charity child into a girls' school and lets her tell it. Oliver gets gruel after a long grace, is called overfed when he strikes Noah, and is foretold the gallows. Jane gets burnt porridge for her soul's sake, is called a mad cat, and is branded a liar, and she answers each charge herself.

from.exact: you may indeed feed their vile bodies, but you little think how you starve their immortal souls!

to.exact: a long grace was said over the short commons

alignments.same: Charity children are kept on thin rations while their keepers give them prayer in place of food.
alignments.differs: Dickens's board starves paupers to save money, and the narrator mocks it from outside; Brocklehurst starves schoolgirls to save their souls, and Jane, one of the girls, hears him say so.

from.exact: Hold her arms, Miss Abbot: she’s like a mad cat.

to.exact: You’ve raised a artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am unbecoming a person of his condition

alignments.same: A dependent child flies at the bigger boy of the house, is dragged off and locked in a dark room, and the elders explain the outburst.
alignments.differs: Bumble blames meat, since a pauper fed too well grows a spirit above his station; Gateshead calls Jane a mad cat, and alone in the red-room she asks why she is always accused.

from.exact: this girl is—a liar!

to.exact: I know that boy will be hung.

alignments.same: A gentleman of the charity's board declares before others what the child is or will become.
alignments.differs: The white-waistcoated gentleman foretells the gallows for a boy who asked for more, and the book hangs Fagin instead; Brocklehurst brands Jane a liar before the school, and Miss Temple clears her name.

question: Dickens's narrator mocks the board from above; Jane meets Brocklehurst in her own voice. Which telling makes the charity's cruelty harder to bear, and why?

substitution.note: Only Oliver Twist has a workhouse board that serves gruel under a long grace, a beadle who blames the boy's outburst on meat, and a board gentleman who foretells his hanging; Vanka is beaten by a master but has no board or sermon, and Heathcliff and Kim are not kept by a charity. On the other side, only Jane Eyre has burnt porridge defended as food for the soul, a girl called a mad cat and locked in a room, and a girl branded a liar before a school.

claim: Dickens sends each man a faceless figure that foreshows a death, and each asks whether it can be averted. Scrooge's Phantom points him to his own grave while there is time, and he wakes to change the end. The signalman's spectre names no place or remedy, and its gesture proves to be the driver's at his death.

from.exact: I never saw the face. The left arm is across the face, and the right arm is waved.

to.exact: It was shrouded in a deep black garment, which concealed its head, its face, its form, and left nothing of it visible save one outstretched hand.

alignments.same: The apparition hides its face and speaks only by the gesture of one arm.
alignments.differs: The Phantom's hand points Scrooge onward and he follows it from scene to scene; the spectre's arm waves the signalman off the line, and when he runs to pull the sleeve away it is gone.

from.exact: Why not tell me how it could be averted—if it could have been averted?

to.exact: Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of things that May be, only?

alignments.same: The warned man asks whether the end the apparition shows is fixed or can still be changed.
alignments.differs: Scrooge gets no answer but argues that changed courses change the ends, and morning bears him out; the signalman cannot tell where the danger lies, dares not telegraph it, and the deaths come.

from.exact: I put this arm before my eyes, not to see, and I waved this arm to the last; but it was no use.

to.exact: read upon the stone of the neglected grave his own name, EBENEZER SCROOGE.

alignments.same: What the apparition foreshowed is the death of the very man who saw it.
alignments.differs: Scrooge reads his own name on a grave in a future he can still undo; the signalman's spectre was the driver's gesture at the moment he was cut down, seen beforehand and past undoing.

question: Scrooge's ghost shows what may be and leaves him time; the signalman's shows what will be and gives him nothing he can do. Why would Dickens, twenty-three years on, write a warning that cannot save?

substitution.note: Only A Christmas Carol has a faceless spirit that shows a man what is to come, ends at his own grave, and is asked whether its shadows are of things that will be or may be. The Haunted and the Haunters' phantoms replay an old crime; the Canterville ghost and Quint and Jessel foretell no death; Whistle's figure warns of nothing; The Monkey's Paw grants wishes but foreshows nothing; the Baskerville hound is a fraud. Replacing The Signal-Man: no other work has an apparition whose gesture repeats the death it forewarns, or a man asking how the shown disaster could be averted.

claim: Both books bring a ghost to a man who first explains it away. Marley speaks at length, wears the chain his life forged, and comes to save his partner's soul. Bulwer's theorist holds that the true soul cannot be called back: what appears is an earth-stained phantom raised by a living brain, and it comes for little or no object.

from.exact: As, then, it was my conjecture that all that was presented, or would be presented to my senses, must originate in some human being gifted by constitution with the power so to present them

to.exact: A slight disorder of the stomach makes them cheats.

alignments.same: Faced with a ghost, the man puts what he sees down to a natural cause in himself or in another.
alignments.differs: Scrooge's undigested beef is a joke to keep down his terror, dropped when the spectre shrieks; Bulwer's narrator holds his theory of a distant living mind through the night and after.

from.exact: compel, not that which ought properly to be called the SOUL, and which is far beyond human reach, but rather a phantom of what has been most earth-stained on earth

to.exact: I wear the chain I forged in life

alignments.same: What comes back from the dead is the part of a man bound to his earthly life.
alignments.differs: Marley's chain of cash-boxes is his own soul's penance, forged link by link of his free will; Bulwer's phantom is no soul at all, only an eidolon that another man's brain compels.

from.exact: if they speak, they utter no ideas above those of an ordinary person on earth

to.exact: I am here to-night to warn you, that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate.

alignments.same: The tale weighs what a returning ghost says and what it comes for.
alignments.differs: Marley comes on an errand of mercy and preaches that mankind was his business; Bulwer's theorist says spectres utter nothing above an ordinary person's ideas, and his phantoms only act out an old crime.

question: Marley's ghost comes to save Scrooge; Bulwer's narrator says a ghost is no soul and comes for nothing. Which book is more afraid of the dead, and which of the living?

substitution.note: Only A Christmas Carol has a dead man's ghost who comes in the chain of his life to save a living friend, after being called indigestion. Usher, Canterville, Turn of the Screw, The Signal-Man and Whistle have apparitions, but none returns to preach a reform: the Canterville ghost wants rest, Quint and Jessel want the children, the signal-man's spectre warns of an accident; Dracula's Count is undead and speaks, but comes to feed, not to warn; Northanger Abbey, Seven Gables and The Yellow Wallpaper have no dead man who returns to speak. Replacing The Haunted and the Haunters: The Signal-Man's narrator also reasons with nerves, and Whistle's professor disbelieves, but neither holds that the soul cannot return and that a phantom is an earth-stained eidolon raised by a living brain.

claim: Oliver Twist shows the workhouse from inside, through a boy the board starves and a white-waistcoated gentleman dooms to the gallows. The Carol puts the board's creed in a rich man's mouth: Scrooge sends the poor to prisons and workhouses. Then a Spirit quotes him back over Tiny Tim and two starved children, and he repents.

from.exact: And the Union workhouses?

to.exact: of being starved by a gradual process in the house, or by a quick one out of it

alignments.same: The workhouse is offered as all the poor need, by men who will not feed them.
alignments.differs: The board's rule is seen from the gruel bowls of the children it starves; Scrooge asks after the workhouses at his desk, to two gentlemen collecting for the poor, as his reason to give nothing.

from.exact: If he be like to die, he had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.

to.exact: than I am that that boy will come to be hung

alignments.same: A comfortable gentleman pronounces the death of a poor child.
alignments.differs: The white waistcoat repeats his prophecy and is never called to account; the Spirit hands Scrooge his own words over the crippled Tiny Tim, and Scrooge hangs his head in penitence and grief.

from.exact: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.

to.exact: where twenty or thirty other juvenile offenders against the poor-laws, rolled about the floor all day

alignments.same: Children of the poor are shown as a class the law has made, hungry and half-clothed.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator mocks the parish for calling infants offenders against the poor-laws; the Spirit shows two wretched children under his robe as Man's own, with Doom written on the boy's brow.

question: Oliver Twist mocks the board but never converts it; the Carol converts one man in a night. Is Scrooge's change an answer to the workhouse, or a way of not answering it?

substitution.note: Only Oliver Twist has a workhouse board whose rule starves the poor 'by a gradual process in the house', a board gentleman who keeps foretelling a pauper boy's hanging, and infants farmed as 'juvenile offenders against the poor-laws'. Jane Eyre's Lowood starves girls but is a school, and Brocklehurst foretells hell, not the gallows; Vanka and Kim have no parish, and Whistle (the Carol's heading peer) has no poor at all. Replacing the Carol: no other work has a rich man who points the poor to prisons and workhouses and then hears a spirit quote his words back over a dying child.

claim: Hard Times turns the parish orphan's story into a rich man's boast. Bounderby claims Oliver's childhood: a mother who left him, hunger, letters learnt under a thief. At the end, as in Oliver Twist, a hidden parent is brought before witnesses; but where Oliver's birth gives him a name, Mrs. Pegler proves Bounderby's misery a lie.

from.exact: ‘My mother left me to my grandmother,’ said Bounderby

to.exact: If he could have known that he was an orphan, left to the tender mercies of churchwardens and overseers, perhaps he would have cried the louder.

alignments.same: A child is left by his mother to keepers who beat and starve him.
alignments.differs: Oliver's narrator tells it for a baby who cannot know it; Bounderby tells it of himself, by the fire on his birthday, as a boast, and it is untrue.

from.exact: under the direction of a drunken cripple, who was a convicted thief, and an incorrigible vagrant

to.exact: You’d like to be able to make pocket-handkerchiefs as easy as Charley Bates, wouldn’t you, my dear?

alignments.same: A London street boy gets his first schooling from a thief.
alignments.differs: Fagin's lessons are a trap Oliver must be rescued from; Bounderby names his thief-tutor with pride, as proof that he made himself.

from.exact: though he come of humble parents, he come of parents that loved him as dear as the best could

to.exact: is your half-brother; the illegitimate son of your father, my dear friend Edwin Leeford, by poor young Agnes Fleming, who died in giving him birth.

alignments.same: Near the end a parent's story is told before a gathered company, and a man's birth is known at last.
alignments.differs: Brownlow's tale gives the workhouse boy a name and a legacy; Mrs. Pegler's tale of a loving mother, paid to keep away, strips Bounderby of the hard childhood he sold.

question: Oliver's suffering is real and his rescue is a gift; Bounderby's suffering is a story he tells for credit. What does Dickens think the self-made man has done with the orphan's tale?

substitution.note: Replacing Oliver Twist: no other work has a workhouse orphan schooled in pocket-picking whose hidden parentage is told before a gathered company. Jane Eyre's charity child learns her uncle's legacy by letter; Wuthering Heights's Heathcliff is taken in, never schooled by thieves; Kim learns his father's name from an amulet, not a witness; Christmas Carol's poor children have no hidden birth. Replacing Hard Times: no other work has a rich man who boasts a foundling's childhood and is shamed when his mother is fetched into his dining-room.

claim: Both books school people against seeing for themselves and shame the parent of a child who looks. Gradgrind wants facts without fancy, so no child of his sees a face in the moon. Forster's Machine wants ideas without facts: Kuno sees a man in the stars and climbs out to see them, and his mother dislikes the stars.

from.exact: The four big stars are the man's shoulders and his knees.

to.exact: No little Gradgrind had ever seen a face in the moon

alignments.same: The book asks whether a child may see a figure in the sky.
alignments.differs: The Gradgrinds dissect the Great Bear and never see a face; Kuno finds a man in Orion for himself, and his mother, raised by the Machine, doubts there is much in it.

from.exact: Let your ideas be second-hand, and if possible tenth-hand, for then they will be far removed from that disturbing element—direct observation.

to.exact: Why, then, you are not to see anywhere, what you don’t see in fact; you are not to have anywhere, what you don’t have in fact.

alignments.same: A lecturer rules what his hearers may take in and forbids the rest.
alignments.differs: Gradgrind's officer bans whatever is not seen in fact; Forster's lecturer bans the seeing itself, and wants the French Revolution at tenth hand, beyond facts.

from.exact: Was he really the little boy to whom she had taught the use of his stops and buttons, and to whom she had given his first lessons in the Book?

to.exact: Thomas and you, to whom the circle of the sciences is open

alignments.same: A parent finds that the child they schooled has gone to look at the forbidden thing, and is ashamed.
alignments.differs: Gradgrind catches Louisa at a hole in the circus booth and leads her home; Kuno has climbed to the surface of the earth, and Vashti, ashamed to have borne him, knows he is fated.

question: Gradgrind starves fancy to feed facts; Forster's lecturer starves facts to feed ideas. Are these opposite mistakes, or one mistake made twice?

substitution.note: Replacing Hard Times: no other work has a schoolroom that forbids fancy, children who never saw a face in the moon, and a father who finds his daughter peeping at a circus. The Country of the Blind calls talk of the sky fancy but schools no children; Flatland's Council forbids talk of a Third Dimension and the Square's grandson takes back his guess, but no schoolroom bans fancy and no child peeps at a show; Candide's Pangloss teaches a creed, not facts. Replacing The Machine Stops: no other work has a lecturer who bans first-hand observation, a son who sees a man in the stars, and a mother taught by a Book who dislikes them; the Time Machine's Eloi are not schooled at all.

claim: Dickens keeps the Grimms' look-alike rescuer but takes away the root of life. Onlookers cannot tell the two men apart, and the double passes for the other to save him, keeping apart from his wife. The Grimm twin loses his head to a jealous brother and is healed; Carton loses his for his rival and stays dead.

from.exact: they were sufficiently like each other to surprise, not only the witness, but everybody present, when they were thus brought into comparison

to.exact: Each of them looks exactly like the other, I cannot tell.

alignments.same: Two look-alike men are set side by side before an authority who must say which is which.
alignments.differs: The Grimm princess finds her husband by her clasp on the lion; at the Old Bailey nobody need choose, because the likeness itself breaks the witness and frees Darnay.

from.exact: Sydney Carton. Advocate. English. Which is he?

to.exact: The sentries, indeed, thought no otherwise than that he was the young King himself, for he looked so like him

alignments.same: Guards at a city gate take one man for the other, and the mistake serves a rescue.
alignments.differs: The Grimm sentries let the free twin in as the lost king; the Paris guards let the drugged Darnay out under Carton's papers, while Carton waits in his cell under his name.

from.exact: between whom and you there is an impassable space

to.exact: but he laid a two-edged sword between him and the young Queen

alignments.same: The double who could stand in the husband's place keeps a barrier between himself and the wife.
alignments.differs: The sword keeps faith for a few nights and is explained to the queen; Carton's space is his own unworthiness, and he keeps it for years while he loves Lucie.

question: The Grimm brother is beheaded for having slept beside the queen and is healed by a root; Carton is beheaded for Lucie's husband and lives on in a child's name. Which story is kinder to the man who stands in?

substitution.note: Replacing Two Brothers: no other work has two look-alikes whom an authority cannot tell apart, gate guards who take one for the other, and a double who keeps apart from the wife. Jekyll's Hyde takes Jekyll's place but looks unlike him; Dorian's double is a picture; The Man Who Was Thursday has men in disguise, none taken for a look-alike. Replacing A Tale of Two Cities: no other work in the view has a double who passes for a rival and dies in his place.

claim: Dickens gives one face to a better and a worse man; Stevenson, two faces to one man. Carton finds nothing to like in his face, wishes to change places with Darnay, and dies in his clothes so Darnay may live. Jekyll welcomes Hyde's face, wills him his place, and Hyde dies in the doctor's clothes.

from.exact: And yet when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome.

to.exact: why should you particularly like a man who resembles you? There is nothing in you to like; you know that.

alignments.same: A man looks at his own face in a glass after meeting his other self.
alignments.differs: Jekyll welcomes the worse self's face as his own; Carton sees the face he shares with the better man, finds nothing in it to like, and says he hates him.

from.exact: the said Edward Hyde should step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes

to.exact: Change places with him, and would you have been looked at by those blue eyes as he was

alignments.same: The worse self imagines taking the better man's place.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's will hands his place to Hyde if he dies or disappears; Carton, drunk at the glass, wishes it only to be loved, and changes places in the end to die.

from.exact: He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor’s bigness

to.exact: Carton dressed himself in the clothes the prisoner had laid aside, combed back his hair, and tied it with the ribbon the prisoner had worn.

alignments.same: The worse of the two dies wearing the better man's clothes.
alignments.differs: Hyde is found poisoned in clothes too big for him, and the doctor is gone with him; Carton's borrowed clothes fit, and the man who wore them rides away alive.

question: Carton dies in Darnay's clothes and Hyde dies in Jekyll's. Is the worse self in each book destroyed, or does it become, at the end, the better one?

substitution.note: Replacing A Tale of Two Cities: no other work has a dissolute man who sees his own face in a better rival, wishes at a glass to change places, and dies in the rival's clothes. The Two Brothers' twins are both good and both live; Dorian's portrait never wears his clothes; Usher's twin is buried, not exchanged. Replacing Jekyll and Hyde: no other work has a will that gives the worse self the better man's place and a death in the doctor's clothes; Dorian dies in his own.

claim: Both orphans are made rich by a man overseas, while a woman who resents them hides the truth about the giver. Jane's dead uncle leaves her a fortune, which she shares openly with her cousins. Pip's comes from the living convict he once fed, and his one good use of it is secret.

from.exact: Yes, Pip, dear boy, I’ve made a gentleman on you! It’s me wot has done it!

to.exact: your uncle, Mr. Eyre of Madeira, is dead; that he has left you all his property, and that you are now rich

alignments.same: A man who went abroad and grew rich proves to be the orphan's benefactor, and the news makes the orphan rich.
alignments.differs: Jane's giver is her father's brother, speaking by will after his death; Pip's is the convict he fed on the marshes, back alive at risk of hanging to see his gentleman.

from.exact: she returned, again nodding steadily, “I let you go on.”

to.exact: I said I was sorry for his disappointment, but Jane Eyre was dead

alignments.same: A woman of the house who bears the orphan a grudge admits she kept the truth about the benefactor from them.
alignments.differs: Mrs. Reed told the uncle Jane was dead, out of hatred; Miss Havisham let Pip think her the giver, to vex her kin, and asks who she is to be kind.

from.exact: The whole business was so cleverly managed, that Herbert had not the least suspicion of my hand being in it.

to.exact: twenty thousand pounds, the sum in question, divided equally between the nephew and three nieces of our uncle

alignments.same: The newly rich orphan turns the money to the good of a friend or kin who has none.
alignments.differs: Jane splits the legacy openly into four shares and gains a family; Pip buys Herbert a partnership in secret, becoming to Herbert the hidden patron Magwitch was to him.

question: Jane insists that the money be shared in the open; Pip hides his gift as his own was hidden from him. Why does Pip choose secrecy, and which book trusts a known gift more?

substitution.note: Replacing Jane Eyre: Oliver Twist's father's will is hidden by his half-brother, not by a woman who resents him, and Oliver shares nothing; The Sign of the Four sends Mary Morstan pearls from an unknown giver in London, with no will and no woman hiding him; Kim's schooling is paid openly by the lama; Wuthering Heights' Heathcliff grows rich abroad but makes no orphan rich. Replacing Great Expectations: no other work in the view has a convict benefactor or an orphan who makes himself a secret patron.

claim: Both books bring a visitor into a shut, rotting house to divert its sick owner, and the house falls when that life ends. Roderick thinks the stones shaped his family for centuries, and the house sinks with its last two. Miss Havisham stopped the clocks herself; her house is auctioned for building materials.

from.exact: I want diversion, and I have done with men and women. Play.

to.exact: with a view of attempting, by the cheerfulness of my society, some alleviation of his malady

alignments.same: A visitor is brought into the dark house to lift the spirits of its sick, shut-in owner.
alignments.differs: Usher writes for his one friend, and they read and paint together; Miss Havisham has a village boy sent, orders him to play, and sets Estella to break his heart.

from.exact: she laid the whole place waste, as you have seen it, and she has never since looked upon the light of day

to.exact: that silent, yet importunate and terrible influence which for centuries had moulded the destinies of his family

alignments.same: The ruin of the house and the sickness of the one who lives in it are one and the same.
alignments.differs: Roderick believes the grey stones, fungi and tarn shaped his family over centuries; Miss Havisham made the waste herself, stopping the clocks at the minute the jilting letter came.

from.exact: The House itself was to be sold as old building materials, and pulled down.

to.exact: the deep and dank tarn at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments of the “House of Usher.”

alignments.same: The house of the last of a family is destroyed once its master or mistress is dead.
alignments.differs: Usher's house splits and sinks the instant its last two die, as if one body with them; Satis House is sold in lots and pulled down for its bricks.

question: Poe's house dies with its family as if it were alive; Dickens's ends at an auction. Did Satis House ever have a life of its own, or only the one Miss Havisham lent it?

substitution.note: Replacing Usher: The House of the Seven Gables has Phoebe come to cheer the shut-in Clifford in a house 'like a great human heart', but the house stands and the family goes on; The Haunted and the Haunters' house is haunted by a living will and only one room is to be pulled down; Jane Eyre's Thornfield burns, but Jane is hired as governess and Rochester lives; Turn of the Screw, Canterville Ghost and Yellow Wallpaper have no house destroyed with its family. Replacing Great Expectations: no other work has an owner who stopped the clocks herself.

claim: Both books turn a man who lives for his coins into father to a child not his own. Scrooge chose Gain over Belle, is shown the daughter he might have had, and wakes to be Tiny Tim's second father. Silas is robbed, and a sleeping child lies where he thought he saw his gold.

from.exact: His gold, as he hung over it and saw it grow, gathered his power of loving together into a hard isolation like its own.

to.exact: I have seen your nobler aspirations fall off one by one, until the master-passion, Gain, engrosses you.

alignments.same: The money a man watches grow draws all his love into itself, until nothing else holds him.
alignments.differs: Scrooge's Gain displaces a living girl who tells him so to his face; Silas's guineas fill a heart already emptied when a false lot cost him his faith, friend and betrothed.

from.exact: instead of the hard coin with the familiar resisting outline, his fingers encountered soft warm curls

to.exact: such another creature, quite as graceful and as full of promise, might have called him father

alignments.same: By a fireside, the man who has loved money is set before a little girl who might be his own.
alignments.differs: Scrooge sees Belle's daughter at another man's hearth, a might-have-been shown by a Spirit; Silas's gold is truly gone, and a stranger's child sleeps on his own floor.

from.exact: the child was come instead of the gold—that the gold had turned into the child

to.exact: to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father.

alignments.same: The tale ends with the lover of money become a father to another man's child.
alignments.differs: Scrooge keeps his fortune and gives it out, raising Bob's salary and saving Tim; Silas has nothing left to give, and the child does not use his money but takes its place.

question: Scrooge is frightened into spending his money on others; Silas loses his and is handed a child he never asked for. Which book thinks a hoarder can choose to change?

substitution.note: Replacing A Christmas Carol: Fagin in Oliver Twist gloats over a hidden box of watches and rings but no child takes its place; the greedy brothers of The King of the Golden River and the townsfolk of Hadleyburg are tested by gold and never become fathers; Oh, Whistle has a haunted bachelor but no money and no child; in Hard Times Gradgrind takes in Sissy, but he is no hoarder and loses no gold. Replacing Silas Marner: no other work has a miser who sees the daughter he lost to Gain and ends a second father. Great Expectations and A Tale of Two Cities, tried later, fail too: Magwitch calls himself Pip's second father but hoards nothing for himself, Miss Havisham's Estella replaces no gold, and no miser in either book is shown the daughter he gave up for Gain.

claim: Both books begin a child's life beside a vagrant mother dead after a long walk, the child bound for the parish. Dickens's surgeon sees no ring; the ring is stolen from the corpse and at last sunk in the river. Eliot's dead woman wears hers, and a weaver keeps the child and the ring.

from.exact: She’s got a wedding-ring on, however. They must fetch her away to the workhouse to-morrow.

to.exact: no wedding-ring, I see

alignments.same: A doctor looks over a ragged young mother dead in the cold, and his first remark is on her wedding-ring.
alignments.differs: Dickens's surgeon finds none and reads the old story of shame; Kimble finds one yet still sends her to the workhouse, while her husband, the squire's son, stands by silent.

from.exact: Will they make me take her?

to.exact: If he could have known that he was an orphan, left to the tender mercies of churchwardens and overseers, perhaps he would have cried the louder.

alignments.same: The orphan's next keepers are to be the parish officers.
alignments.differs: Oliver passes to churchwardens and overseers with no one to object; Silas refuses at once, and Eppie later says that but for him the workhouse would have taken her.

from.exact: had been carefully preserved by him in a little lackered box shaped like a shoe

to.exact: dropped it into the stream

alignments.same: The dead mother's ring outlives her as the one token of the child's birth.
alignments.differs: Old Sally steals it, it is pawned and redeemed, and Monks sinks it to blot out Oliver's claim; Silas keeps it for Eppie, who hardly thinks of the father it stands for.

question: Oliver's ring is a proof that bad men destroy and good men must recover; Eppie's is kept openly and hardly looked at. Why does Eliot let her foundling care so little who her father was?

substitution.note: Replacing Oliver Twist: Jane Eyre and Wuthering Heights have orphans taken in, but no mother dead on the road, no doctor's word on a ring and no parish; Kim carries his father's papers in an amulet, but his mother is not found dead and no parish claims him; A Christmas Carol has Tiny Tim but no dead mother or ring; Hard Times's Sissy is left by a living father, not by a mother dead on the road. Replacing Silas Marner: no other work sets a ring on a dead vagrant mother's finger beside the child the parish would take. Great Expectations and A Tale of Two Cities, tried later, fail too: Pip's mother lies in the churchyard and he is raised by his sister, Estella's mother lives, and neither book has a vagrant mother dead on the road, a ring or a parish.

claim: Cooper takes Irving's psalm-singing master out of a Dutch valley and into a frontier war. Both are drawn as gangling limbs on a poor mount, and both answer terror with a psalm. Ichabod's tune dies in his throat and he vanishes; Gamut sings on through a massacre, and the Hurons spare him as mad.

from.exact: His head was large; his shoulders narrow; his arms long and dangling; while his hands were small, if not delicate.

to.exact: He was tall, but exceedingly lank, with narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, hands that dangled a mile out of his sleeves

alignments.same: The teacher of psalmody is drawn limb by limb for laughter: tall, narrow in the shoulders, with long dangling arms.
alignments.differs: Ichabod has a small flat head and shovel feet, a scarecrow or famine walking; Gamut has a large head and small, almost delicate hands, misbuilt rather than starved.

from.exact: Notwithstanding a constant application of his one armed heel to the flanks of the mare

to.exact: He rode with short stirrups, which brought his knees nearly up to the pommel of the saddle

alignments.same: The singing-master rides a poor beast badly, and horse and man are painted together as a comic picture.
alignments.differs: Ichabod jogs to a frolic on a borrowed plough-horse, elbows flapping; Gamut, one heel spurred, chases soldiers through the forest on a lopsided mare.

from.exact: who now appeared to the astonished natives gifted with the protecting spirit of madness

to.exact: shutting his eyes, broke forth with involuntary fervor into a psalm tune

alignments.same: Facing what may kill him, the singing-master's one answer is to raise a psalm.
alignments.differs: Ichabod's tune dies when his tongue cleaves to his mouth, and he flees and vanishes; Gamut sings on after Cora through the massacre, and the Hurons let him pass as mad.

question: Ichabod's psalm cannot save him from the headless rider; Gamut's carries him unharmed through a massacre. Is Cooper laughing at the singing-master as Irving does, or giving his folly a power Irving denies it?

substitution.note: Replacing Sleepy Hollow: no other work has a lank teacher of psalmody, comic on a poor horse, who strikes up a psalm when terror comes. Moby-Dick's Bildad sings hymns at the helm but is no singing-master and is never in danger for it; Rip Van Winkle's schoolmaster Van Bummel only reads the newspaper. Replacing The Last of the Mohicans: no other work has a psalm-singer whom warriors spare as mad. Christmas Carol, Great Expectations, Hard Times, Silas Marner and A Tale of Two Cities have no singing-master on a poor horse who answers danger with a psalm.

claim: Both tales show an old man of the Hudson country waking to a land with new masters. Rip sleeps twenty years, finds King George repainted as Washington, and settles on the inn bench as the village chronicle. Tamenund has lived every winter of his century, dreams Uncas's youth back, and wakes to see the last Mohican.

from.exact: has Tamenund been a sleeper for a hundred winters?

to.exact: I was myself last night, but I fell asleep on the mountain, and they’ve changed my gun, and everything’s changed, and I’m changed

alignments.same: An old man who has lost hold of the time he is in cries out whether he has slept the years away.
alignments.differs: Rip really slept twenty years in one night and wakes among his own grown village; Tamenund lived all hundred winters and only takes young Uncas for the Uncas of his youth.

from.exact: that the children of the Lenape were masters of the world

to.exact: instead of being a subject to his Majesty George the Third, he was now a free citizen of the United States

alignments.same: The old man learns that rule over the land has passed to others in the years he lost.
alignments.differs: For Rip the new masters are a new face on the inn sign and cost him nothing; Tamenund recalls his people ruling the world and now camps among their enemies' mountains.

from.exact: have I lived to see the last warrior of the wise race of the Mohicans

to.exact: was reverenced as one of the patriarchs of the village, and a chronicle of the old times “before the war.”

alignments.same: The old man ends as the patriarch who keeps the memory of the time before.
alignments.differs: Rip's old times become a tale for every stranger at the hotel while his village thrives; Tamenund speaks at Uncas's burial and says his day has been too long.
