question: Rip's revolution changes a signboard; Tamenund's change of masters ends a people. What does Cooper's old man see on waking that Irving's never has to?

substitution.note: Replacing Rip Van Winkle: no other work has an old man who sleeps twenty years and wakes to find the King's face on the inn sign repainted as Washington. The Time Machine and Connecticut Yankee cross centuries by machine or blow, but neither wakes to a repainted inn sign or sits on as a village chronicle. Replacing The Last of the Mohicans: no other work has a patriarch who asks whether he has slept a hundred winters and lives to see the last of his people's race. A Tale of Two Cities comes nearest: Dr Manette loses eighteen years in the Bastille and takes Lucie for her mother, but he is a Paris prisoner, not a sleeper in the Hudson hills, finds no repainted inn sign and is no village chronicle; Christmas Carol, Great Expectations, Hard Times and Silas Marner have no old man who wakes to new masters.

claim: Both tales end in a frame where a sober man weighs a tall tale told aloud. Irving gives the grave face to a listener who demands the moral; his teller believes half of it. Twain gives the gravity to the teller, who admires his heroes in earnest, and the listener, finding no use in it, walks out mid-yarn.

from.exact: He never smiled, he never frowned, he never changed his voice from the gentle-flowing key to which he tuned his initial sentence

to.exact: one tall, dry-looking old gentleman, with beetling eyebrows, who maintained a grave and rather severe face throughout

alignments.same: While the tall tale is told, one man in the frame keeps a grave, unmoved face from start to finish.
alignments.differs: Irving's grave face belongs to a doubting listener among laughing aldermen; Twain moves it to the teller, who tells of the frog without once seeing anything funny.

from.exact: he regarded it as a really important matter, and admired its two heroes as men of transcendent genius in finesse

to.exact: “Faith, sir,” replied the story-teller, “as to that matter, I don’t believe one-half of it myself.”

alignments.same: The frame reports what the teller himself makes of his tale.
alignments.differs: Irving's teller winks and believes only half; Wheeler believes all of it and holds Smiley and the stranger to be geniuses.

from.exact: I did not think that a continuation of the history of the enterprising vagabond Jim Smiley would be likely to afford me much information concerning the Rev. Leonidas W. Smiley, and so I started away.

to.exact: what was the moral of the story, and what it went to prove?

alignments.same: A sober hearer asks what the tale is good for.
alignments.differs: Irving's burgher stays to demand the moral and is given a mock syllogism; Twain's narrator wanted facts about another Smiley, gets none, and leaves before the end.

question: Irving's teller believes half his tale and his grave listener wants a moral; Wheeler believes all of his and his listener wants none. Who is the joke on in each frame?

substitution.note: Replacing Sleepy Hollow: no other work closes a tale told aloud with a grave listener who demands its moral and a teller who believes half of it. Rip Van Winkle's tale is doubted at the inn but has no grave hearer or winking teller; Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim keep their listeners to the end; Adela Cathcart's and Mugby Junction's frames hear stories without asking what they prove. Replacing the Jumping Frog: no other work has a teller who never smiles at his own tall tale and a listener who walks out mid-yarn. Added at the G21-02 correction: A Christmas Carol, Great Expectations, Hard Times, The Last of the Mohicans, Silas Marner and A Tale of Two Cities make the claim false; the Rainbow's ghost talk in Silas Marner is doubted mid-novel, not a closing frame with a grave hearer or a teller who believes all or half, and David Gamut sings psalms but tells no yarn and asks no moral.

claim: Twain builds the Yankee's frame from the frog's: a stranger met by chance does all the talking and tells of wonders as flatly as of the weather. Wheeler's monotone bores the narrator, who walks out before the end; the Warwick stranger's spell holds his, who waits up by the fire and plies him with whisky to hear the rest.

from.exact: the restfulness of his company—for he did all the talking

to.exact: Simon Wheeler backed me into a corner and blockaded me there with his chair, and then sat down and reeled off the monotonous narrative which follows this paragraph.

alignments.same: A stranger the narrator happens on does all the talking while the narrator only listens.
alignments.differs: Wheeler corners the narrator with a chair and drones; the Warwick stranger talks 'softly, pleasantly, flowingly', and the narrator calls his company restful.

from.exact: just as one might speak of the weather, or any other common matter

to.exact: he never betrayed the slightest suspicion of enthusiasm

alignments.same: The teller speaks of marvels in a level, everyday voice.
alignments.differs: Wheeler's flat voice turns a frog full of shot into a solemn history; the stranger's flat voice delivers 'I did it myself', a hole shot through sixth-century mail, and the narrator is electrified.

from.exact: I also comforted him with a hot Scotch whisky; gave him another one; then still another—hoping always for his story.

to.exact: However, lacking both time and inclination, I did not wait to hear about the afflicted cow, but took my leave.

alignments.same: The frame narrator decides whether he wants the rest of the stranger's story.
alignments.differs: The frog's narrator escapes before Wheeler can start on the one-eyed cow; the Yankee's narrator waits up at the inn and pours whisky until the stranger tells all.

question: Both strangers speak of wonders flatly. Why does one leave his hearer bored and fleeing, and the other leave him spellbound and pouring whisky?

substitution.note: Replacing the Jumping Frog: no other work has a talker who corners the narrator with a chair, drones without a smile, and is left mid-story. Sleepy Hollow's teller is 'pleasant' and finishes; Rip tells his tale at the inn but no frame narrator meets him. Replacing A Connecticut Yankee: no other work has a chance-met stranger who talks of an ancient wonder as of the weather and is plied with whisky for the rest. Added at the G21-02 correction: A Christmas Carol, Great Expectations, Hard Times, The Last of the Mohicans, Silas Marner and A Tale of Two Cities make the claim false; none has a frame narrator who meets a stranger talking of wonders as flatly as of the weather.

claim: In both, a stranger passing through brings down a local boast with lead. The camp stranger fills Smiley's champion frog with quail shot, takes forty dollars and is never caught. Hadleyburg's stranger, nursing an offence for a year, fills a sack with gilded lead disks, and the town's pride in its honesty breaks open in its own hall.

from.exact: “Friends, they are only gilded disks of lead!”

to.exact: turned him upside down and he belched out a double handful of shot

alignments.same: The thing everyone staked on turns out to be loaded with lead.
alignments.differs: Smiley finds the shot alone, after the stranger is gone with the money; the gilded disks are shown to the whole town in its hall, as the stranger planned.

from.exact: Hadleyburg had the ill luck to offend a passing stranger—possibly without knowing it, certainly without caring

to.exact: One day a feller—a stranger in the camp, he was—come acrost him with his box

alignments.same: A stranger passing through comes upon the place that thinks itself unbeatable.
alignments.differs: The camp stranger just sees a bet to win; Hadleyburg's has been slighted, broods a whole year, and wants a plan that will hurt the entire town.

from.exact: was prouder of it than of any other of its possessions

to.exact: Smiley was monstrous proud of his frog

alignments.same: The victim's pride is in a thing it trusts no one can beat.
alignments.differs: Smiley's pride is a trained frog and costs him forty dollars; Hadleyburg's is its own honesty, and losing it costs the town its name.

question: The camp stranger wants forty dollars; Hadleyburg's wants a whole town. Does the later story turn the frog trick into a moral, or keep it a joke?

substitution.note: Replacing the Jumping Frog: no other work has a stranger who weights the local favourite with lead to win. The £1,000,000 Bank-Note's wager has no trick and no lead; Gold-Bug's treasure is real. Replacing Hadleyburg: no other work has a stranger whose sack of gold proves to be gilded lead disks. Added at the G21-02 correction: A Christmas Carol, Great Expectations, Hard Times, The Last of the Mohicans, Silas Marner and A Tale of Two Cities make the claim false; Bounderby's boast falls to his own mother, not a passing stranger, and no prize there is loaded with lead.

claim: Both tales let a dead woman's baby reform men who lived for gold. Eliot's child leads the lone weaver into church and among his neighbours, and lives to choose him. Harte's camp keeps its Luck to itself, with no woman, no parson and no strangers, and the flood takes the child and Kentuck together.

from.exact: It was evident that no plan which entailed parting from their new acquisition would for a moment be entertained.

to.exact: No—no—I can’t part with it, I can’t let it go

alignments.same: Offered a way to hand the orphan to those who could nurse it, its finders refuse to part with it.
alignments.differs: Silas alone claims the child as sent to him; the camp votes as a body against Red Dog and any woman, and gives it to Stumpy and an ass.

from.exact: I proclaim you Thomas Luck, according to the laws of the United States and the State of California, so help me God.

to.exact: Silas, making himself as clean and tidy as he could, appeared for the first time within the church

alignments.same: For the foundling's christening, a man who never prays takes part in a rite of faith for the first time.
alignments.differs: Dolly leads Silas into the parish church among his neighbours; Stumpy stops a mock service in a grove and names the child himself by state law, with no parson.

from.exact: The camp was jealous of its privileges and looked suspiciously on strangers.

to.exact: the child created fresh and fresh links between his life and the lives from which he had hitherto shrunk continually into narrower isolation

alignments.same: The child changes how its keepers stand toward the world beyond their door.
alignments.differs: Eppie draws the recluse out into his neighbours' lives; the Luck makes the camp clean and quiet but walls it in, preempting the land and turning strangers away.

question: Eppie joins Silas to Raveloe; the Luck shuts Roaring Camp off from Red Dog, from women and from strangers. Is the camp's regeneration real if it lets no one in?

substitution.note: Replacing Silas Marner: no other work has a man who lived for gold refuse to give up a dead woman's baby and stand at its christening. Oliver Twist's orphan is kept by a parish that hires and farms; A Christmas Carol's Scrooge is changed by spirits and never takes in a child; Hard Times' Sissy is a schoolgirl, not a foundling. Replacing the Luck: no other work has a band of men refuse a nurse, christen the child by state law and turn strangers away for its sake. Great Expectations' Pip is a boy at his parents' grave, brought up by hand by his sister, and no finder refuses to part with him or stands at a christening.

claim: Both open on a birth with no fit help, in which the mother dies, and ask who will feed and name the child. Dickens's parish farms him out and names him off an alphabet. Harte's camp of outlaws will not send the baby away and names him for its own luck.

from.exact: The door closed on the extempore surgeon and midwife, and Roaring Camp sat down outside, smoked its pipe, and awaited the issue.

to.exact: There being nobody by, however, but a pauper old woman, who was rendered rather misty by an unwonted allowance of beer; and a parish surgeon who did such matters by contract

alignments.same: A fallen woman gives birth with no fit midwife by, and dies of it.
alignments.differs: Dickens's attendants are hired by the parish and leave the dead for the bottle and dinner; Harte's whole camp waits outside, laying bets, and greets the first cry with revolver shots.

from.exact: Tipton proposed that they should send the child to Red Dog,—a distance of forty miles,—where female attention could be procured.

to.exact: whether there was no female then domiciled in “the house” who was in a situation to impart to Oliver Twist, the consolation and nourishment of which he stood in need

alignments.same: With no woman at hand to nurse the orphan, its keepers ask whether to send it away to be fed.
alignments.differs: The parish farms Oliver out to a woman paid by the head; the camp shouts down Red Dog, rears the child on an ass's milk and sends to Sacramento for lace.

from.exact: to take a fresh deal all round. Call him Luck, and start him fair.

to.exact: We name our fondlings in alphabetical order.

alignments.same: The father unknown, the orphan's name is chosen by the men who keep him.
alignments.differs: Bumble takes the next letter off a ready list, so Twist is one charge among many; Oakhurst names the child for the camp's fortune, and Stumpy christens him before them all.

question: Oliver is 'badged and ticketed' a parish child the hour he is dressed; the Luck is wrapped in red flannel and then in lace. Does the camp give its child a freer place than the workhouse gives Oliver?

substitution.note: Replacing Oliver Twist: no other work stages a birth attended by hirelings in which the mother dies, and then has a parish farm out and alphabetically name the child. Silas Marner's Eppie arrives walking, her mother dead in the snow, and no one proposes to farm or name her by list; Jane Eyre's orphan is kept by an aunt. Replacing the Luck: no other work answers the workhouse birth with a camp that refuses to send the baby away and names it for its luck. Great Expectations opens on a boy at his parents' grave, not on a birth, and Pip names himself.

claim: Harte sends the gambler who named the Luck out of Roaring Camp into a snowstorm. The man who dealt a foundling a fresh start now plays a losing game, and the end turns the Luck's over: an innocent girl holds the fallen woman, and the gambler dies alone.

from.exact: this yer young man from Roaring Camp—an entire stranger—carry away our money

to.exact: Oakhurst, a gambler, had the melancholy air and intellectual abstraction of a Hamlet

alignments.same: John Oakhurst, the gambler of Roaring Camp, is one of the men the story sets apart.
alignments.differs: In the Luck he is at home in the camp and gives the child a handkerchief; Poker Flat calls him a stranger and would hang him for his winnings.

from.exact: Luck,” continued the gambler reflectively, “is a mighty queer thing. All you know about it for certain is that it’s bound to change.

to.exact: “It’s better,” said the philosophical Oakhurst, “to take a fresh deal all round. Call him Luck, and start him fair.”

alignments.same: Oakhurst speaks of luck in a card-player's words, as a deal or a streak.
alignments.differs: In the Luck he names a baby for the camp's fortune and a fresh deal; in the snow he says only that luck must change, and pins up his own bad streak.

from.exact: the younger and purer pillowing the head of her soiled sister upon her virgin breast, they fell asleep

to.exact: the strong man, clinging to the frail babe as a drowning man is said to cling to a straw

alignments.same: Each tale ends with a sinner dying in the arms of an innocent, the bodies found by searchers.
alignments.differs: In the flood Kentuck holds the baby; in the snow Piney, the stronger, holds the Duchess, and the two women die together while Oakhurst shoots himself alone.

question: Oakhurst named the Luck and told the camp to start him fair; at Poker Flat no one names him anything but a stranger. Does the second tale take back the first one's hope that a camp of outcasts can be made over?

substitution.note: Replacing the Luck: no other work has John Oakhurst, a camp that named a child for its luck, or a man dying while he holds a baby in a flood. The Jumping Frog's Calaveras camp has gamblers but no Oakhurst and no foundling; Silas Marner's Eppie lives. Replacing the Outcasts: no other work brings back the gambler who named the Luck. Great Expectations (added later): Pip is no gambler and no foundling of a camp, and no one dies in a snowstorm, so the claim fails for it.

claim: Both shut a small band in by the weather within sight of home and ask what the elements mean to them. Harte's snow is a mercy from above that hides the outcasts' stain and makes sinner and virgin equal. Crane's sea is indifferent: no temple to curse, and the strongest drowns.

from.exact: he at first wishes to throw bricks at the temple, and he hates deeply the fact that there are no bricks and no temples

to.exact: from a remote pinnacle of her rocky fastness hurled in that direction a final malediction

alignments.same: Cut off and starving, one of the band wants to hurl something at the power that has left them there.
alignments.differs: Mother Shipton has a target, the smoke of the town that drove her out, and the curse does her good; Crane's man finds no temple to stone and only a high cold star.

from.exact: The cook's arm was around the oiler's shoulders, and, with their fragmentary clothing and haggard faces, they were the babes of the sea, a grotesque rendering of the old babes in the wood.

to.exact: the younger and purer pillowing the head of her soiled sister upon her virgin breast, they fell asleep

alignments.same: Two of the band fall asleep in each other's arms while the cold closes in, like children lost in the wood.
alignments.differs: Harte's women sleep into death as pure and sinful sisters; Crane's two men wake to row again, and the narrator calls the picture grotesque.

from.exact: She did not seem cruel to him then, nor beneficent, nor treacherous, nor wise. But she was indifferent, flatly indifferent.

to.exact: all human stain, all trace of earthly travail, was hidden beneath the spotless mantle mercifully flung from above

alignments.same: At the end the narrator says what nature meant by the storm that kills.
alignments.differs: Harte's snow is flung 'mercifully' from above and makes the sinner and the virgin equal in death; Crane's nature is neither kind nor cruel, and takes the oiler who swam strongest.

question: Harte lets the snow forgive the outcasts; Crane's correspondent finds nature 'flatly indifferent' and still says he can now be an interpreter. Which story gives the band more to understand about why some of them died?

substitution.note: Replacing the Outcasts: no other work shuts a band in by snow and has the snow hide the sinner's stain and two women die embraced. Robinson Crusoe's castaway is alone and lives; A Descent into the Maelstrom's fisherman reads the whirlpool alone; Silas Marner has one death in the snow, not a band. Replacing the Open Boat: no other work answers with a band at sea that sleeps embraced as 'babes of the sea' under a nature 'flatly indifferent'. Great Expectations (added later): the convicts on the marshes are no band shut in by weather, and no storm is read as mercy or indifference, so the claim fails for it.

claim: Stevenson's hunt runs on the lore Tom recites to Huck: a yellow paper of marks, a dead man by the tree, ghosts that keep off by day. Tom has no paper and finds the gold by luck in a robber's cave; the pirates have the paper and dig an empty pit.

from.exact: the chart on yellow paper, with the three red crosses

to.exact: an old yellow paper that tells how to find the marks

alignments.same: The robbers' treasure is found by an old yellow paper that shows the marks.
alignments.differs: Tom knows such papers only by hearsay and has none, so he digs under any dead tree; Jim takes a real one from a dead pirate's chest, and killers fight for it.

from.exact: leastways, he won’t walk by day, and you may lay to that

to.exact: Yes, but, Huck, ghosts don’t travel around only at night. They won’t hender us from digging there in the daytime.

alignments.same: On the way to dig, the leader calms the frightened party: the dead do not walk by day.
alignments.differs: Tom's ghosts are hearsay about blue lights in an empty house; Silver says it beside a shipmate Flint murdered and laid out, and a voice in the trees soon tests him.

from.exact: he had carried it on his back, in many weary journeys, from the foot of the tall pine to a cave

to.exact: We’ll take it to my den.

alignments.same: The buried gold is lifted from its first hiding place and carried to a cave.
alignments.differs: Injun Joe moves it because the boys' pick gave them away, and Tom finds it in the cave; Ben Gunn moves it first, and the pirates dig at the mark for nothing.

question: Every rule Tom recites from his books comes true on Stevenson's island. Does that make Tom right about treasure, or make Treasure Island the boy's book Tom has been reading?

substitution.note: Replacing Treasure Island: The Gold-Bug's paper is a parchment cipher, not a yellow chart, no one in it speaks of ghosts, and its chest lies where it was buried; King Solomon's Mines has a map and a treasure cave, but no one moves the treasure and no one fears the dead by day. Replacing Tom Sawyer: no other work has a boy who recites the yellow paper and the dead man from books, and a robber who carries the dug-up box to his cave. Silas Marner's gold is stolen from under his floor, not hunted by a paper of marks; the Poker Flat and Roaring Camp miners dig for gold but tell no buried-treasure lore.

claim: Tom recites the rules of Legrand's hunt: a paper of signs to cipher out, a dead limb, a first dig that finds nothing. Legrand reads the cipher, finds the error and lifts Kidd's chest. Tom has no paper, blames witches and the hour, and gives the tree up.

from.exact: a paper that’s got to be ciphered over about a week because it’s mostly signs and hy’roglyphics

to.exact: These characters, as any one might readily guess, form a cipher

alignments.same: The robbers' directions are written in signs that must be ciphered out.
alignments.differs: Legrand works out Kidd's characters letter by letter; Tom has no paper, explains that 'hy'roglyphics' are pictures that mean nothing, and says he doesn't want any marks.

from.exact: sometimes in rotten chests under the end of a limb of an old dead tree, just where the shadow falls at midnight

to.exact: ’tis dead limb putty much all de way.

alignments.same: The chest lies under the end of a dead limb of one old tree.
alignments.differs: Jupiter finds Kidd's skull nailed on that limb and drops the beetle from it; Tom digs under every dead-limb tree in reach and guesses where the midnight shadow falls.

from.exact: “Blame it, we must be in the wrong place again. What do you think?”

to.exact: we had reached a depth of five feet, and yet no signs of any treasure became manifest

alignments.same: The first hole at the chosen spot turns up nothing, and the diggers ask what went wrong.
alignments.differs: Legrand traces the error to Jupiter's left eye, moves the peg and strikes the chest; Tom blames witches, then the shadow, then the hour, and leaves the holes.

question: Tom has every rule of the Gold-Bug's hunt but the cipher itself. Is his failure under the dead tree a joke on Tom, or on stories like Poe's?

substitution.note: Replacing The Gold-Bug: Treasure Island's note is a plain bearing, not a cipher, its tree is a live pine, and its empty pit was rifled, not dug in the wrong place; King Solomon's Mines has a map and no dead limb. Replacing Tom Sawyer: no other work has a seeker who recites the cipher and the dead limb from hearsay, has no paper, and gives up after guessing at the hour. Great Expectations, Silas Marner and the Harte camps have money and gold but no cipher, dead limb or failed first dig.

claim: Both heroes toil gladly at what no one asks of them and shirk the chore they owe. Irving calls it the great error in Rip's make-up, and a scolding wife drives him to the woods. Twain makes it a law of work and play; Tom sells his fence as play, and his aunt laughs.

from.exact: Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do, and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do.

to.exact: The great error in Rip’s composition was an insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labor.

alignments.same: The narrator names the rule behind a hero who labours hard yet will not do his own work.
alignments.differs: Irving calls it an error in Rip's own make-up; Twain makes it a law for every body and calls the writer 'a great and wise philosopher' for finding it.

from.exact: they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash.

to.exact: He would never refuse to assist a neighbor even in the roughest toil, and was a foremost man in all country frolics for husking Indian corn, or building stone fences

alignments.same: Hard work on a fence is done gladly when it is a frolic and nobody's duty.
alignments.differs: Rip builds his neighbours' fences while his own farm falls apart; Tom gets the village boys to paint his fence and pay him kites and marbles for the chance.

from.exact: His aunt Polly stood surprised a moment, and then broke into a gentle laugh.

to.exact: Morning, noon, and night, her tongue was incessantly going

alignments.same: The woman of the house scolds the idler for the work he dodges.
alignments.differs: Dame Van Winkle's tongue never stops and drives Rip off with his gun and dog; Aunt Polly, tricked by the boy, laughs and owns she can never learn.

question: Rip's idleness costs him twenty years; Tom's turns a profit by noon. Is Twain's 'law' of work Irving's 'error' made a joke, or a defence of Rip?

substitution.note: Replacing Rip Van Winkle: Bartleby prefers not to work and plays at nothing; Smiley in the Jumping Frog bets but has no chore he shirks; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod works for his board. Replacing Tom Sawyer: no other work has a boy who trades his chore away to others as play and a narrator who states the rule that work is what one is obliged to do. Hard Times sets fact against fancy in a school but has no boy who sells his chore as play; Pip in Great Expectations is scolded by his sister but does not toil gladly at others' work.

claim: Huck starts where Tom Sawyer, a book he says told the truth 'mainly', winds up: the cave gold, the widow, and the robber gang Tom promised. Tom Sawyer ends on that bargain; the sequel spends it. The gang's raid finds a Sunday-school picnic, Huck resigns within a month, and he tries to give the gold away.

from.exact: We got six thousand dollars apiece—all gold.

to.exact: The sum amounted to a little over twelve thousand dollars.

alignments.same: The robbers' gold the two boys found in the cave is counted out and shared.
alignments.differs: Tom Sawyer ends on the town's wonder at the sum; Huck gives it one line as the old book's ending, and soon begs the Judge to take it all off him.

from.exact: I might join if I would go back to the widow and be respectable

to.exact: Well, I’ll go back to the widder for a month and tackle it and see if I can come to stand it, if you’ll let me b’long to the gang, Tom.

alignments.same: Huck goes back to the widow's house for the price of a place in Tom's robber gang.
alignments.differs: Tom Sawyer closes on the bargain as a happy end; Huck tells it as done, plays robber 'about a month', resigns, and the gang breaks up having robbed nobody.

from.exact: You fetch them to the cave, and you’re always as polite as pie to them; and by-and-by they fall in love with you, and never want to go home any more.

to.exact: Well, the women get to loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two weeks they stop crying

alignments.same: Tom lays down the books' rule: women carried to the cave are treated politely and come to love their captors.
alignments.differs: In Tom Sawyer only Huck hears it, and asks; in the sequel Ben Rogers objects that the cave will be cluttered, and the one raid takes doughnuts and a rag doll.

question: Huck says Mr. Mark Twain told the truth 'mainly'. What had Tom Sawyer's happy ending stretched, that its sequel has to undo?

substitution.note: Replacing Tom Sawyer: no other work ends with two boys counting robbers' gold from a cave, a widow who takes one of them in, and a robber gang promised as the price of staying respectable; Treasure Island's gold is shared among men, Oliver Twist's Fagin keeps a school of thieves, not a play gang. Replacing Huckleberry Finn: Treasure Island answers Tom Sawyer's treasure lore but has no widow, no gang and no reckoning of the money; no other work takes up Tom's gang and dissolves it. Recheck with works merged later in order: Great Expectations, The Luck of Roaring Camp, The Outcasts of Poker Flat and A Tale of Two Cities have no two boys counting cave gold, no widow taking one in, no play robber gang; none takes up Tom's gang.

claim: Each boy travels with an elder seeking freedom: Jim from slavery, the lama from the Wheel. Huck's raft hides from people; Kim's road is a river of them. Huck is glad to be named Tom Sawyer; Kim asks who Kim is. A will frees Jim at home; the lama's River is at his feet.

from.exact: a vast improvement on the cramped and crowded Lahore streets

to.exact: Other places do seem so cramped up and smothery, but a raft don’t.

alignments.same: The boy sets the road or river he travels with his companion against the cramped places he has left.
alignments.differs: Huck's raft drifts by night and hides a runaway from every town; Kim's Grand Trunk Road is crowded with castes and weddings, and he wants to see them all.

from.exact: No; I am Kim. This is the great world, and I am only Kim. Who is Kim?

to.exact: it was like being born again, I was so glad to find out who I was.

alignments.same: Among strangers who have given him a new name, the boy turns to the question of who he is.
alignments.differs: Huck is relieved to be Tom Sawyer, a borrowed name that covers his hunt for Jim; Kim, told he is a Sahib, holds to his own name and finds it strange.

from.exact: I have wrenched my Soul back from the Threshold of Freedom to free thee from all sin

to.exact: she set him free in her will

alignments.same: At the end the elder whose freedom the journey sought is free, but not by the journey's road.
alignments.differs: A will freed Jim at home while the boys ran south and Tom staged an escape for sport; the lama finds his River and turns back from freedom for the boy.

question: Huck decides to go to hell to free Jim and finds it was already done; the lama comes back from freedom to free Kim. Which boy is changed more by the old man he travels with?

substitution.note: Replacing Huckleberry Finn: Tom Sawyer has a raft and Jackson's Island but no elder seeking freedom and no borrowed name; Treasure Island's Jim travels with Silver, who seeks gold, and keeps his own name; Oliver Twist is given a name and a past by others, but walks with no companion seeking freedom. Replacing Kim: Treasure Island, Lord Jim and The Man Who Would Be King have no boy guiding an old seeker; A Passage to India's friends seek no freedom, and no other work sets a crowded road against the cramped town the boy left. Recheck with works merged later in order: Great Expectations' Pip helps the convict Magwitch flee by river, but they do not travel together through the book, Pip takes no borrowed name to cover the flight, and the escape fails rather than freedom coming by another road; The Luck of Roaring Camp, The Outcasts of Poker Flat and A Tale of Two Cities have no boy travelling with an elder seeking freedom.

claim: Both towns have a drunk they call harmless who goes 'on the war-path' down the main street, calling one enemy out. Twain's crowd laughs, and the sober colonel shoots Boggs as his daughter runs up. Crane's town hides, and the bride's mere presence ends the feud without a shot.

from.exact: When he's sober he's all right—kind of simple—wouldn't hurt a fly—nicest fellow in town.

to.exact: He’s the best naturedest old fool in Arkansaw—never hurt nobody, drunk nor sober.

alignments.same: A townsman tells the stranger that the raging drunk is the gentlest man in the place.
alignments.differs: Bricksville's loafers trust it and jeer at Boggs in the street; Yellow Sky bars its doors and shutters anyway, for Scratchy's bullets are real.

from.exact: when he goes on the war-trail, we hunt our holes—naturally

to.exact: Cler the track, thar. I’m on the waw-path, and the price uv coffins is a-gwyne to raise.

alignments.same: The drunk's rampage is called going on the war-path, like an Indian raid on the town.
alignments.differs: Boggs says it himself and threatens only in words; the bar-keeper says it of Scratchy, who shoots at a dog, a scrap of paper and his friend's windows.

from.exact: seeming for the first time he saw the drooping drowning woman at the other man's side

to.exact: That young girl screamed out and comes rushing, and down she throws herself on her father

alignments.same: A woman comes into the street where the drunk and his enemy meet.
alignments.differs: Boggs's daughter is sent for to calm him and arrives as he falls dead; the bride is there before any shot, and the sight of her makes Scratchy lower his gun.

question: Sherburn kills the harmless drunk and then scorns the town's cowardice; Scratchy is stopped by nothing but the word 'married'. Which town has outgrown its gunmen?

substitution.note: Replacing Huckleberry Finn: no other work has a town drunk called harmless who rides or walks the street on the 'war-path' calling one man out by name. The Outcasts' Uncle Billy is a drunk but calls no one out; the Mohicans' war-cries are real Indians'; Tom Sawyer's Muff Potter is a harmless drunk but calls no one out and is not shot. Replacing the Bride: no other work answers with a gunman's feud called off by a marriage.

claim: Both end a frontier with the last of an old fighting kind. Cooper's Magua falters before Cora, but the killing goes on, Uncas dies, and Tamenund mourns his race. Crane's 'last one of the old gang' lowers his revolver before a bride and walks home: his frontier ends in a marriage, not a massacre.

from.exact: He's about the last one of the old gang that used to hang out along the river here.

to.exact: for my boy is the last of the Mohicans

alignments.same: A fighting man is named the last of his kind left in the country.
alignments.differs: Chingachgook says it of his son, the last of a chiefly blood; a bar-keeper says it to a drummer of a drunk river tough in a shirt made in New York.

from.exact: He moved a pace backward, and his arm with the revolver dropped to his side.

to.exact: he raised his arm on high, but dropped it again with a bewildered air, like one who doubted

alignments.same: An armed man about to strike stands before a woman and lowers his weapon, bewildered.
alignments.differs: Magua's pause saves no one: a follower stabs Cora and three die on the ledge. Scratchy's lowered arm ends the fight, and he says it is all off.

from.exact: in the presence of this foreign condition he was a simple child of the earlier plains

to.exact: The pale faces are masters of the earth, and the time of the red men has not yet come again.

alignments.same: The last words set the fighter in a time that has passed.
alignments.differs: Tamenund speaks them over a dead chief as a nation's grief; Crane's narrator says them of a drunk outdone by a wedding, who leaves only tracks in the sand.

question: Cooper mourns the last of the Mohicans; Crane makes the last of the old gang a comic figure. Does the Bride laugh at the frontier or at the books that made it tragic?

substitution.note: Replacing the Mohicans: no other work names a warrior the last of his race and has an armed foe falter before a woman. Rip Van Winkle's changed times have no fighter; the Outcasts' Oakhurst is no last of a kind; Huckleberry Finn's Sherburn does not falter; Sleepy Hollow's Brom Bones is a rough rider who wins the bride by a prank, not the last of anything. Replacing the Bride: no other work answers with the last of the old gang disarmed by a marriage.

claim: Both bring a simple pair bound for marriage among the West's men of the gun under a churchly hush. Harte's outcasts shield the lovers from laughter, and the gambler ends with a bullet in his own heart. Crane leaves the pair to the porter's jokes, and the gunman holsters both revolvers and walks home alive.

from.exact: Immediately a solemn, chapel-like gloom was upon the place.

to.exact: There was a Sabbath lull in the air, which, in a settlement unused to Sabbath influences, looked ominous.

alignments.same: A rough frontier town goes quiet as if at church before men of the gun are dealt with.
alignments.differs: Poker Flat's hush is a committee about to hang or banish its sinners; Yellow Sky's is a saloon barred against one drunk.

from.exact: Historically there was supposed to be something infinitely humorous in their situation.

to.exact: Nothing but Mr. Oakhurst’s admonishing foot saved Uncle Billy from bursting into a roar of laughter.

alignments.same: A plain pair come to marry are a joke to the people who watch them.
alignments.differs: Oakhurst kicks Uncle Billy quiet and the camp takes the lovers in; Crane's porter and passengers enjoy the joke, and the narrator only calls it 'historically' humorous.

from.exact: placing both weapons in their holsters, he went away

to.exact: with a Derringer by his side and a bullet in his heart

alignments.same: The man of the gun ends the tale with his weapon at his side and no foe shot.
alignments.differs: Oakhurst turns his Derringer on himself in the snow; Scratchy puts both revolvers away and walks off alive, his feud simply 'all off'.

question: Harte's outcasts die to honour the lovers; Crane's gunman just goes home. Is the Bride kinder to the West than the Outcasts, or does it take away its last chance at tragedy?

substitution.note: Replacing the Outcasts: no other work brings a couple on their way to be married among exiled gamblers and drunks, under a Sabbath hush, with a gambler's Derringer at the end. The Luck's camp has no couple and no suicide; Huckleberry Finn's feuds and shootings have no pair on the way to be married; the Open Boat's band has neither a marrying pair nor a gun. Replacing the Bride: no other work answers with a bride who ends a gunfight by being there.

claim: Both boys learn on deck at night that men of the ship mean murder for gold, and both shoot a seaman at arm's length almost against their will. Jim hides and carries the plot to the captain; David hears the captain himself plot against a hunted rebel, takes the rebel's side, and sobs over his share.

from.exact: It was Mr. Riach, crying out as if upon a sudden thought: “Couldn’t we wile him out of the round-house?”

to.exact: for from these dozen words I understood that the lives of all the honest men aboard depended upon me alone.

alignments.same: On deck at night the boy overhears men of the ship plan a killing for gold.
alignments.differs: Jim's plotters are mutineers and he warns the captain; David's plotters are the captain and his mates, and he warns the outlawed Jacobite.

from.exact: “And see here, David, yon man has a beltful of gold, and I give you my word that you shall have your fingers in it.”

to.exact: But now, you look here: you’re young, you are, but you’re as smart as paint.

alignments.same: The leader of the plot wins over a lad with praise and a share of gold.
alignments.differs: Silver turns young Dick while Jim listens unseen in the barrel; Hoseason tries it on David himself, who says yes and goes straight to Alan.

from.exact: only at the touch of him (and him alive) my whole flesh misgave me, and I could no more pull the trigger than I could have flown.

to.exact: I scarce can say it was by my own volition, and I am sure it was without a conscious aim—both my pistols went off

alignments.same: The boy shoots a seaman at close range almost without willing it.
alignments.differs: Jim's pistols go off with the shock of Hands's dirk and he fears only the fall; David's flesh first refuses, then he fires in terror and weeps at his share.

question: Jim keeps faith with his captain and David breaks with his. What does each book make of a boy's loyalty when the law's side and the honest side part company?

substitution.note: Replacing Treasure Island: The Sea-Wolf's Humphrey kills no one at close range and overhears no plot for gold; Lord Jim, Moby-Dick and Twenty Thousand Leagues have no boy who hears a murder plan on deck; Kim overhears a war decided from the grass but shoots no one; Robinson Crusoe, Sindbad and Gulliver's Travels have no ship's crew plotting for a passenger's gold; King Solomon's Mines and The Gold-Bug have treasure but no voyage plot overheard and no boy who kills. Replacing Kidnapped with any of these fails the same way. Added on correction: Huckleberry Finn's robbers on the wrecked steamboat plot at night to kill a partner for his share, but Huck shoots no one; Tom Sawyer hears a treasure plot in a haunted house, not on a ship, and fires no shot; Great Expectations, A Tale of Two Cities (Miss Pross's pistol goes off on Madame Defarge, no boy, no seaman), The Last of the Mohicans and the rest have no boy shooting a seaman after overhearing a plot on deck.

claim: Stevenson sets his castaway against the books of people cast away. Crusoe climbs a hill to find the sea all round him, rafts the carpenter's chest ashore and scorns his money. David finds the sea round a tidal islet he could wade off, has no tools, and loses his guineas through a hole while he starves.

from.exact: it burst upon me all in a moment that I was cast upon a little barren isle, and cut off on every side by the salt seas.

to.exact: I saw my fate, to my great affliction—viz. that I was in an island environed every way with the sea

alignments.same: The wrecked man goes up the land and learns to his grief that the sea surrounds him.
alignments.differs: Crusoe's island is true; David's is a tidal islet that 'a sea-bred boy would not have stayed a day on', and laughing fishers tell him so.

from.exact: In all the books I have read of people cast away, they had either their pockets full of tools, or a chest of things would be thrown upon the beach along with them, as if on purpose.

to.exact: And it was after long searching that I found out the carpenter’s chest, which was, indeed, a very useful prize to me

alignments.same: Tools from the wreck decide how the castaway will live.
alignments.differs: Crusoe rafts the carpenter's chest ashore and builds; David, inland bred, has only money and a button, and eats raw limpets that poison him.

from.exact: That made a fortune of three pounds and four shillings, English money, for a lad, the rightful heir of an estate, and now starving on an isle at the extreme end of the wild Highlands.

to.exact: “O drug!” said I, aloud, “what art thou good for?

alignments.same: The castaway counts his money and finds it worth nothing where he is.
alignments.differs: Crusoe scorns the heap and then takes it ashore; David watches a guinea glance off into the sea through a hole in his pocket, an heir counting what is left.

question: David says that if he had sat down to think instead of raging at his fate he would have walked off Earraid. Is Stevenson mocking Crusoe's providence, or the boy who expected a book's island?

substitution.note: Replacing Robinson Crusoe: Sindbad's islands give him no carpenter's chest and no hilltop discovery; Gulliver is set ashore, not wrecked alone; Treasure Island's Ben Gunn is marooned, not wrecked, and has neither a chest of tools nor a hilltop discovery; The Open Boat's men reach a mainland beach. Replacing Kidnapped: no other work has a castaway on an island he could have waded off, or one who names the books of castaways to say his case was different. Added on correction: Tom and Huck camp on Jackson's Island by choice and can swim off; The Outcasts of Poker Flat are cut off by snow, not sea, with no wreck and no chest; Huckleberry Finn, Great Expectations, Silas Marner (gold lost, but no castaway), A Christmas Carol and the rest have no wrecked man finding the sea all round him.

claim: Both tales open on twenty thousand pounds staked by English gentlemen on a man lasting a set number of days, and both close by counting a wife the real winnings. Fogg stakes his own fortune, spends it on the road and is hunted as a bank thief; Twain's stranger never spends his note and grows rich.

from.exact: Brother B said he would bet twenty thousand pounds that the man would live thirty days, any way, on that million, and keep out of jail, too.

to.exact: I will bet twenty thousand pounds against anyone who wishes that I will make the tour of the world in eighty days or less

alignments.same: An English gentleman stakes twenty thousand pounds that a man can last a set number of days.
alignments.differs: Fogg stakes his own money on his own journey; Brother B stakes it on a hungry stranger who is never told the terms.

from.exact: Brother A said he couldn’t offer it at a bank or anywhere else, because he would be arrested on the spot.

to.exact: The polished gentleman disappeared to give place to the bank robber.

alignments.same: A man carrying a fortune in Bank of England notes is expected to be taken for a thief.
alignments.differs: Henry is never doubted, since shopkeepers bow to the note; Fogg is matched to a robber's description, tracked round the world and jailed at Liverpool.

from.exact: it never made but one purchase in its life, and then got the article for only about a tenth part of its value.

to.exact: Nothing, say you? Perhaps so; nothing but a charming woman, who, strange as it may appear, made him the happiest of men!

alignments.same: The closing reckoning counts a wife as the true gain of the wager.
alignments.differs: Fogg has spent nearly all his stake to win and gains only her; Henry never spends the note and comes out with two hundred thousand pounds besides.

question: Fogg spends a fortune and is taken for a thief; Henry spends nothing and is taken for a millionaire. What does each book say a bank-note is worth without the man who carries it?

substitution.note: Replacing Around the World: The Bet stakes two millions on fifteen years and has no bank-notes, no suspicion of theft and no wife; Candide and A Connecticut Yankee have no wager; The Necklace lends a jewel, not a bet. Replacing the Bank-Note: The Bet has no twenty thousand pounds, no thief and no marriage; Hadleyburg's sack is a trap, not a wager on days. Works added later in order: none of the Dickens, Twain, Harte, Cooper, Eliot or Crane tales has gentlemen staking twenty thousand pounds on a man lasting a set term; Great Expectations has unearned money but no wager; their prefaces and notes tell no such tale

claim: Chekhov's wager is Fogg's turned inside out. Fogg risks money that he can circle the globe in eighty days; the lawyer risks his freedom that he can sit fifteen years in one room. Both know the world unseen, and both bets turn on five minutes: Fogg's seemingly lost by error, the prisoner's forfeited on purpose.

from.exact: You stake two millions, I my freedom

to.exact: I have a deposit of twenty thousand at Baring’s which I will willingly risk upon it.

alignments.same: Amid an evening's talk among gentlemen, a man risks something on keeping a term the others call impossible.
alignments.differs: Fogg stakes half his fortune on going round the world in eighty days; the lawyer stakes his freedom on sitting fifteen years in one room.

from.exact: True, I saw neither the earth nor the people, but in your books I drank fragrant wine

to.exact: He must have travelled everywhere, at least in the spirit.

alignments.same: A man knows the whole world without having seen it.
alignments.differs: Fogg's knowledge, from papers at his club, sends him round the globe, where he still looks at nothing; the prisoner's, from books in a cell, ends in contempt for it all.

from.exact: I shall come out from here five minutes before the stipulated term, and thus shall violate the agreement.

to.exact: Having made the tour of the world, he was behind-hand five minutes.

alignments.same: The wager seems lost by five minutes.
alignments.differs: Fogg thinks himself five minutes late by bad luck and has really won by a day; the prisoner leaves five minutes early on purpose to throw the money away.

question: Fogg says he wagered for victory, not money; the prisoner waives the two millions out of contempt. Is either man free of the stake?

substitution.note: Replacing Around the World: the Bank-Note's Henry bets nothing himself, knows London only by its streets and is decided by thirty days, not five minutes; Notes from Underground and Bartleby have a shut-in man but no wager. Replacing The Bet: the Bank-Note has no five minutes and no world known from books; Twenty Thousand Leagues has a world seen, not unseen, and no stake. Works added later in order: none of the Dickens, Twain, Harte, Cooper, Eliot or Crane tales has a wager on a term or a world known unseen; Silas Marner shuts himself in but stakes nothing; their prefaces and notes tell no such tale

claim: Verne wrote two tours of the world. Nemo, who has done with society, roams under the sea on no schedule, and his captive guest names every town and wonder he passes. Fogg, a clubman with a timetable, crosses the same Red Sea without looking up and brings back nothing he saw, only a wife.

from.exact: passed through the memorable scenes of the Red Sea with cold indifference; did not care to recognise the historic towns and villages

to.exact: Mocha came in sight, now a ruined town, whose walls would fall at a gunshot

alignments.same: The traveller passes along the Red Sea coast and its old towns.
alignments.differs: Aronnax names Mocha and counts its mosques and forts; Fogg stays below at whist and does not look at the towns at all.

from.exact: But those who knew him best could not imagine how he had made his fortune

to.exact: Captain Nemo must have expended millions in the acquirement of these various specimens, and I was thinking what source he could have drawn from

alignments.same: No one can tell where the silent hero's fortune comes from.
alignments.differs: Nemo's millions turn out to be gold raised from wrecks, beyond any law; Fogg's sits as open credit at Barings, which got him into the Reform.

from.exact: What had he brought back from this long and weary journey?

to.exact: in less than ten months, I have crossed 20,000 leagues in that submarine tour of the world, which has revealed so many wonders.

alignments.same: The book closes by reckoning what a tour of the world brought back.
alignments.differs: Aronnax brings back the wonders of the deep he watched; Fogg, who saw nothing on the way, brings back only a wife.

question: Aronnax is a prisoner who sees everything; Fogg is free and sees nothing. Which of Verne's travellers really goes round the world?

substitution.note: Replacing Twenty Thousand Leagues: Journey to the Centre goes down, not round, and never crosses the Red Sea; Gulliver and Sindbad make voyages, not a tour of the globe, and name no Mocha; Moby-Dick's Ahab hunts, and his money is the owners'. Replacing Around the World: the Bank-Note stays in London; The Sea-Wolf's Larsen has no club and no timetable. Works added later in order: no Dickens, Twain, Harte, Cooper, Eliot or Crane tale circles the globe or crosses the Red Sea; Huckleberry Finn travels a river, not the world; their prefaces and notes tell no such tale

claim: Hope keeps the Grimms' double who is taken for the king in his own palace while the true king lies shut away. The twin lays a sword between himself and the queen and is beheaded by the brother he freed; Rudolf kisses the King's bride, and the freed King calls him his nearest friend.

from.exact: But neither in the face of the princess nor in that of any other did I see the least doubt or questioning.

to.exact: The sentries, indeed, thought no otherwise than that he was the young King himself, for he looked so like him

alignments.same: The double comes into the royal city and nobody, not even the king's bride, doubts that he is the king.
alignments.differs: The twin chooses to pass for his brother so as to find him; Rudolf is dressed as the King by the King's men and crowned while the King lies drugged in a cellar.

from.exact: I forgot the King in Zenda.

to.exact: but he laid a two-edged sword between him and the young Queen

alignments.same: Alone at night with the absent king's bride, the double must choose what he owes the man he stands for.
alignments.differs: The twin lays a sword in the bed and says nothing; Rudolf forgets the King, kisses Flavia and swears he loves her more than truth or honour.

from.exact: and you would have been my best and nearest friend, Cousin Rudolf.

to.exact: he became so jealous and angry that he drew his sword, and struck off his brother’s head.

alignments.same: The king freed from his prison hears what the double did in his place.
alignments.differs: The Grimm king, told the twin slept in his bed, beheads him in jealousy; Hope's King, though Flavia now loves Rudolf, would keep him by him as his nearest friend.

question: The Grimm twin keeps faith with a sword and is killed for it; Rudolf breaks faith with a kiss and is thanked. Which story asks more of the man who stands in for a king?

substitution.note: Replacing Two Brothers: in A Tale of Two Cities Lucie never takes Carton for Darnay and no king or palace is in play; Jekyll's Hyde looks unlike Jekyll and has no bride to face; The Man Who Was Thursday has disguises but no look-alike; Dorian's double is a picture. Replacing The Prisoner of Zenda: no other work in the view has a double who passes for a king in his own palace before the king's bride and then frees the king. The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky has no look-alike: the marshal brings home his own bride and no one is taken for a king.

claim: Both doubles love the woman pledged to the man they resemble, and both save that man from a cell. Dickens makes the double the debauched copy, who confesses asking nothing and dies in his rival's place; Hope makes him the firmer man, who woos the bride in the King's name, frees the King and lives on apart.

from.exact: his mouth lacking something of the firmness (or obstinacy) which was to be gathered from my close-shutting lips

to.exact: Allowing for my learned friend’s appearance being careless and slovenly if not debauched

alignments.same: The likeness of two men is weighed feature by feature, and one is found the lesser copy.
alignments.differs: The Old Bailey finds Carton the slovenly, debauched one; Rudolf finds the King's face fleshier and his mouth weaker, the double the firmer man.

from.exact: true that I love you more than life—or truth—or honour!

to.exact: For you, and for any dear to you, I would do anything.

alignments.same: The double tells the woman bound to the other man that he loves her beyond everything.
alignments.differs: Carton speaks as himself, knowing Lucie loves Darnay, and asks nothing; Rudolf speaks in the King's name, and Flavia, not knowing, loves him back.

from.exact: But if love had been the only thing, you would have let the King die in his cell.

to.exact: It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done

alignments.same: The double's love is proved by saving the woman's destined husband from prison and death.
alignments.differs: Carton goes to the guillotine in Darnay's name so Lucie keeps her husband; Rudolf frees the King from Zenda, leaves Flavia to him, and goes home alive.

question: Carton's love ends in his death, Rudolf's in a lifetime apart from Flavia. Which ending makes the double's love the greater gift, and to whom?

substitution.note: Replacing A Tale of Two Cities: the Grimm twin in Two Brothers neither loves the queen nor tells her anything, and he is the exact copy, not the lesser; Jekyll and Hyde has no woman between the pair; Dorian Gray and The Man Who Was Thursday have no rival saved from a cell. Replacing The Prisoner of Zenda: no other work in the view has a double who declares love to his rival's bride and then frees the rival from prison. The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky has no double and no rival saved from a cell: the marshal faces the drunk gunman with his own bride beside him.

claim: Orczy keeps Dickens's Terror, the knitters at the scaffold and the condemned smuggled past the barrier, but turns the rescue from a sacrifice into a sport. Carton sends Darnay out under his own name and stays to die. The Pimpernel drives the cart out himself, dressed as a knitting hag, and goes home to rescue again.

from.exact: some say it’s the plague! If it is, I sha’n’t be allowed to come into Paris to-morrow.

to.exact: Apparently the English advocate is in a swoon?

alignments.same: At the gate out of Paris the condemned lie in the vehicle, passed off to the guards as a sick traveller.
alignments.differs: Dickens's guards read every paper and pass the drugged Darnay by Carton's name; Orczy's hag scares them off with the word plague, and the driver is feared to be the rescuer himself.

from.exact: He recognized most of the old hags, “tricotteuses,” as they were called, who sat there and knitted, whilst head after head fell beneath the knife

to.exact: the knitting-women who scarcely lifted their eyes to look at it a moment ago when it could think and speak, count One.

alignments.same: Women sit knitting at the foot of the guillotine while the heads fall.
alignments.differs: Dickens's knitters count the heads up to Carton's; in Orczy one knitting hag, with curls on her whip, drives the condemned Comtesse and her children out of the gate.

from.exact: And all for sheer sport and devilry of course!—saving men, women and children from death

to.exact: It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done

alignments.same: An Englishman thought idle and worthless risks his neck to save the French condemned.
alignments.differs: Carton goes once, for love of Lucie, and dies in Darnay's place; Percy's league calls rescue the finest sport, and he comes home with his wife won back.

question: Carton's rescue costs him his head; the Pimpernel's costs him nothing he does not win back. Does Orczy's sport make the Terror lighter, or only make the rescuer brighter?

substitution.note: Replacing A Tale of Two Cities: no other work this step sees is set in Terror Paris; The Two Brothers and Jekyll and Hyde have a double or a change of clothes but no barrier, no knitters and no condemned nobles. Replacing the Pimpernel: Kim and The Thirty-Nine Steps have disguises and flights but no rescue from the guillotine; The Man Who Was Thursday has masked men in France but no condemned to save. The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky has a marshal's bride and a drunk with two revolvers, but no Terror, no barrier and no rescue.

claim: Both books hide dangerous men in parts that look harmless: Orczy's brainless fop and loathed Jew, Chesterton's open ranter and palsied professor. Orczy's masks cover one hero, who drives his own hunter to the trap and is found out by his wife. Chesterton's hunted chief proves to have hired his hunters, and stays a riddle.

from.exact: Why, then, dress up as an anarchist, you fool!

to.exact: The mask of the inane fop had been a good one, and the part consummately well played.

alignments.same: The man his enemies most want hides in a part no one expects to do anything dangerous.
alignments.differs: Gregory hides by shouting what he really is, since no one believes a ranting anarchist; Percy hides by playing the opposite of what he is, a fop who thinks of cravats.

from.exact: I acted the paralytic Professor so well, that now I can’t leave off.

to.exact: wearing already that mask of somnolent indifference which you have never laid aside until . . . until now.

alignments.same: A part is kept up so long that it stays on even among those closest to the wearer.
alignments.differs: The young detective's palsy clings to him among friends as a joke; Percy wears his dull indifference before his own wife, out of wounded pride, until she breaks through it.

from.exact: I am the man in the dark room, who made you all policemen.

to.exact: the soldiers took no notice of the Jew, who had driven Citoyen Chauvelin to this spot.

alignments.same: The hunted man turns out to have been steering the very men who hunt him.
alignments.differs: Percy, as the Jew, drives Chauvelin to the hut and slips the fugitives out under his soldiers' noses; Sunday hired the detectives who chase him, and his double part is never explained.

question: Marguerite learns that the fool was a mask over the hero she loved; Syme learns that the dreaded chief was the man who sent him. Which unmasking leaves the finder more at peace?

substitution.note: Replacing the Pimpernel: The Secret Agent's Verloc is in both camps but plays no harmless part and hunts no one; The Thirty-Nine Steps' Hannay wears a roadman's clothes but steers no hunter; The Blue Cross's priest looks simple but is no fugitive. Replacing Thursday: Kim's disguises and Scandal in Bohemia's clergyman are worn for an hour, not kept on among friends, and no hunted man there hired his hunters. The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky's Scratchy Wilson is just what he looks like and hunts in the open; no one there plays a harmless part or hires his hunters.

claim: Leroux runs the tale backwards. Like the Beast, Erik keeps a girl in his hidden house, begs her love, and lets her go with a ring and a promise to return. Beauty's return makes the Beast her dream prince; Christine's kiss frees her to marry Raoul, and she will return only to bury Erik.

from.exact: All I wanted was to be loved for myself.

to.exact: Do you love me, Beauty? Will you marry me?

alignments.same: The ugly master of a hidden house asks the girl he keeps there to love and marry him.
alignments.differs: The Beast asks once each evening and accepts her 'No'; Erik kneels, wails 'You don't love me!' and gives her till eleven to choose a wedding mass or a requiem.

from.exact: I give you back your liberty, Christine, on condition that this ring is always on your finger.

to.exact: turn this ring round upon your finger and say firmly

alignments.same: The monster lets the girl go back to the world with a ring that ties her to him.
alignments.differs: The Beast's ring is Beauty's road home to him; Erik's is a guard on her freedom, and when she loses it kissing Raoul she fears his revenge.

from.exact: I made Christine swear to come back, one night, when I was dead

to.exact: I was dying because I thought you had forgotten your promise.

alignments.same: The ugly lover's death is bound to the girl's promise to come back to him.
alignments.differs: Beauty comes back in time and her love revives the Beast as a prince; Erik gives Christine the ring as a wedding-present for Raoul, and her return is only to bury him.

question: Beauty's dream prince and the Beast turn out to be one man; Erik and Raoul stay two. Does Christine's kiss on Erik's forehead keep or break the tale's promise that love can see past a face?

substitution.note: Replacing Beauty and the Beast: Frankenstein's creature asks for a mate, not for the girl's love, and gives no ring; Jane Eyre's Rochester is maimed late, not hidden away, and Jane comes back of her own will, with no ring of leave; The Little Mermaid and The Marsh King's Daughter turn on a woman's change, not a monster's plea. Replacing the Phantom: Jane Eyre has no ring of leave and no death waiting on a promise; The Light Princess and The Snow Queen have no ugly lover. Later entries: The Prisoner of Zenda parts its lovers for duty, with no ugly master and no hidden house; Great Expectations and A Tale of Two Cities keep no girl in a monster's house

claim: Both men tear off a cover, force someone who loved them to look at the hidden face, and hold that the sight binds the viewer for life. Dorian's fair face is the mask, and he kills the painter; Erik's ugliness is no mask but his own flesh, and he weeps and keeps the singer.

from.exact: Feast your eyes, glut your soul on my cursed ugliness!

to.exact: Now you shall look on it face to face.

alignments.same: A man makes a horrified viewer look at the face he has kept hidden.
alignments.differs: Christine tore off the mask herself and Erik rages at her curiosity; Dorian, unasked, tears the curtain from its rod and holds up a lamp for Basil.

from.exact: Perhaps you think that I have another mask, eh, and that this ... this ... my head is a mask?

to.exact: It is the face of my soul.

alignments.same: The man tells the viewer what the dreadful face really is.
alignments.differs: Erik's horror is his own head, with nothing behind it; Dorian's true face is the picture, while the face he wears stays fair.

from.exact: who have torn off my mask and who therefore can never leave me again!

to.exact: was to be burdened for the rest of his life with the hideous memory of what he had done.

alignments.same: Whoever has seen the hidden face, the man reckons, is bound to him for life.
alignments.differs: Erik weeps over Christine, keeps her a fortnight and at last lets her go; Dorian, minutes later, kills Basil with a knife in front of the portrait.

question: Erik's mother gave him his first mask so as not to see him; Basil painted the picture that hides Dorian's soul. Who in each book is to blame for the face that must be hidden?

substitution.note: Replacing Dorian Gray: Jekyll and Hyde shows Lanyon a change of body by a drink, with no cover torn and no face called a soul; The Minister's Black Veil never lifts its veil; Beauty and the Beast hides no face. Replacing the Phantom: Frankenstein's creature is seen at once, wears no mask and binds no viewer; The Birth-Mark's mark is on a wife's face, not shown by its bearer. Later entries: The Prisoner of Zenda and The Scarlet Pimpernel turn on a face taken for another's or a mask of folly, never a hidden face forced on a lover's sight

claim: Both books send Englishmen from London by cab and train and bring them back to a London table to count the gain. Fogg packs one carpet-bag, carries Bradshaw and wins a wife by keeping his term to the minute; Jerome's three heap up luggage, find no one who knows their train, and quit halfway for supper.

from.exact: We must not think of the things we could do with, but only of the things that we can’t do without.

to.exact: We’ll have no trunks; only a carpet-bag, with two shirts and three pairs of stockings for me, and the same for you.

alignments.same: Before setting out, the traveller lays down a rule of packing only what the journey needs.
alignments.differs: Fogg's rule fills one carpet-bag in minutes; the three men's list fills a Gladstone, two hampers, rugs, a melon in a bag and a frying pan in brown paper.

from.exact: nobody at Waterloo ever does know where a train is going to start from

to.exact: a red-bound copy of Bradshaw’s Continental Railway Steam Transit and General Guide, with its timetables showing the arrival and departure of steamers and railways

alignments.same: The first leg is a London railway station and the question of which train leaves when.
alignments.differs: Fogg carries the world's timetables under his arm; at Waterloo no porter knows the train, and the three bribe a driver to be the 11.5 for Kingston.

from.exact: Here’s to Three Men well out of a Boat!

to.exact: What had he really gained by all this trouble?

alignments.same: The book closes in London by asking what the journey was worth.
alignments.differs: Fogg's gain is the wife he won by finishing on the minute; the three slip off the river before their time and toast their escape over a French supper.

question: Fogg sees almost nothing of the world he circles; the three men see the Thames and run from its rain. Which of them comes home having travelled?

substitution.note: Replacing Around the World: Twenty Thousand Leagues and Journey to the Centre start from no London station and keep no term; Kidnapped's David packs nothing and is carried off; the Bank-Note has a wager but no journey and no luggage. Replacing Three Men: Huckleberry Finn's raft trip packs nothing, takes no train and ends far from home; The Bet stays in one room; the Bank-Note's Henry never leaves London; Kim's road has no timetable or packing rule Added later: The Prisoner of Zenda's Rassendyll leaves London by train but packs by no rule, loses the princess and closes with no London reckoning; the Scarlet Pimpernel crosses from Dover by boat; Great Expectations, Outcasts of Poker Flat and the Bride come to Yellow Sky have no packing rule, no London station and no return to count the gain.

claim: Strangers in a country inn hear old locals tell of a famous animal that proves heavier than it looks. Twain's hearer is the butt, bored by an endless yarn, and a stranger loaded the frog with shot. Jerome's strangers bait four boasters, and the trout was always plaster.

from.exact: There was an old fellow there, smoking a long clay pipe, and we naturally began chatting.

to.exact: I found Simon Wheeler dozing comfortably by the bar-room stove of the dilapidated tavern in the decayed mining camp of Angel’s

alignments.same: A visitor to a country inn falls in with an old local by the fire.
alignments.differs: Wheeler corners his hearer and reels off a tale with no end; the old angler gives his catch in a few sentences and goes home, and three more claimants follow.

from.exact: I beg your pardon, I hope you will forgive the liberty that we—perfect strangers in the neighbourhood—are taking

to.exact: I told him a friend had commissioned me to make some inquiries about a cherished companion of his boyhood named Leonidas W. Smiley

alignments.same: The hearer opens the tale with a polite inquiry that is really a trap.
alignments.differs: Twain's narrator is the trap's victim, sent by a friend to be bored; Jerome's strangers lay the trap themselves and coax a fourth man to claim the trout.

from.exact: That trout was plaster-of-Paris.

to.exact: Why blame my cats if he don’t weigh five pounds!

alignments.same: The prize animal of the tale is handled at last and is not what it seemed.
alignments.differs: Dan'l is a real frog a stranger filled with quail shot to win forty dollars; the trout was never a fish, so every claimant's catch, weight and bait were lies.

question: Twain's hearer walks out on Wheeler; Jerome's hearers break the trout. Who is the joke on in each tale?

substitution.note: Replacing the Jumping Frog: Rip Van Winkle and Sleepy Hollow have tavern tales but no prize animal and no hearers' trap; Treasure Island's Admiral Benbow has an old sea-talker but no doubted catch. Replacing Three Men: The Luck of Roaring Camp has a camp but no tale told to strangers; the Bank-Note and Hadleyburg have strangers' tricks but no inn yarn; Tom Sawyer has no teller and no hearer Added later: the Bride come to Yellow Sky has a drummer told tales in a saloon, but of a drunk man, not a prize animal, and no hearers' trap; Great Expectations, Outcasts of Poker Flat, the Prisoner of Zenda and the Scarlet Pimpernel have no inn yarn of a famous animal.

claim: Jones names the Sholto case, and Holmes repeats the creed he gave Watson at its start: the chronicles dress his cases up, the cases rescue him from the dull round of existence, and the work counts, not the man. In 1890 the case closes on the cocaine-bottle; here on a yawn and a line of Flaubert.

from.exact: somewhat to embellish so many of my own little adventures

to.exact: You have attempted to tinge it with romanticism

alignments.same: Holmes faults Watson's written accounts of his cases for colouring them.
alignments.differs: In 1890 he says romance spoils an exact science; now he grants Watson a love of the bizarre and says life itself outdoes any imagining.

from.exact: My life is spent in one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence.

to.exact: But I abhor the dull routine of existence.

alignments.same: Holmes says his cases are his escape from the dull round of everyday existence.
alignments.differs: In 1890 he says it with the syringe in his hand, waiting for a case; now he says it as the case ends, yawning, feeling the ennui close in again.

from.exact: ‘L’homme c’est rien—l’œuvre c’est tout,’ as Gustave Flaubert wrote to George Sand.

to.exact: I claim no credit in such cases. My name figures in no newspaper.

alignments.same: Holmes sets the work above any credit to himself.
alignments.differs: In 1890 Jones gets the credit, Watson a wife, and Holmes the cocaine-bottle; now Watson calls him a benefactor of the race, and he shrugs it off in Flaubert's words.

question: In 1890 the finished case leaves Holmes the cocaine-bottle; in 1891 it leaves him a yawn and a line of Flaubert. Is the second ending a cure for his ennui, or the same ennui put more gracefully?

substitution.note: Only Doyle's Holmes books have the three together. A Study in Scarlet has Holmes's complaint that there is no crime to detect but no chronicle yet to fault and no credit given up for the work; A Scandal in Bohemia and the Hound have Watson as chronicler but no ennui speech and no creed of the work above the man. Notes from Underground and Bartleby have the dull round of existence but no detective. The rest have none of these.

claim: Both tales shut a copyist in a city office: he copies with diligence, never leaves the room, and is left behind when the office moves out. Melville's scrivener stays by his own will until he gives up copying; Doyle's pawnbroker stays because the terms forbid leaving, copying pages no one reads, paid only to be away from home.

from.exact: I had written about Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture and Attica

to.exact: As if long famishing for something to copy, he seemed to gorge himself on my documents.

alignments.same: A man is paid to copy by hand, day after day, at a desk in a city office, and does it with diligence.
alignments.differs: Bartleby copies law papers his employer needs and checks; Wilson copies the Encyclopaedia from the letter A, and no one ever reads his pages.

from.exact: Still, of course, I never dared to leave the room for an instant

to.exact: I observed that he never went to dinner; indeed that he never went any where.

alignments.same: The copyist never leaves the office during his hours.
alignments.differs: Bartleby stays because he prefers to and comes to live there; Wilson stays from ten to two because leaving forfeits the post, and his absence from home is what he is paid for.

from.exact: He said that he had never heard of any such body.

to.exact: you are responsible for the man you left there

alignments.same: The employer moves out of the office, and the man left behind is taken up with the landlord or the new tenant.
alignments.differs: Melville's lawyer moves to be rid of a clerk who will not go; the League's men move because they no longer need Wilson away, and he hunts them from landlord to false address.

question: Wilson would gladly copy on into the B's; Bartleby prefers not to copy at all. What does each tale make of a man valued for where he sits rather than for what he writes?

substitution.note: The Overcoat has a copyist who loves copying but who goes home to copy more, and no office moves out on him. Hard Times and A Christmas Carol have clerks and counting-houses but no copying of pages and no man left behind by a vanished office. The rest have neither a copyist nor a man kept at a desk away from home.

claim: Both tales hand a poor man in London rich men's money for next to nothing, picking him out by his looks, as a stake in a game he cannot see. Doyle's pawnbroker reasons his doubts away and copies on while the game is played under his floor; Twain's clerk lets the question go and wins the game himself.

from.exact: You are an intelligent and honest man, as one may see by your face.

to.exact: He has every requirement. I cannot recall when I have seen anything so fine.

alignments.same: The rich men's side picks the poor man out of the street or the crowd by how he looks.
alignments.differs: The brothers choose Henry for the honesty they read in his face; Ross chooses Wilson for his red hair, and tugs it to make sure it is no wig.

from.exact: They’ve got a game, or a scheme, or an experiment of some kind on hand; no way to determine what it is—let it go.

to.exact: I had quite persuaded myself that the whole affair must be some great hoax or fraud, though what its object might be I could not imagine.

alignments.same: The man sees he is part of someone's scheme and cannot guess its object.
alignments.differs: Henry lets the question go and sets out to win the bet; Wilson argues his doubt away by bedtime, goes to copy, and learns the object only from Holmes.

from.exact: I have a bet on you.

to.exact: The £ 4 a week was a lure which must draw him, and what was it to them, who were playing for thousands?

alignments.same: The poor man's money is small beside the stake his patrons are playing for.
alignments.differs: The brothers' stake is a wager on Henry himself, who wins it and earns a situation; the League's thousands lie in the bank vault next door, and Wilson is only got out of the way.

question: Henry turns the brothers' game into his own fortune; Wilson never knows there is a game until Holmes tells him. What does each tale ask of the poor man who is handed money for nothing?

substitution.note: Candide is picked out for his height and handed money by the recruiting officers, but it is a trap he never sees as a game, and there is no stake beside his pay. Around the World has a twenty-thousand-pound wager, but Fogg is the bettor, not the stake. Hadleyburg's sack is a trap for a whole town, not one man picked by his looks. The Bet has a banker's wager but the lawyer knows its terms. Great Expectations hands Pip money for nothing, but from one convict out of gratitude, not rich men's stake in a game, and not for his looks; The Prisoner of Zenda picks Rassendyll by his looks, but he is no poor man paid off and he knows the game. The rest have no poor man handed money for nothing.

claim: Doyle rebuilds Poe's sealed room: walls and floor searched in vain, an opening judged too small for a cat or a rat, and a beast from the East kept by a master with a whip. Poe's ape kills against its master's will; Doyle's master sends his snake to kill, and it kills him.

from.exact: The walls were carefully sounded, and were shown to be quite solid all round, and the flooring was also thoroughly examined, with the same result.

to.exact: The police have laid bare the floors, the ceilings, and the masonry of the walls, in every direction.

alignments.same: A woman dies in a room locked from within, and the searchers find no way in through walls or floor.
alignments.differs: Dupin trusts the police, who tore the room open; Doyle's coroner only sounded the walls, and Holmes still crawls the floorboards with his lens.

from.exact: It was so small that a rat could hardly pass through.

to.exact: will not admit, throughout their extent, the body of a large cat.
