alignments.same: An opening in the sealed room is judged too narrow for any creature to pass.
alignments.differs: Dupin rightly rules the chimney out and finds the way at a window that only seemed nailed; Doyle's window is truly barred, and Watson's rat-hole ventilator is the killer's road.

from.exact: And also with the result of causing it to turn upon its master at the other side.

to.exact: The fury of the beast, who no doubt bore still in mind the dreaded whip, was instantly converted into fear.

alignments.same: The killing beast, kept by a master who handles it with a whip, turns toward its master at the end.
alignments.differs: Poe's ape sees its master's face and turns from fury to fear; Doyle's adder, beaten by Holmes's cane, turns its fury on the master who loosed it.

question: Poe makes the killer a beast without a purpose and clears its owner; Doyle makes the beast a weapon and its owner the murderer. Which is the more frightening: a crime with no mind behind it, or a mind that hides behind a beast?

substitution.note: Replacing the Rue Morgue: The Sign of the Four has a room locked from within and a question of the chimney, but its killer Tonga is a man who comes through a trap-door big enough for him, with no whip and no master who loses control; Styles has a locked door and poison but no beast; Rikki-Tikki-Tavi has a snake in the house but no sealed room or search. Replacing the Speckled Band: the Hound has a beast set on by a schemer but no sealed room; The Moonstone and the Purloined Letter have no beast.

claim: In both, a deadly Indian snake comes at night through a small hole in the wall into a room where people sleep, and the defender sits silent in the dark until it moves. Doyle's adder is sent by a man and kills him; Kipling's cobra comes by its own plan to empty the house, and dies there.

from.exact: At the bottom of the smooth plaster wall there was a brick pulled out to make a sluice for the bath water

to.exact: the rope was there as a bridge for something passing through the hole and coming to the bed

alignments.same: The snake reaches the sleepers through a small hole made in the wall of the room.
alignments.differs: The sluice is an ordinary drain the cobra finds for himself; the ventilator and dummy bell-rope were made by the doctor so his adder would land on the bed.

from.exact: Rikki-tikki stayed still as death.

to.exact: The shutters cut off the least ray of light, and we waited in absolute darkness.

alignments.same: The defenders keep a silent watch through the night in the dark room the snake comes into.
alignments.differs: Rikki watches the cobra coiled asleep by the water-jar and chooses where to bite; Holmes and Watson see nothing and wait for a hiss to strike at.

from.exact: Those who kill snakes get killed by snakes

to.exact: Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit which he digs for another.

alignments.same: A saying holds that the one who deals in death will die by it.
alignments.differs: The muskrat warns the snake-killer, and Rikki lives to kill both cobras; Holmes says it over the snake's master, who has died by his own adder.

question: Kipling gives his cobras a reason of their own, to win back the garden; Doyle's adder has only its master's. Which household war is the more frightening, and why does Kipling let the snake-killer live?

substitution.note: Replacing the Speckled Band: Kaa's Hunting has a great snake but no house, no hole and no vigil; the Hound has a night watch but a hound on a moor; the Rue Morgue's beast climbs in at a window and no one waits for it. Replacing Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: Kaa's Hunting and Kim bring no snake into a sleeping room through a wall, and no other work in the view sets a vigil against one.

claim: A famous stone leaves a great house, and a servant with a thief's past is the ready suspect. Collins makes Rosanna both suspect and hider, and Cuff is wrong about her; Doyle splits her in two, the plumber framed for his record and the thief who hides the stone in a goose.

from.exact: In the larger and older jewels every facet may stand for a bloody deed.

to.exact: the Moonstone passed (carrying its curse with it) from one lawless Mohammedan hand to another

alignments.same: A famous stone is said to carry a train of crimes with it from hand to hand.
alignments.differs: Collins's diamond bears a god's curse and three priests follow it; Holmes's carbuncle is under twenty years old, and its crimes come from greed alone, the devil's bait.

from.exact: You knew that this man Horner, the plumber, had been concerned in some such matter before, and that suspicion would rest the more readily upon him.

to.exact: there was Rosanna Spearman—with the character of a thief—ready to her hand; the person of all others to lead your ladyship off, and to lead me off, on a false scent.

alignments.same: A servant with a thief's past is named as the one the true taker meant to blame.
alignments.differs: Cuff wrongly fancies Rachel used Rosanna, who was not framed; Holmes rightly says Ryder chose Horner and had him arrested, and Horner goes free.

from.exact: I might at any moment be seized and searched, and there would be the stone in my waistcoat pocket.

to.exact: I might find myself taken off, at a moment’s notice, to the police court at Frizinghall, to be charged on suspicion, and searched accordingly.

alignments.same: The one who holds the evidence fears being searched at any moment and must hide it away from the house.
alignments.differs: Rosanna hides the stained nightgown in the Shivering Sand to shield the man she loves; Ryder pushes his own loot down a goose's throat, and loses it to the market.

question: Collins lets the reformed thief carry the suspicion and the secret and die of it; Doyle frees the plumber and lets the thief go. Which tale is kinder to the servant with a past, and which more just?

substitution.note: Replacing the Moonstone: The Sign of the Four has jewels with a train of killings, but no servant with a record is the ready suspect and the treasure is sunk, not hidden to carry; the Purloined Letter hides a stolen thing in plain sight, but no stone and no servant suspected; the Necklace has a lost jewel and no theft or suspect. Replacing the Blue Carbuncle: the Red-Headed League and the Speckled Band have no stolen stone, Sign of the Four is above.

claim: Both are Christmas tales in which a frightened sinner falls down clutching at the one who has laid his guilt bare, and is let off to mend. Dickens's spirits frighten Scrooge into a new life; Holmes lets Ryder go because the fright will keep him honest, and because it is the season.

from.exact: Ryder threw himself down suddenly upon the rug and clutched at my companion’s knees.

to.exact: "Spirit!" he cried, tight clutching at its robe, "hear me! I am not the man I was.

alignments.same: The guilty man drops down, clutching at the one who has shown him his wrong, and swears he will change.
alignments.differs: Scrooge begs to undo the future he has seen and to live better; Ryder begs only to be kept out of court and thinks of his parents' hearts.

from.exact: This fellow will not go wrong again; he is too terribly frightened.

to.exact: I am here to-night to warn you, that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate.

alignments.same: Fright is meant to save a sinner from his course.
alignments.differs: Marley's ghost frightens Scrooge on purpose to give him a chance; Holmes only finds Ryder frightened already, and counts on it as he lets him run.

from.exact: Besides, it is the season of forgiveness.

to.exact: a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time

alignments.same: Christmas is named as the time for forgiving.
alignments.differs: Fred's praise of the season answers a miser's 'Humbug'; Holmes gives it last, as a 'besides' after the practical reason that the case against Horner must collapse.

question: Scrooge is saved by visions sent on purpose; Ryder is saved by a detective who will not do the police's work. Is Holmes's mercy the Christmas spirit, or a dry man's excuse for it?

substitution.note: Replacing the Carol: Great Expectations has a Christmas, a convict and a frightened boy, but no sinner begging the one who exposed him and no pardon for the season; Silas Marner has a theft and New Year, but the thief Dunstan dies unforgiven; the Hammer of God has a confession to a priest, with no Christmas and no fright to reform. Replacing the Blue Carbuncle: no other detective tale in the view ends in a pardon at Christmas.

claim: Both bring the law at night to a dark spot where a smooth crook waits, and his own light shows his face, marked white near the brow. Holmes has old scores with John Clay and takes him by the collar; Patrolman Wells knows the face as his boyhood chum's and sends a plain-clothes man with a note instead.

from.exact: The light showed a pale, square-jawed face with keen eyes

to.exact: Over the edge there peeped a clean-cut, boyish face, which looked keenly about it

alignments.same: The lawman first sees the wanted man's face, keen-eyed, by the light the man himself brings into the dark.
alignments.differs: Clay's lantern comes up through the floor into an ambush laid for him; Bob strikes a match for his cigar, chatting to the patrolman who is the very friend he waits for.

from.exact: a little white scar near his right eyebrow

to.exact: Has a white splash of acid upon his forehead.

alignments.same: The crook is known by a small white mark on his face near the brow.
alignments.differs: Wilson names the mark not knowing what it means, and Holmes reads Clay from it; O. Henry shows the scar in passing, and only the end tells whose it is.

from.exact: Somehow I couldn’t do it myself, so I went around and got a plain clothes man to do the job.

to.exact: I have had one or two little scores of my own to settle with Mr. John Clay

alignments.same: The lawman who sets the trap has known the crook from before.
alignments.differs: Holmes's past with Clay is a running contest, and he seizes him himself; Jimmy's is a boyhood friendship, so he keeps the tryst but leaves the arrest to a stranger.

question: Jones would rather have his bracelets on John Clay than on any criminal in London; Jimmy Wells cannot put them on Bob himself. Is Jimmy's note a kindness or a second betrayal?

substitution.note: Replacing the League: no other work has a night ambush in which the crook's own light shows his face to the hidden law, a white mark near his brow, and a lawman with an old score. Dracula's Count is known in the dark by the red scar on his forehead, but his hunters are no police and have no past with him; Treasure Island's Billy Bones carries a white sabre cut but no one lies in wait to arrest him; Blue Cross's Valentin knows Flambeau by his height, not a mark, and Father Brown, not the light, unmasks him. Replacing After Twenty Years: no other work answers with a lawman who cannot arrest his old friend. The Blue Carbuncle's Holmes traps Ryder by day talk at a goose stall, not by a lying-in-wait; Ryder bears no mark and is let go. The Speckled Band's night watch does see the villain's dark-lantern gleam, but Roylott's brow carries the snake, not a scar, and Holmes neither knows him from before nor arrests him.

claim: Both bring a man back after twenty years to where the old eating-house of his youth stood, now replaced, asking after an old friend. Rip finds his cronies dead or gone and doubts who he is; Bob, sure of himself, sees through the stranger at once and is told the man the years have changed is himself.

from.exact: About that long ago there used to be a restaurant where this store stands—‘Big Joe’ Brady’s restaurant.

to.exact: He now hurried forth, and hastened to his old resort, the village inn—but it too was gone.

alignments.same: After twenty years away the man goes back to the house where he and his friends once ate and drank, and another building stands in its place.
alignments.differs: Rip stumbles on the change and is bewildered by the new hotel and its talk; Bob knows the place is gone, shrugs, and waits in the hardware store's doorway.

from.exact: If Jimmy is alive on earth he’ll be here by that time.

to.exact: Nicholas Vedder? why, he is dead and gone these eighteen years!

alignments.same: The returner asks after the friend of his old evenings and wonders if he is alive.
alignments.differs: Rip's cronies are dead, lost in the war or in Congress; Bob's friend is alive and true to the hour, but has come as the law.

from.exact: “You’re not Jimmy Wells,” he snapped.

to.exact: I’m not myself—I’m somebody else

alignments.same: At the reunion the question turns to who a man really is after twenty years.
alignments.differs: Rip doubts himself on seeing his son as his double; Bob doubts the stranger, knows him false by his nose, and hears that the years made him bad.

question: Rip slept through twenty years and comes back innocent; Bob was awake for all of them. Why does O. Henry make the hustler, not the dreamer, the one who has turned into somebody else?

substitution.note: Replacing Rip Van Winkle: no other work brings a man back after twenty years to a vanished inn or eating-house to ask after old friends and question who someone is. Great Expectations finds Satis House pulled down and Estella changed after eleven years, but asks after no crony and doubts no one's identity; A Tale of Two Cities' Manette, eighteen years in prison, returns to no old haunt; A Connecticut Yankee's leap is thirteen centuries back, not a return home. Replacing After Twenty Years: no other work answers with a tryst kept to the hour by a friend turned lawman. The Blue Carbuncle and The Speckled Band have no return after years, no vanished eating-house and no old friend asked after.

claim: Both bring a New York man with no work or home into the hands of the law. Soapy scorns charity, courts arrest all night, and is taken as he resolves to work; Bartleby declines a home and every post, never asks for the Tombs, and will not eat its dinners.

from.exact: Three months of assured board and bed and congenial company

to.exact: hope you’ll stay with us some time

alignments.same: Jail is pictured as a hotel that gives its guest bed, board and polite company for his stay.
alignments.differs: Soapy longs for the Island's board above all things; Bartleby, offered the grub-man's dinner, prefers not to dine and turns to face the wall.

from.exact: In Soapy’s opinion the Law was more benign than Philanthropy.

to.exact: will you go home with me now—not to my office, but my dwelling

alignments.same: Private kindness and the law stand as the two places that might house the homeless man.
alignments.differs: Soapy refuses charity on principle, because it pries and humbles; Bartleby gives no reason, prefers no change at all, and the landlord's police decide for him.

from.exact: A fur importer had once offered him a place as driver.

to.exact: Would you like a clerkship in a dry-goods store?

alignments.same: A man without an occupation is offered a plain place in trade.
alignments.differs: Soapy resolves to take his place tomorrow and is arrested at once for doing nothing; Bartleby refuses every post and is removed as a vagrant for staying put.

question: Soapy asks for the Island and is refused; Bartleby asks for nothing and is sent to the Tombs. Does the law in either tale see the man it holds?

substitution.note: Replacing Bartleby: no other work sets a homeless New York man between a refused private kindness and the jail, with the jail's board offered as hospitality and a place in trade offered and refused. A Christmas Carol has Scrooge's 'Are there no prisons?', but no poor man there prefers jail or is offered a post; Oliver Twist has the workhouse and the magistrate, but Oliver is a child kept by the parish who asks for more food, not a man refusing charity; The Overcoat's clerk has work and lodging. Replacing The Cop and the Anthem: Red-Headed League, After Twenty Years and The Bet hold men in custody, but none prefers jail to charity. The Blue Carbuncle is false too: its poor man Henry Baker has a home and loses only his hat and goose, and the thief Ryder holds a hotel post and is let go, not taken.

claim: Both follow a New York patrolman twirling his club on a night beat toward an arrest. Wells knows Bob is wanted, walks on, and sends another to take him; Soapy, passed over by every cop he provokes, is taken only when an anthem from his youth turns him to reform.

from.exact: The policeman twirled his club and took a step or two.

to.exact: The policeman twirled his club, turned his back to Soapy

alignments.same: A patrolman twirls his club and turns away from the man before him, leaving him at liberty.
alignments.differs: Wells walks on from a man he knows is wanted, to spare himself the arrest; the Broadway policeman turns from Soapy, who begs to be taken, as a harmless college boy.

from.exact: It sometimes changes a good man into a bad one

to.exact: he had known it well in the days when his life contained such things as mothers and roses and ambitions and friends

alignments.same: The years since youth have turned a man away from what he was.
alignments.differs: Bob, proud of his pile, hears it only from the detective who arrests him; Soapy sees his own fall when the old anthem reaches him and means to climb back.

from.exact: You’ve been under arrest for ten minutes, ‘Silky’ Bob.

to.exact: Soapy felt a hand laid on his arm.

alignments.same: The arrest falls while the man is thinking of his old days and least expects it.
alignments.differs: Bob is taken for a crime done in Chicago; Soapy, whose crimes all night came to nothing, is taken for standing at a church fence doing nothing.

question: Wells will not arrest the guilty friend himself; the cop at the church arrests a man who has just turned honest. What does the law in O. Henry's New York see when it looks at a face?

substitution.note: Replacing After Twenty Years: no other work has a beat patrolman twirling his club who walks away from the man before him, and an arrest that falls as the man dwells on his youth. The Red-Headed League's arrest is an ambush laid by Holmes, not a beat cop; A Tale of Two Cities has arrests by the Revolution, not a patrolman. Replacing The Cop and the Anthem: no other work has the law pass over the man who is guilty or wants to be taken. The Blue Carbuncle is false too: it is set in London with a commissionaire, not a beat patrolman, and Holmes lets the thief go rather than any arrest falling.

claim: Both bring a captive boy to a bargain with a close-fisted Ebenezer who will not pay to have him back. Stevenson's uncle, tricked by a sham kidnapper, would pay to have David kept away; O. Henry's father turns the bargain round, and the real kidnappers pay him to take the boy.

from.exact: The father was respectable and tight, a mortgage fancier

to.exact: if my uncle was certainly a miser, he was one of that thorough breed that goes near to make the vice respectable

alignments.same: The boy's guardian, named Ebenezer, is a miser whose meanness passes for respectability.
alignments.differs: Balfour has already sold his nephew to the sea for his estate; Dorset is the boy's own father, and the kidnappers count on him to pay.

from.exact: I think you are a little high in your demands, and I hereby make you a counter-proposition

to.exact: I take nae manner of interest in the lad, and I’ll pay nae ransome

alignments.same: Ebenezer, met with a demand for the boy, will not pay the ransom asked.
alignments.differs: Balfour blusters that he cares nothing for the lad and is bullied into terms; Dorset counters coolly in writing, and the kidnappers take his terms.

from.exact: You bring Johnny home and pay me two hundred and fifty dollars in cash, and I agree to take him off your hands.

to.exact: either ye liked David and would pay to get him back; or else ye had very good reasons for not wanting him, and would pay for us to keep him.

alignments.same: Money is offered over the captive boy, and nobody pays to get him back.
alignments.differs: Alan's two ways both have the uncle paying, a trap to make him confess; Dorset's way has the kidnappers paying, and they pay gladly.

question: Alan offers Ebenezer Balfour two ways for the money to go, and Ebenezer Dorset finds a third. What does each bargain say the boy is worth to the man who should want him?

substitution.note: Replacing Kidnapped: no other work brings a captive boy to a ransom bargain with a miserly guardian who will not pay. A Christmas Carol has its miser Ebenezer but no captive and no ransom; Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn talk of keeping captives in a cave till ransomed, but no one is asked to pay; Oliver Twist has Monks pay Fagin to ruin the boy, not to keep or return him; The Prisoner of Zenda holds a king, not a boy, and no ransom is asked. Replacing The Ransom of Red Chief: Treasure Island, Kim and Silas Marner have boys or a child changing guardians, but no guardian is asked for ransom.

claim: Both camp a boy in the woods playing Indian, near a robbers' cave whose captive, driven out, comes back. Tom's band scalp each other in play and soon grow homesick; Red Chief misses no home, goes for Bill's scalp in earnest, and is himself the captive who comes back, to his captors' despair.

from.exact: he was industriously and realistically trying to take Bill’s scalp

to.exact: killed and scalped each other by thousands

alignments.same: A boy camping out in the woods plays Indian and sets about scalping.
alignments.differs: Tom's tribes scalp one another in pretence and call it a gory, satisfactory day; Red Chief takes the bacon knife to his grown captor's hair, as he had sentenced him.

from.exact: I showed him the road to Summit and kicked him about eight feet nearer there at one kick.

to.exact: If you drove them out they’d turn right around and come back.

alignments.same: A captive held in a cave for ransom is driven out and turns round to come back.
alignments.differs: Tom gives it as the rule 'in all the books' for rich ladies won by polite robbers; Red Chief just likes the cave better than school, and the robbers are the ones undone.

from.exact: I don’t have any fun at home. I hate to go to school.

to.exact: After the meal they felt rusty, and stiff-jointed, and a little homesick once more.

alignments.same: A boy away from home in a camp in the woods faces the pull of home.
alignments.differs: Tom's pirates ran off by choice and soon turn homesick and must be cheered; Red Chief, taken by force, wants no home and begs not to be sent back.

question: Tom's captives come back because the books say they do; Red Chief comes back because he likes it. Which tale knows more about what a boy wants from the game of robbers?

substitution.note: Replacing Tom Sawyer: Huckleberry Finn has the gang's cave of captives kept 'till they're ransomed' and the cannon fired for Huck, but its captives are 'always trying to get loose', no boy plays Indian and scalps, and Huck is lonesome, not homesick for a family; Treasure Island and Kidnapped have boys far from home but no Indian game or cave of captives; Robinson Crusoe and Sindbad camp alone and do not play. Replacing The Ransom of Red Chief: The Last of the Mohicans has real scalping and captives, but no boy's game and no captive who returns of his own will.

claim: Both weigh a poor young couple's sacrifice for a thing of beauty, seen in the glass and undone by the last lines. Mathilde's lost diamonds cost ten years and prove paste; Della's hair and Jim's watch each buy a gift the other's sacrifice makes useless, and the narrator calls the two the wisest.

from.exact: She looked at her reflection in the mirror long, carefully, and critically.

to.exact: was lost in ecstasy at her reflection in the mirror

alignments.same: A young wife of a poor household studies herself in the glass before the night that should crown her.
alignments.differs: Mathilde sees herself made splendid by a diamond necklace that is not hers; Della sees her own beauty cut to schoolboy curls, sold for her husband's present.

from.exact: I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs.

to.exact: he was laying aside just that amount to buy a gun

alignments.same: The husband gives up the thing he meant for himself to pay for his wife's adornment.
alignments.differs: Loisel gives up a hoped-for gun for a gown, then his inheritance for the jewels; Jim sells his father's gold watch, and says so only after she has sold her hair.

from.exact: two foolish children in a flat who most unwisely sacrificed for each other the greatest treasures of their house

to.exact: Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!

alignments.same: The last lines show that what was given up bought nothing worth what it cost.
alignments.differs: Maupassant stops on the friend's cry and leaves the wasted years unjudged; O. Henry steps in to judge, and calls the couple's foolish waste the wisest giving.

question: Mathilde pays ten years for a necklace worth five hundred francs; Della and Jim are left with combs and a chain they cannot use. Why is one waste a tragedy and the other a blessing?

substitution.note: Replacing the Necklace: no other work has a poor wife before the glass, a husband who gives up his own wish to pay for her adornment, and a last line showing the sacrifice bought nothing of its worth. The Million Pound Bank-Note's note is lent and never spent, and no one sacrifices; The Overcoat's clerk saves for his own coat, with no wife; Madame Bovary's Emma runs up debts her husband learns of only after her death, for her own adornment, not his gift. Replacing the Gift of the Magi: no other work answers with a couple who each sell a treasure for the other.

claim: Both keep Christmas in a household on a small weekly wage that the narrator puns into the husband's name, the husband going without a greatcoat. A rich man's turkey and raise come to the Cratchits after their cheap goose; no benefactor comes to the Youngs, who give each other their treasures instead.

from.exact: Now, when the income was shrunk to $20, though, they were thinking seriously of contracting to a modest and unassuming D.

to.exact: Bob had but fifteen "Bob" a-week himself

alignments.same: The narrator jokes the man's weekly wage into his own name.
alignments.differs: Dickens makes Bob's name the very coin of his fifteen shillings; O. Henry shrinks Jim's 'Dillingham' with his pay, from thirty dollars toward a bare D.

from.exact: He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

to.exact: the clerk, with the long ends of his white comforter dangling below his waist (for he boasted no great-coat)

alignments.same: On Christmas Eve the young husband and father goes about in the cold without the greatcoat he needs.
alignments.differs: Bob slides on Cornhill and runs home to play; Jim comes in thin and serious, having sold his watch for her combs while his own coat goes unbought.

from.exact: Eight dollars a week or a million a year—what is the difference?

to.exact: These held the hot stuff from the jug, however, as well as golden goblets would have done

alignments.same: The narrator insists the poor household's few things serve as well as a rich man's.
alignments.differs: Dickens shows the Cratchits to a rich man who then sends a turkey and raises Bob's pay; O. Henry sends no benefactor, and the only gifts are the couple's own.

question: Dickens lets Scrooge's money reach the Cratchits' door; O. Henry lets no money reach the Youngs at all. Which Christmas story trusts the poor more?

substitution.note: Replacing the Carol: no other work keeps Christmas with a household whose weekly wage is punned into the husband's name and who goes coatless. Great Expectations' Christmas dinner at Joe's has no wage pun and no gift; Silas Marner spends his Christmas alone on a neighbour's gift of meat, with no wife, wage pun or treasure given up; Bartleby's copyist pay is no household's; Oh, Whistle's professor travels alone, with no household, Christmas or wage. Replacing the Gift of the Magi: no other work answers the Carol with a poor couple who give their own treasures because no money comes.

claim: Both give a girl's long hair, the beauty she wraps herself in, to a woman who trades in it for love's sake, and what it buys goes unused. The sisters' knife would save the mermaid by the prince's death, and she flings it away; Della's chain fits a watch already sold.

from.exact: It reached below her knee and made itself almost a garment for her.

to.exact: she had no clothes, so she wrapped herself in her long, thick hair.

alignments.same: A girl's long hair falls round her like the clothing she lacks.
alignments.differs: The mermaid's hair covers her as she first wakes on human legs before the prince; Della lets hers down alone before the glass to see it once more before she sells it.

from.exact: “Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.

to.exact: We have given our hair to the witch

alignments.same: Long hair is handed to a woman who trades in it, to buy something for one who is loved.
alignments.differs: The sisters pay the sea-witch for a knife to save their sister's life; Della sells hers for twenty dollars to buy a Christmas present.

from.exact: let’s put our Christmas presents away and keep ’em a while.

to.exact: then she flung it far away from her into the waves

alignments.same: What the hair bought is put aside unused.
alignments.differs: The mermaid throws the knife away to spare the prince and goes to the foam; the combs and chain are laid by because each sacrifice undid the other.

question: The sisters' hair buys a gift the mermaid will not use; Della's buys one Jim cannot use. Is a sacrifice wasted if what it buys is never used?

substitution.note: Replacing the Little Mermaid: no other work has women give their long hair for a loved one's sake and the purchase go unused. The Fisherman and His Soul's witch takes no hair and the knife she gives is used; Beauty and the Beast's Beauty gives up no part of herself to buy a thing; The Light Princess's prince offers his life, not his hair, and the Marsh King's Daughter sells nothing. Replacing the Gift of the Magi: no other work answers with a woman who sells her hair.

claim: Both give a poor wife money for clothes and a few hours among the rich. Mathilde asks four hundred francs for her own gown, borrows diamonds that prove paste and pays ten years for one night. Mrs. Sommers drops her children's list for silk at $1.98, and the story ends before any reckoning.

from.exact: really absorbed in speculation and calculation

to.exact: She reflected several seconds, making her calculations and wondering also what sum she could ask

alignments.same: A poor wife reckons carefully over a sum of money that will buy clothes.
alignments.differs: Mathilde reckons for her own gown, sizing the sum to what her husband will not refuse; Mrs. Sommers reckons for her children's shoes, shirt waists and caps, then drops the list.

from.exact: She smiled, just as if she had been asked to inspect a tiara of diamonds with the ultimate view of purchasing it.

to.exact: Suddenly she discovered, in a black satin box, a superb diamond necklace, and her heart throbbed with an immoderate desire.

alignments.same: A poor woman's hands fall on a luxury and her desire for it shows at once.
alignments.differs: Mathilde's diamonds are lent and turn out to be paste; Mrs. Sommers's diamonds are only a simile for stockings she can pay for herself.

from.exact: It was like a dream ended.

to.exact: All was ended for her.

alignments.same: The hours of finery end and the woman rides home in a public conveyance.
alignments.differs: Mathilde's end brings at once the lost necklace and ten years of debt; Chopin stops on the cable car, with nothing paid and only a wish that it never stop.

question: Maupassant makes Mathilde pay ten years for one evening; Chopin never shows Mrs. Sommers's bill. Which story judges its spender, and which leaves the judging to us?

substitution.note: Replacing the Necklace: no other work has a poor wife calculate a sum for a gown, hold diamonds with desire and ride home from one evening of finery. The Bank-Note's Henry is no wife and spends nothing; Madame Bovary's spending is months of debt; Paul's Case's money is stolen and he is a boy. Replacing the Stockings: no other work answers with a windfall turned from the children to one afternoon's silk. The Gift of the Magi's Della spends her hair money on a chain for her husband, not on clothes or hours among the rich.

claim: Chopin twice gives a hemmed-in wife a stretch of time to herself. Louise, freed by news of a death, sees clearly, claims years ahead and prays that life be long. Mrs. Sommers, freed by fifteen dollars, does not think at all; she has one afternoon and a cable car she wishes would never stop.

from.exact: A vision of the future like some dim, gaunt monster sometimes appalled her, but luckily to-morrow never comes.

to.exact: It was only yesterday she had thought with a shudder that life might be long.

alignments.same: A wife has dreaded the long future her life holds.
alignments.differs: Louise's dread turns within the hour into a prayer for long life; Mrs. Sommers keeps the monster off only by never looking past today.

from.exact: She was not going through any acute mental process or reasoning with herself

to.exact: A clear and exalted perception enabled her to dismiss the suggestion as trivial.

alignments.same: A wife takes a pleasure kept for herself without stopping to judge it.
alignments.differs: Louise waves off the charge of monstrous joy by a clear perception and whispers her freedom; Mrs. Sommers is not thinking at all, led by a mechanical impulse that frees her of responsibility.

from.exact: a powerful longing that the cable car would never stop anywhere, but go on and on with her forever

to.exact: She breathed a quick prayer that life might be long.

alignments.same: At the height of her freedom the wife wishes it to go on.
alignments.differs: Louise's prayer is for years and is cut off by her husband's return and her death; Mrs. Sommers's wish shows only in her face to a stranger, and the car must stop.

question: Louise dies when her freedom is taken away; Mrs. Sommers simply rides home to hers. Which ending is the harsher?

substitution.note: Replacing the Hour: no other work has a wife who dreaded a long life, wave off the judging of her own joy and pray that it last, all in one sitting. The Awakening's Edna has months and the sea, not an hour and a prayer; the Yellow Wallpaper's teller has no freedom to wish long. Replacing the Stockings: no other work answers with the same dread kept off by spending one afternoon. The Gift of the Magi's Della spends her stretch of time on her husband's gift, not on herself.

claim: Both spend money not meant for pleasure on new clothes, a fine dinner and a show among rich strangers who take them for their own. Paul's money is stolen, and when 'the play was over' he jumps. Mrs. Sommers's is her children's; she rides home, wishing only that the car never stop.

from.exact: His new street suit he put on in the fitting-room

to.exact: Here, in a retired corner, she exchanged her cotton stockings for the new silk ones which she had just bought.

alignments.same: The spender puts on the new finery at once, in the shop, and bundles the old away.
alignments.differs: Paul buys a whole wardrobe and Tiffany silver with endless care; Mrs. Sommers buys one pair of stockings at $1.98 and rolls her cotton ones into her bag.

from.exact: On the part of the hotel management, Paul excited no suspicion.

to.exact: When she entered her appearance created no surprise, no consternation, as she had half feared it might.

alignments.same: The newcomer in fine clothes passes unremarked among the rich.
alignments.differs: Paul feels his surroundings explain him and that no one could humiliate him; Mrs. Sommers half fears exposure and is simply not noticed by the quiet ladies and gentlemen.

from.exact: the sinking sensation that the play was over

to.exact: The play was over, the music ceased, the crowd filed out.

alignments.same: The end of the spree comes as the end of a play when the music stops.
alignments.differs: For Paul it is the news that his theft is known, and it ends in his death; Mrs. Sommers has seen a real matinee, and its end sends her to the cable car.

question: Paul cannot go back to Cordelia Street; Mrs. Sommers goes back to her brood. Is her ride home a mercy Cather denies Paul, or a worse sentence?

substitution.note: Replacing the Stockings: no other work spends money meant for others on clothes put on in the shop, a dinner and a show, ending as 'the play was over'. The Necklace's Mathilde buys a gown for one ball but has no dinner or play and is noticed by all; the Bank-Note's Henry is clothed on credit. Replacing Paul's Case: no other work answers with a thief's spree ended by death. The Cop and the Anthem's Soapy eats a dinner he cannot pay for to be jailed, with no new clothes or show.

claim: Both set a man and a woman talking over money that is not yet theirs. Twain's lovers talk 'salary and love' together, Henry hides his gains only to surprise Portia, and the dream comes true. Chekhov's long-married pair dream apart, each sure the other will hide the prize, and a wrong number leaves them hating.

from.exact: We talked salary; never anything but salary and love; sometimes love, sometimes salary, sometimes love and salary together.

to.exact: they could not have said, could not have dreamed, what they both needed that seventy-five thousand for

alignments.same: A man and a woman spend an evening talking of a sum they have not yet got.
alignments.differs: Henry and Portia's talk of an unclaimed salary is their courtship; Ivan and Masha laugh and stare at the figures but cannot say what they would buy.

from.exact: privately I raised my salary to twelve hundred the first year on the spot. But I didn’t tell her; I saved it for a surprise.

to.exact: she will lock the money up as soon as she gets it.... She will hide it from me

alignments.same: Money is kept back in silence from the one the man means to share his life with.
alignments.differs: Henry hides his own raise to give Portia a surprise; Ivan only imagines his wife hiding her winnings, and the fancy turns him against her.

from.exact: I didn’t know I had been dreaming

to.exact: Hatred and hope both disappeared at once

alignments.same: A man is jolted out of his dream of money he has never held.
alignments.differs: Hastings's envy wakes Henry to his debts, yet the month ends with a million and a bride; the number 46 wakes the Dmitritches to rooms that now seem dark and small.

question: Henry's money talk binds him to Portia; Ivan's turns him against Masha. Is the difference in the couples, in their years together, or in whether the money is to be earned or won?

substitution.note: Replacing the Bank-Note: no other work has a courting pair who talk of a salary not yet granted while the man hides his gains to surprise her. Hadleyburg's couple are old and share their guilt; the Necklace's pair owe a real debt; Around the World's Fogg never talks money with Aouda; The Bet has no couple. Replacing the Lottery Ticket: no other work has a married pair who come to hate each other over a prize neither yet holds. Works added later in the order: the Gift of the Magi's Jim and Della are poor and loving, talk of no sum not yet theirs and come to no hatred; A Pair of Silk Stockings has no man and spends a real windfall; the Ransom of Red Chief's pair are two kidnappers; After Twenty Years, the Blue Carbuncle, the Cop and the Anthem and the Speckled Band have no couple talking over money.

claim: Chekhov twice sets a man reckoning a fortune that another will get. The banker, owing two millions, wants the winner dead and creeps in to smother him; Ivan only hates his wife across the supper table. The prisoner waives the millions in contempt; the Dmitritches lose theirs to a misread number, still wanting them.

from.exact: He will take away my last farthing, marry, enjoy life, gamble on the Exchange, and I will look on like an envious beggar

to.exact: If she won it she would give me a hundred roubles, and put the rest away under lock and key.

alignments.same: A man pictures the one who will get the money living on it while he is left to beg for a share.
alignments.differs: The banker's dread is real, for the two millions fall due tomorrow; Ivan's is fancy about his own wife and a ticket whose number he has not read.

from.exact: The only escape from bankruptcy and disgrace—is that the man should die.

to.exact: And he looked at his wife, not with a smile now, but with hatred.

alignments.same: The coming payout turns a man's thoughts to hatred of the one who will be paid.
alignments.differs: The banker takes the key and goes by night to smother the prisoner; Ivan's worst deed is to read out the losing number to spite his wife.

from.exact: I despise freedom, life, health, and all that your books call the blessings of the world.

to.exact: And in all these pictures he saw himself well- fed, serene, healthy, felt warm, even hot!

alignments.same: Health and the world's comforts are what the money stands for.
alignments.differs: The prisoner has had them all in books and despises them; Ivan wants them in their plainest form: cold soup, warm sand, vodka and a nap on the sofa.

question: The banker is shamed by a man who despises money; Ivan is checked by nothing but a wrong number. Which story judges the money-dreamer more harshly?

substitution.note: Replacing The Bet: no other work has a man who must pay a fortune to another, hates him for it and plans his death, against a winner who renounces the sum. Bartleby's lawyer pays no fortune; Silas Marner's Dunstan steals but owes no prize; Hadleyburg's townsmen hate no winner. Replacing the Lottery Ticket: no other work turns a man's reckoning of another's prize into hatred of his own wife. Works added later in the order: the Speckled Band's Roylott would kill to keep his stepdaughters' income, but no one waives the sum in contempt and he is not Chekhov; the Ransom of Red Chief's kidnappers reckon a ransom they end up paying, with no wife to hate; the Gift of the Magi, A Pair of Silk Stockings, After Twenty Years, the Blue Carbuncle and the Cop and the Anthem have no man reckoning a fortune another will get.

claim: Both sit a long-married couple at home with a fortune not yet theirs. Twain's Richardses share one guilty wish and sit for weeks in a miserable parlour, held together by the money that ruins them. Chekhov's pair dream apart, read each other's greed in a glance, and hate each other until a wrong number ends it.

from.exact: their wives put in the night spending the money, which was easy.

to.exact: spend twenty-five thousand on real property in the shape of an estate

alignments.same: Money not yet in hand is spent in the head, sum by sum.
alignments.differs: Hadleyburg's nineteen households spend for weeks and some buy on credit; Ivan's estate, travels and bank interest last only until he reads the number.

from.exact: It’s no matter, Edward, I was thinking the same question myself.

to.exact: she understood perfectly well what her husband's dreams were

alignments.same: A wife knows without being told what her husband is thinking about the money.
alignments.differs: Mary shares Edward's guilty thought and stands by him in it; Ivan's wife reads his plan to grab her winnings and meets it with hatred of her own.

from.exact: Richards and his old wife sat apart in their little parlour—miserable and thinking.

to.exact: their rooms were dark and small and low-pitched

alignments.same: A couple's own small rooms turn dreary because of a fortune.
alignments.differs: The Richardses' misery lasts weeks while the hope of the money is alive; the Dmitritches' rooms darken the moment the hope dies with one wrong figure.

question: Twain needs a stranger's plot and a whole town to corrupt one old couple; Chekhov needs one column in a newspaper. What does each think it takes?

substitution.note: Replacing Hadleyburg: no other work keeps an old couple at home spending in fancy a fortune they may claim, with the wife reading her husband's thought. The Bank-Note's pair are young lovers; the Necklace's Loisels owe a real debt; Silas Marner hoards alone. Replacing the Lottery Ticket: no other work turns the same evening hope into hatred between husband and wife. Works added later in the order: the Gift of the Magi's young pair hold no fortune and grow only more loving; A Pair of Silk Stockings has one woman spending a real fifteen dollars; After Twenty Years, the Blue Carbuncle, the Cop and the Anthem, the Ransom of Red Chief and the Speckled Band keep no married couple at home over a prize.

claim: Both tie a young life to a painted thing that holds still while the real one fails, and read it as a sign of sin; the painter dies for his masterpiece. Dorian's portrait takes his age and sins until he stabs it; Behrman's ivy leaf, painted in one cold night, shames Johnsy into living and costs him his life.

from.exact: When the last one falls I must go, too.

to.exact: If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old!

alignments.same: A young person looking at a thing on a wall ties their own life to whether it changes.
alignments.differs: Dorian prays that the picture take his age in his stead and is granted it; Johnsy waits for a real leaf to fall and means to die with it.

from.exact: Something has made that last leaf stay there to show me how wicked I was. It is a sin to want to die.

to.exact: The picture, changed or unchanged, would be to him the visible emblem of conscience.

alignments.same: The watcher reads the image on the wall as a sign set there to show their own sin.
alignments.differs: Dorian vows to reform before the portrait and sins on until he stabs it; Johnsy repents at once, asks for broth and a hand-mirror, and lives.

from.exact: Ah, darling, it’s Behrman’s masterpiece—he painted it there the night that the last leaf fell.

to.exact: As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work

alignments.same: The painter's masterpiece and the painter's death are bound together.
alignments.differs: Basil is stabbed by the sitter whose soul his portrait shows; Behrman dies of a night on a ladder in the rain, and his work stays on the wall, taken for a leaf.

question: Basil's portrait tells the truth about a soul and is stabbed for it; Behrman's leaf saves a life by deceiving the one who looks at it. Which painter made the masterpiece?

substitution.note: Replacing Dorian Gray: no other work ties a life to a painted thing that holds still, read as conscience, at the cost of the painter. The Birth-Mark's mark is on Georgiana's own cheek and is removed, not painted; The House of the Seven Gables' portrait of the Colonel binds no living person's life; The Canterville Ghost's repainted bloodstain keeps no one alive; The Moon and Sixpence's wall paintings stand for no life and show no sin. Replacing the Last Leaf: no other work answers Dorian with a painted thing whose stillness saves the one who watches it.

claim: Both tell, after the night, of a man who died of a winter night in the rain by a wall and tree under a woman's window, for her sake. Behrman goes because Johnsy no longer wants to live, and she lives; Michael Furey went because he himself did not, and the telling shows Gretta's husband he has never loved so.

from.exact: He was standing at the end of the wall where there was a tree.

to.exact: An old, old ivy vine, gnarled and decayed at the roots, climbed half way up the brick wall.

alignments.same: Outside a young woman's window stands a wall with a tree or vine on it, where a man keeps a winter night's watch for her.
alignments.differs: Michael stands at the garden wall himself, shivering, to be seen once more; Behrman climbs to the vine on the next house's wall to be unseen, and leaves only a leaf.

from.exact: I implored of him to go home at once and told him he would get his death in the rain. But he said he did not want to live.

to.exact: His shoes and clothing were wet through and icy cold. They couldn’t imagine where he had been on such a dreadful night.

alignments.same: A man takes his death from a night out in the cold rain for a young woman's sake.
alignments.differs: Michael, already ill, comes because he does not want to live without Gretta; Behrman goes because Johnsy does not want to live, and no one knows where he went.

from.exact: “I think he died for me,” she answered.

to.exact: Mr. Behrman died of pneumonia to-day in the hospital.

alignments.same: Afterwards, in a bedroom, the man's death is told as a death for the woman's sake.
alignments.differs: Sue tells Johnsy as the news of what saved her, and she lives on, knitting; Gretta tells it of herself years later, and her husband learns from it that he has never felt such love.

question: Johnsy never saw Behrman go out into the rain; Gretta saw Michael shivering at the wall and still went away. Which woman owes more to the man who died for her?

substitution.note: Replacing the Last Leaf: no other work has a man die of a night in the rain at a wall under a woman's window for her sake. Wuthering Heights' Heathcliff dies in the rain at his own open window, not under a woman's window for her sake; The Outcasts of Poker Flat's dead die of snow and hunger together, not for one woman at a wall; The Sorrows of Young Werther's lover shoots himself. Replacing The Dead: no other work answers the Last Leaf with a boy who goes out to die because he does not want to live, told years later to a husband.

claim: Both put a dying painter's one masterpiece on the wall of a house, among artists who nurse one another through fever. Strickland, nursed by a kind bad painter whose wife he takes, covers his own hut for himself and has it burned; Behrman, a failure, paints one leaf on a neighbour's wall to keep a sick girl alive.

from.exact: Dirk Stroeve, giving up his work entirely, nursed Strickland with tenderness and sympathy.

to.exact: let Sudie go back to her drawing, so she can sell the editor man with it, and buy port wine for her sick child

alignments.same: An artist in a studio nurses another artist through a fever.
alignments.differs: Sue keeps drawing for the magazines to buy her friend's wine; Stroeve gives up his own work for Strickland, who repays him by taking his wife.

from.exact: From floor to ceiling the walls were covered with a strange and elaborate composition.

to.exact: and a palette with green and yellow colors mixed on it

alignments.same: A painter dying of disease makes his masterpiece on the wall of a house, not on canvas.
alignments.differs: Strickland covers his own hut from floor to ceiling with a world for himself; Behrman paints one leaf on the next house's brick in a night of rain, and no one takes it for art.

from.exact: I think Strickland knew it was a masterpiece. He had achieved what he wanted. His life was complete.

to.exact: In one corner was a blank canvas on an easel that had been waiting there for twenty-five years to receive the first line of the masterpiece.

alignments.same: A painter's life is judged by whether he made the masterpiece he lived for.
alignments.differs: Strickland reaches his and has the house burned with it; Behrman, who never began his, makes it at last as a false leaf for a sick girl, and dies of it.

question: Strickland's masterpiece is burned at his order, Behrman's is mistaken for a leaf. Does a masterpiece need anyone to know it is one?

substitution.note: Replacing the Last Leaf: no other work has a dying painter make his one masterpiece on a house wall among artists who nurse each other. Dorian Gray's portrait is on canvas, and Basil is killed, not sick, with no nursing; The Phantom of the Opera's Erik makes music, not a wall; The Gift of the Magi has no painter or illness. Replacing The Moon and Sixpence: no other work answers the Last Leaf with a great painter who paints his walls for himself and has them burned.

claim: Both shut a man in a house whose rotten air seems alive, where his beloved was laid out for dead, and he dies there. Roderick hears the sister he entombed alive and dies as she falls on him; the lodger, never told Eloise died in that bed, takes the gas there.

from.exact: And he breathed the breath of the house—a dank savour rather than a smell—a cold, musty effluvium as from underground vaults mingled with the reeking exhalations of linoleum and mildewed and rotten woodwork.

to.exact: an atmosphere which had no affinity with the air of heaven, but which had reeked up from the decayed trees, and the gray wall, and the silent tarn

alignments.same: The newcomer breathes a house's own air, reeking up from its rotting fabric like a breath.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator feels it hang about an ancient family seat and its tarn; O. Henry's lodger breathes it from linoleum and mildewed woodwork in a cheap lodging house.

from.exact: It seemed incredible that all this malice and injury had been wrought upon the room by those who had called it for a time their home

to.exact: that silent, yet importunate and terrible influence which for centuries had moulded the destinies of his family

alignments.same: A dwelling and those who live in it have marked one another over long tenancy.
alignments.differs: Usher's stones mould one family for centuries; the furnished room is the one marked, chipped and bruised by a thousand homeless lodgers raging at false household gods.

from.exact: Once again he answered loudly: “Yes, dear!” and turned, wild-eyed, to gaze on vacancy

to.exact: Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!

alignments.same: A man cries out to the woman he loves, sure she is near him in the house though he cannot see her.
alignments.differs: Roderick has heard Madeline for days and dared not speak, and she comes in to him; Eloise's scent fades, no one tells the lodger she died there, and he dies alone.

question: Roderick knew what lay in the vault and kept silent; Mrs. Purdy knows what happened in the bed and keeps silent too. Which silence does the killing?

substitution.note: Replacing Usher: no other work shuts a man in a house whose rotten air seems alive, where the woman he loves was laid out for dead, and has him die there. The Haunted and the Haunters' house holds no beloved; Wuthering Heights' Heathcliff dies in Catherine's old room, but the house is not rotting and he entombed no one; The Yellow Wallpaper's room has a smell that creeps, but no one dies; The Cask of Amontillado walls up a rival, not a sister. Replacing the Furnished Room: no other work answers Usher with a lodger who dies in the bed where his lost love died, never told.

claim: O. Henry twice sets young love in a cheap New York furnished room with a pier glass between the windows, and a woman's hair. Jim looks about for Della's sold hair as she stands before him; the lodger hunts for Eloise, finds a common hair-bow, and dies never told she died there.

from.exact: There was a pier glass between the windows of the room. Perhaps you have seen a pier glass in an $8 flat.

to.exact: a foot-wide cheap pier glass between the two windows

alignments.same: A cheap furnished room in New York has a narrow pier glass between its two windows.
alignments.differs: Della, being slender, masters the strip of glass to watch her hair fall before she sells it; the lodger's glass bears only a stranger's name, Marie, scrawled with a diamond.

from.exact: Jim looked about the room curiously.

to.exact: he sprang to wrest from it a token, for he knew he would recognize the smallest thing that had belonged to her or that she had touched.

alignments.same: A young man looks about a room for something of the woman he loves that is gone.
alignments.differs: Jim looks for Della's hair while she stands before him, saying it went for him; the lodger ransacks the room for a token of Eloise, though she died in that bed.

from.exact: Beautiful combs, pure tortoise shell, with jewelled rims—just the shade to wear in the beautiful vanished hair.

to.exact: But the black satin hair-bow also is femininity’s demure, impersonal, common ornament, and tells no tales.

alignments.same: A hair ornament stands for a woman whose hair, or whose self, is gone.
alignments.differs: Jim's combs were bought for Della's very shade and tell his love; the bow in the drawer belongs to any woman and tells the lodger nothing of Eloise.

question: Jim learns at once what Della gave up; the lodger is never told what happened in his room. In each story, who is given the last word on the lovers, and what does it cost them?

substitution.note: Replacing the Furnished Room: no other work in view sets a young man searching a cheap New York room with a pier glass for the woman he loves and a thing of her hair. The Last Leaf has a sick-room and a hand-mirror, no pier glass between windows, no lover and no hair; The Cop and the Anthem and After Twenty Years have no room and no woman; The Necklace's glass is in a Paris flat, and the loss is diamonds, not hair. Replacing the Gift of the Magi: no other work answers the Furnished Room with a couple who keep house in such a room and lose a woman's hair for love.

claim: Both put a newcomer in a let room whose damaged walls tell of earlier occupants, and a woman seems to be within the room. Gilman's narrator blames children, sees a woman behind the paper and becomes her; O. Henry's lodger reads homeless tenants' rage and cannot find the dead girl calling him.

from.exact: Tiny finger prints on the wall spoke of little prisoners trying to feel their way to sun and air.

to.exact: for the windows are barred for little children, and there are rings and things in the walls.

alignments.same: The newcomer reads marks in the room as left by small children once kept there.
alignments.differs: Gilman's narrator takes the bars and rings for a nursery's and is herself shut in there; O. Henry's lodger reads finger prints as little prisoners' and passes to the next sign.

from.exact: the resentful rage at false household gods that had kindled their wrath

to.exact: they must have had perseverance as well as hatred.

alignments.same: The room's injuries are laid to the hatred of those who lived there before.
alignments.differs: Gilman's narrator blames children, then bites the bedstead and peels the paper herself; O. Henry's lodger blames tenants cheated of a home, and harms only his own sheets.

from.exact: unable to perceive that she was there beside, around, against, within, above him

to.exact: And it is like a woman stooping down and creeping about behind that pattern.

alignments.same: The occupant senses a woman present in the fabric of the room itself.
alignments.differs: Gilman's narrator sees her behind the paper, frees her and becomes her; O. Henry's lodger only smells mignonette and finds no trace of the girl who died in that bed.

question: Gilman's narrator finds a woman in the wall and joins her; O. Henry's lodger finds no one and follows Eloise without knowing it. Which room does more to its tenant?

substitution.note: Replacing the Yellow Wallpaper: no other work has a newcomer in a let room lay its damaged walls to earlier occupants and sense a woman within the room. The Haunted and the Haunters' narrator hires a haunted house and finds a woman's letters, but its walls are not damaged by tenants' hatred and no woman is felt in its fabric; Usher's house is a family seat, not let; The Turn of the Screw's Bly is no let room. Replacing the Furnished Room: no other work answers the Yellow Wallpaper with a lodger who reads a room's ravages and seeks a woman who is there unseen.

claim: Both keep a husband from his marriage by the way he takes work, and lose him a night. Rip shuns profitable labour, sleeps twenty years as one night and is glad his scolding wife is dead; Maxwell, a machine of business, forgets the wedding of the night before and proposes again to his tender bride.

from.exact: Pitcher seized a moment to remark to the bookkeeper that the “old man” seemed to get more absent-minded and forgetful every day of the world.

to.exact: In a word, Rip was ready to attend to anybody’s business but his own; but as to doing family duty, and keeping his farm in order, he found it impossible.

alignments.same: Those about the husband see his way with work leave his own household unminded.
alignments.differs: Rip does anybody's business but his own and his family's; Maxwell does only his own business, so hard that his clerks think him forgetful.

alignments.same: Time between a man's last evening and his waking is lost to him, and his family must tell him what happened.
alignments.differs: Rip's one night was twenty years that took his wife; Maxwell's lost night is a single one, and it held his own wedding.

from.exact: “By George, I’ll do it now,” said Maxwell, half aloud. “I’ll ask her now. I wonder I didn’t do it long ago.”

to.exact: Happily, that was at an end; he had got his neck out of the yoke of matrimony, and could go in and out whenever he pleased

alignments.same: A man finds his married state changed without his knowing and takes it gladly.
alignments.differs: Rip rejoices that the yoke of matrimony is off; Maxwell, already married, eagerly asks to take it on again.

question: Rip's wife dins at his idleness for years; Miss Leslie forgives the business that made Maxwell forget her in one night. Which husband has really left his home?

substitution.note: Replacing Rip: no other work keeps a husband from his family by his way with work, loses him a night of his life, and has him glad of his changed married state. Connecticut Yankee's Hank loses Sandy across the centuries and grieves; The Marsh King's Daughter loses a bride on her wedding evening, but she is the one who goes and there is no work in it; The Story of an Hour's freed spouse is a wife whose husband was not dead; After Twenty Years has twenty years but no wife; A Christmas Carol's Scrooge never marries; Sleepy Hollow's Ichabod only courts, The Jumping Frog and Three Men in a Boat have no wife in view. Replacing the Broker: no other work answers Rip with a man who forgets his own wedding night for his trade.

claim: Both set a man of business whom trade engrosses before the woman who loves him, and she names what his business has done to her. Belle sees Gain has displaced her for good and releases Scrooge; Miss Leslie, wed the night before and forgotten, calls it 'for the time', and a scent of lilac has already brought her back.

from.exact: Stocks and bonds, loans and mortgages, margins and securities—here was a world of finance, and there was no room in it for the human world or the world of nature.

to.exact: I have seen your nobler aspirations fall off one by one, until the master-passion, Gain, engrosses you.

alignments.same: A man's business fills him until nothing else has room in him.
alignments.differs: Scrooge's Gain grows in him over years and Belle watches it; Maxwell's finance fills one morning's rush, and the narrator watches a machine.

from.exact: The odour brought her vividly, almost tangibly before him. The world of finance dwindled suddenly to a speck.

to.exact: Another idol has displaced me; and if it can cheer and comfort you in time to come, as I would have tried to do, I have no just cause to grieve.

alignments.same: The woman and the money contend for one place in a man's mind.
alignments.differs: In Scrooge the idol of Gain displaces Belle for good; in Maxwell a drift of lilac displaces the world of finance in a moment.

from.exact: It’s this old business that has driven everything else out of your head for the time.

to.exact: It is enough that I have thought of it, and can release you.

alignments.same: The woman says aloud what his business has done to her place in him.
alignments.differs: Belle, not yet married, releases Scrooge and leaves; Miss Leslie, married last night, forgives it as passing and puts an arm about his neck.

question: Belle leaves because Gain will last; Miss Leslie stays because she thinks business drove her out only 'for the time'. Is she right?

substitution.note: Replacing the Carol: no other work has a woman who loves a man of business say his trade has displaced her. Silas Marner's gold comes after Sarah has jilted him, and no woman speaks of it; Hard Times' Bounderby marries Louisa without love, but she never says his business pushed her out; Bartleby has an office and no woman; Oh, Whistle's professor has no woman; Rip Van Winkle shuns business. Replacing the Broker: no other work answers Belle with a woman already married, whose man forgets her in one day's trade and asks her again.

claim: Both make a baby the visible sign of a secret about its parents. Dimmesdale fears his features in Pearl's face, and at last bares his own breast to the town. Armand reads the baby's face against his wife, and only his dead mother's letter, read alone, tells him the blood was his.

from.exact: She looked from her child to the boy who stood beside him, and back again; over and over.

to.exact: my own features were partly repeated in her face, and so strikingly that the world might see them!

alignments.same: A parent searches a child's face for what it shows of where the child comes from.
alignments.differs: Dimmesdale dreads that the face shows his own guilt; Désirée sees in it a quadroon boy's likeness, Armand says it shows her blood, and the blood is in fact his.

from.exact: our dear Armand will never know that his mother, who adores him, belongs to the race that is cursed with the brand of slavery.

to.exact: my child must seek a heavenly father; she shall never know an earthly one!

alignments.same: A mother vows that her child will never know the truth of its parentage.
alignments.differs: Hester says it aloud on the scaffold to shield the father; Armand's mother writes it privately to her husband, and the kept secret lets her son ruin his own wife and child.

from.exact: "It means," he answered lightly, "that the child is not white; it means that you are not white."

to.exact: It was revealed!

alignments.same: A father brings into the open what the child's body has been taken to mean.
alignments.differs: Dimmesdale bares his own breast before the town and claims his part; Armand lays the mark on his wife and learns alone, after she is gone, that it was his.

question: Hester's silence protects the father; Armand's mother's silence protects the son. Whom does each secret harm most?

substitution.note: Replacing The Scarlet Letter: no other work has a parent who fears his own features in a child's face and a mother's vow that the child shall never know its father; Silas Marner's Godfrey hides his child but no one reads her face, and Oliver Twist's locket, not his face, tells his birth. Replacing Désirée's Baby: no other work answers with a father who blames the face on his wife and learns from a letter that it was his. Also tried the seven later-merged stories: none reads a parent's secret in a baby's face; Red Chief's boy is a hostage, not a sign of his birth.

claim: Chopin twice ends a wife's story on a truth the reader alone holds whole. Louise feels freedom coming, finds she loved her husband only sometimes, and dies when he walks in; doctors call it joy. Désirée feels a menace coming, loves Armand utterly, and walks into the bayou; a letter tells him the stain was his.

from.exact: What was it? She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name.

to.exact: It was at first too subtle to grasp.

alignments.same: A wife feels something coming toward her that she cannot yet name.
alignments.differs: What comes to Louise is her own freedom, which she welcomes; what comes for Désirée is the rumour of her blood, which takes her husband and then her life.

from.exact: And yet she had loved him — sometimes. Often she had not.

to.exact: When he frowned she trembled, but loved him.

alignments.same: A wife weighs her love for a husband whose will governs her.
alignments.differs: Louise finds her love was only sometimes and counts it little beside owning herself; Désirée's love is whole and hangs on his frowns and smiles.

from.exact: When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of the joy that kills.

to.exact: There was the remnant of one back in the drawer from which he took them.

alignments.same: The last lines hand the reader a truth the people in the story misread or keep hidden.
alignments.differs: The doctors misread Louise's death as joy and no one corrects them; Armand alone reads his mother's letter, and no one else learns that the blood was his.

question: Both endings let the reader know more than anyone in the story. Is that knowledge a punishment for Armand, or only for us?

substitution.note: Replacing the Hour: The Awakening's Edna has no named dread coming nor a misread death; Pair of Silk Stockings has no husband at all on stage. Replacing Désirée's Baby: no other work answers with a wife whose whole love hangs on a husband's frown and a closing letter that turns the blame on him. Also tried the seven later-merged stories: Della of the Magi loves her husband wholly but no truth comes for her and no letter turns blame; none is by Chopin.

claim: Chopin twice ends a wife's story with her walking into water. Edna strips on the empty beach and swims on to elude her children. Désirée, cast off by her husband, goes in her thin white gown into the bayou carrying her baby, and the story stays on the bank.

from.exact: she cast the unpleasant, pricking garments from her, and for the first time in her life she stood naked in the open air

to.exact: Désirée had not changed the thin white garment nor the slippers which she wore.

alignments.same: A wife goes to the water with her body barely covered.
alignments.differs: Edna chooses to stand naked and feels newborn; Désirée has simply not changed her house gown, and the field tears it and bruises her feet.

from.exact: The children appeared before her like antagonists who had overcome her

to.exact: She took the little one from the nurse's arms with no word of explanation

alignments.same: A mother's last walk is shaped by her child.
alignments.differs: Edna goes to the sea to escape her children's hold on her; Désirée takes her baby with her into the bayou.

from.exact: She did not look back now, but went on and on

to.exact: She disappeared among the reeds and willows that grew thick along the banks of the deep, sluggish bayou; and she did not come back again.

alignments.same: The wife walks on into the water and the story does not show her death.
alignments.differs: The Awakening follows Edna into the sea and into her memories; Désirée's story watches from the bank, says only that she did not come back, and turns to Armand.

question: Edna walks into the sea to keep herself; Désirée walks into the bayou having lost everything. Do the two endings mean the same act?

substitution.note: Replacing The Awakening: no other work sends a wife naked into the sea against her children's claim; the Hour's Louise dies at home. Replacing Désirée's Baby: no other work has a cast-off wife walk into water with her baby in her own gown, the story staying behind. Also tried the seven later-merged stories: the Furnished Room's girl dies by gas in a let room, not walking into water; no wife there goes into water.

claim: Both send a man out of time and through strange country home to his wife. Rip's twenty years pass as one night, and his house has fallen. Farquhar's instant of falling stretches to a day and a night, and home is as he left it, his wife waiting, because none of it is real.

from.exact: From this state he was awakened—ages later, it seemed to him

to.exact: Rip’s story was soon told, for the whole twenty years had been to him but as one night.

alignments.same: A man who has lost consciousness cannot tell how long he was gone.
alignments.differs: Rip's twenty years shrink to one night; Farquhar's fall of an instant seems to him to last ages.

from.exact: shone great golden stars looking unfamiliar and grouped in strange constellations

to.exact: There were rows of houses which he had never seen before

alignments.same: On the way home a man finds country he knew has gone strange to him.
alignments.differs: Rip's village has really grown and changed in twenty years; Farquhar's forest and stars are strange because he is dying and the road exists only in his mind.

from.exact: He stands at the gate of his own home. All is as he left it

to.exact: He found the house gone to decay

alignments.same: The journey ends at the man's own door, where he looks for his wife.
alignments.differs: Rip finds the roof fallen in and his wife dead, and is glad enough; Farquhar finds his wife smiling on the steps and dies as he reaches for her.

question: Rip loses twenty years and comes out free of his wife; Farquhar loses one instant and dies reaching for his. Which tale treats the time between as the real story?

substitution.note: Replacing Rip Van Winkle: no other work has a man lose all sense of time, find his country strange on the way home and come at last to his house to look for his wife. After Twenty Years returns to a vanished eating-house but seeks a friend, not a wife; the Marsh King's Daughter loses a night in three minutes but never goes home; the Time Traveller comes back to his house, with no wife. Replacing Owl Creek Bridge: no other work answers with a journey home that proves to be the dying instant itself. Later works tried: the Busy Broker forgets overnight that he married, but takes no road home and seeks no wife at a door; the Furnished Room's young man hunts a lost love through lodgings, not his own house; Cop and the Anthem, Gift of the Magi, Last Leaf, Blue Carbuncle, Desiree's Baby and Red Chief lose no sense of time.

claim: Both give a last hour to a mind running ahead to the life beyond it, then end with one flat sentence from outside. Farquhar's escape to his wife is dreamed in the drop and the last line undoes it; Louise's freedom from her husband is real until he walks in, and the doctors misread her death.

from.exact: But she saw beyond that bitter moment a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely.

to.exact: By diving I could evade the bullets and, swimming vigorously, reach the bank, take to the woods and get away home.

alignments.same: At the moment death enters the story, the mind runs ahead to a life that lies past it.
alignments.differs: Louise sees years alone and her own, with the husband gone; Farquhar plans a way back home to his wife and children, with the noose already round his neck.

from.exact: And she opened and spread her arms out to them in welcome.

to.exact: He springs forwards with extended arms.

alignments.same: Arms are thrown open to the future that is dreamed.
alignments.differs: Louise opens hers to empty years without a husband; Farquhar opens his to his wife, and the blow on the neck comes before he can clasp her.

from.exact: When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease — of the joy that kills.

to.exact: Peyton Farquhar was dead; his body, with a broken neck, swung gently from side to side beneath the timbers of the Owl Creek bridge.

alignments.same: A last sentence, from outside the mind we have followed, reports the death.
alignments.differs: Bierce's sentence is true and cancels the whole escape; Chopin's verdict leaves the hour standing and gets the cause wrong, since the joy died before she did.

question: Bierce's last line tells the truth and Chopin's doctors do not. Which ending asks more of the reader to see what the hour before it meant?

substitution.note: Replacing Owl Creek Bridge: no other work follows a mind's flight into the future in the hour of a death, ends on arms held out, and closes with a flat outside report of the death. The Necklace and After Twenty Years turn in their last lines but on a fact about paste or a face, with no dream of the years ahead; Rip Van Winkle's husband walks home but no one dies of it. Replacing The Story of an Hour: no other work answers with a dream of years without the spouse undone by the spouse at the door. Later works tried: Cop and the Anthem comes nearest, with Soapy's mind running ahead to a reformed life, a hand on his arm and a flat sentence from the Magistrate, but no one is dying and no death is reported; the Furnished Room and Last Leaf report a death but follow no dream of the life beyond; Desiree's Baby, Gift of the Magi, Busy Broker, Blue Carbuncle and Red Chief turn at the end on a fact, not on a dying mind's flight.

claim: Both tales bring a house's dead men home at nightfall to a woman watching the window, while a frightened man looks on. Jacobs's son really returns from the grave and is wished away behind the door; Saki's dead walk in alive across the lawn, and the horror that sends the man running exists only in a girl's tale.

from.exact: her eyes were constantly straying past him to the open window and the lawn beyond

to.exact: walked to the window and raised the blind

alignments.same: A woman who expects the dead men of her house to come back keeps her eyes on the window.
alignments.differs: Mrs. White goes to the window for a son she has just wished out of his grave; Mrs. Sappleton watches for living men due home to tea.

from.exact: Here they are at last!” she cried. “Just in time for tea

to.exact: “It’s Herbert!” she screamed. “It’s Herbert!”

alignments.same: When the men arrive, the waiting woman cries out that they have come.
alignments.differs: Mrs. White screams her dead son's name at a knock and fights to unbolt the door; Mrs. Sappleton calls cheerfully about tea and mud, and only the visitor hears a madwoman greeting ghosts.

from.exact: the hall-door, the gravel-drive, and the front gate were dimly-noted stages in his headlong retreat. A cyclist coming along the road had to run into the hedge to avoid an imminent collision.

to.exact: and then to the gate beyond. The street lamp flickering opposite shone on a quiet and deserted road.

alignments.same: The man who dreads the returning dead runs out to the gate and the road.
alignments.differs: Mr. White reaches the gate after his last wish and finds the road empty of the dead; Framton runs from men who are alive, and his road holds a living cyclist forced into the hedge.

question: Saki's story frightens only until its last paragraph. Does the joke need readers who already know tales like Jacobs's, in which the dead really do come home to the woman at the window?

substitution.note: Only The Monkey's Paw has a woman at the window waiting for the dead men of her house, her cry when they arrive, and a frightened man who runs to the gate and an empty road. The Signal-Man's dead are strangers on the line; Usher's Madeline returns to a brother, not a watching wife or mother; The Haunted and the Haunters, The Canterville Ghost, Oh, Whistle and Sleepy Hollow have no one waiting for a dead kinsman; Frankenstein and The Body Snatcher raise the dead but no one watches a window for them; Rip Van Winkle comes home alive to a wife already dead; The Story of an Hour's husband walks in alive, but no one has waited for him and the shock kills the wife, not a visitor; Dorian Gray shares only the wish heading. Of the O.
