Henry tales, The Last Leaf has a woman watching a window, but for a falling leaf, not for dead men coming home, and no one runs; The Furnished Room's dead girl comes back only as a scent to a lodger; The Gift of the Magi, The Ransom of Red Chief and A Romance of a Busy Broker have no returning dead.

claim: Both tales end with a living voice saying aloud, word for word, what a ghost story had given the apparition to say. Dickens leaves the echo a coincidence nobody arranged, and it seals the warning; Saki makes it the last stroke of a girl's lie, because she built the men's song into her tale knowing they would sing it.

from.exact: I said, Bertie, why do you bound?

to.exact: I said, Below there! Look out! Look out! For God’s sake clear the way!

alignments.same: A living man arriving at the end says, beginning 'I said', the very words the tale of the apparition had put in its mouth.
alignments.differs: The engine-driver repeats the spectre's cry by chance and shakes the narrator; Ronnie sings his usual song, which Vera had written into her ghost tale so his arrival would complete it.

from.exact: the nerve cure which he was supposed to be undergoing

to.exact: figures, originating in disease of the delicate nerves that minister to the functions of the eye

alignments.same: The man who sees the apparition is set beside a diagnosis of weak nerves.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator uses nerves to explain the spectre away, and events outrun him; Framton's nerves are the weakness Vera plays on, and nothing outruns her.

from.exact: Romance at short notice was her speciality.

to.exact: the words which I myself—not he—had attached, and that only in my own mind, to the gesticulation he had imitated

alignments.same: The last sentence tells the reader where the frightening words came from.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator closes on a coincidence he can point out but not explain; Saki's last sentence names the liar and leaves nothing supernatural over.

question: In Dickens the echoed words make the reader half believe; in Saki they make only Framton believe. Is Saki mocking the ghost story, or the reader who takes an echo as proof?

substitution.note: Only The Signal-Man ends with a living voice repeating word for word, after 'I said', what the tale of the apparition had made it say, beside a diagnosis of weak nerves. A Christmas Carol's ghosts speak for themselves; The Haunted and the Haunters explains its haunting by a living will, not by echoed words; Sleepy Hollow and The Overcoat leave their spectre a possible trick without any repeated words; The Turn of the Screw's governess sees figures that never speak; The Monkey's Paw's dead son only knocks; Oh, Whistle's figure has no voice; Tobermory repeats overheard words but tells no ghost tale. Of the O. Henry tales, none has an apparition's words repeated by a living voice: The Furnished Room's lodger hears a scent, not words, and the landlady's 'as I said' repeats only her own lie; The Last Leaf, The Gift of the Magi, The Ransom of Red Chief and A Romance of a Busy Broker have no apparition.

claim: Both set a man of sense against a haunting that has already cost lives, and he argues nerves, fancy and coincidence. Dickens's narrator never sees the spectre, and his reasons outlast the signalman. Crawford's Brisbane spends his reasons on the porthole, keeps watch with the captain, and holds the drowned thing in his arms.

from.exact: The Welsh rare-bit I had eaten had disagreed with me. I had been in a nightmare.

to.exact: I showed him how that this figure must be a deception of his sense of sight

alignments.same: A man of sense explains an apparition away as a disorder of the body.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator diagnoses another man's eyes and never sees the figure; Brisbane blames his own supper for a cold, wet arm he has just held.

from.exact: If we see anything now, it must be either imagination or something supernatural.

to.exact: My eyes were on the bell, and my ears were open to the bell, and if I am a living man, it did NOT ring at those times.

alignments.same: Two men watch a fitting of the haunted post together to test whether the haunting is real.
alignments.differs: For Dickens's narrator the bell stays still and only the signalman hears it; the captain and Brisbane both see the brass nut turn and the port open against their hands.

from.exact: There would have remained the disagreeable coincidence of several suicides occurring among men who had slept in the same cabin, but that would have been all.

to.exact: It was not to be denied, I rejoined, that this was a remarkable coincidence, calculated deeply to impress his mind.

alignments.same: Deaths that follow a haunting are weighed as coincidence.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator offers coincidence as the answer, and the tale ends on another; Brisbane says coincidence is all there would have been had he moved out.

question: Dickens's narrator ends on a coincidence he cannot explain; Brisbane ends 'if it was a ghost.' Which sceptic gives up more of his reason, and which tale needs him to?

substitution.note: Replacing The Signal-Man: no other work has a sceptic argue away another man's haunting at its post, test it by watching the fitting, and call the deaths coincidence while never seeing the thing himself. The Haunted and the Haunters' investigator sees every sign himself and explains it by a living will; Whistle's Parkins argues only for himself; A Christmas Carol's Scrooge blames his own supper but keeps no watch and no one has died of the ghost; The Open Window's Framton is a nervous man, not a sceptic, and argues nothing. Replacing The Upper Berth: no other work answers with a sceptic who keeps the watch with a witness and seizes a drowned body. Corrected against the tales that came in before this step: The Furnished Room, The Gift of the Magi, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no sceptic and no haunting, and keep no watch. The Yellow Wallpaper, now sharing the let-room heading, has a rational husband who argues away his wife's fancies, but no haunting has cost lives and no one keeps watch.

claim: Both sea survivors tell a night of terror to listeners and point to their bodies as proof. Poe's fisherman studies the whirl, reads its law in the wreckage, and escapes by it, expecting no belief. Brisbane studies the porthole, finds no law in it, and ends his tale unsure himself of what he held.

from.exact: I watched it intently, fixing its position in my mind, and trying to ascertain whether it changed.

to.exact: This hope arose partly from memory, and partly from present observation.

alignments.same: In the hour of terror the teller fixes his eye on one thing and studies how it moves.
alignments.differs: The fisherman reads from the sinking wreckage how the whirl draws things down, and saves himself by it; Brisbane watches the nut turn and learns nothing that keeps the port shut.

from.exact: the bruises were there on the following morning to testify to the fact, if I myself had doubted it.

to.exact: My hair which had been raven-black the day before, was as white as you see it now.

alignments.same: The teller points to a mark left on his own body to vouch for the night.
alignments.differs: The fisherman's white hair is his whole proof, shown to a stranger; Brisbane's bruises prove only that he was awake, and his broken arm is still to come.

from.exact: That is how I saw a ghost—if it was a ghost. It was dead, anyhow.

to.exact: I told them my story—they did not believe it.

alignments.same: The survivor ends his tale by facing the doubt it meets.
alignments.differs: The fisherman knows what happened and expects his hearer not to believe him; Brisbane, met with 'Bosh!', is himself unsure what he fought, sure only that it was dead.

question: Poe's fisherman is saved by what he observes and Brisbane by nothing he observes. Does the ghost story need its teller's reason to fail where the sea story needs it to work?

substitution.note: Replacing the Maelström: no other work has a sea survivor tell listeners how he studied the thing that nearly killed him, show a mark on his body, and close by facing their disbelief. The Open Boat's correspondent reads the sea's indifference but tells no hearers; Moby-Dick's Ishmael floats out of the vortex on a coffin with no proof on his body; Twenty Thousand Leagues' Aronnax cannot tell how he escaped; Sindbad's hearers do not doubt him; The Open Window has no sea and no survivor. Replacing The Upper Berth: no other work answers with a survivor whose study finds no law at all. Corrected against the tales that came in before this step: The Furnished Room, The Gift of the Magi, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no sea, no survivor telling hearers, and no mark shown as proof. The Yellow Wallpaper, now sharing the let-room heading, has no sea and no survivor telling hearers.

claim: Both hauntings come from the unused bed in a sceptic's room. Parkins blames the maids, beats the wind at the window, and is saved by the Colonel from a thing made of bedclothes. Brisbane blames the steward, loses the port with the captain, and grapples a drowned body that breaks his arm.

from.exact: I disordered the clothes last night in unpacking, and they haven’t made it since.

to.exact: I fancied that Robert had not had the courage to make the bed after the accident of the previous night

alignments.same: The unused bed in a sceptic's room is found disturbed, and he blames a servant for not making it.
alignments.differs: Parkins's bed is only twisted, and he blames maids called away; Brisbane's berth was slept in and smells of the sea, and he thinks the steward afraid to touch it.

from.exact: Parkins was struggling with the small casement, and felt almost as if he were pushing back a sturdy burglar, so strong was the pressure.

to.exact: He was wrestling with all his might, with the brass loop of the port. It seemed to turn against his hands in spite of all his efforts.

alignments.same: A man strains at a window fastening against a force pushing from the other side.
alignments.differs: Parkins wins, and the window latches itself; the captain loses, Brisbane's oak stick snaps, and the port stands open for the thing.

from.exact: There seemed to be absolutely nothing material about it save the bedclothes of which it had made itself a body.

to.exact: It was like the body of a man long drowned, and yet it moved, and had the strength of ten men living

alignments.same: The thing from the other bed has a body that is not its own.
alignments.differs: James's thing is only bedclothes and, the Colonel thinks, could do nothing but frighten; Crawford's is a drowned corpse with the strength of ten men that breaks Brisbane's arm.

question: Parkins never touches his visitor and Brisbane seizes his twice. Does closing with the thing make it more real, or does James's visitor, who can only frighten, leave its sceptic more shaken?

substitution.note: Replacing The Upper Berth: no other work has the haunting rise from the unused bed in a sceptic's room, a fastening wrestled against a force, and a visitor with a borrowed body. The Turn of the Screw keeps its ghosts outside at windows and towers; The Haunted and the Haunters has no second bed and its shapes are shadows; Canterville's ghost is a figure of fun with no bed; The Open Window's window is kept open on purpose and no one sleeps there. Replacing Whistle: no other work answers with a sceptic saved by a witness from a visitor that has only bedclothes for a body. Corrected against the tales that came in before this step: The Furnished Room's lodger dies in a dead girl's bed but no sceptic blames a servant, wrestles a window or meets a body; The Gift of the Magi, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no haunting. The Yellow Wallpaper, now sharing the let-room heading, has a bed nailed down, not an unused one disturbed, and no visitor with a body.

claim: Both keep an opening for men lost and never found, and a man bolts from the room. Crawford's port will not stay shut, the drowned come back through it, and those who run die. Saki's window is open in a girl's tale, the lost walk in muddy and alive, and the runner is a nervous guest.

from.exact: That is why the window is kept open every evening till it is quite dusk.

to.exact: there's nobody on board as can keep this 'ere port shut at night.

alignments.same: An opening stays open every night, and the tale ties it to men who were lost.
alignments.differs: Vera says the aunt keeps the window open for her dead to walk back in; on the Kamtschatka no hand can keep the port shut, and the drowned thing uses it.

from.exact: Their bodies were never recovered.

to.exact: we stopped and lowered boats, but they were not found.

alignments.same: Men swallowed by bog or sea leave no bodies behind.
alignments.differs: Saki's three were never lost and come home for tea; Crawford's sleepers are really gone overboard, and one comes back to the berth as a drowned body.

from.exact: Who was that who bolted out as we came up?

to.exact: They bolt out of bed and run down the passage.

alignments.same: A man flees the room at full speed from what he takes for the dead.
alignments.differs: Framton runs from living men and a spaniel and is laughed at as a crank; Crawford's sleepers run from the upper berth into the sea.

question: Saki's window waits for ghosts that never come and Crawford's port lets one in that no one invited. Which tale is crueller to the man who runs?

substitution.note: Replacing The Upper Berth: no other work has an opening that will not stay shut for men lost and never found, and sleepers who bolt from the room to their deaths. The Monkey's Paw's door is opened for a son whose body was found and buried; Whistle's window lets in no lost men; The Signal-Man's lost are killed on the line, with no one fleeing a room. Replacing The Open Window: no other work answers with lost men who were never lost and a flight that is only a joke. Corrected against the tales that came in before this step: The Furnished Room's window is stopped shut, not kept open, and no one bolts; The Gift of the Magi, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no lost men and no flight. The Yellow Wallpaper, now sharing the let-room heading, has barred windows and no lost men.

claim: Both let a room whose sleepers killed themselves, and its keepers hide the suicides so it can be let again. Crawford's cabin keeps the smell of the sea its dead went into, and a sceptic told the story stays and lives. O. Henry's room keeps the girl's mignonette, and her lover, told nothing, dies by her gas.

from.exact: There be many people will rayjict the rentin’ of a room if they be tould a suicide has been after dyin’ in the bed of it.

to.exact: I don't want the ship to get a bad name, and nothing hangs about an ocean-goer like stories of suicides.

alignments.same: Those who let the room keep its suicides quiet for the sake of trade.
alignments.differs: Mrs. Purdy lies to the lodger who asks and he never learns; the captain tells Brisbane himself and asks only that the other passengers not hear.

from.exact: This enveloping scent of mignonette, the odour that she had loved and made her own—whence came it?

to.exact: Ever since that the place smells of sea-water from time to time.

alignments.same: A smell comes and goes in the room from one who died out of it.
alignments.differs: The mignonette is the dead girl's own scent and calls her lover to her; the sea-water is the road the drowned took, and the captain sniffs it with dread.

from.exact: When all was snug and taut he turned out the light, turned the gas full on again and laid himself gratefully upon the bed.

to.exact: I intended to be the exception to the rule by which every one who slept in that particular state-room went overboard.

alignments.same: Whoever sleeps in the room is drawn to the death of those who slept there before.
alignments.differs: O. Henry's lodger dies by gas in the bed where Eloise died by gas, never knowing it; Brisbane knows the rule, stays, and lives, while his room-mate goes over.

question: Mrs. Purdy's silence lets the lodger die where Eloise died; the captain's candour lets Brisbane stay and live. Does knowing a room's past protect the one who sleeps in it?

substitution.note: Replacing The Upper Berth: no other work has a let room whose keepers hide the suicides of those who slept in it, a smell left by the dead, and a next sleeper drawn to the same end. The Yellow Wallpaper's house is let cheap with no deaths told, and its smell is the paper's; The Haunted and the Haunters' owner tells the tale frankly and lets the house rent free, and no tenant killed himself there; The Open Window and Whistle hide no deaths for trade. Replacing The Furnished Room: no other work answers with a keeper who hides suicides from a lodger who then dies by the same means in the same bed; The Gift of the Magi and The Last Leaf have no death in the room's past, and The Romance of a Busy Broker has no room let. A Christmas Carol's Scrooge keeps the dead Marley's chambers, but no death there is hidden for trade and no sleeper is drawn after him.

claim: Both tales post an apparition on the haunted man's way, crying the same words, while a sceptic blames the eye. Dickens's spectre warns of disaster on the line; Kipling's cries a dead woman's plea for forgiveness to the man who wronged her, and its one warning, at a landslip, only saves him for more haunting.

from.exact: “Jack! Jack dear! Please forgive me,” rang with a wail in my ears

to.exact: It calls to me, for many minutes together, in an agonised manner, ‘Below there! Look out! Look out!’

alignments.same: The apparition cries to the haunted man again and again in the same few words.
alignments.differs: The spectre's cry warns of danger on the line; Mrs. Wessington's repeats the plea she made alive to the man who wore her to death, and he can do nothing with it.

from.exact: Therefore, I conclude that it’s Eyes.

to.exact: figures, originating in disease of the delicate nerves that minister to the functions of the eye

alignments.same: A sceptic beside the seer explains the apparition as a disorder of the eye.
alignments.differs: Dickens's narrator lectures the signal-man and hides his own shiver; Heatherlegh rides beside the rickshaw, asks Pansay where it is, and prescribes liver pills.

from.exact: the ‘rickshaw came to a dead stop under a pine-clad, over-hanging shale cliff

to.exact: Within six hours after the Appearance, the memorable accident on this Line happened

alignments.same: The apparition stands where disaster is about to fall.
alignments.differs: Dickens's spectre comes hours before an accident no one can stop; the rickshaw halts just before the cliff falls, and the men who halt with it live.

question: Dickens's spectre comes from outside the signal-man's life; Kipling's comes out of Pansay's own past. Does the halt before the landslip make the rickshaw something other than a punishment?

substitution.note: Only The Signal-Man posts its apparition at a place of coming disaster, repeating one cry, beside a sceptic who blames a disease of the eye. A Christmas Carol has a sceptic's stomach theory but Marley comes to a room, says many things and marks no place of disaster; The Haunted and the Haunters and Oh, Whistle have no repeated cry and no eye diagnosis; The Turn of the Screw's figures never speak; The Open Window's ghosts are a girl's invention; The Monkey's Paw's dead son only knocks. The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and A Romance of a Busy Broker (tried in the G25-04 correction) have no apparition with a repeated cry and no sceptic blaming the eye; the Furnished Room's dead lover returns only as a scent.

claim: Both tales have the one who sees a dead woman force a loved companion to look at her, and lose the companion for it. Pansay, begging Kitty to speak to the ghost, confesses the wrong that raised it; James's governess accuses Flora of seeing and hiding, and the child, seeing nothing, begs to be taken away.

from.exact: What a dreadful turn, to be sure, miss! Where on earth do you see anything?

to.exact: “What? Where?” she asked. “I can’t see them anywhere.”

alignments.same: Told of the apparition, the companion at the seer's side asks where it is and sees nothing.
alignments.differs: Mrs. Grose's blindness at the lake becomes for the governess proof that the child sees and lies; Kitty's, on a crowded Simla road, only makes her think Jack doubts her riding.

from.exact: there, there, there, and you see her as well as you see me!

to.exact: “Yes, there is a mistake somewhere,” I repeated, “a hideous mistake. Come and look at It.”

alignments.same: The seer presses the companion toward the apparition and insists that she look.
alignments.differs: The governess wants Flora to admit she sees the dead woman; Pansay wants Kitty to tell the ghost they are betrothed, and in pleading lets out his wrong to her.

from.exact: Take me away, take me away—oh, take me away from her!

to.exact: “Thank you, Mr. Pansay,” she said, “that’s quite enough. Syce ghora láo.”

alignments.same: Shown a ghost she does not see, the loved one turns from the seer and leaves.
alignments.differs: Flora flees the governess herself as the cruel one; Kitty leaves because the raving has told her Pansay's past, and cuts him across the face with her whip.

question: James's governess takes the dead to be the wicked ones; Kipling's ghost is the one who was wronged. Does James leave room for the governess's own guilt in what she makes Flora look at?

substitution.note: Only The Phantom Rickshaw has a seer drag a loved companion toward a dead woman she cannot see and lose her for it. The Signal-Man's narrator also looks and sees nothing, but he is a stranger who stays; The Yellow Wallpaper's husband faints at what he sees in the room, with no ghost shown him; Canterville, The Haunted and the Haunters and Dracula show their apparitions to everyone; Usher's Madeline is seen by both men. The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and A Romance of a Busy Broker (tried in the G25-04 correction) have no seer pressing a loved companion to look at a dead woman.

claim: Kipling frames both tales alike: the narrator asks a broken man for his story 'from beginning to end', the man clings to his own name, and an official blames sun or overwork for his death. The Rickshaw opens with that verdict and its narrator rejects it; the King closes on it.

from.exact: Tell me all you can recollect of everything from beginning to end.

to.exact: I suggested that he should write out the whole affair from beginning to end

alignments.same: The narrator asks the broken man to give the whole affair 'from beginning to end'.
alignments.differs: Carnehan tells it aloud across the office table, begging the narrator to keep looking in his eyes; Pansay writes it out in fever, in a magazine diction that does not calm him.

from.exact: I am Peachey—Peachey Taliaferro Carnehan

to.exact: I’m Jack Pansay on leave at Simla—at Simla! Everyday, ordinary Simla.

alignments.same: The broken man says his own name aloud to hold on to who and where he is.
alignments.differs: Carnehan names himself because the narrator does not know the wreck before him; Pansay names himself on a haunted road to prove he is not going mad.

from.exact: He was admitted suffering from sun-stroke. He died early yesterday morning

to.exact: Overwork started his illness, kept it alight, and killed him poor devil.

alignments.same: After the man's death an official gives a plain bodily cause for it.
alignments.differs: The Superintendent's sunstroke is the tale's last word; Heatherlegh's overwork comes first, and the narrator answers 'I do not believe this'.

question: In both tales a doctor's plain cause sits beside a story no doctor could certify. Why does Kipling let the official verdict close the King but put it first, and refuse it, in the Rickshaw?

substitution.note: Only The Phantom Rickshaw pairs with the King in all three: the narrator's request for the whole story 'from beginning to end', the broken man naming himself to hold on, and an official bodily cause of death. Frankenstein's Walton hears Victor's tale unasked and gives no official cause; Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim are told by Marlow, not by the broken man; The Signal-Man's narrator hears the tale but gives no verdict on the death; Jekyll's statement is found, not asked for; Bartleby tells nothing. The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and A Romance of a Busy Broker (tried in the G25-04 correction) have no narrator taking down a broken man's story and no official cause of death set against it.

claim: Both shut a lord in his house with what he fears, and a tall figure in bloody grave-clothes comes to him and he falls dead. Usher buried his sister alive in his vault; she is flesh, and a guest escapes to see the house sink. Prospero welds his gates against a plague; the shroud is empty, and none survive.

from.exact: And these—the dreams—writhed in and about taking hue from the rooms, and causing the wild music of the orchestra to seem as the echo of their steps.

to.exact: Through the red-litten windows, see Vast forms that move fantastically To a discordant melody

alignments.same: Fantastic shapes move through rooms lit red by their windows, to wild music, in a ruler's house.
alignments.differs: Usher's ballad shows the dance after evil things have taken the king's palace, a figure for his own mind; Prospero's dreams dance before the blow, a revel he chose and dressed himself.

from.exact: His vesture was dabbled in blood

to.exact: There was blood upon her white robes

alignments.same: A tall figure in grave-clothes, with blood on them, comes through the shut house to its master.
alignments.differs: Madeline is a living body broken out of the vault her brother shut her in; the Red Death's shroud holds no one, and Prospero's walls were built to keep it out.

from.exact: upon which, instantly afterwards, fell prostrate in death the Prince Prospero

to.exact: bore him to the floor a corpse, and a victim to the terrors he had anticipated

alignments.same: The master of the house drops dead as the shrouded figure reaches him.
alignments.differs: Usher dies under his sister's weight while his guest flees and sees the house sink; Prospero dies at a look, dagger drawn, and every reveller dies after him.

question: Usher's terror is already inside, under his own floor; Prospero's is kept beyond iron gates. If both houses fall the same way, does it matter where the thing was shut?

substitution.note: Replacing Usher: no other work brings a figure in bloody grave-clothes through a shut house to kill its master on the spot. The Cask of Amontillado walls a man in but nothing comes out; Dracula, The Haunted and the Haunters and The Canterville Ghost have no lord killed by a shrouded comer; The Tell-Tale Heart's dead man stays under the floor. Replacing the Masque: no other work answers with a plague welded out and an empty shroud. The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no shut house and no figure in grave-clothes.

claim: Both bring a shrouded figure with no body in it to a rich man who leaves the dying poor outside. Prospero welds his gates, chases the figure with a dagger, and dies with all his guests. Scrooge kneels, follows where it points, and wakes holding his own bedpost, with time to mend.

from.exact: said Scrooge, "they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.

to.exact: The external world could take care of itself.

alignments.same: A man of means leaves those dying beyond his door to their fate.
alignments.differs: Prospero shuts the plague-struck country out and feasts a thousand friends; Scrooge refuses a coin for the poor in his counting-house, and a Ghost later gives his words back to him.

from.exact: It was shrouded in a deep black garment, which concealed its head, its face, its form

to.exact: shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave

alignments.same: A tall, silent figure wrapped in grave-clothes moves slowly before the rich man.
alignments.differs: Scrooge kneels to the Phantom and goes where it points; Prospero takes the mummer for an insult and runs at it with a dagger.

from.exact: It shrunk, collapsed, and dwindled down into a bedpost.

to.exact: untenanted by any tangible form

alignments.same: At the end the shroud is grasped and found to hold no body.
alignments.differs: Scrooge's Phantom shrinks into his own bedpost and he wakes to Christmas morning; the revellers who seize the Red Death's cerements fall dead where they stand.

question: Prospero gets no warning but the clock; Scrooge gets three spirits and a morning. What does each tale think a rich man owes the world outside his door?

substitution.note: Replacing the Masque: no other work sets an empty shroud before a rich man who has shut out the dying poor. The Signal-Man's spectre warns but is never grasped; The Haunted and the Haunters' shapes have a living will behind them; Oliver Twist and Hard Times show the poor shut out but no shrouded figure. Replacing the Carol: no other work answers with a rich man who kneels to the figure and is given time to change. The Romance of a Busy Broker has a rich man too busy for love but no shroud and no dying poor; The Furnished Room and The Last Leaf have no shrouded figure.

claim: Both lead a grown man like a child through a place run by an order he cannot sense, and his tests prove nothing. Nunez has the sight the blind lack and is mocked until he must flee or lose his eyes; the father lacks his son's ear and is left watching the nursery.

from.exact: Must you be led like a child? Cannot you hear the path as you walk?

to.exact: Gip tugged my finger forward.

alignments.same: A grown man is led through the strange place by another's hand or voice, as a child is led.
alignments.differs: A blind man scolds Nunez, who can see, for needing a guide; the father is led in by his own small son, who soon lets go of him for the shopman's finger.

from.exact: they could hear and judge the slightest gesture of a man a dozen paces away—could hear the very beating of his heart

to.exact: I myself haven't a very quick ear and it was a tongue-twisting sound, but Gip—he has his mother's ear—got it in no time.

alignments.same: The place's power runs on a quickness of ear that the grown man lacks.
alignments.differs: The blind have trained their ears in place of the eyes Nunez still has; the father lacks his son's ear, and only Gip catches the word that wakes the soldiers.

from.exact: They mocked Nunez when Pedro did not arrive

to.exact: I have taken occasion to drop in upon him once or twice, unannounced, when the soldiers were about, but so far I have never discovered them performing in anything like a magical manner.

alignments.same: The man sets his own watch to prove what the strange order hides, and it shows nothing.
alignments.differs: Nunez's sight was true, and the blind laugh him down for it; the father spies on his son's nursery and cannot tell whether the magic is there at all.

question: Nunez climbs out of the valley to keep his eyes; the father walks out of the shop with his son and no answer. Which man is more shut out by what he can perceive?

substitution.note: Replacing The Magic Shop: no other work has a man led in by his son's hand, lacking the ear that wakes the toys, and spying on the nursery afterwards. The Turn of the Screw's governess watches children too, but she has seen the ghosts herself and no child leads her; Flatland's Square is led by the Sphere into a sense he gains, not one he lacks. Replacing The Country of the Blind: Flatland's Square also cannot prove a sense others lack, but no one scolds him for not hearing his path and no prophecy is mocked; Herland's men are held in a closed land but are not led like children or outheard. No other work answers with a sighted man outheard by a whole people.

claim: Both bring a seller of marvels before a father who takes the wonder for a skilled fake, and the son vanishes by it before his eyes. The Indian asks a daughter for his horse and is jailed for the lost prince; Wells's shopman names no price and gives the boy back at once.

from.exact: I had seen the trick done at entertainments endless times before—it's part of the common stock of conjurers

to.exact: except a clever imitation of a real one; and any skilled workman might do as much.

alignments.same: The father first takes the marvel for craftsman's work that any skilled hand could copy.
alignments.differs: One flight wins the king over, and he longs to own the horse; the father goes on calling the goods faked even as the magic grows 'a little too genuine'.

from.exact: We make no charge for glass balls

to.exact: I can only deliver up my horse in exchange for the hand of the princess your daughter.

alignments.same: The seller of the marvel will not take a common price for it.
alignments.differs: The Indian asks the king's daughter for his horse; the shopman charges nothing, says only that 'we pay in the end', and never sends the bill the father waits for.

from.exact: In that instant my boy had utterly disappeared?

to.exact: before he had finished, the young man turned the screw, and was soon out of sight.

alignments.same: The father's son vanishes by the marvel before his eyes, and the father turns on the seller.
alignments.differs: The king jails the Indian for three months against the prince's return; the father snatches at the shopman, who slips away, and finds Gip beside him on Regent Street.

question: The Indian's price is named and outrageous; the shopman's is never named. Which father has more reason to fear the bill?

substitution.note: Replacing The Enchanted Horse: no other work has a marvel-seller whom a father first takes for a skilled faker, a price that is not money, and the son carried out of sight by the marvel before the father. Beauty and the Beast's Beast asks a daughter, but sells nothing and no son vanishes; The Monkey's Paw's sergeant gives a talisman, but the son dies at work, not before his father's eyes; The Snow Queen's Kay is carried off with no father and no seller. Replacing The Magic Shop: no other work answers with a seller who names no price and gives the boy back at once.

claim: Both set a motherless boy with a stern father before a door to an enchanted palace, and end with his body by the railway. Paul must steal his way in and finds money the wall; Wallace has the success Paul lacked, passes his open door for it, and goes through a door only to his death.

from.exact: came through a broad shaded colonnade to a spacious cool palace, full of pleasant fountains, full of beautiful things

to.exact: as though he were exploring the chambers of an enchanted palace, built and peopled for him alone

alignments.same: The world the boy longs for is an enchanted palace where he feels at home at last.
alignments.differs: Wallace's palace is given him free, full of kind people and playmates who call him back; Paul's is a hotel paid for with stolen money, where he wants to know no one.

from.exact: “If that was my success,” he said, and crushed it, and held it out for me to see.

to.exact: money was everything, the wall that stood between all he loathed and all he wanted

alignments.same: Worldly success is weighed against the world the man longs for.
alignments.differs: For Paul money is the wall he must break through to get in; Wallace has the success and crushes it like a walnut, for it is what kept him outside.

from.exact: By our daylight standard he walked out of security into darkness, danger and death. But did he see like that?

to.exact: There flashed through his brain, clearer than ever before, the blue of Adriatic water, the yellow of Algerian sands.

alignments.same: At the death by the railway the tale asks what the dreamer saw as he went.
alignments.differs: Cather shows Paul's last sight and his regret for 'the folly of his haste'; Wells's narrator cannot say whether Wallace saw the pit or the garden.

question: Paul is shut out by having no money; Wallace by having too much success. Which of them was nearer the door?

substitution.note: Replacing Paul's Case: Araby's boy longs for an enchanted bazaar and has no mother at home, but no money stands between him and it and he does not die; Madame Bovary's Emma longs for a palace-world and dies of debt, but she is no motherless boy and dies by poison at home, not by the railway; The Magic Shop's door admits a boy but no one dies. Replacing The Door in the Wall: Araby and The Moon and Sixpence weigh a dream against work, but neither hero holds the success Paul lacks and dies at a railway through a door; no other work ends with a successful man's body found where the door led. Also tried (works merged later): The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no motherless boy, no door to an enchanted palace and no death by the railway.

claim: Both set a boy's longing for an enchanted place against school and the clock, and end in a judgment of vanity. Joyce's boy scorns school, reaches the bazaar too late, finds it dark, and calls his own longing vanity; Wallace keeps time, never enters the garden again, and calls his career the vanity.

from.exact: I had hardly any patience with the serious work of life which, now that it stood between me and my desire, seemed to me child’s play, ugly monotonous child’s play.

to.exact: But I seem to remember the attraction of the door mainly as another obstacle to my overmastering determination to get to school.

alignments.same: The schoolboy weighs the wonder he longs for against the work of school.
alignments.differs: Joyce's boy holds school to be child's play beside his desire; Wallace's schoolboy holds the door to be an obstacle and runs past it to school.

from.exact: saw by the lighted dial of a clock that it was ten minutes to ten

to.exact: I ran past tugging out my watch, found I had ten minutes still to spare

alignments.same: At the threshold of the wonder the boy looks at the time and finds ten minutes.
alignments.differs: Joyce's boy has come too late and the bazaar is closing; Wallace has ten minutes to spare and spends them on getting to school.

from.exact: Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

to.exact: I will go in out of this dust and heat, out of this dry glitter of vanity, out of these toilsome futilities.

alignments.same: The tale ends in a judgment of vanity.
alignments.differs: Joyce's boy, in the dark hall, judges his longing for the bazaar to be vanity; Wallace judges the world of work to be vanity and the garden the way out of it.

question: Joyce's boy loses the bazaar by being late; Wallace loses the garden by being on time. Which of them does his story blame?

substitution.note: Replacing The Door in the Wall: Paul's Case also scorns school for a world of wonder, but Paul is never punctual for it and never calls his longing or his world vanity; The Magic Shop's boy is led in by his father and is never late or early. Replacing Araby: Paul's Case sets the theatre against school but has no clock at the threshold and no closing hall; Story of an Hour and The Dead end in a judgment, but not of a boy's longing set against school and time. Also tried (works merged later): The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no boy who weighs an enchanted place against school and the clock, and none ends in a judgment of vanity.

claim: Both open a London street door onto wonders that lets a boy in and is not found again by seeking. Wells's father is led in by his son and leaps through the last door to land safe on Regent Street; Wallace, once that boy, passes the door as a man and goes through another into a pit.

from.exact: that the door was unfastened, and that he could go in as he chose

to.exact: “It's only the Right Sort of Boy gets through that doorway.”

alignments.same: The door to the wonder-place opens for one boy.
alignments.differs: The shop door is locked to the spoilt child and opens to Gip, who tugs his father in; Wallace's door stands unfastened for him alone, and he alone must choose.

from.exact: I knew enough by this time not to seek again belatedly that which is not found by seeking

to.exact: I have been up and down Regent Street several times, looking for that shop.

alignments.same: The grown man goes looking for the place and does not find it.
alignments.differs: The father looks for the shop to pay a bill he expects; Wallace has learned that the door comes only unsought, and when it comes he passes it.

from.exact: The doorway was left unfastened through a misunderstanding between two gangers, and through it he made his way

to.exact: I leapt after him—into utter darkness.

alignments.same: The man goes through a last door into darkness.
alignments.differs: The father comes out at once on Regent Street with Gip beside him; Wallace's body is found at the bottom of a railway shaft.

question: Gip is the Right Sort of Boy and comes home with his soldiers; Wallace was such a boy and was marched home weeping. Why does Wells let one child keep the magic?

substitution.note: Replacing The Magic Shop: Paul's Case has a door to an enchanted palace, but the hotel is found whenever Paul pays and no boy is chosen by it; The Country of the Blind's valley is entered by a fall, not a street door; Rip Van Winkle seeks the glen again and finds no trace of its opening, but no boy was let in there and no last door leads him into darkness. Replacing The Door in the Wall: no other work has a street door that admits a boy, cannot be found by seeking, and a last door into darkness. Also tried (works merged later): The Furnished Room, The Last Leaf and The Romance of a Busy Broker have no London street door onto wonders that lets a boy in.

claim: Both carry a soft-bred creature into a world where the strong eat the weak, and harden it. Buck obeys that law as an ancestral mandate, sheds morality as a handicap and is proud to kill men; Van Weyden hears it preached, feels his joy in brutality as sin, and will not stamp on others.

from.exact: The big eat the little that they may continue to move, the strong eat the weak that they may retain their strength.

to.exact: Kill or be killed, eat or be eaten, was the law; and this mandate, down out of the depths of Time, he obeyed.

alignments.same: The law that rules the newcomer's new world is put as eating: the strong eat the weak to go on living.
alignments.differs: Larsen argues it aloud to a gentleman who disputes it; Buck obeys it without a word, as a mandate from the dogs before him.

from.exact: My reason dictated that the beating Thomas Mugridge had received was an ill thing, and yet for the life of me I could not prevent my soul joying in it.

to.exact: It marked, further, the decay or going to pieces of his moral nature, a vain thing and a handicap in the ruthless struggle for existence.

alignments.same: Under the new rule the newcomer's morality from the soft South gives way, and the book marks the moment.
alignments.differs: Van Weyden is frightened by his joy at a beating and calls it sin; Buck's first theft marks him fit to survive, and his lost morality is called a handicap.

from.exact: “I may have learned to stand on my own legs,” I retorted. “But I have yet to stamp upon others with them.”

to.exact: He had killed man, the noblest game of all, and he had killed in the face of the law of club and fang.

alignments.same: The soft newcomer has learned the hard world's lesson and is strong in it.
alignments.differs: Van Weyden refuses to turn his strength on others, and Larsen calls his education half done; Buck kills the Yeehats and feels a pride greater than any before.

question: Larsen says Van Weyden's education is only half completed. Has Buck completed it, and would London have Van Weyden follow him?

substitution.note: Replacing The Call of the Wild: Kidnapped also carries a gentle youth onto a brutal ship, but no one preaches or obeys a law that the strong eat the weak, and David never shrugs off his morality; Heart of Darkness has Kurtz gone savage, but he is not a soft-bred newcomer marked fit to survive by a theft. Replacing The Sea-Wolf: Moreau's Prendick learns to rule the Beast Folk, but no one preaches eating the weak to him and he feels no joy in a beating. No other work answers with a newcomer who learns the law and refuses to use it.

claim: Both teach a beast a master's law by pain and give a Saint Bernard's devotion to one man, then let the creature slide back to the wild. Moreau's Beast Folk worship the hand that wounds, and the Dog-man sinks dumb and dies; Buck never fawns, and once Thornton dies he leads the wolf pack.

from.exact: a man with a club was a lawgiver, a master to be obeyed, though not necessarily conciliated.

to.exact: “His is the House of Pain. “His is the Hand that makes. “His is the Hand that wounds. “His is the Hand that heals.”

alignments.same: The beast learns that the man who hurts it is the giver of its law and must be obeyed.
alignments.differs: The Beast Folk chant a litany to the hand that wounds them and cringe before Moreau; Buck obeys the club but never fawns, though he sees beaten dogs lick the man's hand.

from.exact: Love, genuine passionate love, was his for the first time.

to.exact: “The Master’s will is sweet,” said the Dog-man, with the ready tact of his canine blood.

alignments.same: A creature of Saint Bernard blood gives his devotion to one man, and the man calls it his dog's nature.
alignments.differs: The Dog-man calls Prendick Master as he called Moreau and wants the rest killed; Buck gives Thornton, who saved his life, an adoring love and is cold to other men.

from.exact: John Thornton was dead. The last tie was broken. Man and the claims of man no longer bound him.

to.exact: My Dog-man imperceptibly slipped back to the dog again; day by day he became dumb, quadrupedal, hairy.

alignments.same: The devoted beast passes out of man's world back into the animal's.
alignments.differs: The Dog-man sinks by unnoticed degrees at Prendick's side and is killed by the Hyena-swine; Buck turns only when his master is dead, and leads the pack.

question: Wells's beasts lose speech and the upright walk as they revert; Buck loses nothing he values. Is going back to the wild a fall in one book and a rise in the other?

substitution.note: Replacing Moreau: Kaa's Hunting has a law taught by blows ('I hit him, very softly, when he forgets'), but its pupil is a man-cub, no dog is devoted to one master, and no one slips back to the beast; Rikki-Tikki-Tavi has an animal devoted to a family, but no law of pain and no reversion. Replacing The Call of the Wild: no other work has a Saint Bernard's devotion to one man, a law of the club or whip, and a beast turned wild. No other work answers with a reversion that is a triumph.

claim: London runs The Call of the Wild backwards. Buck is stolen from a judge's place in the Santa Clara Valley and sits by Thornton's fire only on his way out; White Fang, born a wolf, comes in to man's fire by choice and ends at home on a judge's estate in that valley.

from.exact: Here, in Sierra Vista, which was the name of Judge Scott’s place, White Fang quickly began to make himself at home.

to.exact: Buck lived at a big house in the sun-kissed Santa Clara Valley. Judge Miller’s place, it was called.

alignments.same: A judge's estate in the Santa Clara Valley is the dog's home, where he lives at ease among the judge's family.
alignments.differs: Buck's story starts there and he is stolen north to the Klondike; White Fang is carried south out of the Klondike, and his story ends there.

from.exact: Of his own choice, he came in to sit by man’s fire and to be ruled by him.

to.exact: He was a thing of the wild, come in from the wild to sit by John Thornton’s fire, rather than a dog of the soft Southland stamped with the marks of generations of civilization.

alignments.same: The dog is said to have come in from the wild to sit by a man's fire.
alignments.differs: Buck's fire is a halt, and a call in the forest soon pulls him from it; White Fang chooses the fire and the rule that goes with it, and stays.

from.exact: Here he was compelled to violate his instinct of self-preservation, and violate it he did, for he was becoming tame and qualifying himself for civilisation.

to.exact: The domesticated generations fell from him.

alignments.same: The narrator names the moment the dog crosses the line between the tame and the wild.
alignments.differs: Buck, a pet, sheds the habits of the tame and goes back to the wild; White Fang, a wolf, lets boys stone him unpunished and becomes tame.

question: Buck ends running at the head of a wolf pack, White Fang asleep in the sun at Sierra Vista. Does London count either ending a loss?

substitution.note: Replacing The Call of the Wild: The Sea-Wolf has a soft-bred man hardened, but no judge's estate, no dog at a fire and no crossing from the tame to the wild; Moreau has beasts sliding back, but no home in the Santa Clara Valley to be lost or won. Replacing White Fang: no other work brings a wild-born beast in to a man's fire and to a judge's house. Only White Fang turns each of the three scenes round.

claim: Both mould a beast under men it takes for gods, with a hand that wounds and a law against flesh. Moreau's knife-made Beast Folk fear the hand, break the Law and slide back; London's wolf, moulded by blows and then by kindness, takes the hand's pat and keeps the law.

from.exact: It was another instance of the plasticity of his clay, of his capacity for being moulded by the pressure of environment.

to.exact: to find out the extreme limit of plasticity in a living shape.

alignments.same: A beast is plastic matter that can be moulded into another shape.
alignments.differs: Moreau moulds with the knife on his table; White Fang is moulded by the men and dogs around him, first into a fiend, then into a pet.

from.exact: There it came now, the god’s hand, cunning to hurt, thrusting out at him, descending upon his head.

to.exact: His is the Hand that wounds.

alignments.same: The beast takes a man for a god and knows him first by a hand that hurts.
alignments.differs: The Beast Folk chant that the hand wounds and heals and fear it to the end; Scott's hand comes down only to pat, and fear turns to love.

from.exact: Thus it was he learned the law, and ere he left the domain of the chickens, he had learned to ignore their existence.

to.exact: Not to eat Fish or Flesh; that is the Law.

alignments.same: The masters lay down a law against the beast's taste for flesh.
alignments.differs: The Beast Folk recite the Law and break it once they taste blood; White Fang, his nose held to the dead hens, learns it in one lesson and keeps it.

question: Moreau cannot make his creatures keep the shape he cut; Scott changes White Fang without a knife. Is London saying that kindness, not surgery, moulds a beast for good?

substitution.note: Replacing Moreau: Frankenstein has a made creature turned fiend by cruelty, but no master's hand, no law against flesh and no beast moulded; Kaa's Hunting has a law taught by blows, but its pupil is a man-cub and no god's hand pats him. Replacing White Fang: The Call of the Wild has a club as lawgiver, but Buck takes no man for a god and keeps no law of the tame. No other work answers Moreau with a beast that keeps its new shape.

claim: London twice sets a Klondike dog beside a man who goes on against an old hand's warning, and lets the dog outlive him. Buck balks at the rotten ice and is saved by a master he loves and later mourns; the husky, caressed only by the whip, obeys, and trots off to other fire-providers.

from.exact: The old-timer had been very serious in laying down the law that no man must travel alone in the Klondike after fifty below.

to.exact: The bottom’s likely to drop out at any moment. Only fools, with the blind luck of fools, could have made it.

alignments.same: An old hand of the North warns a newcomer that the trail ahead will kill him, and the newcomer goes on.
alignments.differs: Hal sneers at Thornton to his face and drives on with his party; London's newcomer goes alone, calls the old-timers womanish while his fire burns, and owns them right only as he dies.

from.exact: The dog did not want to go. It hung back until the man shoved it forward, and then it went quickly across the white, unbroken surface.

to.exact: it seemed that he sensed disaster close at hand, out there ahead on the ice where his master was trying to drive him.

alignments.same: A dog senses the danger hidden under the snow or ice and holds back, and its master drives it on.
alignments.differs: Buck refuses under the club and so is off the ice when it gives way; the husky yields to a shove, breaks through, and must bite the ice from its toes.

from.exact: Then it turned and trotted up the trail in the direction of the camp it knew, where were the other food-providers and fire-providers.

to.exact: brooding and mourning by the pool

alignments.same: A dog stays by its dead master for a while, then leaves him for the life it will go on with.
alignments.differs: Buck, who adored Thornton, mourns by the pool where he was killed; the husky, never caressed but by the whip-lash, smells death, backs away and goes to other men.

question: In The Call of the Wild love between a man and a dog saves the dog from the ice; in To Build a Fire the dog is 'not concerned in the welfare of the man'. Is the later story London taking back the bond of the earlier book?

substitution.note: Replacing The Call of the Wild: White Fang has the husky and the fire, but no old hand's warning, no dog that balks at hidden danger, and no master who dies; The Sea-Wolf and Moreau have no dog on a trail. Replacing To Build a Fire: The Open Boat, Moby-Dick and The Sea-Wolf have no dog, and no other work has a dog driven over a hidden danger that then outlives its master.

claim: Both bring a man near death in a nature that would not miss him and let him find dying comfortable. Crane's correspondent thinks out that indifference himself and lives by a brotherhood that spells him at the oars; London's newcomer never thinks it, goes without a partner, and sleeps into death.

from.exact: It did not lead him to meditate upon his frailty as a creature of temperature, and upon man’s frailty in general, able only to live within certain narrow limits of heat and cold

to.exact: When it occurs to a man that nature does not regard him as important, and that she feels she would not maim the universe by disposing of him

alignments.same: Mortal danger in nature raises the question of man's frailty and his place in a universe that would not miss him.
alignments.differs: Crane's correspondent comes to the thought himself and rages at it; London's newcomer, without imagination, never has it, so the narrator states it over his head and the cold proves it.

from.exact: If he had only had a trail-mate he would have been in no danger now. The trail-mate could have built the fire.

to.exact: Then he touched a man in the bottom of the boat, and called his name.

alignments.same: Life in the killing cold or sea depends on a second man who takes over the work when one man's body gives out.
alignments.differs: In the dingey the oiler, rowing past exhaustion, wakes the correspondent to spell him all night; London's newcomer went without a partner, and no one takes the matches from his dead fingers.

from.exact: A good idea, he thought, to sleep off to death. It was like taking an anæsthetic.

to.exact: drowning must really be a comfortable arrangement, a cessation of hostilities accompanied by a large degree of relief

alignments.same: Worn out by the struggle, the man finds that death would be comfortable, a relief rather than a horror.
alignments.differs: The correspondent thinks it while still swimming, and a wave and a rescuer bring him ashore; London's man stops running, sits in the snow to meet death decently, and sleeps into it.

question: Crane's survivors come ashore able to be 'interpreters' of the sea; London's man dies having learned only 'what real cold was'. Does either story need its man to understand what nature has shown him?

substitution.note: Replacing The Open Boat: The Sea-Wolf opens with Van Weyden in cold water, but alone, picked up by a ship, with no partner spelling him; Descent into the Maelström has a man who lives by thinking and a brother who dies clinging, but no cold, no turn at the work and no comfortable death; Robinson Crusoe is alone and lives; The Outcasts of Poker Flat lets two women die asleep in the snow, but no one thinks out nature's indifference, no partner spells another to save him, and the women die together, not for want of one. Replacing To Build a Fire: The Call of the Wild and White Fang have the cold but no man who dies of it alone.

claim: Crane twice puts men within reach of death and has them ask nature what she thinks of them. Henry, having run from his regiment, reads a squirrel's flight as her sign that he was right; the correspondent, kept at the oars by a silent brotherhood, finds her flatly indifferent and his own faults plain.

from.exact: She did not seem cruel to him then, nor beneficent, nor treacherous, nor wise. But she was indifferent, flatly indifferent.

to.exact: He conceived Nature to be a woman with a deep aversion to tragedy.

alignments.same: A man just out of reach of death looks at the land about him and makes nature a woman who has a view of his plight.
alignments.differs: Henry, hiding in the woods, finds her timid of blood and on his side; the correspondent finds her neither cruel nor kind, and sees his own faults.

from.exact: he at first wishes to throw bricks at the temple, and he hates deeply the fact that there are no bricks and no temples

to.exact: The youth turned, with sudden, livid rage, toward the battlefield. He shook his fist.

alignments.same: A death the man cannot stop turns his grief into rage at whatever rules the world.
alignments.differs: Henry, over Jim Conklin's body, shakes his fist under a sun pasted like a wafer; the drowning man finds no temple to stone and wishes to plead on one knee.

from.exact: It would be difficult to describe the subtle brotherhood of men that was here established on the seas.

to.exact: He felt the subtle battle brotherhood more potent even than the cause for which they were fighting.

alignments.same: Crane names, in nearly the same words, a 'subtle brotherhood' that binds men facing death side by side.
alignments.differs: Henry's holds through one charge and he runs in the next; the boat's, never spoken, warms four men through a night and a day until she swamps.

question: Henry finds nature on his side when he has run; the correspondent finds her indifferent when there is nowhere to run. Does the boat teach what the battle could not, or only take away the chance to flee?

substitution.note: Replacing The Red Badge: no other work in view has a man fresh from danger read nature as a woman approving him, shake his fist at the sky over a friend's death, and name a 'subtle brotherhood' with the men beside him. The Maelström's fisherman wonders at God's power in the whirlpool; Crusoe reads providence; Ahab strikes through a mask at a malice he believes in; Owl Creek's Farquhar sees nature sharpened in a dream of escape, not judging him. Replacing The Open Boat: no other work in view finds nature flatly indifferent to men kept together in a small boat.

claim: Both follow a young man who leaps from his post at the first terror and later argues the case was not plain. Henry's flight is never found out, so he counts himself a man; Jim's was tried in open court, and he says the jump itself must be lived down.

from.exact: “I had jumped . . .” He checked himself, averted his gaze.

to.exact: Directly he began to speed toward the rear in great leaps.

alignments.same: At the first terror the young man leaves the place his duty holds him, in a leap, before he knows he has chosen.
alignments.differs: Henry runs because the men beside him run; Jim jumps alone from a ship of sleeping pilgrims into the officers' boat, and can only add 'It seems.'

from.exact: There was not the thickness of a sheet of paper between the right and the wrong of this affair.

to.exact: He had done a good part in saving himself, who was a little piece of the army.

alignments.same: Afterwards the runaway argues his own case, that leaving was not plainly wrong.
alignments.differs: Henry argues it to himself as strategy until news that the line held makes him feel wronged; Jim argues it aloud to Marlow, granting it was not the truth.

from.exact: “I had jumped—hadn’t I?” he asked, dismayed. “That’s what I had to live down. The story didn’t matter.”

to.exact: He had performed his mistakes in the dark, so he was still a man.

alignments.same: The runaway weighs his flight against what others know of it.
alignments.differs: Henry, sure nothing can now be discovered, feels still a man and patronizes his friend; Jim, whose jump is public, says the officers' story did not matter, only the jump.

question: Henry is saved by nobody having seen; Jim is ruined by everybody having heard. Which of them comes nearer to facing what he did?

substitution.note: Replacing The Red Badge: Moby-Dick's Pip leaps from the whale-boat in fright but argues nothing and goes mad; The Open Boat's men never leave their boat; Kidnapped's David and Treasure Island's Jim stand their ground; Owl Creek's Farquhar escapes only in a dream. Replacing Lord Jim: no other work in view has a young man who runs from his post at the first terror, reasons afterwards that it was sense, and is restored because no one knows.

claim: Both bring a danger from space upon a world busy with its affairs, set Martians watching, and leave men a new brotherhood. In The Star the danger is blind matter and the Martians only remark how little the earth was hurt; in the novel the watching Martians are the danger.

from.exact: this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own

to.exact: The Martian astronomers—for there are astronomers on Mars, although they are very different beings from men—were naturally profoundly interested by these things.

alignments.same: Minds on Mars, unlike men's, watch what befalls the earth.
alignments.differs: The novel's Martians watch with envious eyes and plan to take the earth; the tale's astronomers only note from afar how little it was hurt.

from.exact: With infinite complacency men went to and fro over this globe about their little affairs, serene in their assurance of their empire over matter.

to.exact: As a matter of fact, use and wont still ruled the world, and save for the talk of idle moments and the splendour of the night, nine human beings out of ten were still busy at their common occupations.

alignments.same: Men go about their common business while a danger out of space draws near.
alignments.differs: In the novel no one has thought of danger from the sky; in the tale the star blazes overhead, the mathematician has warned the world, and common-sense still goes to bed.

from.exact: it has done much to promote the conception of the commonweal of mankind

to.exact: But of the new brotherhood that grew presently among men, of the saving of laws and books and machines

alignments.same: The disaster from space leaves men with a new sense of a common humanity.
alignments.differs: The novel's narrator weighs this gain against a lasting dread of the sky; the tale names the brotherhood, refuses to tell it, and ends with Martians who see no damage.

question: In The Star nothing means the earth harm; in The War of the Worlds the Martians do. Which leaves men more humbled?

substitution.note: Every novel and story in the graph this step sees was put in place of each side; none has the passages the alignments pair (see the LOG line).

claim: Both watch a planet fall sunward, the earth seem to stop turning, and a black disc cross the light. The Time Traveller sees these ends slowly, alone, after man is gone; The Star crowds them into a week, and men live through them under a hotter sun.

from.exact: everywhere the days were hotter than of yore, and the sun larger

to.exact: the planets must ultimately fall back one by one into the parent body. As these catastrophes occur, the sun will blaze with renewed energy

alignments.same: A planet falling into the sun leaves the earth under a hotter sun.
alignments.differs: The Star makes the fall happen in a week, to men who live to feel the heat; the Time Traveller only guesses at such a fall to explain a far future's warmth.

from.exact: It seemed to those who in Europe watched for the rising of the star that the world must have ceased its rotation.

to.exact: The earth had come to rest with one face to the sun, even as in our own time the moon faces the earth.

alignments.same: The earth seems to stop turning under a great light in the sky.
alignments.differs: In The Star it only seems so, for the star has fallen behind the sky and the earth turns on; the Time Traveller finds it truly stopped by tidal drag after ages.

from.exact: Men looking up, near blinded, at the star, saw that a black disc was creeping across the light.

to.exact: Suddenly I noticed that the circular westward outline of the sun had changed; that a concavity, a bay, had appeared in the curve.

alignments.same: A black disc creeps across the blazing light, and a cold wind follows.
alignments.differs: The Star's eclipse is the moon and brings respite to crowds crying to God on the minarets; the Traveller's brings final darkness on a beach where no man is left.

question: Wells first imagined the end of the earth with no one left to see it. Why does The Star give it survivors and a brotherhood?

substitution.note: Every novel and story in the graph this step sees was put in place of each side; none has the passages the alignments pair (see the LOG line).

claim: Both make beings from another world survey the earth's seas and poles and judge it by its surface. Voltaire's dwarf wrongly finds no one there and the tale laughs at his haste; Wells's Martians find the earth unharmed after millions have died, and the tale grants that at their distance they are right.

from.exact: All the familiar continental markings and the masses of the seas remain intact

to.exact: the nearly imperceptible pond we call the Mediterranean, and the other little pool that, under the name Ocean, encircles the molehill

alignments.same: Observers from another world take in the earth's lands and seas at a glance.
alignments.differs: Wells's Martians read the markings like a map through a telescope and report them intact; Voltaire's giants walk round the globe in 36 hours and find its ocean a pool.

from.exact: it is astonishing what a little damage the earth, which it missed so narrowly, has sustained

to.exact: The dwarf, who was a bit hasty sometimes, decided straightaway that the planet was uninhabited.

alignments.same: The observer judges the earth by its surface and misses its people.
alignments.differs: Wells's Martians miss millions of dead and no one corrects them; Voltaire's dwarf denies there is anyone at all and is shown wrong by a microscope.

from.exact: Which only shows how small the vastest of human catastrophes may seem at a distance of a few million miles.

to.exact: But he was fooled by appearances, which happens only too often, whether one is using a microscope or not.

alignments.same: The narrator closes an outside view of the earth with a maxim on judging from afar.
alignments.differs: Wells's maxim grants that from a few million miles the catastrophe really is small; Voltaire's faults the observer for being fooled.

question: Voltaire's visitors are corrected by a microscope; Wells's Martians are not. Is the last sentence of The Star a joke on the Martians or on us?

substitution.note: Every novel and story in the graph this step sees was put in place of each side; none has the passages the alignments pair (see the LOG line).

claim: Both print a dead young man's own papers under an editor's preface and weigh his despair against a pistol. Goethe's editor asks for tears, and Werther shoots himself as a sacrifice for Charlotte; Lermontov's editor is glad of the death, and Pechorin's despair is one no pistol cures, in a man who never sacrificed for love.

from.exact: The news afforded me great delight; it gave me the right to print these notes

to.exact: To his spirit and character you cannot refuse your admiration and love: to his fate you will not deny your tears.

alignments.same: An editor sets the private writings of a young man now dead before the public and, in a preface, tells the reader how to take him.
alignments.differs: Goethe's editor asks the reader's love and tears; Lermontov's is delighted by the death, which frees him to print, and gives the book's ironic title as his opinion.

from.exact: not that despair which is cured at the muzzle of a pistol, but the cold, powerless despair concealed beneath the mask of amiability and a good-natured smile

to.exact: It is not despair: it is conviction that I have filled up the measure of my sufferings

alignments.same: The young man names his despair and measures it against death by the pistol.
alignments.differs: Werther calls his resolve to shoot himself conviction, not despair; Pechorin calls his despair the kind no pistol cures, hidden under a smile, and tells it to Mary to win her pity.

from.exact: To none has my love brought happiness, because I have never sacrificed anything for the sake of those I have loved

to.exact: One of us three must die: it shall be Werther.

alignments.same: On the eve of facing a pistol, the young man sums up what his love has meant to those he loved.
alignments.differs: Werther gives his life so that Charlotte and Albert may live; Pechorin, the night before his duel, owns that he loved for his own pleasure and never sacrificed anything.

question: Pechorin says his despair is not the kind a pistol cures. Is A Hero of Our Time a Werther for an age that no longer believes in dying for love?

substitution.note: Replacing Werther: Jekyll and Hyde ends in a dead man's written statement, but no editor prefaces it and no pistol or beloved is weighed; Madame Bovary and The Awakening end in a despairing death, but with no editor's papers and no sacrifice for a lover; Notes from Underground has an editor's note, but its writer is alive and no pistol is named. Replacing the Hero: no other work prints a dead young man's papers with an editor glad of his death.

claim: Both measure the man of their generation against a novel's hero, call him a cripple, and set him against an officer over a point of honour. Pechorin mocks Grushnitsky's pose, sends his second and shoots; the Underground Man owns himself the anti-hero, never sends his challenge, and tells his readers they are all cripples too.

from.exact: a novel needs a hero, and all the traits for an anti-hero are expressly gathered together here

to.exact: His aim is to make himself the hero of a novel.

alignments.same: The man of the day is measured against the hero of a novel, and found to be playing a part.
alignments.differs: Pechorin scorns Grushnitsky for posing as a novel's hero; the Underground Man turns the charge on himself and calls his own notes the portrait of an anti-hero.

from.exact: we are all divorced from life, we are all cripples, every one of us, more or less

to.exact: I became a moral cripple.

alignments.same: The man of the generation calls himself a cripple, his life withered from within.
alignments.differs: Pechorin says it of himself alone, to Mary, to win her pity; the Underground Man says 'we are all' and throws it at readers who would call him the exception.

from.exact: Oh, if only that officer had been one of the sort who would consent to fight a duel!

to.exact: I shall have the honour to send my second to you to-day

alignments.same: An insult turns the man of the generation toward a duel with an officer.
alignments.differs: Pechorin, an officer, sends his second at once and shoots Grushnitsky off the ledge; the clerk nurses the insult for years, never sends his challenge, and bumps the officer on the Nevsky.

question: The Underground Man says 'we are all cripples'; Pechorin calls only himself a moral cripple. Which of the two is the hero of our time?

substitution.note: Replacing the Hero: The Overcoat has a clerk slighted by a man of rank, but no hero of a novel, no cripple and no duel; Werther has a young man and a pistol, but no officer and no point of honour; Lord Jim and The Red Badge of Courage weigh a young man's honour, but against a ship and a battle, not a duel over an insult. Replacing Notes: Jekyll and Hyde names no novel's hero and no duel. No other work answers with an anti-hero whose challenge is never sent.

claim: Both set their generation's cold sceptic beside a materialist doctor, at a duel and facing death. Lermontov keeps the doctor at the hero's side: Pechorin shoots his man dead and trusts his exalted destiny. Turgenev makes the hero the doctor: Bazarov dresses the wound he gave, and dying owns that Russia does not need him.

from.exact: I am no longer a duellist, but a doctor, and must examine your wound.

to.exact: Doctor, these gentlemen have forgotten, in their hurry, no doubt, to put a bullet in my pistol. I beg you to load it afresh—and properly!

alignments.same: A duel over a point of honour turns on the young sceptic's shot, with a doctor on the ground.
alignments.differs: Pechorin has his second, Doctor Werner, reload and shoots Grushnitsky off the ledge; Bazarov, himself the doctor, wounds Paul Petrovitch and turns at once to dress the wound.

from.exact: And the sequel was that I cut myself, and, on repairing to the district physician, found that he did not possess what I wanted.

to.exact: He has mastered all the living chords of the human heart, just as one learns the veins of a corpse, but he has never known how to avail himself of his knowledge.

alignments.same: A sceptic and materialist trained in medicine knows men as an anatomist knows a corpse.
alignments.differs: Lermontov's Werner is the hero's friend, an anatomist who cannot use what he knows; Turgenev makes the materialist the hero, and opening a typhus corpse he cuts his finger and finds no cure.

from.exact: Russia needs me, indeed! Evidently she does not need me.

to.exact: A purpose there must have been, and, surely, mine was an exalted destiny

alignments.same: Facing death, the young man asks what his life was for and what great part was meant for him.
alignments.differs: Pechorin, on the eve of a duel he survives, is sure an exalted destiny was his and he missed it; Bazarov, really dying, calls his father's talk of a loss to Russia rubbish.

question: Pechorin kills his man and keeps faith in his exalted destiny; Bazarov wounds his man, dresses the wound, and dies of a cut finger. Is Bazarov Lermontov's hero grown up, or his refutation?

substitution.note: Replacing the Hero: Notes from Underground has a hero of his time and a duel never fought, but no doctor; Werther has a pistol and a death, but no duel and no doctor; Madame Bovary has a doctor and a death, but no duel and no sceptic hero; Jekyll and Hyde has a doctor but no duel. Replacing Fathers and Sons: no other work makes the sceptic hero a doctor who dresses the wound he gave and dies of a dissection.

claim: Both ask whether natural science explains a man. Bazarov says yes: men are frogs on hind legs, a rectified society will cure moral sickness, and all else may be denied. The Underground Man denies the one thing Bazarov keeps, the laws of nature, and says men act against their advantage to prove they are not piano-keys.

from.exact: the whole work of man really seems to consist in nothing but proving to himself every minute that he is a man and not a piano-key!

to.exact: You and I are frogs too, except that we walk upon our hind legs.

alignments.same: Natural science would explain a man as a mechanism, a frog to be opened or a key in an instrument.
alignments.differs: Bazarov opens frogs to learn what is taking place in ourselves; the Underground Man says a man's whole work is to prove he is no piano-key, by madness if need be.

from.exact: if he were enlightened, if his eyes were opened to his real normal interests, man would at once cease to do nasty things

to.exact: Rectify that body, and moral sickness will soon cease to be.

alignments.same: Vice is traced to a fault that reform can remove, so that men will cease to do evil.
alignments.differs: Bazarov states the cure in earnest to Madame Odintsov; the Underground Man quotes it as the reformers' creed and answers 'Oh, the babe!', for men choose against their own advantage.

from.exact: what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic, when, for some reason I dislike those laws and the fact that twice two makes four?

to.exact: We have decided merely to deny everything.

alignments.same: A man of the new generation refuses what his elders hold settled.
alignments.differs: Bazarov denies every authority and principle but trusts chemistry and his frogs; the Underground Man refuses the one thing Bazarov keeps, the laws of nature and twice two makes four.

question: Bazarov denies everything but natural science; the Underground Man denies natural science itself. Which of the two is the real nihilist?

substitution.note: Replacing Fathers and Sons: Hard Times comes nearest (Gradgrind's facts and statistics answer to the reckoning of advantages), but it has no frogs, no cure of vice by a rectified society spoken by a young man, and no denial of all authority; Frankenstein and The Island of Doctor Moreau trust science to make life, not to explain or cure men. Replacing Notes: Hard Times answers Gradgrind with the circus and the heart, not with a man who acts against his advantage to prove he is not a piano-key.

claim: In both, a man kills someone old, denies it was for money, and his nerves, not evidence, bring the truth out before officers. Poe's murderer shrieks it in one night to officers he fancies mock him; Dostoevsky's lawyer openly waits on those nerves, and Raskolnikov half-says it as a question, telling his cause, a test of daring, to Sonia.

from.exact: I didn’t do the murder to gain wealth and power and to become a benefactor of mankind

to.exact: For his gold I had no desire.

alignments.same: The murderer, telling why he killed the old victim, denies that he did it for the money.
alignments.differs: Poe's man names the old man's filmed eye, a fixation he cannot explain; Raskolnikov names a test of himself, whether he dared to step over, and tells it to Sonia, not to the police.

from.exact: he knew what he was doing, but could not restrain himself

to.exact: I talked more freely to get rid of the feeling

alignments.same: Sitting with an officer who talks easily of the crime, the murderer feels the truth rising in him and cannot hold it back.
alignments.differs: Poe's man hears it as a sound and talks louder to drown it, then shrieks; Raskolnikov leans to the police clerk and asks 'what if it was I', and the clerk disbelieves him.

from.exact: He’ll come of himself, or maybe do something which will make it as plain as twice two are four

to.exact: They heard!—they suspected!—they knew!—they were making a mockery of my horror!

alignments.same: The officers seem to know and to wait, smiling, for the murderer's own nerves to give him up.
alignments.differs: Poe's officers were 'satisfied' and the mockery is the murderer's fancy; Porfiry tells Raskolnikov outright that he is leaving him free so that suspicion and terror will bring him in of himself.

question: Poe's murderer is undone in one night by a sound he alone hears; Raskolnikov is left free for weeks while the lawyer waits for him to come of himself. Is either confession chosen, or are both forced out by nerves?

substitution.note: Replacing The Tell-Tale Heart: The Black Cat's murderer kills his wife in a drunken rage and is betrayed by the cat's cry after his own bravado, with no old victim and no money disclaimed; The Diamond Lens kills Simon for the diamond; The Cask of Amontillado has no officers; Jekyll and Hyde's murder of the old Carew is confessed in writing, never before officers. Replacing Crime and Punishment: Notes from Underground has no murder; in Dorian Gray, The Secret Agent and the Holmes and Brown stories the killer is not undone before officers by his nerves.

claim: Both set a man who has reasoned past common morals beside a young prostitute whose death he paints to her. The Underground Man scorns arithmetic yet stays in his corner, works on Liza for power and lets her go; Raskolnikov acts on a murder reckoned as simple arithmetic, and at Sonia's knees finds life taking the place of theory.

from.exact: One death, and a hundred lives in exchange—it’s simple arithmetic!

to.exact: such positiveness is not life, gentlemen, but is the beginning of death

alignments.same: Whether a man may do a thing is put as a sum, as certain as arithmetic.
alignments.differs: The Underground Man refuses the sum in the name of life and does nothing; a student's sum weighs the pawnbroker's death against a hundred lives, and Raskolnikov, who thought the same, kills her.

from.exact: you get ill and are taken to the hospital, what will happen then?

to.exact: it would be happy for you if you were to die soon of consumption in some corner

alignments.same: Alone with a young prostitute, the man presses her pitilessly with a picture of sickness and of what will become of her.
alignments.differs: The Underground Man paints Liza's death in a cellar for 'the exercise of my power'; Raskolnikov presses Sonia on her family's fate, then bows down to her as to 'all the suffering of humanity'.

from.exact: He wept and threw his arms round her knees.

to.exact: She came close to me, put her arms round me and stayed motionless in that position.

alignments.same: The man breaks down in tears before the woman he has tormented, and they hold each other.
alignments.differs: Liza holds the sobbing Underground Man, and he answers with spite and a note thrust into her hand; Raskolnikov falls at Sonia's knees in Siberia, and 'Life had stepped into the place of theory'.

question: The Underground Man calls twice two makes four the beginning of death, yet it is he who stays in his corner and Raskolnikov, who killed by a sum, who is raised again. Is the novel Dostoevsky's answer to his own underground?

substitution.note: Replacing Notes from Underground: Hard Times reckons life in facts and figures but has no prostitute and no man who refuses the sum; Oliver Twist's Nancy is pressed by no reasoning man with her death; The Bet's prisoner reasons alone with no woman. Replacing Crime and Punishment: no other graph work sets a moral sum, a young prostitute told of her death and the man's breakdown in her arms together; Madame Bovary, The Awakening and The Moon and Sixpence have none of the three, nor have the works shelved with Notes under heading:double (Jekyll and Hyde, Dorian Gray, Young Goodman Brown and others) or The Tell-Tale Heart.
